en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Path of Purification (Second Part).
12. Exposition of the Supernormal Powers (Iddhividha-niddesa):

Discussion of the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññā-kathā) 365. Now, it was stated that this development of concentration has the higher knowledges as its benefit by way of those mundane higher knowledges; [here follows the exposition].
In order to accomplish those direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the practitioner must apply himself to the practice having attained the fourth jhāna in the earth-kasina and other objects.
For in this way, his cultivation of concentration will both attain its intended benefits and become more stable.
Possessing that cultivation of concentration which has attained its benefits and become more stable, he will easily undertake the cultivation of wisdom.
He will accomplish it. Therefore, we shall first begin the discussion on direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

For the Blessed One, in order to show the benefits of the cultivation of concentration to clansmen who have attained the fourth jhāna absorption, and in order to teach the progressively higher and more sublime states, said:
"When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, and bright..."

When his mind is free from blemish, devoid of defilement, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhā*).
In this manner, he experiences the various supernormal powers, such as: being one, he becomes many;
[the knowledge of the divine ear-element, the knowledge of the minds of others, and the knowledge of recollecting past lives].
"Knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings" refers to the five mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).

Regarding these, a beginner yogi who wishes to perform the supernormal transformations of psychic power—such as "being one, he becomes many," and so forth—should first develop eight attainments (*samāpatti*) for each of the eight kasiṇas, ending with the white kasiṇa.

Then, by way of the kasiṇas in direct order, by way of the kasiṇas in reverse order, by way of the kasiṇas in both direct and reverse order, by way of the jhānas in direct order, and by way of the jhānas in reverse order...
By way of conformity with and reversal from the jhānas; by skipping jhānas; by skipping kasiṇas; by skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas;
by transferring factors; by transferring objects; by transferring both factors and objects; by defining the factors;
and by defining the objects—in these fourteen ways the mind should be thoroughly tamed.
366. What, then, here is the "conformity with the kasiṇas" … [and so on] … what is the "definition of the object"?
Here, a bhikkhu enters jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa, and from there into the water-kasiṇa;
thus, entering in this sequence through the eight kasiṇas even a hundred times or a thousand times—this is called "conformity with the kasiṇas."
Starting from the white-kasiṇa and proceeding in reverse order in the same manner is called the "reverse order of the kasiṇas.

Starting from the earth-kasiṇa up to the white-kasiṇa, and starting again from the white-kasiṇa down to the earth-kasiṇa—attaining them repeatedly in this way by way of forward and reverse order—is called the "forward and reverse order of the kasiṇas.

Starting from the first jhāna and proceeding in regular succession up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attaining them repeatedly in that sequence is called the "forward order of the jhānas."
Re-entering repeatedly from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the first jhāna is called "the reverse order of jhānas.
Re-entering repeatedly from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and again from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception back down to the first jhāna—
in this way, re-entering repeatedly by way of direct and reverse order is called "the direct and reverse order of jhānas."
In the case of the earth-kasiṇa, however, having attained the first jhāna, one attains the third right there;
then, having emerged from that very state, one attains the base of infinite space, and from that, the base of nothingness.

Thus, skipping over the kasiṇa and leaping by way of the jhānas alone in alternate order is called "leaping through the jhānas" (*jhānukkantika*). The same application should be made for those based on the water-kasiṇa and so forth.
Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, one then proceeds through the fire kasiṇa, then the blue kasiṇa,
then the red kasiṇa, and so on; skipping the jhānas in this manner and skipping directly from one kasiṇa to another is called "skipping the kasiṇas" (kasiṇukkantika).
Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, then the third jhāna in the fire kasiṇa, the base of infinite space after breaking through the blue kasiṇa,
and the base of nothingness from the red kasiṇa— in this manner, the skipping of both the jhānas and the kasiṇas is called "skipping over jhānas and kasiṇas" (jhānakasiṇukkantika).
Furthermore, having attained the first jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa, to attain the others in that very same [object] is called "transference of factors" (*aṅga-saṅkantika*).

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa, to attain that same [jhāna] in the water-kasiṇa... and so on up to... the white-kasiṇa; thus, attaining the same single jhāna in all the kasiṇas is called "transference of the object" (*ārammaṇa-saṅkantika*).
Having attained the first jhāna in the earth-kasiṇa, [to attain] the second in the water-kasiṇa, and the third in the fire-kasiṇa... [and so forth].
The fourth [jhāna] is attained with the air kasiṇa; having removed the blue kasiṇa, the base of infinite space; from the yellow kasiṇa, the base of infinite consciousness;
from the red kasiṇa, the base of nothingness; and from the white kasiṇa, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, the shifting of both the factors and the objects by way of skipping every other one is called "shifting of factors and objects."

Having defined the first jhāna as having five factors, one defines the second as having three factors, the third as having two factors, and likewise the fourth, the base of infinite space... pe ...the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this defining of the mere factors of the jhānas is called "definition of factors."
Likewise, having defined "this is the earth-kasiṇa," "this is the water-kasiṇa," and so on up to "this is the white-kasiṇa"—
such defining of the mere object is called "defining the object. Some also maintain that there is a "defining of the factors and the object," but since this is not mentioned in the Commentaries,
it certainly cannot be a method for meditation.

367. Furthermore, it is impossible for a beginner practitioner who has not previously developed his meditation and has not tamed his mind in these fourteen ways to achieve the transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*).

For a beginner, even the preliminary work on the *kasiṇa* is a heavy burden; perhaps only one in a hundred or a thousand is capable of it. This applies even to one who has completed the preliminary work on the *kasiṇa*.
Producing the sign is a burden; among hundreds or thousands, only one is able to do it. Once the sign has arisen, developing it to attain absorption (appanā) is a burden;
among hundreds or thousands, only one is able to do it. For one who has attained absorption, taming the mind in fourteen ways is a burden;
among hundreds or thousands, only one is able to do it. Even for one whose mind has been tamed in those fourteen ways...
The transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbana*) is indeed a heavy burden; among hundreds or thousands, only one is capable of it.
Even for one who has attained such transformations, the state of rapid response is a heavy burden; among hundreds or thousands, only one possesses such quickness of response.
This was seen when about thirty thousand possessors of psychic power came to attend upon the Elder Mahā-Rohaṇa-Gutta while he was ill at Therambatthala.
One who has been ordained for eight years is like the Elder Rakkhita.
His power is described precisely in the *Pathavīkasiṇaniddesa*. Having seen that power, the elder said:
"Friends, if Rakkhita had not existed, we would all have fallen into reproach, [thinking], 'They were unable to protect the Naga king. Therefore, one should wander about having taken it up oneself."
"One must first cleanse the defilement called 'weapon' before it is fit to go about taking it up.
Following the Elder's advice, all thirty thousand bhikkhus became quick-witted.
Yet, even when one possesses quick wit, the burden of being a support for others lies with only one among hundreds or thousands.
It occurs, just like the Elder who was the protector against the rain of embers when Māra rained down embers during the Giribhaṇḍavāhana festival, having created earth in the sky; however,
for those with powerful past applications— such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the Chief Disciples— even without this aforementioned method.
It is precisely through the attainment of Arahantship by means of the sequence of meditative development (bhāvanā) that this transformation of psychic power (iddhi-vikubbana) and other qualities,

such as the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), come to success. Therefore, just as a goldsmith who wishes to fashion a decorative ornament makes the gold soft and workable by heating and hammering it with fire, and just as a potter who wishes to fashion a vessel...

Just as one makes clay workable by kneading it well until it becomes soft, even so, a beginner, having tamed the mind through these fourteen modes, should make it soft and wieldy by means of mastery over desire,
mastery over the mind, mastery over energy, and mastery over investigation, as well as by means of mastery over adverting and the other [mental functions],
and then apply himself to the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividha*). This applies to one who is endowed with the prior causes.
However, it is also permissible for one who has attained mastery even in the fourth jhāna alone among the kasiṇas to perform this.
To show the method by which the practice should be undertaken here, the Blessed One said, "When his mind is thus concentrated," and so forth.
368. Herein, this is the analytical exposition according to the sequence of the canonical text. Therein, "he" refers to one who has attained the fourth jhāna.
The yogi. Thus, this is a demonstration of the sequence of the fourth jhāna.

By this it is meant that he has attained the fourth jhāna through the sequence beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna. "In one who is concentrated" (samāhite) means in one who is concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna.

"In the mind" (citte) refers to the fine-material-sphere mind (rūpāvacara-citta). Regarding "purified" (parisuddhe) and so forth, however, [it is due to] the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi).
"Pure": because of its very purity, it is "cleansed"; what is meant is that it is luminous.
Because the stains of lust and so forth have been destroyed by the removal of the conditions for pleasure and the rest, it is "without blemish.

Because it is without blemish, it is "free from defilement," for it is by means of the blemish that the mind becomes defiled. Because it has been well-developed, it is "become malleable," meaning it has attained mastery.
For the mind that is proceeding [in meditation] is called "pliant. And because of that very pliancy, it is said to be "workable," meaning capable of work and fit for work.
For a pliant mind becomes workable like well-tamed gold; and both of these states arise precisely from being well-developed.
As it has been said: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other thing..."
"That which, when thus developed and cultivated, becomes pliant and wieldy—just like this mind, monks. Because it stands upon these qualities such as complete purity, it is "steadfast" (*ṭhita*).
Precisely because of that steadfastness, it has reached imperturbability; what is meant is that it is immovable and free from agitation.
Alternatively, it is "steadfast" because it stands under its own control by virtue of its pliancy and wieldiness. It is so called because it is embraced by faith and the other [faculties].
It has reached imperturbability. For a mind embraced by faith does not waver through lack of faith; one embraced by energy does not waver through laziness;
one embraced by mindfulness does not waver through negligence; one embraced by concentration does not waver through restlessness;
one embraced by wisdom does not waver through ignorance; and one that has attained illumination does not waver through the darkness of the defilements.
It moves. When embraced by these six qualities, it reaches imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*).

Thus, a mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of directing itself toward the realization through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) of those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.

Another method: when concentrated by means of the fourth jhāna absorption; when purified by the removal of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); and by the surmounting of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest.
It is "purified" (*pariyodāta*). It is "stainless" (*anaṅgaṇa*) due to the absence of the spheres of desire that are conditions for the attainment of jhāna.

It is "free from defilement" (*vigatūpakkilesa*) through the removal of covetousness and other such defilements of the mind. Both of these [qualities] are to be understood according to the *Anaṅgaṇa-sutta* and the *Vattha-sutta*.

It is "pliable" (*mudubhūta*) by virtue of having attained mastery. It is "workable" (*kammaniya*) by virtue of having reached the state of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). By virtue of the fulfillment of development...
It stands having attained refinement and reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*). The meaning is that it stands in such a way as to have reached imperturbability.
Thus, the mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of being directed toward the realization through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) of those states to be realized by direct knowledge;
it serves as the basis and the foundation for the realization through direct knowledge.
Dasaiddhikathā 369.
Regarding the phrase "he directs and inclines the mind toward the modes of supernormal power" (*iddhividhā*): here, "supernormal power" (*iddhi*) is in the sense of succeeding;
it is said to be in the sense of accomplishment and in the sense of acquisition. For that which is accomplished is acquired.
And that which succeeds is called "iddhi. As it is said: "For one who desires sensual pleasures, this succeeds for him.
Likewise: "Renunciation succeeds, thus it is *iddhi*; it repels [the opposite], thus it is a *pāṭihāriya*. The path to arahantship succeeds, thus it is *iddhi*;
it repels [the defilements], thus it is a *pāṭihāriya*."

Another method: success (*iddhi*) is so called in the sense of succeeding. This is a designation for the perfection of means. For the perfection of means succeeds because it brings forth the intended fruit.
As it was said: "This householder Citta is virtuous and of good character;
if he should make a resolution, 'In the future, may I be a wheel-turning monarch,' this will indeed succeed for him."
“The mental aspiration of one who possesses virtue is purified.
Another method: beings succeed by means of this, thus it is *iddhi*. “They succeed” means they become successful, prosperous, and reach the highest excellence;
this is what is meant. It is tenfold. As it is said: “How many kinds of *iddhi* are there? There are ten kinds of *iddhi*. Furthermore, it is said:
“What are the ten kinds of success (iddhi)? Success by resolution, success by transformation, success consisting of mind-made [body], success through the pervasion of knowledge,
success through the pervasion of concentration, noble success, success born of the ripening of kamma, success belonging to one possessed of merit, success consisting of science (vijjā),
and success in the sense of succeeding through the condition of right application here and there.”

370. In this context, the supernormal power (iddhi) demonstrated by analyzing it thus—“By nature one person adverts to being many; having adverted to a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand, he resolves with knowledge:
‘May I be many’”—is called *adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi* because it is accomplished by means of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
371. “Thus, having abandoned his natural form, he displays the form of a youth, or the form of a nāga...

[and so on] ...or he displays various military arrays”—such supernormal power (iddhi) as it is described here is called “supernormal power of transformation” (vikubbanā-iddhi), because it proceeds by way of the alteration of abandoning one’s natural form.
372. “In this case, a bhikkhu produces from this body another body, material, mind-made”— according to this method,

the supernormal power (iddhi) described here is called ‘mind-made power’ (manomayā iddhi), because it proceeds by way of the production of another, distinct mind-made body within the interior of one’s own body.

373. However, the distinction produced by the power of knowledge—whether prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with the arising of that knowledge—is called the supernormal power of the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphārā iddhi*).
For this has been said: "The meaning of the abandoning of the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence succeeds;
thus it is the supernormal power of the expansion of knowledge... [and so on] ...the meaning of the abandoning of all defilements through the path of Arahantship succeeds."
“Success through the expansion of knowledge; the success through the expansion of knowledge of the Venerable Bākkula; the success through the expansion of knowledge of the Venerable Saṅkicca;
the success through the expansion of knowledge of the Venerable Bhūtapāla.
In this regard, while the Venerable Bākkula was still young, being bathed in a river on an auspicious day, he was left by his nurse through negligence.
He fell asleep. A fish swallowed him and went to the bathing place at Bārāṇasī. There, a fisherman caught him and sold him to the merchant’s wife.

Having conceived an affection for the fish, she thought, "I shall cook it myself," and while cutting it open, she saw a boy inside the belly of the fish like a golden image. Thinking, "A son has been found by me," she was filled with joy.
Thus, the state of being healthy within the belly of a fish was produced by the power of the knowledge of the Noble Path to Arahantship to be attained by the Venerable Bakkula in his final existence;
therefore, it is called the "success (iddhi) consisting in the expansion of knowledge" (*ñāṇavipphārā iddhi*).
However, the full account of the story should be told in detail.
However, while the Elder Saṅkicca was still in the womb, his mother passed away.

After she had been placed upon the funeral pyre and pierced with stakes, as she was being consumed by fire, the boy received a blow on the bridge of his nose from the tip of a stake and let out a cry.
Then, thinking "the boy lives," they lowered her, slit open her belly, and gave the child to his grandmother. He was then raised by her.
Having gone forth with increasing maturity, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Thus, in the manner already described, the fact that the Venerable Saṅkicca remained free from illness while on the wood-pile is called the supernormal power (*iddhi*) consisting in the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphārā*).
As for the boy Bhūtapāla, his father was a poor man in Rājagaha; he [was carrying] a cartload of wood...
Having gone to the forest and made a load of wood, he arrived near the city gate in the evening. Then his oxen broke the yoke and entered the city.
He, having seated his little son at the base of the cart, followed after the oxen and entered the city itself.
Before he had even departed, the gate was closed. Although the place where the child was was frequented by fierce *yakkhas*,...
The state of health for three watches of the night outside the city is, by the method already described, called success through the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphārā iddhi*).
The narrative account, however, should be expanded in detail.

374. The excellence produced by the power of serenity (*samatha*), whether before, after, or at the very moment of concentration, is called success through the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphārā*).

Supernormal power (*iddhi*). For this has been said: "The meaning of the abandoning of the hindrances succeeds by means of the first jhāna; thus it is supernormal power through the pervasion of concentration... up to...
the meaning of the abandoning of the perception of the base of nothingness succeeds by means of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
thus it is supernormal power through the pervasion of concentration. There is supernormal power through the pervasion of concentration for the Venerable Sāriputta, for the Venerable Sañjīva..."
“The psychic power resulting from the expansion of concentration belongs to the Venerable Khāṇu Koṇḍañña, to the female lay follower Uttarā, and to the female lay follower Sāmāvatī. In that context,
when the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna at Kapotakandara,
on a moonlit night, sitting in the open air with his hair recently shorn, a certain wicked yakṣa—
Although he was being restrained by his companion yakkha, he struck him on the head with a blow that sounded like the thundering of a cloud.
At the moment of that blow, the elder entered into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Consequently, he suffered no injury whatsoever from that strike.
This was the elder’s supernormal power (*iddhi*) arising from the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphārā*). The account of this incident, however, is already recorded in the *Udāna*.

However, perceiving that the Elder Sañjīva had passed away while absorbed in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the cowherds and others gathered grass, wood, and cow dung and set fire to them.
Not even a single thread of the Elder’s robe was consumed by the flames.

This was a supernormal power (*iddhi*) produced through the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphārā*), arising from the power of serenity (*samatha*) as it proceeded by way of successive attainments. The background story (*vatthu*), however, is already recorded in the Sutta.
The Elder Khāṇukoṇḍañña, however, was naturally abundant in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). One night, he sat in a certain forest having entered an attainment.

Five hundred thieves, having plundered their goods while traveling, thought, "Now there is no one coming along our path," and desiring to rest, they were unloading their goods when [the Elder] said, "This is a stump!"
Thinking thus, they placed all their belongings on top of the elder.
As they were departing after resting, at the moment they reached for the first item they had set down, the elder emerged according to the predetermined time limit.
Seeing the elder’s movement, they cried out in fear. The elder said, “Do not be afraid, lay followers; I am a bhikkhu.”
Having come and paid homage, they went forth with faith directed toward the Elder and, together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), attained Arahantship.

This, in this context, was the Elder’s freedom from illness despite being overwhelmed by five hundred loads of goods; it was a supernormal power (*iddhi*) resulting from the expansion of concentration (*samādhi-vipphāra*).
Now, the female lay follower Uttarā was the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇa. A courtesan named Sirimā, driven by jealousy toward her, [prepared] a cauldron of boiling oil.
She poured it upon her head. At that very moment, Uttarā attained the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettā-samāpatti*). The oil rolled off like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
This was her supernormal power (*iddhi*) resulting from the expansion of concentration (*samādhi-vipphārā*).
The background story, however, should be related in detail: Sāmāvatī was the chief queen of King Udena. The brahmin Māgaṇḍiya [desired] the position of chief queen for his own daughter.

Seeking to harm her, he had a venomous snake placed inside that lute and said to the king, "Great King, Sāmāvatī, desiring to kill you, carries a venomous snake hidden within her lute. When the king saw this, he became enraged;
thinking, "I shall put Sāmāvatī to death," he strung his bow and fixed a poisoned arrow to it. Sāmāvatī, together with her retinue, [approached] the king...
She suffused him with loving-kindness (*mettā*). Unable either to shoot the arrow or to lower it, the king stood trembling.
Then the queen said to him, “Why are you weary, Great King? “Yes, I am weary. “In that case, lower the bow,” she said.
The arrow fell at the very feet of the king. Then the queen said to him, “Great King, one should not be malicious toward one who is without malice.”

...he exhorted him. Thus, the King’s inability to discharge his arrow was the psychic power (*iddhi*) resulting from the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphārā*) of the female lay follower Sāmāvatī.
(375) However, dwelling with the perception of non-repulsiveness toward repulsive things and so forth is called "noble psychic power" (*ariyā iddhi*).
As it is said: "What is noble psychic power? Here, a bhikkhu, if he should wish: 'May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive'..."
“He dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive... [and so on] ...he dwells there with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This is called the noble supernormal power (*ariyā iddhi*) because it occurs only in noble ones who have attained mastery over the mind.
For a monk whose taints are destroyed, when endowed with this power, performs the suffusion of loving-kindness toward a repulsive and undesirable object.

Or, while performing attention to the elements, he dwells with a perception of non-repulsiveness. Toward a desirable object that is not repulsive, while performing either the pervasion of foulness (*asubha*) or the attention "it is impermanent," he dwells with a perception of repulsiveness.

Likewise, toward both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, while performing either the pervasion of loving-kindness (*mettā*) or the attention to the elements, he dwells with a perception of non-repulsiveness.

He dwells. Regarding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, he dwells perceiving the repulsive by either performing that same pervasion of foulness (*asubha*) or by attending to them as "impermanent" (*anicca*).

Furthermore, by practicing the sixfold equanimity described in the passage beginning with, "Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad," he dwells [with equanimity] toward both the repulsive and the unrepulsive.
Having turned away from it, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Indeed, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, this very meaning is analyzed according to the method beginning:
"How does one dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in the repulsive? One pervades an undesirable object with loving-kindness, or resolves it by way of the elements," and so forth.
Because this occurs only for Noble Ones who have attained mastery over the mind, it is called "noble supernormal power" (*ariyā iddhi*).

376. Furthermore, the supernormal power (iddhi) consisting of traveling through the air and so forth, which belongs to birds and others, is called "born of the maturation of kamma" (kammavipākajā). As it is said:

"What is the supernormal power born of the maturation of kamma? It is that of all birds, all deities, certain humans, and certain beings in the states of misery—this is the supernormal power born of the maturation of kamma. For in this context, the meditative absorption (jhāna) of all birds...
Or, traveling through the air even without insight (vipassanā) occurs for all devas,

for the beings of the first eon, and for certain humans. Likewise, for certain beings in the states of misery (vinipātika)— such as the yakkhinīs Piyaṅkaramātā, Uttaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and others—
traveling through the air is a supernormal power (iddhi) born of the ripening of kamma.

377. Furthermore, the power of one possessing merit (*puññavato iddhi*) refers to such things as the flight through the air of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) and others. As it is said: "What is the power of one possessing merit?
A wheel-turning monarch travels through the air together with his fourfold army, including even the men who tether the horses and the men who tether the oxen.
This is the power of the merit of the householder Jotika. Of the matted-hair ascetic..."
"The success of the merit-possessing householder; the success of the merit-possessing householder Ghosita; the success of the merit-possessing householder Meṇḍaka;

the success of the five great merit-possessors. In brief, however, the specific accomplishment that arises when the equipment of merit has reached its full maturity is "the success of the merit-possessor."
And herein, for the householder Jotika, a jeweled palace arose after splitting the earth; and sixty-four *kappa*-trees [appeared].
This was the supernatural power (*iddhi*) of that meritorious one. For Jaṭilaka, a golden mountain eighty cubits high manifested.
And for Ghosita, despite attempts being made in seven places to kill him, his state of health was due to his merit.
Supernatural power (*iddhi*). The appearance of rams made of the seven precious gems on a single *karīsa* plot of land was the supernatural power of the meritorious Meṇḍaka.

There were five who were called "of great merit": the merchant Meṇḍaka, his wife Candapadumasirī, his son the merchant Dhanañjaya, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, and his slave named Puṇṇa. Among them, when the merchant had washed his head and was looking up at the sky—
Twelve thousand five hundred granaries were filled from the sky with red rice.
Even when his wife took only a single measure of boiled rice and served it to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, the food was never exhausted.
When his son took a purse containing a thousand coins and gave them even to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, the kahāpaṇas were never exhausted. His daughter-in-law [took] one basket of paddy...
Even when distributing grain to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa after taking it up, it is not exhausted.
When a slave plows with a single plow, there are fourteen furrows—seven on this side and seven on that. This is the supernormal power (*iddhi*) of one possessing merit. 378.

However, the supernormal power consisting of knowledge (*vijjāmayā iddhi*) refers to the traveling through the air and so forth of those such as the *vidyādharas*. As it is said: "What is the supernormal power consisting of knowledge?"
What is success (*iddhi*)? Knowledge-holders (*vijjādhara*), having recited their spells, go through the air. In the sky, in the firmament, they show even an elephant...
[and so on] ...they show various military arrays.
By this or that correct application, the accomplishment of this or that action occurs; therein, it is due to the condition of correct application.
Success (*iddhi*) is so called in the sense of succeeding (*ijjhana*). As it has been said: "By means of renunciation, the state of abandoning sensual desire succeeds;

thus, through the condition of right application in various instances, there is success in the sense of succeeding... up to ... by means of the path of arahantship, the state of abandoning all defilements succeeds;
thus, through the condition of right application in various instances, there is success in the sense of succeeding. Herein—
And the textual passage (pāḷi) that follows is identical to the preceding one, as it serves to illustrate right application (sammāpayoga) in the sense of practice itself.
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated that this includes any craft-work such as arranging troops in the formation of a chariot (sakaṭabyūha),
any medical practice, the study of the three Vedas, the study of the three Piṭakas, and even down to such tasks as plowing and sowing.
Having performed various deeds, the specific result produced therein arises through the condition of right application; thus it is known as "success" (*iddhi*) in the sense of being accomplished.

(10) Thus, among these ten kinds of success, in this term *iddhividhā*, only the success of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) is mentioned. However, in this context, the success of transformation (*vikubbanā*) and the success of the mind-made body (*manomaya*) must also certainly be included.
380. *Iddhividhāya* means for the category of success or for a particular mode of success. One directs and inclines the mind.

When that state of mind has arisen as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) in the manner described, that bhikkhu directs the preliminary mind toward the attainment of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhā*);
having withdrawn it from the kasiṇa object, he sends it forth facing toward the supernormal powers.
"He inclines" means he makes the mind lean toward and tend toward the supernormal power to be attained. "He" refers to that very person who has thus directed the mind.
"Bhikkhu. "Anekavihitam" means manifold, of various kinds. "Iddhividham" means a portion of psychic power (*iddhi*).
"Paccanubhoti" means he experiences; the meaning is that he touches, realizes, and attains it.
Now, showing its manifold nature, he said, "Having been one," and so forth. Therein, "having been one" refers to his natural state prior to the exercise of psychic power.
"Having been one, he becomes many": wishing to walk back and forth, recite, or ask questions in the presence of many people, he becomes a hundred or even a thousand. But how does he become thus?
By accomplishing the four planes, the four bases, the eight steps, and the sixteen roots of supernormal power (*iddhi*), and then resolving through knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
381. In this context, "four planes" should be understood as the four jhānas. For this was said by the General of the Dhamma: "What are the four planes of psychic power?
The plane born of seclusion is the first jhāna; the plane of rapture and happiness is the second jhāna;
the plane of equanimity and happiness is the third jhāna; the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is the fourth jhāna. [These are] the planes of psychic power..."

"These four stages lead to the acquisition of psychic power, the attainment of psychic power, the transformation of psychic power, the manifestation of psychic power, mastery over psychic power, and confidence in psychic power. And herein,
because one has entered upon the first three jhānas through the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of pleasure,
and having attained the perception of lightness and the perception of softness, one’s body becomes light, soft, and wieldy.

One attains supernormal power (*iddhi*); therefore, because they lead to the acquisition of supernormal power by this method, they should be understood as the "ground of requisites" (*sambhāra-bhūmi*).
However, the fourth jhāna is the actual "ground" (*pakati-bhūmi*) for the acquisition of supernormal power.
382. "The four bases": the four bases of supernormal power (*iddhipāda*) should be understood. For this has been said: "Which are the four [bases] of supernormal power?"
The bases of power (*iddhipāda*): Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis of power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis of power endowed with concentration of energy... concentration of mind... and concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
These four bases of power lead to the attainment of success (*iddhi*)... and to fearlessness in success. And herein, that which has desire as its cause...

Concentration characterized by predominance of desire is "desire-concentration" (*chandha-samādhi*). This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire of "wishing to act" (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) predominant.

"Exertive formations" (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) refers to the formations that constitute exertion; this is a designation for the energy of right effort (*sammappadhāna-viriya*) which accomplishes the four tasks.

"Endowed with" means possessed of both desire-concentration and the exertive formations. "Basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*)— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "Iddhipādanti". The full definition of *iddhipāda* would typically conclude with the phrase "the foundation of spiritual power," but as per the instructions, only the provided text is translated.*

Alternatively, in the sense of accomplishment (*nipphatti*), or by way of the term "success" (*ijjhana*)—meaning that by means of this [concentration], beings succeed (*ijjhanti*), become prosperous (*iddhā*), grow (*vuddhā*), and reach excellence—it is the basis for those mental factors associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) that are reckoned as "successes" (*iddhi*).

The meaning is that it is the remaining aggregate of consciousness and mental concomitants which serves as the foundation (*pāda*) in the sense of being the support (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the volitional formations of exertion (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) associated with concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*). For this has been said: "The base of success (*iddhipāda*)."
“For one who has become thus, there is the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness.
Alternatively, it is called a *pāda* (foot) because one goes by means of it; the meaning is that one reaches [the goal]. A *iddhipāda* (basis of psychic power) is a foot for psychic power (*iddhi*).
This is a designation for desire and the rest. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu, relying upon desire, attains concentration, he attains...”
“Unification of the mind—this is called concentration through desire (*chandasamādhi*). He exerts himself so that unarisen evil states do not arise...

[and so on]... these are called the formations of striving (*padhānasaṅkhārā*). Thus, this desire and this concentration through desire, together with these formations of striving—this, monks, is called the basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) endowed with concentration through desire and the formations of striving. Thus.
The meaning should also be understood in the *Sesiddhipāda* [treatises]. 383.
Regarding "eight bases," the eight beginning with desire (*chanda*) should be understood. For this has been said: "What are the eight bases of psychic power (*iddhi*)?
If a bhikkhu, relying on desire, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—this is desire..."
Concentration is not desire; desire is not concentration. Desire is one thing, concentration is another.
If a bhikkhu, by relying on energy... if a bhikkhu, by relying on the mind... if a bhikkhu, by relying on inquiry, gains concentration, he gains one-pointedness of mind.
Inquiry is not concentration; concentration is not inquiry. Inquiry is one thing, concentration is another. These are the eight factors of psychic power (*iddhi*).
“They lead to the attainment of supernormal power (iddhi)... [and so on]... to confidence in supernormal power.

For here, the desire (chanda) arising from the wish to produce supernormal power, when conjoined with concentration (samādhi), leads to the attainment of supernormal power; likewise for energy (vīriya) and the others.
Therefore, it should be understood that these eight factors have been stated.
384. "The sixteen roots": by way of these sixteen aspects, the imperturbability of the mind is to be understood.
For this has been said: "How many roots are there for psychic power? There are sixteen roots: a mind that is not depressed does not waver in indolence, thus it is imperturbable;
a mind that is not elated does not waver in agitation, thus it is imperturbable; a mind that is not drawn forward does not waver in lust..."

The imperturbable: because the mind is not withdrawn, it does not waver in ill-will, thus it is the imperturbable; because the mind is independent, it does not waver in views, thus it is the imperturbable;
because the mind is unattached, it does not waver in desire-and-lust, thus it is the imperturbable;

because the mind is fully liberated, it does not waver in sensual lust, thus it is the imperturbable; because the mind is dissociated, it does not waver in the defilements, thus it is the imperturbable.

The mind made boundless by the limit of the self does not waver within the limit of the defilements; thus it is "imperturbable" (*āneñja*). The mind that has attained unity does not waver amidst the defilements of diversity;
thus it is "imperturbable. The mind embraced by faith does not waver in lack of faith;
thus it is "imperturbable. The mind embraced by energy does not waver in laziness; thus it is "imperturbable. The mind embraced by mindfulness...
"It does not waver in negligence, thus it is imperturbable (*āneñja*); the mind embraced by concentration does not waver in agitation, thus it is imperturbable;
the mind embraced by wisdom does not waver in ignorance, thus it is imperturbable; the mind that has reached illumination does not waver in the darkness of ignorance, thus it is imperturbable.
These sixteen roots of psychic power lead to the attainment of psychic power... [and so on] ...to fearlessness in psychic power."

Granted that this meaning is already established by the passage beginning with "When the mind is thus concentrated," it is stated again for the purpose of showing that the first jhāna and so forth are the foundation, the basis, and the root of psychic power (iddhi). The former method is that which appears in the Suttas;
this one is from the *Paṭisambhidā*. Thus, it is stated again for the sake of non-confusion regarding both contexts.
385. "Resolving by means of knowledge" means that, having mastered these states which serve as the soil and the footings for psychic power,
one enters the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, emerges from it, and if one desires to become a hundred,
performs the preliminary work by thinking, "May I be a hundred, may I be a hundred," then again enters the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, emerges from it, and resolves.
It becomes real together with the mind of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-citta*). The same method applies to a thousand and so forth.
If it does not succeed in this way, one should perform the preliminary work again, enter the attainment a second time, emerge, and then resolve.

For it is stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā* that it is permissible to enter [the attainment] once or twice. In that context, the foundational jhāna-consciousness has the sign (*nimitta*) as its object.
The preliminary consciousnesses have either a hundred objects or a thousand objects, and these are by way of color, not by way of a conceptual designation (*paññatti*).
The resolving consciousness is likewise either with a hundred objects or a thousand objects.

Like the previously mentioned absorption consciousness, it arises immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū*) as a single instance of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

386. As for what is stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*: “By nature, one person adverts to many—whether a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand—and having adverted, he resolves with knowledge, ‘May I become many. He becomes many, just as the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka did.
There too, the phrase “he adverts” is spoken by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*) alone. Having adverted, [he resolves] with knowledge...
"He resolves" is said by way of the knowledge of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*). Therefore, he adverts to being many;

then, at the conclusion of those preliminary minds (*parikamma-citta*), he enters attainment. Having emerged from attainment, he adverts again, "May I be many," and thereafter, immediately after three or four preceding access-minds (*pubbhāga-citta*) have occurred, by means of the finalizing mind that has arisen, [he becomes many].
“Adhiṭṭhāna” means that one resolves by means of a single knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa) which has already been acquired; this is how the meaning should be understood here.
As for what was said, “just as the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka,” that was stated for the purpose of showing bodily witness (kāyasakkhi) regarding the state of being manifold.
That, however, should be illustrated by way of a story: it is said that those two brothers were called “Panthakas” because they were born on a road (panthe).
They received their names. Among them, the eldest was Mahāpanthaka; having gone forth, he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having become an Arahat, he ordained Cūḷapanthaka, saying:
"Just as a fragrant red lotus may be in full bloom at dawn, its fragrance not yet dissipated;"
"Behold Aṅgīrasa shining forth, glowing like the sun in the sky"—this verse he gave him.
He was unable to master it within four months. Then the Elder expelled him from the monastery, saying, "You are incapable of this Dispensation.
At that time, the Elder was the distributor of meals. Jīvaka [approached] the Elder...
Having approached, she said, "Venerable sir, please come to our house tomorrow with five hundred bhikkhus and accept almsfood from us.
The Elder also consented, saying, "I accept for all except Cūḷapanthaka.
Cūḷapanthaka stood at the gatehouse and wept. The Blessed One, seeing this with his divine eye, approached him.
"Why do you weep? he asked. He explained the situation to him. The Blessed One said, "One who is unable to perform recitation is not called 'incapable' in my teaching;

do not grieve, monk. Taking him by the arm, he led him into the monastery, miraculously fashioned a piece of cloth, and gave it to him, saying, "Come now, monk, while rubbing this, [use it as] a dust-remover."
"‘Dust-remover’ means: perform recitation again and again. As he did so, his complexion became black.

Perceiving that the cloth was pure and that there was no fault in it, but rather that this was a fault of his own person, he applied his knowledge to the five aggregates, developed insight, and brought it to the stage of conformity (anuloma) near the state of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu).
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses of illumination:
“Lust is not called ‘dust,’ nor is it called ‘grit’;
‘Dust’ is a designation for lust.”
Having utterly abandoned this dust, the wise dwell in the teaching of one who is free from dust.
“Hatred… [and so on]” … [as above].
“Dust is not called ‘dust’;
this is a designation for delusion.
Having abandoned this dust, the wise—”
“They dwell in the teaching of Him who is free from passion.

At the conclusion of that verse, the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), accompanied by the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā), became as if already held in his hands.
On the following day, the Teacher went to Jīvaka’s house together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then, at the conclusion of the offering of the ceremonial water (dakkhiṇodaka)...
While the rice gruel was being given, he covered the bowl with his hand. Jīvaka asked, "Venerable sir, what is it?

[The Buddha replied,] "There is a certain monk in the monastery. He sent a man, saying, "Go, take the noble one and come back quickly. But when the Blessed One had departed from the monastery, [the man returned].
"Having manifested himself a thousandfold,
Paṇḍaka sat in the delightful mango grove until the announcement of the time.
Then that man went there and, seeing the monastery glowing with a single light from the saffron robes, returned and reported that it was filled with bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir, this is the monastery, but I do not know which noble one that is,” he said. Then the Blessed One told him, “Go;
when you see the first person, take hold of the corner of his robe, say, ‘The Teacher summons you,’ and bring him here.
He went there and took hold of the corner of the Elder’s robe. At that very moment, all the other created forms vanished.
The Elder, having dismissed him with the words, “Go,” and having completed his bodily duties such as washing his face, went first and sat down on his seat.
It was with reference to this that it was said, “just as the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka.

In that regard, those many created forms, because they were created without being specifically distinguished, are identical to the possessor of psychic power (iddhimat) in standing, sitting, and so forth.
Or, whatever the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) does—whether speaking, remaining silent, or other such acts—they do exactly that.
But if he wishes to make them of various colors, some in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, and some in the final stage;
likewise, some with long hair, some half-shaved, some shaven, some with mixed hair; or some with half-red robes, some with yellow robes; [he can do so].

Or, wishing to perform other various kinds of tasks— such as reciting the words of the text, delivering a Dhamma talk, engaging in scholarly debate (*sārabhañña*), asking questions, answering questions,
dyeing cloth, sewing robes, or washing them— he should emerge from the foundational jhāna,
perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) by way of resolving, "Let so many bhikkhus be in their prime age," and then, having re-entered attainment, emerge again.
It must be resolved: "By means of the mind of resolution, may they become exactly of whatever form is desired.
This same method applies to such cases as "having become many, may I become one," and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: after this bhikkhu has thus manifested multiplicity, he resolves again, "Having become one, I shall walk up and down."
Having thought, "I shall recite the scriptures; I shall ask a question," or else, out of fewness of desires, thinking, "This monastery has few bhikkhus;
if anyone should arrive, they will wonder, 'Whence have these so many identical bhikkhus come?
Surely this is the power of the Elder,' and thus recognize me"—desiring to be alone in the meantime, he enters the foundational jhāna.
Having entered [the attainment] and emerged, one should perform the preliminary work (parikamma) with the thought, "May I be one," and then, having entered again and emerged, one must resolve:
"May I be one. Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, one becomes one. However, for one who does not act in this way, one becomes one by oneself according to the duration previously delimited.
387. "They appear and disappear" means here that one makes them appear and makes them disappear.
It is with reference to this very point that it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "'Appear' means it becomes unobstructed by anything, uncovered, open, and manifest.
'Disappear' means it becomes obstructed by something, covered, shut away, and concealed."

In this regard, one possessing psychic power (iddhimā), desiring to make something manifest, turns darkness into light, or the concealed into the revealed, or brings that which is outside the range of vision into the range of vision. How so?

For he, wishing to make himself or another appear as if visible even when concealed or standing at a distance, emerges from the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna) and [perceives] this place of darkness...

Having adverted [to the object] with the thought, "Let there be light," or "Let this concealed thing become revealed," or "Let this thing not in the range of vision come into the range of vision," and having performed the preliminary work, he resolves in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolving consciousness, it becomes exactly as resolved.
Others see it even though they are standing at a distance; and he himself, if he wishes to see, sees it.
388. But by whom was this miracle performed previously? By the Blessed One.

For when the Blessed One, invited by Cūḷasubhaddā, was traveling from Sāvatthī to Sāketa—a distance of seven yojanas—by means of five hundred gabled houses fashioned by Vissakamma, he caused the inhabitants of Sāketa city to see those dwelling in Sāvatthī, and the inhabitants of Sāvatthī to see those dwelling in Sāketa.
While they were watching, he made this resolve: having descended into the middle of the city, he split the earth in two and displayed everything down to the Avīci hell;
and having parted the sky in two, he displayed everything up to the Brahma-world.

This matter should also be clarified by means of the Descent of the Gods (*Devorohana*). It is said that after the Blessed One had performed the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), eighty-four thousand beings—
Having released them from their bonds, he reflected on where the past Buddhas had gone at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle;

he saw that they had gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Then, placing one foot upon the surface of the earth and the second upon Mount Yugandhara, he raised his first foot again, stepped onto the summit of Sineru, and there, upon the Paṇḍukambala stone slab—
Having entered the rains retreat, he began a discourse on the Abhidhamma for the ten thousand deities of the world-systems who had assembled there, starting from the very beginning.
At the time for the alms-round, he manifested a created Buddha (nimmitabuddha), who preached the Dhamma.
The Blessed One, having chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* and washed his face at Lake Anotatta, took alms-food in Uttarakuru and returned to the shore of Lake Anotatta.
He partook [of the meal]. The Elder Sāriputta went there and paid homage to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One gave a hint to the Elder, saying, "Today I have taught this much Dhamma. In this manner, he delivered discourses on the Abhidhamma without interruption for three months.
Upon hearing them, eighty koṭis of devas attained penetration of the Dhamma.
Although the assembly gathered for the Twin Miracle extended for twelve yojanas, it remained encamped with its baggage trains, thinking, "We shall depart only after we have seen the Blessed One.
The merchant Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika alone attended upon them with all necessary provisions.
The people requested the Elder Anuruddha to find out where the Blessed One was. The Elder, expanding his vision, [beheld him].
Having seen with his divine eye that the Blessed One had entered the rains retreat there, he informed them.
They requested the Elder Mahāmoggallāna to go for the purpose of paying homage to the Blessed One.
Right there in the midst of the assembly, the Elder sank into the great earth, emerged from Mount Sineru, and appeared at the feet of the Tathāgata.

Emerging while prostrating at the Blessed One’s feet, he said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa say that they will depart only after they have paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet and seen him. The Blessed One asked:
“But where, Moggallāna, is your elder brother, the General of the Dhamma, at this time? “In the city of Saṅkassa, venerable sir. “Moggallāna, me—”
“Those who wish to see me should come to the city of Saṅkassa tomorrow; I shall descend at the city of Saṅkassa tomorrow on the full-moon uposatha day of the Great Pavāraṇā.

“Very well, Bhante,” the Elder replied, and having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, he descended by the same path he had come and reached the presence of the people. And as he was going and coming, so that the people might see him—
Thus he made his resolve. This, then, was the miracle of manifestation that the Elder Mahāmoggallāna performed there.
Having arrived thus, he reported what had transpired and said, "Do not perceive it as being far away; depart after you have already taken your morning meal.
The Blessed One informed Sakka, the king of the gods: "Great King, tomorrow I shall go to the world of men."
The King of the Devas commanded Vissakamma: "Dear son, tomorrow the Blessed One intends to go to the world of men;
construct three flights of stairs—one made of gold, one made of silver, and one made of jewels. He did accordingly.
On the second day, the Blessed One stood upon the summit of Sineru and surveyed the eastern world-system, seeing many thousands of world-spheres.
Having become opened, they shone as if they were a single courtyard.
Just as it was to the east, so too he saw everything opened to the west, to the north, and to the south. He saw downward as far as the Avīci hell and upward as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm.
It is said that on that day there was what is called the "Opening of the World. Humans saw the gods, and the gods saw humans.
There, neither humans looked upward nor did the gods look downward; everyone saw one another face-to-face.

The Blessed One descended by a central staircase made of jewels, the gods of the six sense-sphere heavens by a golden staircase on the left side, and the Suddhāvāsa gods and Mahābrahmā by a silver staircase on the right side. The king of the gods [held] the bowl and robe.
Mahābrahmā took up a white parasol three *yojanas* in size; Suyāma took up a yak-tail fan;
and Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabbas, descended while making an offering to the Tathāgata, having taken a yellow *beluva*-wood lute measuring three *gāvutas*.
On that day, there was no being who, upon seeing the Blessed One, failed to conceive a longing for Buddhahood. This is the point here.
The Blessed One performed the miracle of manifestation.
Furthermore, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, sat upon the courtyard of the shrine at the Tissamahāvihāra and said:
"Monks, a monk endowed with three qualities has entered upon the unerring path."
While preaching the *Apaṇṇaka-sutta*, saying, “It happens,” the Elder turned the fan downward; from the Avīci hell upward, everything became one vast expanse.
Then he turned it upward; as far as the Brahma-world, everything became one vast expanse.

The Elder, having terrified them with the fear of hell and enticed them with the bliss of heaven, taught the Dhamma. Some became stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), some once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*), non-returners (*anāgāmī*), and arhats.
389. But when he wishes to make himself invisible, he turns light into darkness, or what is uncovered into covered, or what is within range of sight into what is beyond range. How so?

For just as one might not be seen even though uncovered or standing nearby, so wishing to make himself or another thus, he emerges from the basic jhāna and [directs his mind]: "This place is to be light."

Having adverted [to the object] with the thought, "Let there be darkness," or "Let this which is uncovered become covered," or "Let this which is in the range of vision become outside the range of vision," and having performed the preliminary work, he resolves in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolving consciousness, it becomes exactly as resolved.
Even those standing nearby do not see it; and he himself, wishing not to see it, does not see it.
390. But by whom was this miracle performed before? By the Blessed One.
For the Blessed One, while the noble youth Yasa was sitting right nearby, acted in such a way that his father did not see him.

Likewise, having gone out to meet Mahākappina from a distance of two hundred leagues, he established him in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and established his thousand ministers in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).
Following in his wake, Queen Anojā, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand women, arrived and sat nearby;
yet she acted in such a way that the king did not see her or her company. When asked, "Venerable sir, do you see the king?", she replied, "What is better for you:
to search for the king, or rather, yourself? To which she said, "Myself, venerable sir."
As she sat there, he taught her the Dhamma in such a way that she, together with a thousand women, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala),
the ministers in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and the king in arahantship. Furthermore,
this was exactly what the Elder Mahinda did by acting in such a way that on the day he arrived in Tambapaṇṇi Island, the king could not see the rest of those who had come with him.
Furthermore, every manifest miracle is called "manifestation" (*āvi-bhāva*), while a non-manifest miracle is called "disappearance" (*tiro-bhāva*).

Among these, in a manifest miracle, both the psychic power (*iddhi*) and the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) are perceived; this should be illustrated by the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya*).
For in that case: "Here the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with his disciples."
"A mass of fire issues from his upper body, and a stream of water issues from his lower body"—thus both were manifested.
In a manifestation that is not public, only the supernormal power (*iddhi*) is manifested, not the possessor of supernormal power (*iddhimā*).
This should be illustrated by the Mahaka Sutta and the Brahmanimantanika Sutta; for there, [the supernormal power of] the Venerable Mahaka and the Blessed One...
And it was the psychic power itself that appeared, not the possessor of psychic power.
As it is said:
"Seated to one side, the householder Citta said this to the Venerable Mahaka: 'It would be well for me, Bhante...'"
“May the noble Mahaka display a wonder of psychic power, a superhuman feat.

“In that case, householder, spread out your upper robe on the veranda and scatter a bundle of grass. “Very well, venerable sir,” Citta the householder replied to the Venerable Mahaka, and having spread out his upper robe on the veranda, he scattered a bundle of grass.

He gave him permission. Then the Venerable Mahaka entered the dwelling and performed such a feat of supernormal power that a flame issued forth through the keyhole and the gap between the door panels, burning the grass but not burning his upper robe.
And as it is said:
“Then, monks, I performed such a feat of psychic power that Brahmā,
the assembly of Brahmā, and the followers of Brahmā would hear my voice but not see me;
having vanished, I uttered this verse:”
“Having seen fear in existence, and having seen existence as something to be sought after by those who desire non-existence,
I did not praise any form of existence, nor did I cling to delight. “In this regard,
he goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, just as if through space.”
"Beyond the wall" (*tirokuṭṭa*) means beyond another's wall; that is to say, to the other side of the wall. The same method applies to the others.
"Wall" (*kuṭṭa*) is a designation for the wall of a house. "Rampart" (*pākāra*) is the surrounding rampart of a house, monastery, village, and so forth.
"Mountain" (*pabbata*) refers either to a mound of earth or a mountain of rock. "Without clinging" (*asajjamāno*) means not adhering. "Just as in the air" (*seyyathāpi ākāse*) means in the sky.

In this way, one who wishes to go should enter the space-kasiṇa attainment, emerge, and—having performed the preliminary work by directing the mind toward a wall, a rampart, or any mountain such as Sineru or the Cakkavāḷa mountains—resolve: "Let there be space.
There is space alone. For one wishing to descend or wishing to ascend, [there must be] a hollow opening...
There is a hole for one who wishes to go by piercing through; he goes there without being obstructed.
However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said here: "Friend, what is the purpose of attaining the space-kasiṇa?
Does one who wishes to manifest elephants, horses, and so forth, attain the elephant-kasiṇa, horse-kasiṇa, and so on? Is it not rather [the case that] wherever..."
"In some cases, having performed the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, mastery over the eight attainments itself is the measure; whatever one wishes for, that very thing comes to be.
The bhikkhus said, "Venerable sir, only the space-kasiṇa has come down in the Text;
therefore, this must certainly be stated. Herein, this is the Text:
“By nature he is an attainer of the space-kasiṇa absorption. He adverts to what is beyond walls, beyond enclosures, and beyond mountains.
Having adverted, he resolves with knowledge: ‘Let there be space. There is space.
Unobstructed, he passes through what is beyond walls, beyond enclosures, and beyond mountains, just as ordinary people who lack supernormal powers pass through any place that is not enclosed.”

"Just as those who are unencumbered walk without obstruction over what is not fenced off, even so that possessor of psychic power, having attained mastery over the mind, passes through walls, through enclosures,
and through mountains without obstruction, just as if through open space. But if,
while that bhikkhu is walking after having made a resolution, a mountain or a tree should arise in his path, [he would pass through it].
But must it be resolved again after having attained [the meditative state]? There is no fault in this.

For resolving again after attaining is like receiving formal dependence (*nissaya*) in the presence of one’s preceptor. Moreover, because this bhikkhu has resolved, "Let there be space," there is indeed space.
And by the power of that previous resolution alone, even if another mountain [should appear] in the interval...

Or that a tree will arise by the power of the seasons—this is simply impossible. However, when something is created by another possessor of psychic power (*iddhimant*), the first creation is the stronger;
the other must go either above or below it. 393.
Regarding "they dive and emerge even in the earth": here, "emerge" (*ummujjanti*) means to rise up, and "dive" (*nimujjanti*) means to sink down.

Sinking down; emerging and submerging is "emerging-and-submerging. One who wishes to do this should attain the water-kasina, then rising up, delimit the area, thinking, "Let there be water on this much ground," and perform the preliminary work. It should then be resolved in the manner already described.
Simultaneously with the resolution, the earth in the delimited area becomes water alone.
Thus he performs the act of emerging and diving therein. Here is the canonical text:
"By nature he is an obtainer of the attainment of the water-kasiṇa. He adverts to earth. Having adverted, he resolves with knowledge:
'Let there be water. There is water. He performs the act of emerging and diving upon that earth, just as people do."

"Just as those naturally lacking supernormal power perform diving and surfacing in water, even so that possessor of supernormal power, having attained mastery over mind, performs diving and surfacing in earth just as if in water.
And it is not only diving and surfacing; [he does so] in bathing, drinking, washing the face, washing clothes, and so forth—whatever [is required].

Whatever he desires, that he makes. And it is not only water; regarding ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, whatever he desires—having adverted to it with the thought, "Let this and that be just this much," and having performed the preliminary work, he resolves—and it becomes exactly as resolved.
When he draws it out and places it into a vessel, the ghee remains ghee.
Oil is indeed oil; water is indeed water. He wets it because he wishes to wet it; one who does not wish to wet it does not wet it.
And for him alone that earth becomes water, while for other people it remains earth.
There, people go on foot, they go by means of vehicles and so forth, and they even perform agricultural work and other tasks. But if this...

He wishes, "May there also be water for them," and indeed there is. However, once the delimited period has passed, with the exception of that water which naturally remains in jars, ponds, and so forth, the remainder of the delimited area becomes earth alone.
394. Regarding the phrase "even on water that does not break": here, that water which sinks when stepped upon is what is called "breaking."

This is called "the opposite, which does not break through. However, one who wishes to go [through water] should enter the earth-kasiṇa attainment, emerge, delimit a certain area saying, "Let there be earth in this place," perform the preliminary work, and then resolve according to the method already described.
Simultaneously with the resolution, the water in the delimited area becomes earth itself.
Thus he goes there. Here is the canonical text regarding this:
“He is naturally a master of the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa. He adverts to water. Having adverted to it, he resolves with knowledge:
‘Let it be earth. It becomes earth. He walks upon the water that does not break, just as...

“Just as people who naturally lack supernormal power walk upon solid ground that cannot be pierced, even so that possessor of supernormal power, having attained mastery over his mind, walks upon water that cannot be pierced, just as if on solid ground.
Not only does he walk; whatever posture he desires, that he performs. And not only this...

He turns even water into earth; likewise, regarding gems, gold, mountains, trees, and so forth, whatever he desires, having adverted to it in the manner already described, he resolves, and it becomes exactly as resolved.
To him alone that water becomes earth, while for other people it remains water;
and fish, turtles, water-crows, and the like, move about therein according to their pleasure. If...
Furthermore, when he wishes to turn that earth into other things for other people as well, it indeed becomes so; yet, once the limited period has elapsed, it becomes water again.
"He moves by means of a cross-legged posture" (pallaṅkena kamati) means he goes by means of a cross-legged posture. "A winged bird" (pakkhī sakuṇo) means a bird endowed with wings.

However, for one who wishes to do so, having entered the earth-kasiṇa attainment and emerged from it, if he wishes to go while sitting, he should delimit an area the size of a cross-legged seat, perform the preliminary work, and resolve it in the manner already described.
If he wishes to go while lying down, [he should delimit] an area the size of a bed; if he wishes to go on foot, [he should delimit] an area the size of a path.
Having thus delimited the place accordingly, one should resolve according to the method already described, saying, "Let there be earth.
Simultaneously with the resolution, it becomes earth itself. Here is the canonical text regarding this:
"He travels cross-legged even through the air, just like a winged bird. [This is] by means of the natural attainment of the earth-kasiṇa."
He becomes a possessor [of this power] and adverts to space. Having adverted to it, he resolves with knowledge: "Let there be earth. There is earth.
On that space in the sky, he walks, stands, sits, and lies down.
Just as ordinary people who lack supernormal powers walk, stand, sit, and lie down upon the earth, even so... [he does likewise].
“Thus, possessing supernormal power and having attained mastery over the mind, he walks back and forth in the sky, in the atmosphere...
[and so on] ...and even makes his bed there. A bhikkhu who wishes to travel through the air must also be a possessor of the divine eye. Why?

Because in between there may be mountains, trees, and so forth, produced by the seasonal elements, or nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others who might create obstacles out of envy; it is for the purpose of seeing these that one must have the divine eye.
Having seen them, what should be done? One should enter the foundational jhāna, emerge, perform the preliminary work by resolving, "Let there be space," and then fix the mind upon it.
However, the Elder said: "Friend, what is the purpose of entering the attainment?
Is his mind not already concentrated? Whatever place he resolves upon, saying 'let there be space,' that very place becomes space."
Although he spoke thus, nevertheless, one should proceed according to the method already described for the power of passing through walls.
Furthermore, for the purpose of descending into a secluded place, this person must possess the divine eye;
for if he were to descend into a non-secluded place—such as a bathing ford or at the village gate—he would become visible to the multitude. Therefore, by means of the divine eye...
"Having seen [the way], he avoids a place that is not suitable and descends into a place that is suitable.
(396) "He touches and strokes with his hand even these sun and moon, so powerful and so majestic"—
here, their great power consists in their movement forty-two thousand yojanas above [the earth].

His great power (*mahānubhāvatā*) is to be understood by his ability to produce light simultaneously over the three continents. Likewise, he possesses great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*) through his walking above [the earth] and his production of light.
"He touches" (*parāmasati*) means he grasps or touches in one place. "He strokes" (*parimajjati*) means he strokes all around, as if upon the surface of a mirror.
This psychic power (*iddhi*) of his, moreover, occurs solely by way of the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññāpādaka-jhāna*).
It succeeds; there is no fixed rule here regarding the kasiṇa attainments. For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:

"He even rubs these sun and moon... [omission] ...he touches. Here, that possessor of psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind adverts to the sun and moon, and having adverted, he resolves with knowledge:
"Let them be within the reach of my hand. They come to be within the reach of his hand. He...
Whether sitting or lying down, he touches, strokes, and rubs the moon and sun with his hand.

Just as ordinary people who lack supernormal power might touch, stroke, and rub some visible form when it is within reach of their hands, even so does that possessor of supernormal power... [and so on] ...rub it.”
If he wishes to go and touch it, he goes and touches it. But if, while sitting or lying right here, he wishes to touch it, he resolves:

"Let it come within arm's reach. By the power of that resolution, it comes like a palm fruit released from its stalk and stands within arm's reach, whereupon he touches it, or he extends his hand and touches it.

But when one increases [the body], what is it that increases: the appropriated (*upādiṇṇaka*) or the unappropriated (*anupādiṇṇaka*)? It is the unappropriated that increases by depending upon the appropriated.
Regarding this, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said: "But, friends, is the appropriated small or large?"
"It does not exist; for when a bhikkhu emerges through a palm-leaf opening or the like, his appropriated [body] is small.
When he makes his personal existence large, it becomes large, as in the case of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
—The Story of the Taming of the Nandopananda Nāga.
It is said that on one occasion, after hearing the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika invited him, saying, “Venerable sir,
please accept alms at our home tomorrow together with five hundred bhikkhus,” and then departed.
The Blessed One consented, and having spent the remainder of that day and the night, at the time of dawn he [surveyed] the ten-thousandfold world system.
He looked around. Then, a nāga king named Nandopananda came within the range of his knowledge.
The Blessed One thought, "This nāga king has come within the range of my knowledge; does he possess the necessary potential (upanissaya)?
As he reflected, he saw that "this one holds wrong views and lacks faith in the Three Jewels. [He considered: "Who then can lead him away from this wrong view?"
Reflecting on how he should investigate this, he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, having attended to his bodily needs, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, announce to five hundred bhikkhus that the Tathāgata is going on a journey to the deva realm. And on that day...
They prepared the banquet hall for Nanda and Upananda. There, the king sat upon a celestial jewel-couch while a divine white parasol was held over him;
surrounded by the three types of theatrical performances and the assembly of nāgas, he sat gazing at the varieties of food and drink served in celestial vessels.
Then the Blessed One acted so that the nāga king could see [him].
Having made that canopy, he set out toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with five hundred bhikkhus, traveling right over the very summit of it.
Now at that time, a wicked and pernicious view had arisen in the Nāga king Nandopananda:
"These shaven-headed recluses are indeed passing above our heads, over the realm of the Tāvatiṃsa devas."
“They enter the celestial abode and they depart from it; from this day forward, I will no longer allow them to go about scattering the dust of their feet upon my head.
Having risen and gone to the base of Sineru, he discarded that physical form, encircled Sineru seven times with his coils, spread his hood over it, and [proceeded] to the Tāvatiṃsa abode.
Having seized him with his hood turned downward, he made him disappear from sight.
Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, formerly, standing in this place, I saw Sineru, I saw the slopes of Sineru, I saw the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and I saw the Vejayanta palace."
“I see the banner atop the Vejayanta Palace. What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, that at present I no longer see Sineru... nor do I see the banner atop the Vejayanta Palace?
“Rāṭṭhapāla, this Nāga king named Nandopananda is angry with you; he has [submerged] Sineru seven times...”
“Having surrounded him with his coils and covered him above with his hood, he stands there having created darkness.
“I shall subdue him, Bhante,” [said Ānanda]. But the Blessed One did not grant permission. Then the Venerable Bhaddiya and the Venerable Rāhula—gradually, all the bhikkhus stood up.
But the Blessed One did not grant permission.
At the conclusion, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, "Venerable Sir, I shall subdue him.
"Subdue him, Moggallāna," the Blessed One granted permission. The Elder, casting off his own form, manifested the great appearance of a royal nāga;
he encircled Nandopananda fourteen times with his coils and placed his own hood upon the tip of the other's hood.
Setting him aside, he pressed him down together with Sineru. The Naga king emitted smoke.
The Elder also emitted smoke, saying, "Smoke exists not only in your body; it exists in mine as well.

The smoke of the Naga king did not afflict the Elder, but the smoke of the Elder did afflict the Naga king. Thereupon, the Naga king burst into flames. The Elder also [emitted flames], saying, "Not only yours..."
"There is fire in his body; there is fire in me too," [the Elder] thought, and he blazed up.
The power of the Nāga king did not afflict the Elder, but the Elder’s power did afflict the Nāga king. The Nāga king, thinking, "This man is oppressing me with Mount Sineru;
he is smoking and blazing," asked, "Sir, who are you? "I am Nanda, O King."
“Moggallāna. “Venerable sir, remain in your own state as a bhikkhu.
The Elder abandoned that form and entered through the opening of his right ear and emerged from the opening of his left ear;
