he entered through the opening of his left ear and emerged from the opening of his right ear; likewise through the opening of his right nostril...
Having entered, he emerged through the left nostril; having entered through the left nostril, he emerged through the right nostril.
Then the Naga king opened his mouth. The Elder entered through the mouth and walked back and forth within the belly from east to west.
The Blessed One said, "Moggallāna, pay attention; this Naga is possessed of great psychic power. The Elder—

“Venerable sir, my four bases for psychic power have been developed, cultivated, made the vehicle, made the foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken. Let alone Nandopananda, venerable sir;
I could tame even a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand royal nāgas like Nandopananda,” he said.
The Nāga king thought, "He was not seen while entering; now, at the time of his departure, I shall seize him between my fangs and crush him.
Having thought this, he said, "Come out, venerable sir; do not trouble me by pacing back and forth inside my belly.
The Elder came out and stood outside. The Nāga king recognized him, saying, "This is he!"
Seeing him, he did not release his breath. The Elder entered the fourth *jhāna*. Not even a single pore of his body could the wind move.

It is said that while the remaining monks might have been able to perform all the miracles from the beginning, having reached this point, they would not have been able to enter such a state with such rapid reflexes.
The Blessed One did not grant them permission to subdue the nāga king.
The nāga king thought, "I was unable to move even a single hair-pore of this ascetic with my nāga-wind; this ascetic possesses great psychic power.
The Elder, casting off his own form, manifested the shape of a garuḍa and [emitted] a garuḍa-wind.

As he proceeded, he followed the king of the nāgas. The king of the nāgas, abandoning that form and manifesting the appearance of a young brahmin, said, "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to you," and bowed at the elder’s feet.
The elder, having tamed the king of the nāgas and rendered him free from venom, said, "Nanda, the Teacher has arrived; come, let us go. Thus he subdued the king of the nāgas.
Having taken him, he went into the presence of the Blessed One. The Naga king, having paid homage to the Blessed One, said, "Venerable Sir, I go for refuge to you.
The Blessed One, saying, "May you be happy, O Naga king," proceeded to the residence of Anathapindika, surrounded by the community of monks.
Anāthapiṇḍika said, "Venerable sir, why have you arrived so late? [Moggallāna replied,] "A battle took place between Moggallāna and Nandopananda.
"Venerable sir, who won and who lost? "Moggallāna won; Nanda was defeated.
Anāthapiṇḍika said, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept from me a week’s stay, one after another."
Having said, "I shall provide food for seven days and perform honors for the Elder," he made great offerings for seven days to the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Thus, this was said with reference to that great physical form manifested on this occasion of subduing Nandopānanda: "When he assumes a great physical form..."

"It becomes great, like that of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Even when this was said, the bhikkhus replied, "Supported by what is grasped (*upādiṇṇaka*), only that which is not grasped (*anupādiṇṇaka*) increases. And this alone is the logical reasoning here.
Having done this, he does not merely touch the moon and sun; if he so desires, having made a footstool...
He places it at his feet; he makes it a seat and sits upon it; he makes it a bed and lies down upon it; he makes it a backrest and leans against it.
As it is with one, so it is with another. For even when many hundreds of thousands of monks do this, it succeeds for each and every one of them in exactly the same way.
Even the movement of the moon and sun, and their illumination, proceed in the very same manner.

It is so. For just as when thousands of bowls are filled with water, the disks of the moon are seen in every bowl, yet the movement and the illumination of the moon remain exactly as they are in their natural state—such is this miracle.
"As far as the Brahma-world" means taking even the Brahma-world as the limit. "He wields mastery with his body" means...
Therein, he exercises mastery over himself with his body as far as the Brahma-world. The meaning of this should be understood by following the text. Here is the text:

"He exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world. If that possessor of psychic power, having attained mastery over mind, desires to go to the Brahma-world, he resolves upon what is distant as being near, saying, 'Let it be near,' and it becomes near. Even if it is near..."
If he resolves, "Let it be far," it becomes far. Even if it is much, he resolves, "Let it be little," and it becomes little.
Even if it is little, he resolves, "Let it be much," and it becomes much.
With the divine eye, he sees the form of that Brahmā; with the divine ear-element, he hears the sound of that Brahmā.
He hears. With the knowledge of penetration of minds, he understands the mind of that Brahmā.

If that possessor of psychic power, having attained mastery over the mind, desires to go to the Brahma-world with a visible body, he directs his mind in accordance with the body and resolves his mind in accordance with the body;
having directed his mind in accordance with the body and resolved his mind in accordance with the body...
Having descended into the perception of lightness and the perception of ease, he goes to the Brahma-world with a visible body.
If that possessor of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind wishes to go to the Brahma-world with an invisible body, he transforms the body by means of the mind;
he resolves upon the body by means of the mind. Having transformed the body by means of the mind, by means of the mind...
Having resolved upon the body and entered into the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness, he goes to the Brahma-world with an invisible body.
There, in the presence of that Brahmā, he manifests a mind-made form, complete in all its limbs and parts, with no faculties lacking.
If that possessor of psychic power walks back and forth, the manifested form also walks there. If that possessor of psychic power...
He stands, sits, and lies down; the emanation also lies down there.
If that possessor of psychic power emits smoke, blazes up, preaches the Dhamma, asks a question, or answers a question when asked, the emanation also answers a question when asked there.
If that possessor of psychic power [interacts] with that Brahmā...
He stands together with him, converses, and engages in discussion;

even as a created being, he stands together with that Brahmā there, converses, and engages in discussion. For whatever that possessor of psychic power does, the created being does that very same thing.”

In this context, "he resolves that what is distant shall be near" means: having emerged from the foundational jhāna, he adverts to a distant world of the devas or the Brahmā-world, thinking, "Let it be near.
Having so adverted and performed the preliminary work, he enters the attainment once more and resolves with knowledge, "Let it be near";
thus it becomes near. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
In that regard, who took what was distant and made it near? The Blessed One.
For at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle, while departing for the world of the gods, the Blessed One brought Yugandhara and Sineru close together;
placing one foot upon the surface of the earth at Yugandhara, he placed the second upon the summit of Sineru. Who else did so? The Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

For the Elder, having finished his meal duties at Sāvatthī, condensed the thirty-yojana road to the city of Saṅkassa—by which a retinue of twelve yojanas had set out—and brought them there at that very moment.
Moreover, the Elder Cūḷasamudda did the same on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. It is said that during a time of famine, [people] approached the Elder...
Early in the morning, seven hundred bhikkhus arrived. The Elder, wondering, "Where will this great Saṅgha of bhikkhus go for alms?
and seeing that they would not find anyone throughout the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, perceived that they would find them on the opposite shore at Pāṭaliputta.
He had the bhikkhus take up their bowls and robes and said, "Come, friends, let us go for alms," and [he stepped] upon the earth.
Having condensed [the journey], he went to Pāṭaliputta. The monks asked, "Venerable sir, which city is this? "Pāṭaliputta, friends.
"Venerable sir, the place called Pāṭaliputta is far away. "Friends, those who are called 'senior elders' (mahallaka-thera) take even what is distant and make it near.
"Venerable sir, where is the great ocean? "Is it not, friends, right here in between?"
"Did you come after passing over one blue lotus? "Yes, venerable sir. "But the great ocean is vast," [the Elder said].
"Friend, those called 'senior elders' can make even something vast appear small.

And just as this [Elder] did, so too the Elder Tissa Datta, having bathed in the evening and put on his upper robe, when the thought arose, "I shall pay homage to the Great Bodhi Tree," made it appear close at hand.
But who made what was near far? The Blessed One. For the Blessed One made the interval between himself and Aṅgulimāla far, even though it was near.
And who made what was much little? The Elder Mahākassapa.
It is said that on a festival day in Rājagaha, five hundred young women, taking moon-cakes (*candapūva*), were going out for a festival celebration when they encountered the Blessed One.
Seeing him, they said nothing. But when they saw the Elder approaching from behind, thinking, "Our Elder is coming;
we shall give him some cakes," they all took their cakes and approached the Elder. The Elder drew out his bowl and made everything fit into it, filling it to the brim with a single bowlful.
The Blessed One sat down in front, waiting for the Elder. When the Elder had brought the food, he gave it to the Blessed One.
In the story of the merchant Illisa, however, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna performed a small amount of merit;

and in the story of Kākavaliya, the Blessed One did so. It is said that the Elder Mahākassapa, having spent seven days in meditative attainment, stood at the door of the house of a destitute man named Kākavaliya while providing for the poor. His wife [saw] the Elder...
Seeing this, he poured boiled rice with unsalted sour gruel into his own bowl. The Elder took it and placed it in the hands of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One made a resolution that it should suffice for the great community of monks. What was brought in a single bowl became enough for everyone.
And on the seventh day, Kākavaliya attained the status of a wealthy merchant.
And it is not only the transformation of a small amount into much;
for one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*), everything succeeds according to his wish—whether sweet becomes unsweet, or unsweet becomes sweet, and so forth.
For instance, when the Elder Mahā-Anula and many other monks, having gone for alms and received only dry rice, sat down on the bank of the Ganges and were about to eat it...
Having seen this, he resolved that the water of the Ganges was the cream of ghee and gave the signal to the novices.
They brought it in basins and gave it to the community of monks. Everyone ate with the sweet cream of ghee.
"With the divine eye" means: standing right here, by extending his vision, he sees the form of that Brahmā. Right here...
And standing there, he hears every sound that person speaks. He understands the mind.
"He transforms the mind according to the body" means he transforms the mind by means of the physical body (karaja-kāya). Taking the mind of the foundational jhāna, he applies it to the body.
He makes it conform to the body, moving slowly; for the movement of the body is indeed slow. [He develops] the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness.

"He descends" means that he descends into, enters, touches, and attains the perception of pleasure (*sukhasaññā*) and the perception of lightness (*lahusaññā*) that are co-nascent with the supernormal power-consciousness (*iddhicitta*) which has the foundation-jhāna as its object. The "perception of pleasure" is the perception associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*).
For equanimity is said to be "peaceful pleasure. And that very perception, by means of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and their opposites such as applied thought (*vitakka*), etc., [is purified].
And because of this liberation, it should also be understood as a "perception of lightness. For one who has entered that state, even the body born of karma becomes as light as a tuft of cotton.
With such a body—which is visible and as light as a tuft of cotton blown by the wind—he goes to the Brahma-world.
And while going thus, if he so desires, he creates a path in space by means of the earth-kasiṇa.
Having created [the body], he goes on foot. If he wishes, by means of the air-kasiṇa, he resolves upon the air and travels with the wind like a tuft of cotton-wool.
Moreover, the mere desire to go is the measure here.
For when there is the desire to go, one who has thus performed the resolution of mind travels as if flung by the force of that resolution, appearing like an arrow shot by an archer.
"He transforms the body by means of the mind" means that, having taken hold of the body, he places it upon the mind.
He makes it conform to the mind, moving swiftly; for the movement of the mind is indeed swift.

"He enters upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness" means that he enters upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness co-nascent with the supernormal power consciousness (iddhicitta) which has the material body as its object. The rest...
This should be understood in the manner already stated. However, this is merely the movement of consciousness.

When it was asked, "As he goes with an invisible body, does he go at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of that resolving-consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*), or at the moment of its presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*), or at the moment of its dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*)?", the Elder replied, "He goes during all three moments. But does he go by himself?
"He sends a created being" means he makes it according to his wish. But here, his own going is what is intended.
"Mind-made" (manomaya) means it is made by means of the resolve of the mind. "With unimpaired faculties" is said with reference to the shape of the eye, ear, and so forth;
however, there is no sensitivity (pasāda) in the created form. If the possessor of psychic power walks, [the created being follows].
The statement beginning with "Even the created [being] walks there" and so forth is said with reference to everything created by a disciple.
However, that which is created by a Buddha performs whatever the Blessed One does; furthermore, it may perform other things according to the Blessed One’s own wish.
And herein, when that possessor of psychic power, remaining right here, sees a form with the divine eye or hears a sound with the divine ear-element...
He hears the voice; he understands the mind by means of the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*); yet, to this extent, he does not exercise mastery over him with his body.

Even when, remaining right here, he stands together with that Brahmā, converses with him, and engages in discussion with him—to this extent as well, he does not exercise mastery over him with his body.
Furthermore, regarding his resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) such as "he resolves that what is distant becomes near," and so forth...

Even to this extent, he does not exercise mastery over the body. Even when he goes to the Brahma-world by means of a body that is either visible or invisible, even to this extent, he does not exercise mastery over the body.
But when he enters upon the procedure described in the manner beginning with "he creates a form in the presence of that Brahmā," it is to this extent that he exercises mastery over the body.
It is called "wielding mastery. The remainder here, however, is stated for the purpose of showing the preliminary stage for wielding mastery by means of the body;
this, first of all, is supernormal power as resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*). 398.
Now, this is the distinction between the supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbanā*) and that of the mind-made (*manomaya*): first, by one performing a transformation, [he thinks]: "So..."
Having abandoned his natural form, he displays the form of a youth, or displays the form of a nāga, or displays the form of a supaṇṇa, or displays the form of an asura,
or displays the form of Indra, or displays the form of a deva,
or displays the form of Brahmā, or displays the form of the ocean, or displays the form of a mountain, or displays the form of a lion.
"or shows the form of a tiger, or shows the form of a leopard, or shows an elephant,
or shows a horse, or shows a chariot, or shows a foot soldier, or shows various military arrays"—
when these forms of boys and so forth have been mentioned, whatever one desires must be resolved upon. By one who resolves:
And having emerged from the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) by means of any one object such as the earth-kasiṇa, one should advert to one’s own form as a youth.
Having so adverted, at the conclusion of the preliminary work (parikamma), one should enter again, emerge, and resolve: "May I become a youth of such-and-such a kind.
Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, one becomes a youth, just like Devadatta. This same method applies in all cases.
The passage beginning with "He even displays an elephant" is stated here by way of displaying elephants and so forth externally as well.
In that context, one should not resolve, "May I become an elephant," but rather resolve, "Let there be an elephant. This same method applies to horses and the rest as well.
This is the supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbanā-iddhi*).
399. However, one who wishes to create a mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) emerges from the foundational jhāna, adverts to his own body, and resolves according to the method already described:

"Let it become hollow. It becomes hollow. Then, having adverted to another body within it and performed the preliminary work, he resolves according to the method already described: "Let there be another body within this one. He [extracts that body] from the reed...
He draws it out like a reed from its sheath, a sword from its scabbard, or a snake from its slough. Therefore it is said:
"Here, a bhikkhu emanates from this body another body—material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, not lacking any faculties.
Just as a man might pull a reed from its sheath, and it would occur to him: 'This is the sheath; this is the reed.'"
"The muñja grass is one thing, the sheath is another; yet the sheath is drawn out from the muñja grass itself," and so forth.

In this context, these similes were spoken to show that just as the sheath and so on are similar to the muñja grass and so on, so too mind-made form (manomayarūpa) is exactly like the possessor of psychic power (iddhimat).
This is mind-made supernormal power (manomayā iddhi).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, called the Exposition of the Supernormal Powers, in the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of virtuous people.
13. Exposition of the Higher Knowledges:
Discussion of the Divine Ear Element. 400.
Now, the sequence for the exposition of the divine ear element has arrived. Therein, [this follows] after that and the other three higher knowledges.
The meaning of "with his mind thus concentrated" and so forth should be understood in the same manner already explained. However, we shall describe only the specific distinctions in each case.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the divine ear-element": here it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine [hearing].
For the hearing of devas, produced by well-performed kamma, is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth; and due to its freedom from such defilements, even at a great distance...

The divine ear-element is capable of receiving objects. And this ear-element of knowledge produced by the power of the bhikkhu’s development of energy is exactly like that; thus it is "divine" because it resembles the divine.
Furthermore, it is "divine" because it is obtained through the divine abiding and because it itself is supported by the divine abiding. In the sense of hearing...
And it is the "ear-element" (sotadhātu) in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (nijjīva). It is also called the "ear-element" because it performs the function of the ear-element.
By means of that divine ear-element—purified means completely cleansed and free from defilements; transcending the human means having gone beyond the sphere of human experience.
"By means of hearing sounds" means having transcended and passed beyond the human faculty of the fleshly ear, and remaining [with it].
"Hears both kinds of sounds" means he hears two kinds of sounds. Which two? Celestial and human; that is to say, the sounds of both gods and humans.
By this, the exhaustion of the specific categories should be understood. "Those far and near" refers to those...
It is said that he hears sounds far away—even those in other world-systems—as well as those nearby, including even the sounds of tiny creatures inhabiting his own body.
By this, it should be understood that there is a comprehensive inclusion of all sounds without exception.
But how is this [clairaudience] to be produced? That bhikkhu, having entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and having emerged from it...

With the mind of preparatory concentration (*parikamma-samādhi*), one should first direct attention to a coarse sound in the forest, such as the roar of lions and other wild animals, which is at a distance within the range of the natural ear.

Or, [one may attend to] the sound of a monastery bell, the sound of a drum, the sound of a conch, or the sound of the recitation of novices and young bhikkhus who are reciting with all their might, or the sound of those engaged in ordinary conversation, saying, "What, venerable sir? and so forth.
The sounds beginning with "What, friend? and so forth; the sound of birds; the sound of wind; the sound of footsteps; the hissing sound of boiling water;

the sound of palm leaves drying in the sun; and the sound of ants, termites, and so on—in this way, one should attend to all sounds from the coarsest upwards in their proper sequence, starting with subtle sounds. By means of that, [one perceives] the sign of sound among the sounds in the eastern direction.

One should attend to them. One should attend to the sign of sound in sounds from the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, the lower direction, the upper direction, the eastern intermediate direction, the western intermediate direction, the northern intermediate direction, and the southern intermediate direction.
One should attend to the sign of sound in both gross and subtle sounds. Even for one whose mind is ordinary, those sounds...
They become clear. However, they are exceedingly clear to the mind of concentration resulting from preliminary work (*parikamma-samādhi*).

As he thus attends to the sign of sound, thinking, "Now the divine ear-element will arise," mind-door adverting consciousness arises taking one of those sounds as its object. When that has ceased, four or five...

Or, they speed along with the impulsions (*javana*), the first three or four of which are called the preliminary (*parikamma*), access (*upacāra*), conformity (*anuloma*), and change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) consciousnesses belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while the fourth or fifth is the absorption consciousness (*appanā-citta*) of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) belonging to the fourth jhāna.
Therein, the knowledge that arises together with that absorption consciousness should be understood as the divine ear element (*dibba-sotadhātu*). From that—
However, he has fallen into that stream. While making that [stream] firm, he should expand it by delimiting a space of only one finger's breadth, thinking, "I hear a sound within this interval.

Thereafter, he should expand it by repeatedly delimiting it according to two fingers, four fingers, eight fingers, a span, a ratana, the interior of a room, a front chamber, a palace, a courtyard, a monastery, a grazing ground, a village, a district, and so forth, up to the world-system (cakkavāḷa) or even beyond that.
Thus, having attained direct knowledge (abhiññā), even when a sound enters the space touched by the object of the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna),

he hears it by means of the knowledge of direct knowledge (abhiññāñāṇa) without again entering that foundational jhāna. And while hearing in this way, even if there were a single tumultuous uproar from the sounds of conchs,
kettledrums, and small drums reaching as far as the Brahma-world, should he desire to discern each [sound] individually—
When it exists, one is indeed able to discern: "This is the sound of a conch," and "This is the sound of a drum.
The discussion on the divine ear-element is finished.
Now follows the discussion on the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*).
401. Regarding the discourse on the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*): here, "penetrating" (*pariya*) means that which goes around; the sense is that it delimits.
"Penetration of mind" (*cetopariya*) is the penetration of the mind. That which is both the penetration of mind and knowledge is "knowledge of penetrating others' minds.
This means "for the purpose of that. "Of other beings" (*parasattānaṃ*) means of all beings excluding oneself. "Of other persons" (*parapuggalānaṃ*)—this too [is the same].

This has the same meaning [as the previous phrase]. However, a diversity of phrasing (*byañjana-nānatta*) was employed due to the nature of those to be trained (*veneyya*) and the elegance of the teaching (*desanā-vilāsa*).

"With his own mind, he understands their minds" means: with his own consciousness (*citta*), he understands their consciousness. "He understands thoroughly" (*paricca pajānāti*) means: having delimited them, he knows them in their various modes according to whether they possess lust (*sarāga*) and so forth.
But how is this knowledge to be developed? For it is accomplished by means of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), which serves as its preliminary exercise (*parikamma*).

Therefore, that bhikkhu, having increased the light and seen with the divine eye the color of the blood existing in dependence upon the heart-matter (*hadayarūpa*) of another, should search for the mind. For when there is a mind of joy (*somanassacitta*), [the blood appears red].
When a mind of joy prevails, it is like a ripe *nigrodha* fruit;
when a mind of grief prevails, it is like a black *jambu* fruit; when a mind of equanimity prevails, it is like clear sesame oil.
Therefore, by means of that [knowledge], he discerns: "This material form is originated by the faculty of joy; this is originated by the faculty of grief..."

"This is originated from the equanimity faculty. Having thus seen the blood-colored heart of another and sought after their mind, one must make the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa) firm.
For when that [knowledge] has become firm, by gradually transferring from mind to mind, one understands all sense-sphere minds as well as fine-material and immaterial sphere minds.

Even without seeing the material form of the heart. And this is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “When one desiring to know another’s mind in the immaterial realm (*ārūpa*) asks, ‘Whose heart-form does he see?
Whose alteration of the faculties does he observe?’—it is no one’s at all. This is the domain of one possessing supernormal power (*iddhimant*):
namely, that by attending to a mind anywhere, he knows the mind in its sixteenfold division. For one who has not yet formed a mental resolution...”
"But this discussion is by way of [the presence of] lust.
Furthermore, in such passages as "a mind with lust" (*sarāgaṃ cittaṃ*), the eightfold consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood as "a mind with lust.
The remaining wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is "free from lust" (*vītarāga*). The two types of unhappy consciousness...
As for the two types of consciousness—doubt and restlessness—these four states of mind do not fall within this dyad.
However, some elders include them as well. The two kinds of unhappy consciousness are called "consciousness with hatred.
All wholesome and indeterminate consciousness belonging to the four planes is "without hatred. The remaining ten unwholesome types of consciousness [are with hatred].
These do not fall within this dyad. However, some elders include them as well.

Regarding the terms "with delusion" (*samoha*) and "free from delusion" (*vītamoha*): here, according to the method of individual classification (*pāṭipuggalika-naya*), only the two types of consciousness accompanied by doubt and restlessness are "with delusion.
Yet, because delusion is possible in all unwholesome states, all twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousness are also "with delusion."
It should be understood as "mind. The remainder is free from delusion (*vītamoha*). That which is accompanied by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) is contracted (*saṃkhitta*).

That which is accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) is distracted (*vikkhitta*). That which belongs to the fine-material and immaterial spheres is exalted (*mahaggata*). The remainder is unexalted (*amahaggata*). All that pertains to the three planes is surpassable (*sauttara*).

That which is supramundane (*lokuttara*) is unsurpassable (*anuttara*). That which has attained access (*upacāra*) and that which has attained absorption (*appanā*) is concentrated (*samāhita*). That which has not attained either is unconcentrated.

It is unconcentrated. It is liberated when it has attained liberation by way of its own factor (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), subsiding (*paṭipassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*). This fivefold liberation, when not yet attained, should be understood as "unliberated.
Thus, a monk who possesses the knowledge of penetration of others' minds knows this mind in all its aspects—whether it is a mind with lust... [and so on]... or an unliberated mind as "unliberated."
"He understands the mind.
The discussion on the knowledge of penetration of others' minds is finished.
Now begins the discussion on the knowledge of recollection of past lives.

402. Regarding the discourse on the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*): "For the sake of the knowledge of recollecting past lives" means for the purpose of that knowledge which consists in the recollection of past lives.
"Past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) refers to the aggregates (*khandha*) in which one dwelt in previous, past births. "Dwelt" (*nivuttha*) means having resided in, having experienced;
having arisen and ceased within one's own continuum (*santāna*). Alternatively, it refers to the phenomena (*dhamma*) in which one dwelt. "Dwelt" (*nivuttha*) [is explained as follows]:...

Those [beings] who have dwelt in a particular sphere of experience and have been known and delimited by one's own consciousness—or even those known by the consciousness of others, as in the recollection of past lives (*chinnavaṭumaka-anussaraṇa*) and so forth—these are obtainable only for Buddhas.

"Recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*) refers to that mindfulness (*sati*) by which one recollects past lives; "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge associated with that mindfulness.

Thus, it is said: "for the sake of this knowledge of recollection of past lives" means for the purpose of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, for the attainment and acquisition of this knowledge.
"Of many kinds" (*anekavihitam*) means manifold, or that which has proceeded in various ways; the meaning is "described."
"Past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) refers to the continuum of existence that has dwelt here and there, beginning from the immediately preceding past existence.

"Recalls" (*anussarati*) means that one remembers by following along step by step, either according to the succession of the aggregates (*khandha*) or according to the process of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*).
Indeed, six types of persons recall this past life: followers of other sects (*titthiya*), ordinary disciples (*pakatisāvaka*), great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*), and chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*).
[The categories are] Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas.
In that regard, the followers of other sects (titthiyā) recollect only forty eons, and not beyond that. Why?
Because their wisdom is weak. For, due to their lack of discernment regarding name-and-form (nāmarūpa), their wisdom is weak. Ordinary disciples [recollect] even a hundred eons...
They indeed recollect even a thousand eons because their wisdom is powerful. The eighty great disciples recollect one hundred thousand eons.
The two chief disciples recollect one incalculable and one hundred thousand eons. Private Buddhas recollect two incalculables and one hundred thousand eons;
such is the extent of their resolve. But for the Buddhas, there is no limit at all.
The sectarians (titthiyā) remember only the succession of the aggregates; they are unable to remember by way of death and rebirth-linking apart from that succession.
For them, there is no reaching of a desired destination as there is for those with sight.
Just as the blind go without ever letting go of their staff, so too do they remember without ever letting go of the succession of the aggregates.
Ordinary disciples recollect both by way of the succession of aggregates and by way of death and rebirth-linking.
The same is true for the eighty great disciples. However, for the two chief disciples, there is no requirement to follow the succession of aggregates;
having seen the death of one individual existence, they see its rebirth-linking, and then, having seen the death of another, they see its rebirth-linking.
In this way, those who pass on do so by means of death and rebirth-linking alone; the same applies to Paccekabuddhas.
However, for Buddhas, there is neither the function of a succession of aggregates nor the function of passing on by means of death and rebirth-linking.
For them, in many millions of eons—whether below or above—whatever place they desire, that [place]...

That becomes quite clear. Therefore, even though there are many millions of eons, they condense them like a string of elisions (*peyyāla*) and, entering exactly wherever they wish, they proceed by way of a "lion's leap" (*sīhokkanta*).
And for those proceeding in this manner, their knowledge is like that of an archer such as Sarabhaṅga, who has mastered the practice of shooting at a moving target.

Just as an arrow shot [at a target], without striking against trees, creepers, or other obstacles along the way, falls upon the target itself—neither sticking nor veering off—so too, one does not stick or veer off amidst various intervening births; and without sticking or veering off, it reaches exactly the place desired.
Furthermore, among those who recollect past lives, the insight into past lives of the non-Buddhist sectarians (tīrthikas) is like the light of a glowworm.
Having been offered, it appears: to ordinary disciples, like the light of a lamp; to great disciples, like the light of a torch;
to chief disciples, like the light of the medicinal star (the morning star); to paccekabuddhas, like the light of the moon;
and to Buddhas, it appears like the orb of the autumn sun adorned with a thousand rays.
The recollection of past lives by the followers of other sects is like the groping of blind men with the tips of their staffs. That of ordinary disciples is like walking upon a bridge made of sticks.
That of the great disciples is like walking upon a bridge made of logs. That of the chief disciples is like walking upon a bridge made of carts.
That of the paccekabuddhas is like traveling on a great path for logs. And that of the Buddhas is like traveling on a great path for carts.

In this context, however, what is intended is the recollection of past lives by the disciples. Therefore it was said: “He recollects means that he remembers by following along the succession of aggregates or by following along the succession of death and rebirth.

403. Thus, a beginner monk who wishes to recollect in this way, having returned from his almsround after the meal, should go into seclusion alone and, entering the four jhānas in sequence, [emerge] from the fourth jhāna which serves as the basis for direct knowledge.
Having arisen, one should first bring to mind the very last sitting. Then, the arranging of seats, the entering of the lodging,
the putting away of the bowl and robes, the time for eating, the time of returning from the village, the time of wandering for alms in the village,
the time of entering the village for alms, the time of departing from the monastery, and the time of paying homage at the shrine terrace and the Bodhi terrace.
The time for washing the bowl, the time for receiving the bowl, the duties performed from the receiving of the bowl up to the rinsing of the mouth,
the duties performed at dawn, the duties performed during the middle watch, and the duties performed during the first watch— in this way,
one should bring to mind all the duties performed throughout the entire day and night in reverse order. However, this much is evident even to the ordinary mind.
It becomes clear. However, the mind of preliminary concentration (*parikamma-samādhi*) is already quite evident.
But if anything here remains unclear, one should again enter the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna*), emerge, and reflect upon it.
By this much, it becomes as clear as a lamp that has been lit. In this same reverse order, on the second day, and likewise on the third, fourth, and fifth days.
One should bring to mind what was done on the tenth day, on the half-month, on the month, and even as far back as a year.

By this same method, as one brings to mind [the past] for ten years, twenty years, and so on, until reaching one's own rebirth-linking in this present existence, one must bring to mind the name-and-form that occurred at the moment of death in the previous existence. For a wise bhikkhu is indeed capable of this.
At the very first moment, having displaced the rebirth-linking consciousness, one is able to take the mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) at the moment of death as the object.

However, because the mind-and-matter of the previous existence has ceased without remainder and another has arisen, that place becomes as dense and pitch-black as a deep darkness, difficult to see for one of dull wisdom. Therefore, he too [thinks]: "I am not able to [see] the rebirth-linking..."
One must not abandon the task with the thought, "I shall open [the door] and take as my object the mind-and-matter that occurred at the moment of death.
Rather, one should enter that same foundational jhāna again and again; and emerging from it time and again, one should advert to that state.
For one acting in this way is just like a strong man who, while cutting down a great tree for the sake of the rafters of a peaked house,
finds that the blade of his axe has become blunted by merely cutting the branches and foliage; yet, although unable to cut the great tree with the blunt axe,
he does not abandon his task, but goes to a smithy, has a sharp axe made, and returns again.
He would cut it down; and when it had grown again, he would do the same and cut it down once more.
Cutting it in this way, because there is nothing further to be cut once it has been cut, and because he continues to cut what remains uncut, he would before long topple the great tree.
In the very same way, having emerged from the foundational jhāna, instead of reviewing what was previously adverted to, he [directs his mind] back to the rebirth-linking itself.
As he adverts, before long, having discarded the rebirth-linking [consciousness], he would take as his object the mind-and-matter that occurred at the moment of death.
This point may also be illustrated by the example of the wood-gatherers, the grass-cutters, the hair-cutters, and so forth.
In this context, the knowledge that occurs taking as its object everything from the final sitting down until the moment of rebirth-linking—
What is called "knowledge of past lives" does not yet exist; rather, it is what is called "knowledge of preparatory concentration.
Some say it is "knowledge of the past," but that is not tenable when referring to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

However, when for that bhikkhu, having bypassed the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), mind-door adverting arises taking as its object the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that occurred at the moment of death (*cutikkhaṇa*), [then that knowledge arises].
When that [preliminary consciousness] has ceased, four or five impulsion moments (javana) arise, taking that same object. The rest is exactly as described previously:

the preceding ones, termed "preparation" (parikamma) and so forth, belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); the final one is the absorption consciousness (appanā-citta) of the fourth jhāna belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
At that time, the knowledge that arises together with that consciousness is as follows:
This is called the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*). By means of that knowledge, through mindfulness associated with it, one recollects manifold past lives.
That is to say: one birth, two births... [and so on] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, one recollects manifold past lives.

404. Therein, “even a single birth” (*ekampi jātiṃ*) refers to a single continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) included within one existence (*ekabhava*), beginning with rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and ending with death (*cuti*).
This same method applies to “two births” (*dvepi jātiyo*) and so forth.

However, in expressions such as “many aeons of dissolution” (*anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe*), it should be understood that an aeon during which [the world] is contracting is an “aeon of dissolution” (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*), while one during which it is expanding is an “aeon of evolution” (*vivaṭṭakappa*). Therein, by means of dissolution...
The period of dissolution and its duration are included because they are the root of it. And by means of evolution, the period of evolution and its duration are included;
for when this is so, those which were stated as, "Bhikkhus, there are these four incalculables of an eon. Which four?
The period of dissolution, the duration of dissolution, the period of evolution, and the duration of evolution"—these are fully encompassed.

In this regard, there are three kinds of destruction: destruction by water, destruction by fire, and destruction by wind. There are three limits of destruction: the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala realms.
When the eon is destroyed by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by flames.
When it is destroyed by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it is destroyed by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm...
It is destroyed by wind. In detail, however, even at all times one Buddha-field perishes.
There are three kinds of Buddha-fields: the field of birth (*jātikhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakhetta*).
Among these, the field of birth extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). This is [the extent] during the Tathāgata’s taking of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth.

It vibrates. The field of its command extends as far as a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), where the efficacy of these protective discourses (*paritta*)—namely, the *Ratana-sutta*, the *Khandha-paritta*, the *Dhajagga-paritta*, the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta*, and the *Moraparitta*—prevails.
The field of its range is infinite and immeasurable; that which is called "or as far as one might wish" refers to where [its power extends].
Whatever the Tathāgata desires, that he knows. Thus, among these three Buddha-fields, one—the field of authority—is destroyed.
When that is destroyed, the field of birth is also necessarily destroyed.
It is destroyed all at once, and it re-forms all at once. In this way, its destruction and its re-formation are to be understood.

405. For at the time when a world-age (*kappa*) is destroyed by fire, first of all a great cloud that destroys the world-age arises and pours down a single great rain over a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). People, joyful and delighted, bring out all their seeds and sow them.
But when the crops have grown only as far as they are trampled by cattle, [the wind] shrieks like a donkey and does not let fall even a single drop.
When it does not rain, then the rain is truly cut off, time after time. It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said:
"There comes a time, monks, when for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, the rain does not fall.
Beings who subsist on rain, having passed away...
They are reborn in the Brahma-world, as are the deities who subsist on flowers and fruits.

Thus, when a long period of time has passed, the water in various places becomes exhausted; then, in due course, even the fish and turtles die and are reborn in the Brahma-world, as do the beings in the hells.
Regarding this, some say that the hell-beings perish upon the appearance of the seventh sun.
Without jhāna there is no rebirth in the Brahma-world. As for some among these who were oppressed by famine and others who were incapable of attaining jhāna, how do they attain rebirth there?
It is by means of the jhāna obtained in the world of the devas.
For at that time, when it is known that "after the passing of one hundred thousand years, the arising of a new aeon will occur," the sense-sphere devas known as Lokabyūhas [arise].

With their veins showing, their hair disheveled, their faces weeping, wiping away tears with their hands, dressed in red garments and wearing extremely hideous attire, they wandered along the public highways proclaiming thus:
"O noble sirs, after the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, the end of the eon will occur;
this world will be destroyed, and even the great ocean will dry up. And this...
"The great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn up and perish. There will be a dissolution of the world as far as the Brahma-world.
Friends, cultivate loving-kindness; friends, cultivate compassion, gladness, and equanimity.
Serve your mother; serve your father; be respectful toward the elders of the family."
Having heard their words, most humans and earth-deities become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);
becoming soft-hearted toward one another, they perform meritorious deeds such as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and are reborn in the world of the devas.

There, having partaken of divine ambrosial food and performed preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the air-kasiṇa, they attain meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Others, however, [attain it] through karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya*).
They are reborn in the deva world through kamma. Indeed, there is no being wandering in saṃsāra who is devoid of kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
They too attain jhāna there in that very same way. Thus, by virtue of the jhāna attained in the deva world, they all are reborn in the Brahma world.
But after the cessation of the rains, following the passage of a long period of time, a second sun appears.
And this was said by the Blessed One: "There comes a time, monks... [and so on], the full account of the seven suns should be recited here.
And when that [second sun] has appeared, no distinction between night and day is discerned; there is only one sun.
One rises and one goes to its setting. The world becomes like a place where the sun’s heat is uninterrupted.
And whereas in the ordinary sun there is a son of the gods named Sūriyadevaputta, such a being does not exist in the sun that destroys an eon.
While the ordinary sun is in operation, clouds and columns of smoke move through the sky; but while the eon-destroying sun is in operation, it is free from smoke and clouds.
The sky becomes as stainless as the surface of a mirror. With the exception of the five great rivers, the water in all other small streams and such dries up.
After a long period has passed from that, a third sun appears; through its appearance, even the great rivers dry up.
After a long period has passed from that, a fourth sun appears; through its appearance, [the waters] in the Himavat...
The seven great lakes that are the sources of the great rivers—namely, Sīhapapāta, Haṃsapātana, Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Rathakāradaha, Anotattadaha, Chaddantadaha, and Kuṇāladaha—dry up.
After the passing of a long period from that time as well, a fifth sun appears. With its appearance, gradually not even enough water to fill the tip of a finger joint remains in the great ocean.
After that, with the passing of a long period of time, a sixth sun appears.

With its appearance, the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) becomes a single mass of smoke, its moisture consumed by the smoke; as it is here, so it is with hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
After that, with the passing of a further long period of time, a seventh sun appears. With its appearance, the entire world-system...
There is a single mass of flame together with hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

Even the peaks of Mount Sineru, distinguished by their hundreds of *yojana* heights and so forth, crumble and vanish right there in space. That mass of fire, having arisen, seizes the realm of the Four Great Kings (*Cātumahārājika*).
There, having incinerated the golden palaces, the jewel palaces, and the gem-studded palaces, it seizes the abode of the Thirty-three (*Tāvatiṃsa*). By this very same [process]...
By means of skillful method, it reaches as far as the plane of the first *jhāna*. Having consumed the three [lower] Brahmā-worlds there, it stands reaching up to the Ābhassara realm.
As long as even the slightest trace of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) remains, it does not go out.
However, with the total exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena, it goes out like the flame of a fire that has consumed ghee and oil, leaving not even soot behind. By way of the space below—
Above, there was a single vast expanse of darkness.
Then, after the passing of a long period of time, a great cloud arose and first rained down very fine, delicate drops.
Gradually, raining with torrents as large as lotus stalks, bamboo poles, pestles, palm trunks, tree trunks, and so forth, it poured down.
Having filled every place burnt by the fire throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), that water vanishes.
Then, winds arising from below and from the sides condense that water into a solid mass, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf.
If it is asked how they condense such a vast mass of water into a solid mass, it is because of the provision of openings (*vivara*). For in that [process], within that...
It makes way for that [water]. As it is thus compressed by the wind, condensed, and whirled about, it gradually sinks downward.

As each layer of water has sunk, the Brahma-worlds appear in the place of the Brahma-world, and the worlds of the four sense-sphere devas appear above in the place of the four sense-sphere deva-worlds.
But when it has descended to the previous earth-level, powerful winds arise.
These confine it, making it breathless like water standing in a covered water-vessel. As the sweet water is being exhausted, it brings forth a layer of flavor-earth above it;
this is endowed with color, as well as with fragrance and taste, like a crust on top of waterless thickened milk-rice.

And at that time, the beings who had been reborn earlier in the Ābhassara Brahma-world, having passed away from there due to the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit, were reborn here. They possessed their own radiance and moved through the air.
Having tasted that earth of flavor according to the method described in the Aggañña Sutta, they became overcome by craving and began to attempt to eat it by making balls of it.
Then their own radiance disappears and darkness arises. Seeing the darkness, they are afraid.
Then, to dispel their fear and inspire courage in them, the solar disk—five hundred yojanas in full extent—appears.
Seeing it, they become joyful and delighted, thinking, "We have regained light," and [they say], "To us who were afraid..."
Having dispelled their fear and generated courage, he arose; therefore, they gave him the name "Sūriya" (the Sun), saying, "Let there be a sun.
Then, when the sun had made light during the day and set, they became afraid again, thinking, "Even that light we obtained has vanished.
It occurred to them, "It would be well indeed if we could obtain some other light."
As if knowing their thoughts, the lunar disc appears at a distance of forty-nine yojanas.
Seeing it, they become even more exceedingly joyful and satisfied, and thinking, "He has arisen as if knowing our desire;
therefore, let him be called 'Canda' (the Delighter)," they give him the name Canda. Thus, when the moon and sun had appeared, the constellations [also appeared].
The forms of stars appear.
From that time on, nights and days become discernible, and gradually months, fortnights, seasons, and years follow.
However, on the very day the moon and sun appear, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavanta mountains also appear. And these—
They appear simultaneously, on the full-moon day of the month of Phagguna itself. How so?

Just as when rice mixed with *kaṅgu* grain is being cooked, bubbles arise all at once—some places becoming high and prominent, some low-lying, and some level—even so, in the places where there were high elevations, mountains arose; and in the places that were low-lying...
The oceans and the islands in places of equal depth.
Then, as those beings were consuming the savory earth (*rasapathavī*), gradually some became beautiful and others became ugly.
Thereupon, the beautiful ones began to despise the ugly ones. Due to that pride (*atimāna*), even that [savor]...
The savory earth disappears. A crust of earth appears. Then, by that same process, that too disappears.
A creeping vine appears. By that same process, that too disappears.
Unplowed rice appears—without husks, without powder, pure, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains.
Then their vessels appear. They place the rice in the vessel and set it upon a stone slab;
spontaneously, a crest of flame arises and cooks it. It becomes boiled rice resembling the jasmine flower, and there is no need for it to be accompanied by soup or curry.
Whatever flavor they desire to eat, [that very flavor it possesses].
It becomes like that very essence for them. As they consume that coarse food, from that time forward urine and feces arise.
Then, for the purpose of their discharge, orifices break open; the male faculty appears in the male, and the female faculty appears in the female.
There, indeed, the woman excessively gazes upon the man, and the man excessively gazes upon the woman.
Due to that excessive gazing, a fever of sensual desire arises in them. From that, they engage in sexual intercourse.
Being censured and harassed by the wise on account of engaging in that unrighteous practice, they [abandon] that unrighteous practice.
For the sake of concealment, they built houses. While dwelling in those houses, by following the example of a certain indolent being, they gradually began to store up food.
From that time on, even the husk and the bran enveloped the grain, and the ground where it had been harvested no longer grew it again.
Having gathered together, they lamented: "Alas, friends, evil things have appeared among beings! For formerly we were mind-made.
This should be expanded upon according to the method stated in the *Aggañña Sutta*. Then they established boundaries.
Afterward, a certain being took another's portion without it being given. Having rebuked him twice, [they continued...]
On the third occasion, they struck one another with hands, clods of earth, and sticks.
When these instances of taking what was not given, censuring, speaking falsehood, and inflicting punishment had arisen, they gathered together and reflected:
"What if we were to appoint one being who would, on our behalf, censure those who deserve censure, reprove those who deserve reproach, and banish those who deserve banishment? We..."
“We shall provide him with a portion of the rice.
When the beings had thus reached a consensus, during this very eon, at that time, among those beings, this very Blessed One— while still a bodhisatta—
was the most handsome, the most beautiful, the most influential, and the most endowed with wisdom.
He was capable of exercising restraint and encouragement. They approached him, made their request, and formally elected him.

Because he was elected by that great multitude, he was known as Mahāsammata (“Greatly Elected”); because he was the lord of fields, he was known as Khattiya (“Field-Lord”); and because he delighted others through righteousness and equity, he was known as Rāja (“King”).
Thus he became renowned by these three names. For whatever is a source of wonder in the world, it is the Bodhisatta alone who [possesses it].
In that regard, beginning with the "First Man" (Ādipuruṣa) as the Bodhisatta, once the circle of Kṣatriyas was established,
the other castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth were gradually established in turn.
Therein, from the great cloud that destroys the eon until the final cutting off of the flame, this is called one incalculable aeon of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa).

From the cessation of the fire that destroys the eon until the great rain-cloud of prosperity that fills a hundred thousand million world-systems—this is called the second incalculable aeon, the period of subsistence during the contraction.
From the great rain-cloud of prosperity until the manifestation of the moon and sun—this is called the third incalculable aeon, the period of expansion.
From the manifestation of the moon and sun until the great rain-cloud that once again destroys the eon—this is the fourth incalculable aeon.
He is called "one who stands for the turning away" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). These four incalculables constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*).
Thus, first of all, the destruction by fire and the re-establishment [of the world] are to be understood.
407. But at the time when the aeon is destroyed by water, from the very beginning a great cloud that destroys the aeon arises.
This should be expanded upon according to the method already stated. However, this is the distinction:
whereas there [in the previous case] was a second sun, here a great cloud of caustic water arises to destroy the aeon.

Starting by raining very fine drops, it gradually rains with great torrents, filling hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). Wherever it is touched by the caustic water, [it is destroyed].
The earth, mountains, and so forth dissolve; the water is held on all sides by the winds. The water takes up everything from the earth up to the plane of the second jhāna.
Having caused even the three Brahmā-worlds there to dissolve, it remains striking against the Subhakiṇha realm.
It does not subside as long as there exists even a minute atom of anything belonging to the conditioned (*saṅkhāra*). However, that which has followed into the water...
Having overcome all conditioned formations, it is suddenly pacified and passes away.
"The upper space becomes one with the lower space, and there is a great darkness"—all this is as previously described.
However, here the world reappears beginning with the Ābhassara Brahma-world. Beings pass away from the Subhakiṇha realm and are reborn in the stations of the Ābhassaras and so forth.
In this context, from the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the water that destroys the aeon, this constitutes one incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeyya*).
From the cessation of the water until the great cloud of prosperity (*sampatti-mahāmegha*), this is the second incalculable period. From the great cloud of prosperity...
[and so on] ...these four incalculable periods constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*). In this way, both the destruction by water and the re-establishment [of the world] are to be understood.

408. At the time when the aeon is destroyed by wind, it should be explained in detail according to the method previously stated, beginning with: "First of all, a great cloud that destroys the aeon arises. However, this is the distinction:
whereas in that case there is a second sun, here a wind arises for the purpose of destroying the aeon. It first stirs up coarse dust; then—
Fine dust, fine sand, coarse sand, gravel, stones, and so forth— even up to rocks the size of a gabled house and great trees standing on uneven ground—
he causes to rise up from the earth into the sky, and they do not fall back again;
right there they become pulverized and vanish into non-existence.
Then, in due course, a wind arises from beneath the great earth, overturns the earth, turns it upside down, and hurls it into the sky.

Portions of the earth measuring a hundred yojanas, as well as those measuring two, three, four, or five hundred yojanas, break apart and, cast by the force of the wind, are reduced to fine dust in the very sky and pass into non-existence. Even the Cakkavāḷa mountain...
The wind even lifts up Mount Sineru and hurls it into the sky. Striking one another, they are reduced to powder and destroyed.

By this very same method, destroying the terrestrial celestial mansions (*bhūmaṭṭhaka-vimāna*) and the aerial celestial mansions (*ākāsaṭṭhaka-vimāna*), and having destroyed the six realms of the sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva-loka*), it destroys hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). Therein—
The world-systems collide with world-systems, the Himavat mountains with Himavat mountains, and Mount Sinerus with Mount Sinerus;
having met one another, they are ground to powder and destroyed. The wind seizes everything from the earth up to the plane of the third jhāna.
Having destroyed even the three Brahmā worlds therein, it stands striking against the Vehapphala realm. Thus, all conditioned phenomena pass away.
Having destroyed it, he himself perishes. Together with the lower space, the upper space becomes one vast darkness;
all else is as previously described. However, here the world manifests beginning from the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world.
After falling away from the Vehapphala realm, beings are reborn in the abodes of the Subhakiṇha and other such places.
In this context, from the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the wind that destroys the aeon, this constitutes one incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeyya*).
From the cessation of the wind until the great cloud of prosperity, this is the second incalculable period...
[and so on] ...These four incalculable periods constitute one great aeon (*mahākappa*). Thus should the destruction by wind and the re-establishment [of the world] be understood.
409. For what reason does the world thus perish? It is because of the root of unwholesomeness. Indeed, when the roots of unwholesomeness have become predominant, the world perishes in this way.
Furthermore, when passion (*rāga*) is more predominant, it perishes by fire; when hatred (*dosa*) is more predominant, it perishes by water.
Some, however, say that when hatred is more predominant, it perishes by fire, and when passion is more predominant, it perishes by water.
They say: when delusion (*moha*) is more predominant, it is destroyed by wind. Even while being destroyed in this manner, it is destroyed by fire for seven consecutive eons;
on the eighth eon, it is destroyed by water. Again, for seven eons it is destroyed by fire; on the eighth eon, it is destroyed by water.
Thus, being destroyed on every eighth eon, after having been destroyed by water seven times, again for seven eons—
It is destroyed by fire. At this point, sixty-three eons have passed. During this interval, even when the occasion for destruction by water arrives, it is warded off;
then, having gained its opportunity, the wind destroys the world, disintegrating the Subhakiṇha realm where the lifespan is a full sixty-four eons. 410.
Furthermore, a monk who recollects past lives and remembers eons [recollects] many [lives] within these eons.
He recollects many aeons of world-dissolution, many aeons of world-evolution, and many aeons of both world-dissolution and evolution. How?
By way of the method beginning with, "I existed there," and so forth.

In that context, "I existed there" means: in such-and-such an aeon of world-dissolution, I existed in such-and-such a state of being, or in such-and-such a mode of birth, or in such-and-such a destination.
"I existed in a station of consciousness, or in an abode of beings, or in a class of beings. "Of such a name" means Tissa or Phussa.
"Of such a clan" means Kaccāna or Kassapa. This is stated by way of his recollection of his own name and clan in his past existence.
Furthermore, if at that time he [recalls] his own excellence of physical appearance, or whether his livelihood was coarse or refined—
If one wishes to recollect the abundance of pleasure and pain, or the state of being short-lived or long-lived, one recollects that as well.
Therefore he said: "Of such a complexion... [and so on] ...of such a limit to his lifespan.
Therein, "of such a complexion" means fair or dark. "Of such food" means one whose food was boiled rice with meat, or one who subsisted on wild fruits.

Or: "Experiencing pleasure and pain in this way" means experiencing physical and mental pleasures and pains of various kinds, such as those with and without worldly objects (*sāmisa-nirāmisa*), and so forth.
"Having such a limit to one's lifespan" means having a lifespan limited to one hundred years, or having a lifespan limited to eighty-four hundred thousand eons (*kappa*).
"Passing away from there, I arose elsewhere" refers to myself.
Then, having passed away from such-and-such a birth, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings,
I was reborn again in such-and-such a birth, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings.
There too, indeed, in that birth, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings...
Or again, "I existed. "With such a name," and so forth, is exactly as previously described.

Furthermore, because "I was there" is the recollection of one ascending step by step as far as desired, whereas "having passed away from there" is the reviewing of one returning, therefore, regarding this present rebirth expressed as "reborn here":
It should be understood that the statement "he arose there" was spoken with reference to his place of rebirth immediately following [the previous one].

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "there he was named... was spoken for the purpose of showing the recollection of his name, clan, and so forth, in that place of rebirth immediately following this present birth.
"Having passed away from there, I have arisen here" means: having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, I am now born here.

"Having passed away from there, he has been reborn here in such-and-such a khattiya family or a brahmin family. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way. "With its aspects and its particulars" (*sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ*): it is "with its particulars" by way of name and clan; it is "with its aspects" by way of complexion and so forth.
For by name and clan a being is designated as "Tissa Kassapa"; by complexion and so forth, he is known through his diversity as "dark" or "fair."
Therefore, name and clan are the enumeration; the others are the modes. "He recollects his manifold past lives"—this is of plain meaning.
The discussion on the knowledge of recollection of past lives is finished.
The discussion on the knowledge of passing away and rebirth follows.

411. Regarding the discourse on the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (*sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇa*): "for the knowledge of passing away and rebirth" means for the sake of knowing both passing away (*cuti*) and rebirth (*upapāta*).
By means of that knowledge by which the passing away and rebirth of beings are known—for that purpose—it is said to be "for the purpose of the knowledge of the divine eye.
"He directs and inclines his mind" means he directs the preparatory mind (*parikamma-citta*) and inclines it.
And he directs it. This refers to that bhikkhu who has performed the mental application. Regarding the phrase "with the divine" and so forth:
it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine. For deities possess a divine eye of sensitive flesh (pasādacakkhu) produced by their well-performed kamma;

being unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and the like, and being free from defilements, it is capable of receiving objects even at a distance. And this [eye] is likewise produced by the power of the development of energy.
"The eye of knowledge is just like that": it is "divine" (*dibba*) because it resembles the divine;

it is "divine" because it is acquired by means of the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*) and because it itself is supported by the divine abidings; it is "divine" because it possesses great radiance through its mastery of light;
and it is "divine" because it has a vast range through the seeing of forms situated beyond walls and so forth. All of this should be understood according to the rules of grammar (*saddasattha*).
It is "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing; it is also "eye" because it performs the function of the eye.
It is "purified" (*visuddha*) because it is the cause for the purification of view through the seeing of death and rebirth.

For he who sees only death and not rebirth adopts the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*); he who sees only rebirth and not death adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings (*nava-satta-pātubhāva-diṭṭhi*).
But he who sees both of these transcends that twofold course of views;
therefore, his vision of them becomes a cause for purification of view. And the sons of the Buddha see both of these. Hence it is said:
“It is ‘purified’ because the vision of passing away and rebirth is a cause for purification of view.”
It should be understood that it "surpasses the human" by seeing forms after having transcended the sphere of human reach;

or, because it surpasses the human fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), it is called "surpassing the human. "With that divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings" means that he surveys beings just as humans do with their fleshly eyes.
Regarding the phrase "passing away and being reborn": it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the precise moment of death (*cutikkhaṇa*) or the precise moment of rebirth (*upapattikkhaṇa*).
However, those who are near to death and will pass away shortly are called "passing away" (*cavamāna*);

and those who have already taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and have just been born are intended by the term "being reborn" (*upapajjamāna*). It is these kinds of beings who are passing away and being reborn.
And he shows that "he sees.
"Inferior" means despised, reviled, looked down upon, and disregarded by way of birth, family, wealth, and so forth, because they are associated with the outflow of delusion (*moha*).
"Superior" means the opposite of those, because they are associated with the outflow of non-delusion. "Beautiful" means because they are associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adveṣa*).

"Endowed with a desirable, lovely, and pleasing appearance" means possessed of a form that is agreeable, beautiful, and charming. "Ugly" (*dubbaṇṇa*) means possessed of a form that is undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasing due to being associated with the outflow of hatred;

it also means unsightly or deformed. "Well-gone" (*sugata*) means one who has gone to a good destination; or, because of being associated with the outflow of non-greed, it means wealthy and possessing great riches.
"Ill-gone" (*duggata*) means one who has gone to a bad destination; or, because of being associated with the outflow of greed, it means poor, lacking food and drink.

"According to their deeds" (*yathākammūpaga*) means that they have gone according to whatever karma has been accumulated. Therein, the function of the divine eye is described by the preceding phrases beginning with "passing away from the previous [existence].
By this present phrase, however, the function of the knowledge of passing away according to deeds is indicated. And this is the sequence of the arising of that knowledge:
here, a bhikkhu, having extended light downward toward the hells, [beholds] the beings in hell...
He sees beings undergoing great suffering. That vision is precisely the function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). He then attends to it thus:
"What deed have these beings performed that they now undergo this suffering?
Then, the knowledge having that specific karma as its object arises in him, [knowing] "Having done such-and-such a deed. Likewise, he increases the light directed toward the higher deva-worlds.
He sees beings experiencing great prosperity in the Nandana Grove, the Missaka Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and so forth.
That seeing is also merely the function of the divine eye. He then attends to it thus: "What deed have these beings performed that they experience this prosperity?
Then, [he understands], "Having performed such-and-such a deed," and that becomes the object of his kamma-recollection.
Knowledge arises. This is called the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma (*yathākammupagañāṇa*). There is no separate preliminary exercise for this;
as it is with this, so it is also with the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*). For these two depend on the divine eye as their basis and succeed together with the divine eye.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccaritena*), misconduct (*duccarita*) means that which is badly conducted, or that which is wickedly conducted because it is rotten with defilements.
"Bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*) means misconduct committed by the body, or misconduct that has arisen from the body; the same method applies to the other two [forms of misconduct].

"Endowed with" (*samannāgatā*) means possessed of. "Revilers of the noble ones" (*ariyūpavādakā*) refers to those who, being ill-disposed toward the noble ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, including even householders who have attained the stream-entry—speak against them either by imputing faults or by disparaging their virtues.
Or rather, it means they are revilers, abusers, and reproachers. In this context, one who says, "These have no ascetic quality (samaṇadhamma);

these are not ascetics," reviles them by means of the final ground (antimavatthu). One should understand that one reviles them by way of destroying their virtues when saying such things as, "These have no jhāna, nor liberation, nor the path, nor the fruit."
Whether one reviles [an Ariyan] knowingly or unknowingly, in either case it is indeed a reviling of an Ariyan.
This is a grave offense, similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) deed; it is an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path, yet it is remediable.
To clarify this, the following story should be understood.
It is said that in a certain village, an elder and a young bhikkhu were walking for alms.
At the very first house, they received a bowlful of warm gruel. The elder was suffering from a stomach ailment, and he thought, "This gruel is suitable for me;
I shall drink it before it becomes cold. While the people were [preparing] a threshold-crossing...
When a piece of wood was brought, he sat down and drank from it. The other, feeling disgusted, said, "This old man is overcome by extreme hunger; he has done something for which we should be ashamed.
Later, after the elder had wandered through the village and returned to the monastery, he asked the young bhikkhu, "Friend, do you have a firm footing in this Teaching?
"Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer," he replied.
"Therefore, friend, do not exert yourself for the sake of the higher paths. An arahant has been slandered by you.
He asked his forgiveness, and because of that, his karma was restored to its natural state.
Therefore, whoever else slanders a noble one should go and, if he is senior to the other, squat on his heels;
Having sat down, he should ask for forgiveness, saying: "I said this and that to the Venerable One; may you forgive me for that.
If he is junior, he should pay homage, sit in the kneeling position (ukkuṭika), raise his joined palms, and ask for forgiveness, saying: "Venerable Sir, I said this and that to you;
may you forgive me for that. If he has gone away to another region, [he himself...]
Or, having gone himself, or having sent a co-resident (saddhivihārika) or someone else, he should ask for forgiveness.
And if he is unable neither to go nor to send anyone, he should go into the presence of those monks who reside in that monastery;
if they are junior, he should sit down on his heels, and if they are senior, [he should address] the elders...
Having proceeded in the manner already described, one should say, "Venerable sir, I said such and such to the Venerable [Name];
may that Venerable one forgive me," and thus seek forgiveness. Even if he does not forgive in person, this same procedure must be performed.
If the monk is traveling alone, and neither his place of residence nor his destination is known, then for one...
Having approached a learned bhikkhu, one should say: "Venerable sir, I spoke thus and so to the Venerable named so-and-so;
as I recall that, remorse has arisen in me. What should I do? He will reply: "Do not worry;
the Elder forgives you. Settle your mind. Then, by that [advice] of the Noble One...
Facing the direction where [the deceased] has gone, one should raise one’s hands in añjali and say, “May you forgive me.
If he has attained final Nibbāna, one should go to the place of his parinibbāna, and even if it is as far as a charnel ground, one must ask for forgiveness.
When this is done, there is neither an obstruction to heaven nor an obstruction to the Path; it becomes exactly as it was before.

"Those of wrong view" means those with perverted vision. "Those who undertake actions based on wrong view" refers to those who, by way of wrong view, have undertaken various kinds of kamma, as well as those who encourage others in bodily actions and so forth rooted in wrong view.
