And here, by the inclusion of verbal misconduct, the disparagement of noble ones is included; and by the inclusion of mental misconduct, wrong view is included.
It should be understood that even though these two have already been included [in the previous categories], they are mentioned again for the purpose of showing their extreme blameworthiness.
For slandering the Noble Ones is extremely blameworthy, because it is similar to an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). And this has also been said:
"Sāriputta, just as a bhikkhu who is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom might attain final knowledge (*aññā*) in this very life..."

"It is in this way, Sāriputta, that I declare: if one does not abandon that speech, does not abandon that mind, and does not relinquish that view, then as one is carried away, so one is placed in hell.
And indeed, there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other thing..."
“Thus, monks, this wrong view is extremely blameworthy. Monks, wrong views are the supreme among blameworthy things.
“At the breaking up of the body” means at the relinquishing of the appropriated aggregates. “After death” means immediately thereafter, at the grasping of the rebirth-aggregates.
Alternatively, “at the breaking up of the body” means the cutting off of the life-faculty. “After death” means subsequent to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).
"Apāya," and so forth—all these are synonyms for hell (*niraya*).
For hell is called "apāya" because it is devoid of the "ayas" (merits) that serve as the cause for heaven and liberation, or because it is a lack of the "āya" (arrival) of happiness.
It is called "duggati" because it is a destination or refuge of suffering, or because it is produced by defiled (*duṭṭha*) karma due to an abundance of hatred.
"Gati" means an unhappy destination (*duggati*). It is called a "fall into ruin" (*vinipāta*) because those who commit evil deeds fall into it helplessly;

or alternatively, it is a "fall into ruin" because they fall there while perishing, their limbs and members being shattered. It is called "hell" (*niraya*) because there is no pleasure (*sukha*)—which is synonymous with "essence" (*rasa*)—therein.

Alternatively, by the mention of the "state of loss" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm (*tiracchānayoni*); for the animal realm is a state of loss because it is removed from a happy destination.

There is no miserable destination (*duggati*) for those of great authority, such as the Nāga kings and others, because of their birth [there]. By the mention of "miserable destination," the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) is intended;
for that is both a state of loss (*apāya*) and a miserable destination, since it is departed from the happy destinations (*sugati*) and has become a place of suffering.
But it is not a "fall" (*vinipāta*), because they have not fallen like the Asuras. By the mention of "fall," the host of Asuras is intended; for that, in the sense already stated, is...
It is called a "state of loss" (*vinipāta*) because it is a state of falling away from all elevations, being both a place of woe and a miserable destination.

By the mention of "hell," it refers specifically to the various types of hell, such as Avīci and others. "Reborn" (*upapanna*) means having arrived; the intention is that they have been produced there through rebirth.
The bright side [of the teaching] should be understood by reversing what has been stated.
However, this is the distinction: there, by the inclusion of "a happy destination" (*sugati*), the human destination is also comprised;

by the inclusion of "heaven" (*sagga*), only the divine destination is meant. Therein, a "happy destination" (*sugati*) is a beautiful destination. A "heaven" (*sagga*) is a supreme (*agga*) state through its objects such as forms and so forth.
All of that is called a "world" (*loka*) in the sense of being subject to breaking up and falling away; such is the etymological meaning.
“Thus, with the divine eye,” and so forth—all this is the concluding statement. “In this way, with the divine eye... he sees”: such is the summary meaning here.

However, a clansman who is a beginner and desires to see in this manner must, in every respect, make the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) with a kasiṇa object capable of being directed toward these three: the fire-kasiṇa, the white-kasiṇa, and the light-kasiṇa.
One of the three kasiṇas should be made proximate. Having made it the object of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), it should be expanded and established.
The intention is that absorption (appanā) should not be induced therein. For if one were to induce it, it would have the basic jhāna as its support, not the preliminary work (parikamma).
And among these three, the light-kasiṇa (āloka-kasiṇa) alone is the most excellent. Therefore...

Having produced that or one of the other kasiṇas in the manner described in the "Description of the Kasiṇas," one should expand it while remaining on the level of access concentration (upacāra-bhūmi) itself.
The method for expanding it should also be understood from the manner described therein.
One should perceive the visible form only within the area where it has been expanded. For one who perceives the visible form during this preliminary work (parikamma), [the following occurs]:
The watch passes away. Then the light disappears. When that has disappeared, even the visible form is no longer seen.
Thereupon, having repeatedly entered the basic jhāna and emerged from it, one should pervade [the area] with light.
In this way, the light gradually becomes firmly established; thus, as much space as one delimits, thinking, "Let there be light," [is filled].
In that place, light remains. Even sitting there during the day, one sees forms as they appear.
At night, the simile is of a man traveling along a path by means of a grass torch.
It is said that one man set out on a path at night with a grass torch, but his torch went out. Then, for him, the even and uneven [parts of the path]...
They were not visible. He struck that torch against the ground and relit it. Once it blazed up, it produced a light even greater than the previous one.
As he repeatedly relit it whenever it went out, the sun eventually rose.
When the sun had risen, he thought there was no further need for the torch; so, discarding it, he continued on his way throughout the day.
In this context, the light of the kasiṇa during the stage of preliminary work (parikamma) is like the light of a torch.

Just as when the torch is extinguished there is no seeing of even or uneven ground, so too, for one who sees forms, when the light disappears after the preliminary work has exceeded its limit, there is no seeing of forms.
Repeated entry [into the kasiṇa] is like the rubbing of the torch. Making a light greater than the previous light by means of the torch is like the following.
For one who performs the preliminary work again, there is a more powerful pervasion by light.

Just as the rising of the sun is the abiding of light that has become stable within its defined limits, so too, after discarding the small light, there is the seeing of forms for even a whole day by means of the light that has become stable.
After discarding the limited light, there is the seeing of forms for even a whole day by means of the light that has become stable.
In this context, when that bhikkhu’s physical eye has not reached its range, yet this form— situated within the belly, dependent on the heart-basis,
resting upon the surface of the earth below, or located beyond walls, mountains, and ramparts,
or even in another world-system— comes within the range of his eye of knowledge, it becomes as if seen by the physical eye; at that time, it is the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
It should be understood that [the consciousness] has arisen. And herein, it is this very [consciousness] that is capable of seeing forms, not the preceding stages of consciousness.

Furthermore, this becomes an obstacle for the worldling. Why? Because wherever he resolves, "Let there be light," that very place—even piercing through earth, ocean, and mountains—becomes filled with light; yet for him...
In that regard, fear arises for one who sees terrifying forms such as those of *yakkhas* and *rakkhasas*.
Since this leads to distraction of mind and causes one to fall away from *jhāna*, one must be diligent in the viewing of forms.
Herein, this is the sequence for the arising of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). Taking the aforementioned type of form as its object, there occurs an adverting of the mind-door (*manodvārāvajjana*).
Once it has arisen and ceased, four or five impulsion moments arise taking that very same form as their object;

all this is to be understood in the same manner as previously described. Here too, the preliminary consciousnesses are of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and possess both applied and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*).
At the conclusion, the consciousness that accomplishes the purpose is of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and belongs to the fourth jhāna. The knowledge co-arising with that [consciousness]—
The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is called both "knowledge" and "divine-eye-knowledge.
The Discussion on the Knowledge of Passing Away and Rebirth is finished.
The Miscellaneous Discussion.
Thus the Knower of the Five Aggregates, the Protector, spoke of the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Having understood them, this miscellaneous discussion regarding them should also be understood.

For among these, that which is called the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), consisting of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*), includes both the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the destination according to karma (*yathākammupaga-ñāṇa*).

There are also two kinds of knowledge regarding the surrounding area (*paribhaṇḍa*). Thus, these two together with the five beginning with the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha*) constitute the seven kinds of direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) that have come down here.
Now, for the sake of non-confusion regarding the classification of their objects, the four triplets of objects (*ārammaṇattika*) spoken by the Great Seer (*mahesi*) are stated:
One should illuminate the occurrence of these seven kinds of knowledge among them.

Herein, this is the illumination. For four triplets of objects were taught by the Great Sage. Which four? The triplet of limited objects, the triplet of path-objects, the triplet of past objects, and the triplet of internal objects.
414. Therein, the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power has as its object the limited, the sublime, the past, the future, the present, the internal, and the external.
It occurs with respect to seven kinds of objects.

How so? For when, desiring to go by means of an invisible body after making the body dependent upon the mind, one transforms the body through the power of the mind and merges it into or elevates it within a sublime consciousness, then—considering that the object is obtained through application—it has a limited object because its objective basis is the material body.
And when, having made the mind dependent on the body, one desires to go with a visible body and thus transforms the mind according to the body—
merging the foundational jhāna-consciousness into the material body and superimposing it upon it— then,
considering that the object is obtained through application, it becomes "of exalted object" because its object is an exalted state of consciousness.
However, because that very same consciousness takes as its object what has already passed and ceased, it therefore has a past object.
When those such as the Elder Mahākassapa resolve upon the future—as when they were establishing the Great Relic Treasury—it has a future object.
It is said that while the Elder Mahākassapa was constructing the Great Relic Treasury, he resolved: "In the future, eighteen years..."
He made this resolution: “For two hundred years, let these perfumes not dry up; let the flowers not wither; let the lamps not go out.

And it was exactly so. When the Elder Assagutta saw the Saṅgha of bhikkhus eating dry rice at the Vattaniya monastery, he resolved that the water cistern should become the taste of curd every day before the meal.
He made a resolution: "Let there be the taste of curd taken before the meal; let it be ordinary water after the meal.
However, when he makes the body dependent upon the mind and travels with an invisible body, the object is present.
This occurs at the time of transforming the mind according to the body, or the body according to the mind, or at the time of manifesting his own form as that of a youth and so forth.

Furthermore, because it takes one’s own body and mind as its object, it has an internal object (*ajjhattārammaṇa*). However, at times when one sees external elephants, horses, and so forth, it has an external object (*bahiddhārammaṇa*).
In this way, first of all, the functioning of the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*) among the seven types of objects should be understood.

415. The knowledge of the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātuñāṇa*) functions with respect to four types of objects by way of being limited (*paritta*), present (*paccuppanna*), internal (*ajjhatta*), and external (*bahiddhā*).
It occurs. How so? Because it takes sound as its object, and sound is limited, it therefore has a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*).
Furthermore, because it occurs by taking only an existing sound as its object, it has a present object (*paccuppannārammaṇa*).
At the time of hearing the sound within one's own belly, it has an internal object (*ajjhattārammaṇa*); at the time of hearing the sound of others, [it has an external object].
"An external object": in this way, the operation of the knowledge of the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātuñāṇa*) upon its four objects should be understood.
416. The knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) operates upon eight objects by way of being limited, sublime, immeasurable, pertaining to the path, past, future, present, and external.
How so? For when it knows the sense-sphere mind (*kāmāvacaracitta*) of others at that time, it has a limited object.

It exists. At the time of knowing a fine-material-sphere or immaterial-sphere consciousness, it has a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*). At the time of knowing a path or fruition, it has an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇa*).
And herein, an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) does not know the mind of a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), nor does a stream-enterer know the mind of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*); thus it is said.
This should be understood up to the point of the Arahant. However, the Arahant knows the minds of all;

furthermore, this distinction should be understood: that one who is higher [on the path] also knows the mind of one who is lower. At the time when the path-consciousness is the object, it has the path as its object.
But when one knows the minds of others within the past seven days and within the future seven days, then—
It has the past as its object and the future as its object.
How does it have the present as its object? The "present" is threefold:

momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*), serial present (*santatipaccuppanna*), and temporal present (*addhāpaccuppanna*). Among these, that which has reached the stages of arising, presence, and dissolution is the momentary present.

The "present by continuity" (*santati-paccuppanna*) is comprised of one or two moments of continuity. In this regard, for one who has been sitting in darkness and then goes to a place with light, the object does not become manifest immediately;
rather, it should be understood that between the time it first appears and the time it becomes fully manifest, there are one or two moments of continuity.
Likewise, for one who has been wandering in a place with light and then enters a small inner room, the visible form does not become manifest all at once.
However, until that [sound] becomes manifest, one should understand that there are one or two hundred vibrations in this interval.
Furthermore, even after seeing from a distance the movement of the washermen’s hands and the striking of the gong or drum, one does not yet hear the sound;
until that sound is heard, one should understand that there are likewise one or two hundred vibrations in this interval. Thus...
Thus far [the views of] the Majjhimabhāṇakas.

The Saṃyuttabhāṇakas, however, having stated two continuities—namely, material continuity and immaterial continuity—[hold that] for one who has stepped into water, [the continuity lasts] until the line made by the water where he stepped upon the bank has subsided;
and for one who has come from a journey, [it lasts] as long as [the heat remains] in the body...
The state of being smoke does not subside; for one who has entered the womb after coming from the heat, the state of darkness does not disappear until [the end].
For one who, having attended to the meditation subject within the womb, looks out by opening the window during the day, the flickering of the eyes does not subside;
this is called the continuity of form (*rūpa-santati*). Two or three impulsion-moments (*javana-vāra*).
Having stated that "the immaterial continuity is called [present]," they say that both of these are what is termed "present by way of continuity" (*santati-paccuppanna*).
However, that which is delimited by a single existence is termed "present by way of duration" (*addhā-paccuppanna*). It is with reference to this that it is said in the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*:
"Friends, whatever is the mind and whatever are mental objects—both of these are present. If, regarding that which is present, one is bound by desire and lust..."
“Consciousness exists; because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in it;

delighting in it, one is swept away by present phenomena. Thus it is said. Herein, “present by continuity” (santatipaccuppanna) is what appears in the Commentaries, while “present by duration” (addhāpaccuppanna) is [the sense] found in the Suttas.
In this regard, some say that the mind of the present moment is the object of the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*).
For what reason? Because the mind of the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimant*) and that of another arise at the same moment.
And their illustration is as follows: just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the air, inevitably one flower strikes the stalk of another with its own stalk.

One penetrates [the mind] thus: "I shall know another's mind. When one adverts to the minds of a great multitude by way of a mass, one necessarily penetrates the mind of a single person with one's own mind—at the moment of its arising, its presence, or its dissolution.
Furthermore, even when one adverts for a hundred years or a thousand years, the mind with which one adverts—

Because those two [the object and the consciousness] lack a common locus, and because there is the fault of the advertence and the impulsion reaching the state of having different objects when the object is undesirable, this [view] is rejected as improper in the Commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
However, it should be understood that the object is the present by way of continuity (*santati*) and the present by way of duration (*addhā*). In that regard:

Whatever another’s mind [is perceived] during the time measured by two or three thought-moments (*javana-vīthi*)—counting from the present thought-moment back through the past and forward into the future—all that is called "present by way of continuity" (*santati-paccuppanna*). However, it is stated in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*:
"But 'present by way of duration' (*addhā-paccuppanna*) should be illustrated by means of a sequence of impulsion-moments (*javana-vāra*). That has been well said.
Herein, this is the explanation: One possessing supernormal power (*iddhimā*), desiring to know another’s mind, adverts (*āvajjati*).
That act of adverting ceases together with the object it takes as its focus, which is present at that very moment. Following that, there arise four or five impulsion moments (*javana*);

the last of these is the supernormal consciousness (*iddhicitta*), while the rest are sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara*). For all of them, that very same [other person's] mind which has already ceased serves as the object.
They exist, yet they do not have different objects because their objects are present by way of duration (*addhā*).

Even when they share a single object, only the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*) knows the other's mind, not the others. Just as in the eye-door, only eye-consciousness sees visible form, not the others.
Thus, this [consciousness] pertains to both the present by way of continuity (*santati*) and the present by way of duration (*addhā*).

Furthermore, it has a present object by way of its own continuity. Or, since even what is present by way of continuity falls under that which is present by way of temporal duration (*addhā*), it should be understood as having a present object precisely by way of temporal duration.

Moreover, because it has another's mind as its object, it has an external object. Thus should the occurrence of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) among the eight types of objects be understood.

417. Knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects by way of being limited (*paritta*), exalted (*mahaggata*), immeasurable (*appamāṇa*), path (*magga*), past (*atīta*), internal (*ajjhatta*), external (*bahiddhā*), and indeterminate (*anavattabba*).
How so? For when it recollects the aggregates belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), its object is limited.

When it recollects the aggregates belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), its object is exalted. [When it recollects] in the past [events] by oneself or by others...
When recollecting the path developed and the fruit realized, it has an immeasurable object. When recollecting only the path developed, it has the path as its object.
However, by way of necessity, this has only the past as its object.
In that regard, although the knowledge of penetration of minds and the knowledge of rebirths according to karma also have the past as their object, nevertheless...
For those [knowledges], the object of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is only the mind that has passed away within seven days.
For it does not know any other aggregate (khandha) or anything associated with the aggregates.

However, because its object is the mind associated with the Path (magga), it is said to have the Path as its object in a figurative sense (pariyāyato). And for the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (yathākammupagañāṇa), the object is merely past volition (cetanā).
As for the object: regarding the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), there are no past aggregates or anything connected with the aggregates that is not its object.
For that knowledge follows the course of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) with respect to all phenomena within past aggregates and things connected with those aggregates;
this is the distinction to be understood. This is the method of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) in this context. Furthermore, because "wholesome aggregates... [the text continues].

“It is a condition for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of penetration into others’ minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to one’s kamma, and the knowledge of future existences, by way of object-condition,” so it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*.

Therefore, all four aggregates are objects for the knowledge of penetration into others’ minds and the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to one’s kamma; therein, for the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to one’s kamma, they are specifically wholesome and unwholesome states.
When recollecting one’s own aggregates, this has an internal object. When recollecting another’s aggregates, it has an external object.

When recollecting by way of name, clan, the earth-sign, and so forth—according to the method beginning with, "In the past there was the Blessed One Vipassī; his mother was Bandhumatī, his father was Bandhumā"—it has an indeterminate object. "Name and clan" refers to...
And here, the meaning of the expression "bondage to the aggregates" should be understood as established by conventional designation (*sammuti*), not as the literal expression itself.

For the expression, being included within the sense base of sound (*saddāyatana*), is limited (*paritta*). As it is said: "The analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) has a limited object.
This is our position in this matter. Thus should the occurrence of the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsāñāṇa*) with respect to the eight types of objects be understood.
418. The knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) operates upon four types of objects by way of being limited, present, internal, and external.
How so? Since it takes visible form (*rūpa*) as its object, and visible form is limited (*paritta*), it therefore has a limited object.

And because it operates only upon visible form that actually exists, it has a present object. At the time of seeing visible forms such as those within one's own womb, etc., [it has an internal object].

It has an internal object. At the time of seeing another's form, it has an external object. Thus should the occurrence of the knowledge of the divine eye be understood with respect to the four objects.
419. The knowledge of future possibilities has as its objects: the limited, the sublime, the immeasurable, the path, the future, the internal, the external, and the inexpressible.
It occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects. How so? For when it knows, "This person will be reborn in the future in the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara)," its object is limited (paritta).
When it knows, "He will be reborn in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara)," its object is exalted (mahaggata).
When it knows, "He will develop the path and realize the fruit," its object is immeasurable (appamāṇa).
At the moment of knowing, "He will develop the path," it has the path as its object. However, by way of necessity, that [knowledge] has only the future as its object.
In this regard, although the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) also has the future as its object, nevertheless, its object is only the mind within seven days in the future.
For it does not know any other aggregate (khandha) or anything connected with the aggregates. As for the knowledge of future possibilities (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa):
In the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), according to the method already explained, there is no such thing as a future object that lacks an objective referent.

At the time of knowing, "I will be reborn in such-and-such a place," it has an internal object (*ajjhattārammaṇa*). At the time of knowing, "So-and-so will be reborn in such-and-such a place," it has an external object (*bahiddhārammaṇa*). [One may also know]:
"In the future, the Blessed One Metteyya will arise; a brahmin named Subrahmā will be his father."

Furthermore, when one knows the name and clan by way of the method beginning with “The mother was the brahmin lady named Brahmavatī,” it is an object that cannot be stated [as a specific category] according to the method explained under the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsāñāṇa*).
Thus should the occurrence of the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) in respect of its eight objects be understood.

420. The knowledge of the destination according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) has five objects by way of being limited (*paritta*), sublime (*mahaggata*), past (*atīta*), internal (*ajjhatta*), and external (*bahiddhā*).
It occurs with respect to objects. How so? For when it knows kamma belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), its object is limited (paritta).

When it knows kamma belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), its object is exalted (mahaggata). It knows only what is past; thus, its object is past (atīta).
When it knows its own kamma, its object is internal (ajjhatta); when it knows another's kamma, its object is external (bahiddhā).
Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of rebirth according to karma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*) with respect to its five objects should be understood.
As for what was stated here—that it has both an internal object and an external object—this means that at times it knows internally and at times externally;
thus, at the time of knowing, it indeed possesses both an internal and an external object.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Direct Knowledge," in the Visuddhimagga composed for the delight of virtuous people.
14. Exposition of the Aggregates:
Discourse on Wisdom 421.
Now, since [the practitioner] possesses thus a more stable development of concentration that has attained its benefits by way of direct knowledge (abhiññā),...
When a wise man, established in virtue, is endowed with these qualities, he develops both the mind and wisdom;
herein, concentration—indicated by the term "mind"—is developed in every aspect.

Immediately after that, however, wisdom must be developed. But because it was taught so very concisely, it is not even easy to understand, let alone to develop. Therefore, this series of questions is presented in order to show its detailed exposition and the method of its development.
What is wisdom? In what sense is it wisdom? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? How many kinds of wisdom are there? How is it to be developed?
What is the benefit of developing wisdom? 422. Herein, this is the answer: "What is wisdom? Wisdom is of many kinds and various types.
If one were to begin by explaining all of that, the answer would fail to achieve its intended purpose and would lead instead to further distraction.

It would follow [that all knowledge is wisdom]. Therefore, we speak here with reference only to that which is intended [in this context]. Wisdom (*paññā*) is insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) associated with a wholesome state of consciousness.
In what sense is it "wisdom"? It is wisdom in the sense of understanding (*pajānana*). What is this so-called "understanding"?

It is knowing in various ways, distinguished by the modes of perceiving (*sañjānana*) and cognizing (*vijānana*). For although perception (*saññā*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and wisdom (*paññā*) are alike in their nature as knowing, perception [knows] "this is blue,"...

"Yellow" is merely the perception of the object; it is not able to bring about the penetration of the characteristics [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self] as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Consciousness knows the object—such as "blue" or "yellow"—and brings about the penetration of the characteristics;
however, it is not able to bring about the manifestation of the path by progressing further. Wisdom, according to the method already stated...
It knows the object, brings about the penetration of its characteristics, and, having exerted effort, brings about the manifestation of the path.
For example, when three people— a child of undeveloped intellect, a village dweller, and a money-changer— are looking at a heap of kahāpaṇa coins placed on a money-changer’s board,
the child of undeveloped intellect perceives only the mere state of the coins being variegated, multicolored, long, square, or round.
The village dweller knows, "This is the enjoyment and utility for humans, esteemed as a jewel," yet he does not know [its specific qualities].
The money-changer knows both its variegated nature and so forth, as well as, "This is the enjoyment and utility for humans, esteemed as a jewel";
however, he does not know this distinction: "This one is clever, this one is counterfeit, this one is of half-value. The money-changer...
He knows all those various modes; and knowing them, he recognizes a coin even by looking at it, by hearing the sound of it when struck,
by smelling its scent, by tasting its flavor, or by holding it in his hand,
and he knows whether it was made in such-and-such a village, town, city, mountain, or riverbank, and by such-and-such a master.
It knows; this should be understood in this very way.

For perception (saññā) is like a child who has not yet developed the faculty of understanding seeing a kahāpaṇa coin, because it grasps merely the mode of appearance of the object as it presents itself through blue and other colors.
Consciousness (viññāṇa), however, is like a villager seeing a kahāpaṇa coin.
Because it grasps the mode of the object by way of blue and so forth, and because it leads to the penetration of the characteristics even beyond that;

wisdom is like a money-changer’s examination of a coin, for after grasping the mode of the object by way of blue and so forth, and leading to the penetration of the characteristics, it further leads to the manifestation of the path.
Therefore, this [wisdom] is distinguished by the modes of perceiving and cognizing.
Knowing in various ways—this should be understood as "clear comprehension" (*pajānana*). It is with reference to this that it was said:
"Wisdom (*paññā*) is in the sense of clear comprehension.
However, wherever there are perception (*saññā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), wisdom does not necessarily exist there. But when it does exist, it is inseparable [from them].
Having analyzed those phenomena—distinguishing them as “this is perception, this is consciousness, this is wisdom”—they are subtle and difficult to see because no diversity can be found among them.
Therefore, the Venerable Nāgasena said: “It was difficult, Great King, that was accomplished by the Blessed One.
“What, venerable Nāgasena, was difficult for the Blessed One to accomplish? “It was difficult, Great King, that was accomplished by the Blessed One...”
"It has been said: 'That which is the discernment of formless mental states—the mind and mental factors—occurring with a single object, such that it is declared:
"This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness"—this is [the definition].
What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? Herein, its characteristic is the penetration of the individual essence of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*)."
Wisdom has the function of destroying the darkness of delusion that conceals the intrinsic nature of phenomena; it is manifested as non-delusion.
Furthermore, because of the statement, “One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are,” concentration is its proximate cause.
This concludes the exposition on the classification of wisdom.
425. As to how many kinds of wisdom there are: first, it is of one kind by way of its characteristic of penetrating the individual essence (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.

It is of two kinds by way of the mundane and the supramundane; likewise, by way of being with taints (*sāsavā*) or without taints (*anāsavā*), etc.; by way of the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); by way of being accompanied by joy or equanimity;

and by way of the planes of seeing and development (*bhāvanā*). It is of three kinds by way of being consisting of reflection, hearing, and mental development (*bhāvanāmayā*). Likewise, it is [of three kinds] by way of having limited, exalted, or immeasurable objects (*ārammaṇa*).

By way of skill in means regarding gain and loss, and by way of internal adherence and so forth. It is fourfold by way of knowledge regarding the four truths and by way of the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).

426. Among these, the singlefold section has its meaning already explained. Regarding the twofold section: those associated with the mundane path are mundane; those associated with the supramundane path are supramundane. Thus, they are twofold by way of being mundane or supramundane.
In the second dyad, those that have become objects for the taints (*āsava*) are "with taints" (*sāsava*). Those that do not have them as objects are "without taints" (*anāsava*).

In terms of meaning, however, this [term] refers only to the mundane and supramundane. The same principle applies in such cases as "associated with taints" being "with taints," and "dissociated from taints" being "without taints.
Thus, they are twofold by way of being with or without taints, and so forth.
In the third dyad, the wisdom that analyzes the four immaterial aggregates for one who wishes to begin insight is "wisdom analyzing name";
the wisdom that analyzes the material aggregate is "wisdom analyzing form.
Thus, it is twofold by way of analyzing name-and-form.
In the fourth dyad, wisdom is accompanied by joy in two types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness and in the path-consciousnesses of the fourfold jhāna according to the fivefold method;
it is accompanied by equanimity in two types of sense-sphere wholesome consciousness and in the four path-consciousnesses of the fifth jhāna.
Thus, it is twofold by way of being accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity.

In the first pair of twos, the wisdom of the first path is the plane of seeing (*dassanabhūmi*); the wisdom of the remaining three paths is the plane of development (*bhāvanābhūmi*). Thus, it is twofold by way of the planes of seeing and development. Regarding the triads:
in the first triad, wisdom acquired without hearing from another is "consistently produced by reflection" (*cintāmayā*), because it is accomplished through one's own reflection.
Wisdom acquired by hearing from another is "consistently produced by learning" (*sutamayā*), because it is accomplished through the power of what has been heard. [The third type is] as it is...
Or, the wisdom produced by means of meditation, having reached absorption (*appanā*), is "consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya*). For this has been said:

"In that regard, what is wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayā paññā*)? It is the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakata*) or conformity to the truths (*saccānulomika*) with respect to the spheres of work prescribed by yoga, or the spheres of craft prescribed by yoga, or the branches of science (*vijjāṭṭhāna*), [contemplating] that 'form is impermanent'..."
Or [the understanding that] feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is impermanent;

whatever such conformable acceptance, view, preference, conviction, perspective, or acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma one acquires without hearing it from another—this is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*). ...
Whatever one acquires after hearing it—this is called wisdom born of hearing (*sutamaya-paññā*). All [wisdom] is also...
“The wisdom of one who has attained [jhāna] is wisdom consisting in cultivation.
Thus, it is threefold by way of being produced through reflection, hearing, and cultivation.

In the second triad, wisdom that occurs with reference to phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) has a limited object (parittārammaṇa). [Wisdom occurring with reference to] the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara)...
That which occurs directed toward the limited is of limited object; that which occurs directed toward the sublime is of sublime object. That is mundane insight.
That which occurs directed toward Nibbāna is of immeasurable object. That is supramundane insight. Thus, it is threefold by way of having limited, sublime, and immeasurable objects.

In the third triad, "gain" (āya) means increase; it is twofold: from the abandoning of what is harmful and from the arising of what is beneficial. Skill in this regard is skill in gain. As it has been said:
“In this regard, what is skill in acquisition? When I attend to these states, unarisen unwholesome states do not arise and arisen unwholesome states are abandoned;
or when I attend to these other states, unarisen wholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states increase and reach full maturity.”
“Those things that lead to the fulfillment of development: whatever therein is wisdom, understanding...
[as above] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view—this is called skill in acquisition.
Furthermore, “decline” (apāya) means non-increase; it is twofold: through the loss of what is beneficial and through the arising of what is harmful. Skill in this regard—
Skill in decline (*apāyakosalla*). As it is said: "In this regard, what is skill in decline? When one attends to these states, wholesome states that have not yet arisen do not arise," and so forth.

In all instances, however, regarding the means and the causes for the production of those various states, there is that which occurs at that very moment, arising spontaneously with the situation (*ṭhānuppattika*).
Skillfulness (*kosalla*) is skill in means (*upāyakosalla*). As it is said: "All wisdom regarding the means to that [end] is skill in means.
Thus, it is threefold by way of skill in means regarding gain, loss, and so forth.
In the fourth triad, the wisdom of insight undertaken by taking one's own aggregates as the object is "inwardly directed" (*ajjhattābhinivesa*). [The wisdom] of another...

Adherence directed externally is that which is undertaken by taking the aggregates or external matter not bound up with the faculties as its object. Adherence directed both internally and externally is that which is undertaken by taking both as its object.
Thus, there are three kinds [of adherence] according to the internal, etc., modes. 428.
Among the sets of four, in the first tetrad, knowledge that occurs with reference to the truth of suffering is "knowledge of suffering. [Knowledge of] the origin of suffering...
Knowledge that occurs with reference to the origin of suffering is knowledge of the origin of suffering.

Knowledge that occurs with reference to the cessation of suffering is knowledge of the cessation of suffering. Knowledge that occurs with reference to the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Thus, it is fourfold by way of knowledge regarding the four truths.
In the second tetrad, the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) refer to the four types of knowledge that have reached differentiation regarding meaning and so forth. For it has been said:

“Knowledge regarding meaning is the analytical insight of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). Knowledge regarding phenomena is the analytical insight of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*). Knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation of those phenomena is the analytical insight of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding these knowledges is the analytical insight of ingenuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*)”.
In this context, "meaning" (*attha*) is, in brief, a designation for cause and fruit.
For that which is cause and fruit is called "meaning" because it is refined (*ariyati*), attained (*adhigamiyati*), and reached (*sampāpuṇiyati*) by following the cause.
In detail, however, these five phenomena are "meaning": whatever is produced by conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what has been spoken, fruition (*vipāka*), and functional (*kiriya*).

It should be understood thus: for one who reflects upon that meaning, the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).

"Dhamma" is, in brief, a designation for condition (*paccaya*). For a condition is called "dhamma" because it upholds (*dharati*), causes to proceed, or allows [something] to reach its respective state; therefore, it is called "dhamma. As for its differentiation, whatever...
The cause that produces a fruit, the noble path, what has been spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five things should be understood as "dhamma.
For one who reflects upon that dhamma, the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that dhamma is the discrimination of dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā).
Indeed, this very meaning is stated in the Abhidhamma:

“Knowledge regarding suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). Knowledge regarding the origin of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena. Knowledge regarding the fruit of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning.
Knowledge regarding those phenomena that have been born, become, produced, brought forth, and manifested—knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning.”

Knowledge regarding those phenomena from which other phenomena are born, become, produced, generated, fully manifested, and made apparent—that is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*). Knowledge regarding the origin of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.

… [and so on] … Knowledge regarding the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
Knowledge of the way is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*). Here, a monk knows the Dhamma: the discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*)...
[and so on] ...the expositions (*vedalla*). This is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena. He knows the meaning of each and every statement:
"This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement. This is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
"What phenomena are wholesome? At whatever time a wholesome consciousness pertaining to the sense sphere has arisen...

these phenomena are wholesome. Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā).
Having analyzed in this manner, it is thus shown.

"Knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic designation of phenomena (*dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ*): In that context, the "linguistic designation of phenomena" refers to the natural language, the non-deviant conventional usage, concerning both the meaning and the phenomenon.
Regarding its "expression"—that is, its utterance or articulation—upon merely hearing that which is spoken, uttered, or articulated, one discerns:
"This is natural language; this is not natural language. Thus, it is with respect to that natural language known as the linguistic designation of phenomena... [that knowledge arises]."
The analytical knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding the Magadhi, the root language of all beings, is the discrimination of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

For one who has attained the discrimination of language, upon merely hearing such statements as "contact is feeling," they know: "This is a natural linguistic expression. However, upon hearing such statements as "feeling is contact," they know: "This is not a natural linguistic expression."
"Knowledge regarding knowledges" means that for one who reviews by making all knowledges the object, there is knowledge having knowledge as its object;

or, in detail, it is the analytical insight of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*) which is knowledge regarding those aforementioned knowledges by way of their respective domains, functions, and so forth.
These four analytical insights also undergo differentiation in two stages: the stage of the trainee (*sekkha-bhūmi*) and the stage of the adept (*asekkha-bhūmi*).
Among these, the [insight] of the Chief Disciples and the Great Disciples reaches its differentiation on the plane of those beyond training (asekkha-bhūmi).

That of the Venerable Ānanda, the householder Citta, the lay follower Dhammika, the householder Upāli, the female lay follower Khujjuttarā, and others, reaches its differentiation on the plane of those still in training (sekkha-bhūmi).

Thus, although these reach their differentiation in two planes, they become clear through five modes: by means of realization, the scriptures (pariyatti), hearing, interrogation, and previous application.
In this context, "attainment" (adhigama) refers to the realization of Arahatship. "Mastery of the scriptures" (pariyatti) refers to the thorough study of the Buddha’s word.

"Hearing" (savana) refers to listening to the Dhamma with due respect and attention. "Inquiry" (paripucchā) refers to discussions concerning the resolution of difficult passages and the meaning of words within the Canon and its commentaries.
"Past application" (pubbayoga) refers to having followed the practice of going forth and returning [to lay life] under the dispensation of previous Buddhas.
The application of insight continues as far as the stage of conformity (anuloma) which is proximate to the lineage (gotrabhū).
Others have said:
"Prior practice, extensive learning, the local dialect, and traditional lore;"
"Thorough inquiry, attainment, reliance upon a teacher, and likewise excellence of friends—these are the conditions for the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
In this context, prior application is as previously described. "Great learning" refers to [mastery] in various scriptures and fields of craft.
And proficiency. "Local dialect" refers to proficiency in one hundred and one modes of expression; specifically, however, it is skill in the Māgadhī language.
"Scriptural tradition" refers to the mastery of even as much of the Buddha’s word as a single chapter of similes.
"Inquiry" refers to asking questions regarding the determination of the meaning of even a single verse. "Realization" refers to the state of being a stream-enterer... up to ... arhatship.
Or: "Dependence on a teacher" means dwelling in the presence of teachers who are abundant in learning and inspired eloquence.
"Success through friends" means the acquisition of such friends as those very same ones.
In that regard, Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas [attain] the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) by depending upon their past application (*pubbayoga*) and their realization (*adhigama*).

[They] attain them. Disciples attain all these causes. However, there is no separate application of meditation on a subject (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanānuyoga) for the attainment of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

For those in training (sekkhā), the attainment of the analytical knowledges culminates in the liberation of the fruit of training; for those beyond training (asekkhā), the attainment of the analytical knowledges culminates only in the liberation of the fruit of non-training.
Indeed, just as the Tathāgatas possess the ten powers (dasabala), so too do the Noble Ones [possess] the analytical knowledges by means of the Noble Fruit itself.
"The analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) succeed": this was said with reference to these analytical knowledges; thus, they are "fourfold" by way of the four analytical knowledges.
430. The Definition of the Ground, Root, and Body of Wisdom:

As for the question "How should it be developed?", here, because through this wisdom [the various categories] such as the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), faculties (indriya), truths (sacca), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and so forth...
The phenomena (dhammā) are the ground. These two purifications—purity of virtue and purity of mind—are the root.

The five purifications—purity of view, purity by overcoming doubt, purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path, purity of knowledge and vision of the way, and purity of knowledge and vision—are the body.
Therefore, among those phenomena that constitute the ground...

Having cultivated familiarity with knowledge by means of learning and interrogation, and having accomplished the two purifications that serve as the root, it should be developed by one who accomplishes the five purifications that constitute the body. This is the summary here. 431.
This, however, is the detailed exposition: first, regarding what was stated [as being] "divided into the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, and so forth..."

Regarding the phrase “the aggregates are the ground,” here “aggregates” refers to the five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
This concludes the discussion on the aggregate of form.

432. Therein, whatever class of phenomena possesses the characteristic of being disturbed by cold and so forth, all that, taken together, should be understood as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).
Although this is of one kind by virtue of its characteristic of being disturbed, it is twofold through the division into primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*).
Among these, primary material form is fourfold: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Of these—

The characteristics, functions, and manifestations of these [elements] have been explained in the analysis of the four elements. As for their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), however, all of them have the remaining three elements as their proximate cause.

Derived matter (*upādārūpa*) is of twenty-four kinds: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, visible form, sound, odor, [taste, nutritive essence, the faculty of femininity, the faculty of masculinity, the faculty of life, the physical basis, the heart-base, the faculty of bodily pleasure, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of grief, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the mark of the male, the mark of the female, the lightness of matter, the malleability of matter, the wieldiness of matter].
Taste, the femininity faculty, the masculinity faculty, the life faculty, the heart-base, bodily intimation, verbal intimation,
the space element, lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter, integration of matter,
continuity of matter, decay of matter, impermanence of matter, and edible food.

433. Therein, the eye has the characteristic of being susceptible to impact by visible forms, or the characteristic of the sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to see;
its function is to seize upon visible forms; it is manifested as the support for eye-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see.
The ear has the characteristic of being susceptible to impact by sounds, or the characteristic of the sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to hear.

Or the ear has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements capable of striking sounds; or it has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to hear.

Its function is to attract sounds. It is manifested as the support for ear-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to hear. The nose has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements capable of striking odors; or it has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma rooted in the desire to smell.
Its function is to attract odors. It is manifested as the support for nose-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to smell.

The tongue has the characteristic of being sensitive matter capable of being struck by tastes; or alternatively, it has the characteristic of being sensitive matter originated by kamma rooted in the desire to taste.
Its function is to apprehend tastes. It is manifested as the basis for tongue-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to taste.

The body has the characteristic of being sensitive matter capable of being struck by tangible objects; or alternatively, it has the characteristic of being sensitive matter originated by kamma rooted in the desire to touch. Its function is to apprehend tangible objects. It is manifested as the basis for body-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to touch.

Or, the body has the function of impinging upon tangible objects; it is manifested as the support for body-consciousness; its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma, which originate from the desire to touch.

However, some say: "The sensitive matter of the elements with fire predominant is the eye; the sensitive matter of the elements with air, earth, and water predominant are the ear, nose, and tongue respectively;
and the body is that of all [four]. Others say: "The sensitive matter of those with fire predominant is the eye..."

Some say that the ear, nose, tongue, and body are predominant over the space-element, air-element, water-element, and earth-element respectively. They should be asked: “Produce a scriptural passage (sutta) [to support this].
Certainly, they will not find any such sutta. However, some here offer the reason: “Because visible forms and so forth are supported by the qualities (guṇa) of fire and the other elements.
They should be asked: “Who says that visible forms and so forth are the qualities of fire and the other elements? [For] in those things that exist inseparably (avinibbhoga-vutti),...
"Indeed, among the primary elements (bhūta), it is impossible to say, 'This is the quality of this one; this is the quality of that one.

Furthermore, they might argue: "Just as you accept the functions of supporting and so forth for earth and the other elements due to the predominance of each respective element within their various constituent parts, so too must this [distinction] be accepted because the predominance of visible form and the rest is observed in those constituent parts where fire and the others predominate."

“Form and so forth are their qualities. They should be told: “We would like that, if the fragrance of cotton—which has earth as its predominant element—were stronger than the fragrance of fermented liquor which has air as its predominant element, and if the color of cold water were inferior to the color of hot water which has fire as its predominant element.
Since neither of these two cases exists, therefore, setting this aside, for them...
The conceptualization of distinctions among those [elements] that serve as a basis should be understood thus:

"Just as the visible form, taste, and so forth of the elements within a single group are mutually distinct even though there is no distinction [in their nature], so too are the eye-sensitivity and the others distinct, even in the absence of any other specific cause.
What, then, is that which is unique to each? Karma alone is their specific cause. Therefore, due to the distinction in karma...

The distinction between these [faculties] is not due to a distinction in the primary elements (*bhūta*). For if there were a distinction in the primary elements, the sensitive matter (*pasāda*) would not even arise.
As the ancients have said: "The sensitive matter belongs to those that are equal, not to those that are unequal.
(435) Thus, although these possess distinctions based on the distinction of karma, among them, the eye and the ear grasp objects that do not come into contact [with the faculty].
Because they are causes of consciousness with respect to objects that do not adhere to their own support (*nissaya*). The nose, tongue, and body grasp their objects when those objects are in contact;
this is because, both by way of their support and by themselves, they are causes of consciousness with respect to objects that do adhere to their own support. 436.
And here, the eye is that which in the world is variegated with black and white circles, interspersed with dark eyelashes, resembling the petals of a blue lotus.

It is called "the eye. In the center of the black circle (the iris) of that composite eye, which is surrounded by a white circle (the sclera), there are seven layers of membranes—like cotton-pads soaked with oil—spread across the area where the body's shape arises when facing those standing before it.
These seven ocular membranes perform the functions of supporting, washing, adorning, and fanning [the eye].
Supported by the four elements—which perform the functions of sustaining, binding, maturing, and moving like the four nurses of a kṣatriya prince;
sustained by temperature, mind, and nutriment; maintained by vitality;

and surrounded by color, fragrance, taste, and so forth—it is, in measure, no larger than the tip of a louse's head, [serving as the basis] for visual consciousness and the rest, each according to its respective capacity.
It remains establishing itself as the state of being the door for the physical basis (vatthu). And this was said by the General of the Dhamma:
“That translucent eye-organ by which one perceives forms— This is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse.”
Within the ear-canal, which possesses its constituent materials (*sasambhāra*), is a region covered with fine, tawny hairs and shaped like a finger-stall; there the ear—
assisted by the elements in the manner described, supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment,
and maintained by vitality— remains, surrounded by color and other qualities, performing its function as the appropriate physical basis and door for ear-consciousness and the rest.

Within the nostril cavity, which possesses its constituent parts, the nose— situated in a place shaped like a goat’s hoof and accompanied by its respective supports and protective coverings— remains, effecting its status as the appropriate basis and door for olfactory consciousness and the rest.

Above the center of the tongue, which possesses its constituent parts, the tongue— situated in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal and accompanied by its respective supports and protective coverings—
remains, effecting its status as the appropriate basis and door for gustatory consciousness and the rest.
However far as there is what is called "appropriated matter" (upādiṇṇa-rūpa) in this body, throughout it all the body remains—
like moisture on a cotton pad— surrounded by the aforementioned types of support and maintenance,
fulfilling its role as the appropriate basis or door for body-consciousness and the rest.

Furthermore, these [faculties] such as the eye should be regarded as being inclined toward their respective spheres—namely, what is designated as an anthill, water, space, a village, and a charnel ground—and as being inclined toward the spheres of snakes, crocodiles, birds, dogs, jackals, and forms, and so forth.
Regarding the objects beginning with visible form that follow next: visible form has the characteristic of impinging upon the eye;

its function is to serve as the objective field for eye-consciousness; its manifestation is the presentation of that same consciousness's sphere; and its proximate cause is the four great elements. And just as this...
Likewise, all derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) are included here. However, where there are specific distinctions, we shall explain them there.
This [visible form] is of many kinds, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.

Sound has the characteristic of striking the ear; its function is to be the objective domain of ear-consciousness; and it is manifested as the range of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds according to the method of "the sound of a drum," "the sound of a kettle-drum," and so on.

Odor has the characteristic of striking against the nose; its function is to serve as the objective field for nose-consciousness; its manifestation is as the range of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds according to the method of "root-odor," "heartwood-odor," and so forth.

Taste has the characteristic of striking against the tongue; its function is to serve as the objective field for tongue-consciousness; its manifestation is as the range of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds according to the method of "root-taste," "stem-taste," and so forth.
438. The female-faculty has the characteristic of the female state; its function is to manifest "this is a woman"; its manifestation is the female sex-signs, marks, postures, and behaviors.
It is manifested as the state of being the cause [of masculinity]. The male faculty has the characteristic of the male state; its function is to manifest one as "a man";
it is manifested as the cause of the male sex signs, marks, postures, and deportment. Both of these pervade the entire body just like the sensitivity of the body;
however, they do not exist in the same way as the sensitivity of the body, which exists in the places where it is present and does not exist in the places where it is absent.
It attains the state of being called "stationary," for there is no mutual confusion among them, as there is none between the color and taste of a fruit.
439. The life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining conascent material phenomena; its function is their occurrence; its manifestation is their stabilization;

its proximate cause is the primary elements that are to be maintained. And although there exists this arrangement of characteristics such as maintenance, it exists only at the very moment of presence.
It protects those co-nascent forms just as water protects lotuses and the like; it protects the phenomena arisen from their respective conditions just as a nurse protects a child;
and it functions solely through its connection with the phenomena that have already set themselves in motion, like a pilot.
It does not function beyond the moment of dissolution, because of the absence of both itself and of those things it would have to set in motion.
It does not establish [the object] at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself dissolving—just as the oil in a wick does not support the flame of a lamp while it is being consumed.
Yet, it should be understood that it is not devoid of the powers of preservation, occurrence, and establishment, for it acts as the respective means (sādhana) during the aforementioned moments.
440. The heart-base has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element; it belongs to those very elements.
Its function is to serve as a basis; its manifestation is flowing. It depends on the blood of the kind described in the discourse on mindfulness directed to the body within the heart;
it is assisted by the primary elements through their functions such as supporting; it is sustained by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment;
it is maintained by vitality; and it serves as the physical basis for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental states associated with them.
It remains while accomplishing [its task].

441. Bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) is a modification of form that serves as the condition for the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body by means of the air-element originated by the consciousness occurring in the process of approaching and so forth;
its function is to manifest intention, and it is manifested by being the cause of bodily vibration.
It has the air element produced by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-vāyodhātu*) as its proximate cause.

Furthermore, this is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*) because it is the cause for making one's intention known through bodily movement, and because it is itself cognizable by the body in the form of that bodily movement.

And because of its connection with those moving material phenomena born of consciousness, even those things born of the seasons (*utu*) and so forth move; thus, there are [actions such as] advancing and so on.
It should be understood that they proceed.

Vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) is the modification of shape that serves as the condition for the impact upon the appropriated earth-element originated by the consciousness that sets vocal expression in motion;
its function is to reveal intention; it is manifested as the causal state of the sound of speech; and its proximate cause is the earth-element originated by consciousness.

This [intimation], moreover, is called "verbal intimation" (*vacīviññatti*) because it is the cause for making one's intention known through the sound of speech, and because it is itself cognizable by means of that speech designated as the sound of words.

For just as water is known to exist in a forest upon seeing signs of water such as the hoofprints of cattle left after they have wallowed, so too is the intention known by apprehending both the movement of the body and the sound of speech.
Bodily and vocal intimation are also cognized. 442.
The space element has the characteristic of delimiting matter; its function is to manifest the boundaries of matter;
it is manifested as the limit of matter, or alternatively, as the state of non-contact and the state of fissures and apertures; its proximate cause is delimited matter. By means of which...
In delimited material phenomena, there is the notion: "this is above, below, or across from that. 443.

The characteristic of lightness of matter is the state of being unweighed down; its function is the removal of heaviness in material phenomena; it is manifested as quick transformation; its proximate cause is light matter.
The characteristic of plasticity of matter is the state of being unrigid; its function is the removal of rigidity in material phenomena.
It has non-opposition toward all activities as its manifestation and softness as its proximate cause. The wieldiness of matter is characterized by a state of pliancy suitable for bodily activity;
it has the dispelling of unwieldiness as its function, the absence of rigidity as its manifestation, and wieldy matter as its proximate cause.
These three, however, do not abandon one another. Nevertheless, that lightness of matter which is like that of one who is free from illness—

Lightness of matter (*rūpalahutā*) is a mode of non-sluggishness characterized by rapid transformation; it arises from conditions that counteract the disturbance of the elements which cause the sluggishness of matter.
It is a modification of matter consisting in the softness of material phenomena, characterized by pliancy and the capacity for mastery over all specific functions;
it arises from conditions that counteract the disturbance of the elements which cause the rigidity of matter.

That modification of matter which is the plasticity of matter is as follows: that state of workability in matter—like well-refined gold—which consists in being suitable for bodily actions, and which arises from conditions opposed to the disturbances of the elements that are unsuitable for bodily actions; that modification of matter is the "workability" (*kammaññatā*) of matter.
In this way, the distinction between these two should be understood.
444. Accumulation has the characteristic of heaping up matter; its function is to cause matter to emerge from the past;
it is manifested as the act of conveying [matter] forward, or as the state of fullness; its proximate cause is accumulated matter. Continuity has the characteristic of the occurrence of matter;
its function is to link together; it is manifested as non-interruption; its proximate cause is matter that links together. Both of these...

This is a synonym for the very same birth-form (*jātirūpa*); however, because of the diversity of its modes and for the sake of those to be trained, the teaching was presented by way of the headings "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*).
Since there is no difference in meaning here, therefore, in the exposition of these terms it is said:
"That which is the accumulation of the bases (*āyatana*), that is the accumulation of form; that which is the accumulation of form, that is the continuity of form."

It has been stated thus. In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, after stating, "Arising (*ācaya*) is birth; accumulation (*upacaya*) is growth; continuity (*santati*) is occurrence," the following analogy was given:
"Arising is like the time when water begins to rise in a pit dug on a riverbank;
accumulation is like the time when it becomes full; continuity is like the time when it overflows and flows away."
And at the conclusion of the simile it is said: "What is stated here? By means of the base (āyatana), accumulation (ācaya) is stated;
by means of accumulation, the base is stated. Therefore, that which is the initial manifestation of material phenomena is accumulation.

That which is their subsequent manifestation, as well as the manifestation of others arising thereafter, is "growth" (upacaya) because it appears in the mode of increasing. That which belongs to those...

Furthermore, it should be understood that the repeated arising of other [phenomena] as they are being produced above [the preceding ones], because it appears in the form of a continuous succession, is called "continuity" (*santati*).

Aging has the characteristic of the maturation of material form; its function is to lead [it] toward [its end]; and its manifestation is the disappearance of novelty even while the intrinsic nature [of the phenomenon] has not yet departed.

Like the state of rice becoming old, [aging] has as its proximate cause matter that is reaching maturity. This was said with reference to manifest aging, because changes such as brokenness and so forth are seen in the teeth and other parts.
However, for immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā), there is what is called "concealed aging" (paṭicchannajarā);
it has no such visible change. And there is also what is called "uninterrupted aging" (avīcijarā) in earth, water, mountains, the moon, the sun, and so forth.

The impermanence of matter has the characteristic of disintegration; its function is to fall away; it is manifested as destruction and vanishing; and its proximate cause is matter in the process of disintegrating.

Edible food has the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*); its function is to sustain matter; it is manifested as support; and its proximate cause is the substance that must be taken after being made into mouthfuls. This is a designation for that nutritive essence by which living beings subsist. These, first of all, are the material phenomena mentioned in the canonical texts (*pāḷi*).
However, in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), there are also the material phenomena of strength (*bala-rūpa*) and the material phenomena of production (*sambhava-rūpa*).
According to the opinion of some, the form of birth (*jātirūpa*) is the form of disease (*rogarūpa*), and for others it is the form of torpor (*middharūpa*).

Having thus brought forward other forms as well and stated, "Surely you are a Sage, a Perfectly Awakened One; there are no hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) in you," and so forth, the form of torpor is first rejected as being simply non-existent.

Among the others, the form of disease is already included by the inclusion of aging (*jaratā*) and impermanence (*aniccatā*); the form of birth is included by the inclusion of accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*).
The material quality of cohesion is included by the inclusion of the water element, and the material quality of motion is indeed included by the inclusion of the air element.
Therefore, the conclusion is made that not even one of these exists separately.
Thus, these twenty-four kinds of derived matter together with the four kinds of primary matter mentioned previously constitute twenty-eight kinds of matter, neither more nor less.
447. All of that is of one kind in such ways as: it is not a cause, causeless, dissociated from causes, conditioned, mundane, and subject to taints (sāsavam).

It is twofold by way of being internal or external, gross or subtle, distant or near, produced or unproduced, sensitive matter or non-sensitive matter, faculty or non-faculty, and clung-to (upādiṇṇa) or not-clung-to.
Therein, the fivefold [matter] beginning with the eye is "internal" because it occurs in dependence upon the personal body (attabhāva); the remainder is [external].

It is "external" because it is external. The twelvefold [form]—consisting of the nine beginning with the eye and the three elements excluding the water element—is "gross" because it must be apprehended by way of impact;
the remainder is "subtle" because it is the opposite of that.
That which is subtle is "distant" because its nature is difficult to penetrate, while the other is "near" because its nature is easy to penetrate. The four...

The eighteen kinds of material phenomena—the thirteen beginning with the eye-element and physical nutriment—are "produced" (nipphanna) because they must be discerned by way of their own intrinsic nature, having transcended the states of delimitation and transformation.
The remainder are "unproduced" (anipphanna) due to being the opposite of that.
The fivefold [materiality] beginning with the eye, because it is the condition for the apprehension of visible forms and so forth, is like the surface of a mirror in its extreme clarity.
Sensitive matter (*pasāda-rūpa*) is so called; the other is non-sensitive matter (*napasāda-rūpa*) because it is the opposite of that.

Only sensitive matter, together with the triad beginning with the female faculty (*itthindriya*), is a faculty (*indriya*) in the sense of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭhena*); the rest are non-faculties (*anindriya*) because they are the opposite of that.

That which we shall later describe as "born of kamma" (*kammaja*) is "clung-to" (*upādiṇṇa*) because it is appropriated by kamma; the rest are not clung-to (*anupādiṇṇa*) because they are the opposite of that.
448. Furthermore, all material form (rūpa) is threefold by way of the triads beginning with "visible and kamma-born.
Therein, gross form is visible and impinging; the remainder is invisible and impinging. All subtle form is invisible and non-impinging.
Thus, first, it is threefold by way of the triad of the "visible. By way of the triad of the "kamma-born," etc.:

Furthermore, that which is born from karma is "kamma-born"; that which is born from other conditions than that is "not kamma-born"; that which is not born from anything at all is "neither kamma-born nor not kamma-born.
That which is born from consciousness is "consciousness-born"; that which is born from other conditions than that is "not consciousness-born";

that which is not born from anything at all is "neither consciousness-born nor not consciousness-born. That which is born from nutriment is "nutriment-born"; that which is born from other conditions than that is "not nutriment-born."
