That which is not born from anything at all is neither born of nutriment nor not born of nutriment. That which is born from temperature is "temperature-born" (*utuja*); that which is born from conditions other than that is "not-temperature-born" (*anutuja*);
that which is not born from anything at all is neither temperature-born nor not-temperature-born. Thus, it is threefold by way of the triad beginning with "kamma-born.
Furthermore, it is fourfold by way of the four tetrads beginning with "seen," "visible form," "base," and so on. Among these, the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*)...
The visible is so called because it is the object of seeing; the sound base is so called because it is the object of hearing;

the triad of odors, flavors, and tangibles is so called because they are objects for faculties that grasp what has reached them; and the rest are so called as "cognized" because they are the objects of consciousness alone.
Thus, first of all, it is fourfold by way of the tetrad beginning with the seen.
Furthermore, herein, produced matter is called "material matter" (rūparūpa); the space element is called "delimiting matter" (paricchedarūpa);
bodily intimation and so forth, ending with wieldiness, are called "alteration matter" (vikārarūpa); and birth, aging, and dissolution are called "characteristic matter" (lakkhaṇarūpa).
Thus, it is fourfold by way of these four tetrads beginning with material matter.
Furthermore, that which here is called heart-materiality is a base (*vatthu*) but not a door (*dvāra*). The two types of intimation (*viññatti*) are doors but not bases.
The sensitive materiality (*pasāda-rūpa*) is both a base and a door. The remainder is neither a base nor a door. Thus, it is fourfold by way of the tetrad of bases and so forth.
(450) Again, it is fivefold by way of these: born from one, born from two, born from three, born from four, and not born from anything at all.

In this context, that which is born of karma alone and that which is born of consciousness alone are called "born of one" (*ekaja*). Among these, the materiality of the sense faculties together with the heart-base is born of karma alone.
The two types of intimation are born of consciousness alone. That which is born from both consciousness and temperature is called "born of two" (*dvija*);
that is the sense-sphere of sound alone. That which is born from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment is called "born of three" (*tija*); and that, moreover—

The triad of lightness and so forth is likewise. That which is produced by all four—kamma and the rest—is called "fourfold-born" (*catujam*); this excludes the characteristic material phenomena (*lakkhaṇarūpa*) and consists of the remainder.
However, the characteristic material phenomena are not produced from anything. Why? Because there is no arising of arising;

and for that which has already arisen, the other two [subsidiary characteristics] are merely its maturation and dissolution. As for what was said: "the visible-object base, the sound-base, the odor-base..."
In such passages as, "The taste-base, the tangible-base, the space-element, the water-element, lightness of matter, malleability of matter,
wieldiness of matter, integration of matter, continuity of matter, and edible food—
these phenomena are mind-originated," the fact that birth arises from something else is admitted; however, that [birth] pertains to the conditions that produce matter.
It should be understood that [the Buddha] was seen at the moment of his performance of the task.
This, then, is the introductory section of the detailed exposition on the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). Now follows the discourse on the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha).
451. Furthermore, whatever has the characteristic of being felt, all that taken together is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha);
whatever has the characteristic of perceiving, all that taken together is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha);

whatever has the characteristic of volitional formation, all that taken together is the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); whatever has the characteristic of cognizing, all that taken together—

Having done so, the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) should be understood. In this context, since the other aggregates are easily understood once the aggregate of consciousness is understood, we shall provide the exposition beginning with the aggregate of consciousness.
For it is said: "Whatever has the characteristic of cognizing, all that taken together should be understood as the aggregate of consciousness."

It has been said: "And what is consciousness? Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. As it was said: 'Friends, it cognizes, it cognizes; therefore it is called consciousness. Consciousness, mind, and thought are one in meaning.
Although this is of a single kind by its intrinsic nature through the characteristic of cognizing, it is threefold according to its genus: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
452. Therein, the wholesome is fourfold according to the division of planes: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane.
Therein, the sense-sphere wholesome is eightfold according to the division of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and volitional effort.
That is to say: accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, without volitional effort, and with volitional effort; and likewise—

It is dissociated from knowledge. It is accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and both without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*) and with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*); likewise, it is dissociated from knowledge.

For when, having encountered the excellence of the object to be given, the recipient, and so forth, or some other cause for joy, one is exceedingly glad and—preceded by right view occurring in the manner of "there is giving," etc.—neither desponding nor being urged on, [one gives].
When one performs meritorious deeds such as giving for the sake of others, at that time one’s consciousness is accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge,
and without volitional effort (asaṅkhāra). However, when one— being joyful and elated according to the method described—

performs such acts either while sinking due to a lack of generosity and so forth despite being preceded by right view, or when encouraged by others, then that same consciousness is with volitional effort (sasaṅkhāra).
For in this context, "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) is a designation for the preliminary effort that occurs either on one's own account or on behalf of others.
However, when young children— who have become accustomed through witnessing the conduct of their kinsmen— see monks and, having conceived a sense of joy,
suddenly give whatever is in their hands or pay homage, then the third consciousness arises.
But when, being urged by relatives with words such as "Give! Pay homage!", they act in this way, then the fourth consciousness arises.

However, when—due to the deficiency of the object to be given, the recipient, and so forth, or the absence of other causes for joy—they are devoid of joy in all four modes of application, then the remaining four are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
"...arise. Thus, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness should be understood as eightfold, according to the distinctions of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and volitional formations.

The fine-material-sphere consciousness, however, is fivefold according to the distinction of the association with jhāna factors. Namely: the first, associated with initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), pleasure (sukha), and concentration (samādhi);
the second, which has transcended initial application; the third, which has further transcended sustained application; and the fourth, from which rapture has faded away.
The fourth [jhāna], and the fifth, which is associated with equanimity and concentration and has its bliss subsided.

The formless-sphere consciousness is fourfold by way of association with the four formless attainments. For, as previously described, that associated with the jhāna of the base of infinite space is the first;
those associated with the base of infinite consciousness and so forth are the second, third, and fourth. The supramundane is [fourfold] due to association with the four paths.
Thus, in this way, wholesome consciousness alone is of twenty-one kinds. 453.

Unwholesome consciousness, however, is of one kind according to plane, being exclusively of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*). According to roots, it is of three kinds: rooted in greed (*lobha*), rooted in hatred (*dosa*), and rooted in delusion (*moha*).
Therein, that rooted in greed is of eight kinds through its division into [states associated with] joy, equanimity, views, and formations. Namely:
[There are] states accompanied by joy, associated with views, both without effort and with effort; likewise, those dissociated from views.
[There are] states accompanied by equanimity, associated with views, both without effort and with effort; likewise, those dissociated from views.
For when one, having placed wrong view foremost in such a manner as "there is no danger in sensual pleasures," is joyful and elated...

When one enjoys sensual pleasures, or when one regards such things as "auspicious sights" and the like as being essential with a mind that is naturally sharp and incited [by desire], then the first unwholesome consciousness arises.
When it is with a mind that is dull and incited [by desire], then the second [unwholesome consciousness] arises.
When, without placing wrong view at the forefront, one engages in sexual intercourse merely out of being joyful and delighted, [then the third arises].
When one covets the prosperity of others or seizes another's property with a mind that is naturally sharp and uninstigated, then it is the third [type of unwholesome thought].
When it is with a dull mind instigated by external factors, then it is the fourth.
However, when—due to the lack of success in sensual pleasures or the absence of other causes for joy—it occurs across all four permutations...

When they are devoid of joy, then the remaining four arise accompanied by equanimity. Thus, the root of greed should be understood as eightfold according to the distinctions of joy, equanimity, views, and formations (*saṅkhāra*).

The root of hatred, however, is twofold: accompanied by displeasure and associated with aversion, being either without formations or with formations; its occurrence should be understood as taking place at times when it functions intensely or weakly in acts such as killing living beings.

It is twofold: rooted in delusion and accompanied by equanimity, associated with doubt, and associated with restlessness. Its occurrence should be understood at the times of decision and distraction. Thus, unwholesome consciousness is of twelve types. 454.
Indeterminate consciousness is twofold according to its classification by birth: resultant (*vipāka*) and functional (*kiriya*). Therein, resultant consciousness is fourfold according to plane:
sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere, and supramundane. Therein, sense-sphere resultant consciousness is twofold: wholesome-resultant and...
And unwholesome-resultant. Wholesome-resultant is also twofold: rootless and with roots.

Therein, that which is devoid of the roots of resultants such as non-greed is "rootless. That is eightfold: eye-consciousness; ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; the mind-element whose function is receiving; and the two mind-consciousness-elements whose functions are investigating and so forth.
Therein, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing visible form dependent on the eye; its function is to have mere visible form as its object.
It has the manifestation of being directed toward visible forms, and its proximate cause is the absence of the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) that takes visible forms as its object.

Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness have the characteristic of cognizing sounds and so forth dependent on the ear and other sense bases; they have the flavor of taking mere sounds and so forth as their objects;
they have the manifestation of being directed toward sounds and so forth; and their proximate cause is the absence of the functional mind-elements that take sounds and so forth as their objects.

Immediately following eye-consciousness and the others, there is the mind-element (*manodhātu*), which has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so forth; its function is the reception of visible forms and so forth; it is manifested as such a state; and its proximate cause is the cessation of eye-consciousness and the rest.
The mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—which is of two kinds, being either rootless-resultant or associated with roots—is characterized by the cognition of the six objects;
its functions include investigating and so forth; it is manifested as such a state; and its proximate cause is the heart-base. [It is distinguished] by its association with joy or equanimity.
Furthermore, its classification is according to two and five bases. Among these, one [type] is associated with joy (*somanassa-sampayutta*) because it occurs exclusively with desirable objects;
it has two bases because it functions as investigation (*santīraṇa*) and registration (*tadārammaṇa*) in the five doors, and because it occurs at the conclusion of the impulsion (*javana*) process.
One [other type] is associated with equanimity (*upekkhā-sampayutta*) because it occurs with objects that are neither-desirable-nor-undesirable.
Having been offered as a sacrifice, it occurs in five locations by way of investigation, registration, rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.

Furthermore, this eightfold rootless resultant consciousness is twofold because its objects are either determinate or indeterminate, and threefold through the distinction of equanimity, pleasure, and joy.
Herein, the pentad of sense-sphere consciousness has determinate objects, as they proceed respectively only toward visible forms and so forth.

The remainder has an indeterminate object. For therein, the mind-element (manodhātu) occurs with respect to all five [objects] beginning with visible form, while the two mind-consciousness-elements (manoviññāṇadhātu) occur with respect to all six.
Furthermore, among these, body-consciousness is associated with pleasure; the mind-consciousness-element in two instances is associated with joy, and the remainder is associated with equanimity.
Thus, first of all, the eightfold wholesome resultant rootless consciousness should be understood.

However, that which is associated with the root-cause of non-greed and so forth is "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*). Like wholesome states of the sense-sphere, it is eightfold according to the divisions of joy and so forth.
But unlike the wholesome state, which occurs toward six kinds of objects by way of giving and so forth, this is not the case.
For this [rootless consciousness] occurs only toward those things included within limited phenomena (*parittadhamma*), by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, death, and registration.
It proceeds with respect to the six objects. However, the state of being volitional or non-volitional here should be understood by way of its origin and so forth.

Furthermore, although there is no difference in the associated states, it should be understood that the resultant is effortless, like the reflection of a face in a mirror or similar surfaces, while the wholesome is effortful, like the face itself.
For the unwholesome resultant is exclusively rootless (*ahetuka*). That consists of seven types: eye-consciousness; ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness;
the mind-element with the function of receiving; and the five instances of the mind-consciousness-element with the functions of investigating and so forth.
This should be understood according to its characteristics and other features in the same manner as was explained for the wholesome rootless resultants.
For while exclusively wholesome-resultants have desirable or desirable-neutral objects, these have undesirable or undesirable-neutral objects.
Furthermore, those [resultants] are threefold according to the distinction of equanimity, pleasure, and joy, whereas these are twofold by way of pain and equanimity.
For here, body-consciousness is accompanied only by pain, while the remaining ones are accompanied by equanimity. And that equanimity in them—
The inferior [equanimity] is not too sharp, like suffering; the superior equanimity among the others is not too sharp, like pleasure.
Thus, by way of these seven unwholesome resultants and the preceding sixteen wholesome resultants, sense-sphere resultant consciousness is twenty-three-fold.

The fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) wholesome consciousness, however, is fivefold, just like the wholesome [consciousness of the sense sphere]. But the wholesome [fine-material-sphere consciousness] occurs in the cognitive process (javanavīthi) by way of attainment (samāpatti).
This [fine-material-sphere consciousness] occurs in rebirth by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti).

And just as it is with the fine-material-sphere, so too the immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) wholesome consciousness is fourfold. Its classification of occurrence is also according to the same method stated for the fine-material-sphere.
Supramundane resultant consciousness is fourfold because it is the fruit of the four paths;
it occurs in two ways: by way of the cognitive process of the path and by way of meditative attainment. Thus, there are thirty-six kinds of resultant consciousness in total across the four planes.
Furthermore, functional consciousness (kiriya) is threefold according to the division of planes: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, and immaterial-sphere.
Among these, the sense-sphere is twofold: rootless (ahetuka) and with roots (sahetuka). Therein, that which is devoid of the functional roots such as non-greed is rootless;
it is twofold by way of the division between mind-element (manodhātu) and mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu).

Therein, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so forth that precede eye-consciousness and the rest; its function is adverting; it is manifested as being directed toward visible forms and so forth; its proximate cause is the interruption of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); and it is invariably associated with equanimity.

The mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), however, is twofold: common and uncommon. Therein, the common [mind-consciousness-element] is accompanied by equanimity, is rootless, is functional (*kiriya*), and has the characteristic of cognizing the six kinds of objects.
By way of its function, it performs the roles of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) and adverting in the five doors and the mind door.
It is manifested as suchness; it has as its proximate cause any one of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) moments following a rootless resultant mind-consciousness element.
It is unique, accompanied by joy, and rootless; its characteristic is the cognition of the six objects.
By way of function, it has the production of a smile toward inferior objects for Arahants as its essence; it is manifested as suchness, and is exclusively...
"Having the heart-base as its proximate cause. Thus, the rootless functional consciousness of the sense sphere is threefold.
The root-cause-accompanied, however, is eightfold according to the division of joy and so forth, just like the wholesome.

For while the wholesome arises in both trainees and worldlings, this [functional] arises only in Arahants; this is the distinction here. In this way, first, the sense-sphere consciousness is elevenfold.
The wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere, however, is fivefold and fourfold respectively, just like the wholesome [consciousness].
Its distinction from the wholesome should be understood by way of its arising in Arahants alone. Thus, there are twenty types of functional consciousness in all across the three planes.
455. Thus, there are twenty-one wholesome consciousnesses, twelve unwholesome, thirty-six resultants, and twenty functionals;

all together, these constitute eighty-nine types of consciousness. These operate in fourteen modes: as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), adverting (*āvajjana*), seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, receiving (*sampaṭicchana*), investigating (*santīraṇa*), determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), impulsion (*javana*), registration (*tadārammaṇa*), and death (*cuti*).

How so? For when beings are reborn among gods and humans through the power of the eight wholesome kamma-formations of the sense-sphere, they then take as their object at the time of death one of these three: kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of the destination.

Based on this, there arise the eight wholesome-resultant consciousnesses of the sense-sphere accompanied by roots; and in the case of those attaining the state of eunuchs and so forth among humans, there arise the weak two-rooted wholesome-resultants and the rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity.
Thus, nine resultant consciousnesses proceed by way of rebirth-linking.

When beings are reborn in the fine-material or immaterial realms through the power of wholesome kamma of the fine-material or immaterial spheres, then at the time of death, taking only the sign of the kamma (kamma-nimitta) that has appeared before them as their object,
nine resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material or immaterial spheres proceed by way of rebirth-linking.
But when they are reborn in a state of misery through the influence of unwholesome kamma,

then at the time of their death, having taken as an object one of the three— kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of the destination— that presents itself, a single unwholesome resultant rootless mind-consciousness element occurs by way of rebirth-linking.
Thus, first of all, the occurrence of the nineteen resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking should be understood here.
But when the rebirth-linking consciousness has ceased, there arises a stream of life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-viññāṇa) that follows upon each respective rebirth-linking consciousness;
it is the result of that very same karma, occurs with that very same object, and is of the same nature.
Again, it is of the same nature—thus, in the absence of another mental state to interrupt the continuity, it flows like the current of a river.
Even for one who does not see dreams, [this stream] indeed continues in an immeasurable number during times such as the onset of sleep;

thus, the occurrence of those very same consciousnesses should be understood by way of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) as well. Now, when, in the course of such a continuum of the life-continuum, the faculties of sentient beings become capable of grasping objects—
When that occurs, once a visible form has come within the range of the eye, there is an impact upon the eye-sensitivity conditioned by that form;
through the power of that impact, there is a vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Then, when the life-continuum has ceased, the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) performs the function of adverting, as if cutting off the life-continuum by taking that very form as its object.
It arises. The same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well.

However, in the mind-door, when any of the six kinds of objects have come into range, immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), a rootless functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity arises, performing the function of adverting as if it were cutting off the life-continuum.
Thus, the occurrence of the two types of functional consciousness should be understood by way of adverting.
Immediately following adverting, however, eye-consciousness—which has the sensitive eye-faculty as its basis—arises at the eye-door, performing the function of seeing;
and ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness arise at the ear-door and so forth, performing their respective functions of hearing and so on.

These [consciousnesses] are wholesome-resultants when directed toward desirable or desirable-neutral objects, and unwholesome-resultants when directed toward undesirable or undesirable-neutral objects.

Regarding the unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses] among the objects: thus, the occurrence of the ten resultant consciousnesses should be understood by way of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching.

Furthermore, from such statements as, "Immediately after the eye-consciousness element has arisen and ceased, there arises the mind, the mentation, the mental faculty, the corresponding mind-element," it is understood that immediately following the eye-consciousness and the others, their very objects [are apprehended].

When receiving [the object], the mind-element (manodhātu) arises as wholesome-resultant immediately after wholesome-resultant [consciousness], or as unwholesome-resultant immediately after unwholesome-resultant [consciousness].
Thus, the occurrence of two resultant consciousnesses by way of reception should be understood.
"Immediately after the mind-element has arisen and ceased, consciousness arises—the mind, the mentation, the mind-consciousness-element born thereof."
As for the verbal description: the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipākāhetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu), which investigates the very same object that was received by the mind-element (manodhātu)—

arising immediately after an unwholesome resultant mind-element when it is unwholesome-resultant, and immediately after a wholesome resultant mind-element when the object is desirable, accompanied by joy, or when the object is desirable-neutral, accompanied by equanimity— thus [is the sequence] of the three resultant consciousnesses.
Its occurrence should be understood as being by way of investigating.

Immediately after the investigating [consciousness], however, there arises the functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity, which determines that very same object; thus, the occurrence of a single functional consciousness should be understood as being by way of determining.
Immediately after the determining [consciousness], if the object—be it visible form or otherwise—is great, then, in accordance with what has been determined...

Regarding the object, six or seven impulsion moments (javana) proceed by way of one or another of the eight sense-sphere wholesome states, the twelve unwholesome states, or the nine remaining sense-sphere functional states;
this, first of all, is the method for the five doors.

In the mind door, however, immediately after the mind-door adverting consciousness, those same [impulsions] arise, starting from the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and extending upward to the fine-material sphere.
The five wholesome [consciousnesses], the five functional [consciousnesses], from the formless realm the four wholesome and four functional [consciousnesses],
and from the supramundane the four path-consciousnesses and four fruition-consciousnesses— whichever among these obtains the necessary conditions, that very one runs. Thus,
the occurrence of the fifty-five wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and resultant consciousnesses should be understood by way of their running (javana).
But at the conclusion of the javana, if there is an extremely strong object at the five sense doors or a clear object at the mind door,
then— at the end of the sense-sphere javanas for sense-sphere beings— whichever condition has been obtained by way of desirable objects and so forth,
or by way of previous kamma-javana consciousnesses and so forth, [the resultant occurs] accordingly among the eight sense-sphere resultant states accompanied by roots.
In the three resultant rootless mind-consciousness elements, a resultant consciousness arises either twice or once,
following upon a javana that has impelled toward an object other than the life-continuum's (bhavaṅga) object— just as a boat following a current might follow after something else in the water—
and which has thus moved against the stream. This occurs at the conclusion of the javana, regarding the object of the life-continuum.
Because it proceeds by taking as its object the same object as that impulsion which was worthy of proceeding, it is called "registering" (*tadārammaṇa*).
In this way, the occurrence of the eleven resultant consciousnesses should be understood by way of registration.
At the conclusion of the registration, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) proceeds once more; when the life-continuum has ceased, there again arise the adverting consciousness and the others.

Thus, with its mental continuum having obtained the necessary conditions, the process proceeds again and again by the fixed order of consciousness: first the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), followed by adverting (*āvajjana*), and after adverting, seeing and so forth, until the exhaustion of the life-continuum within a single existence.
For that final life-continuum consciousness in a single existence is called "death" (*cuti*) because of the passing away from it.
Therefore, that [resultant consciousness] also consists of exactly nineteen types. Thus, the occurrence of the nineteen resultant consciousnesses should be understood by way of death.
From death there is again rebirth-linking; from rebirth-linking there is again the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
In this way, for beings wandering through the realms of existence, destinies, stations, and abodes, the mental continuum proceeds without interruption. As for one who here attains Arahantship...
It reaches [the next state], and when his death-consciousness has ceased, it has indeed ceased.
This is the section on the detailed exposition of the aggregate of consciousness.
Now follows the discussion on the aggregate of feeling.

456. Now, regarding what was said: “Whatever has the characteristic of being felt, all that, taken together, should be understood as the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha)”—here too, that which is called the “characteristic of being felt” is simply feeling itself. As it is said:
“It feels, it feels, friend; therefore it is called ‘feeling. And although that [feeling] is of one kind by way of its intrinsic nature through the characteristic of being felt, it is...
By way of kind, it is threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Among these, the wholesome [consciousness] is associated with wholesome consciousness—described by the method beginning with "the eightfold sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, distinguished by joy, equanimity, knowledge, and volitional formations"—the unwholesome is associated with unwholesome [consciousness], and the indeterminate is associated with indeterminate [consciousness].

It should be understood as indeterminate (*abyākata*). By way of its own specific nature, it is fivefold: pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*dukkha*), mental joy (*somanassa*), mental grief (*domanassa*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
Among these, pleasure is associated with wholesome-resultant body-consciousness; pain is associated with unwholesome-resultant [body-consciousness].

From the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), [it arises] from four wholesome states, four root-cause-accompanied resultant states, one root-cause-free resultant state, four root-cause-accompanied functional states, one root-cause-free functional state, and four unwholesome states;

from the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), excluding the consciousness of the fifth jhāna, from four wholesome states, four resultant states, and four functional states; and from the supramundane (lokuttara).
However, since there is no such thing as a supramundane consciousness that is not associated with jhāna, the eight supramundane types become forty by way of the five jhānas.
Among these, excluding the eight associated with the fifth jhāna, they are associated with the remaining thirty-two wholesome-resultants;
thus, mental joy (*somanassa*) is associated with sixty-two types of consciousness. Mental grief (*domanassa*) is associated with two unwholesome types. Equanimity (*upekkhā*)...
[They] are associated with the remaining fifty-five types of consciousness.

Therein, pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object; its function is to nourish associated states; it is manifested as bodily gratification; and its proximate cause is the body faculty.

Pain has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable tangible object; its function is to wither associated states; it is manifested as bodily affliction; and its proximate cause is the body faculty.

Mental joy has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object; its function is to enjoy a desirable mode in whatever way it may be; it is manifested as mental gratification; and its proximate cause is tranquility.

Mental grief has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object; its function is to enjoy an undesirable mode in whatever way it may be; it is manifested as mental affliction; and its proximate cause is exclusively the heart-base.

Equanimity has the characteristic of feeling neutrality; its function is neither over-excitement nor depression toward associated states; it is manifested as a state of peace; and its proximate cause is a mind devoid of rapture.
This concludes the section on the detailed exposition of the aggregate of feeling. Now follows the discussion of the aggregate of perception.

457. Now, as for what was said: “Whatever has the characteristic of perceiving, all that, taken together, should be understood as the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha),” here too, that which is called the characteristic of perceiving is simply perception itself. As it is said:
“It perceives, it perceives, friend; therefore it is called ‘perception. And although this perception is of one kind in its intrinsic nature by virtue of its characteristic of perceiving, it is...
By way of its moral quality (*jāti*), it is threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Among these, that which is associated with wholesome consciousness is wholesome; that associated with unwholesome [consciousness] is unwholesome;

and that associated with indeterminate [consciousness] is indeterminate. Indeed, there is no such consciousness as is dissociated from perception (*saññā*); therefore, to whatever extent there is consciousness...
As for the classification [of perception], how many kinds of perception are there?
Although this [perception] is classified in the same way as consciousness, it has, from the perspective of its characteristic, the single characteristic of perceiving.
Its function is to make a sign of the object as "this is that very thing," just as carpenters and others do with wood and so forth; it acts according to the sign as it was previously grasped.
It has the manifestation of forming an adherence, like blind men [seeing] an elephant;
its proximate cause is the object as it presents itself, like the perception "man" that arose in young deer regarding grass-figures.
This is the section on the detailed exposition of the aggregate of perception.

458. As for what was said, “Whatever has the characteristic of volitional formation (abhisaṅkharaṇa), all that, taken together, should be understood as the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)”:
here, the characteristic of volitional formation means the characteristic of piling up. But what is that?
They are simply formations (*saṅkhārā*). As it is said: "Monks, because they construct the conditioned, they are therefore called 'formations'.
They have the characteristic of constructing; their function is exertion; they are manifested as an outburst; and their proximate cause is the other three aggregates.

Thus, although they are of one kind according to their characteristics and so forth, they are of three kinds by way of genus: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Among these, those associated with wholesome consciousness are wholesome; those associated with unwholesome [consciousness] are unwholesome; and those associated with indeterminate [consciousness] are indeterminate.

Therein, first, those associated with the first wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere are thirty-six: twenty-seven fixed factors that have come down by their own names, four "ye-vāpanaka" (miscellaneous) factors, and five unfixed factors. Among these, they are:
contact, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, zest, energy, life-faculty, concentration, faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

Tranquillity of body, tranquillity of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, malleability of body, malleability of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body, proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, and rectitude of mind—these twenty-seven have come down in their own form.
Then there are: desire, resolve, attention, and equanimity.

These are the four [factors] that are invariably included. Compassion, appreciative joy, abstention from bodily misconduct, abstention from verbal misconduct, and abstention from wrong livelihood—these five are indeterminate.
For these arise only at certain times, and even when they do arise, they do not arise all together.
459. Therein, it "touches," thus it is contact (*phassa*). This has the characteristic of touching. Its function is impinging; its manifestation is the meeting [of the three];

its proximate cause is the object that has come into the range [of the senses]. For although this is a non-material phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*), it occurs toward the object solely by way of the mode of touching.
And although it does not adhere to it in part, the mind—like the eye to visible form or the ear to sound—[engages with the object].

It impinges upon the object; it has "convergence" as its manifestation because it is described by way of its own cause, which is the convergence of the triad [of sense organ, object, and consciousness].

It is said to have "the object that has come into the range" as its proximate cause, because it arises without interval when the object has been prepared by the appropriate attention and the sense faculty.
Furthermore, because it is the basis for feeling, it should be regarded like a flayed cow.

460. It is called *cetanā* because it intends; the meaning is that it binds together. This *cetanā* has the characteristic of being a state of volition, the function of exertion, and the manifestation of purposeful application.
It accomplishes its own task and the tasks of others, like an eldest pupil, a master builder, and so forth.
Furthermore, in cases such as the recollection of urgent duties, this [volition] becomes manifest as it operates through the state of instigating the associated mental factors.

Whatever needs to be said regarding applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and zest (*pīti*) has all already been stated in the commentary on the first jhāna in the description of the earth-kasiṇa.
461. Virility (*vīrabhāva*) is energy (*vīriya*). Its characteristic is exertion; its function is to support co-nascent states; it is manifested as non-collapse.
Because of the statement, “One who is stirred strives thoroughly,” its proximate cause is spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); its proximate cause is also the basis for the arousal of energy.
Or rather, it should be understood that when rightly undertaken, it becomes the root of all success.
462. That by which beings live, or which itself lives, or which is merely the act of living—that is life (*jīvita*).

Its characteristics and other attributes, however, should be understood in the same manner as those stated for material life (*rūpa-jīvita*). For that [material life] is the life of material phenomena, while this [mental life] is the life of immaterial phenomena.
This alone is the distinction here. 463.
It is *samādhi* because the mind is placed evenly (*samaṃ*) upon the object, or it is rightly placed (*sammā*) upon it;

or else, it is simply the state of being concentrated (*samādhāna*) of the mind. Its characteristic is non-distraction (*avisāra*), or its characteristic is non-wavering (*avikkhepa*); its function is to bind together the co-nascent states.

It should be understood as having the manifestation of tranquility (*upasama*), specifically having happiness as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), and being the steadiness of the mind like the steadiness of a lamp’s flame in a windless place.
(464) It is called *saddhā* because by means of it one has faith, or because it itself has faith, or because it is merely the act of believing. That [is faith].
It has the characteristic of believing, or the characteristic of conviction; its function is to clarify, like a water-clearing gem, or its function is to leap forward, like one crossing a flood.

It is manifested as freedom from turbidity, or it is manifested as resolve. Its proximate cause is a thing worthy of faith, or its proximate cause is the factors for stream-entry such as hearing the true Dhamma. It should be regarded as being like hands, wealth, or seeds.
465. It is *sati* because they remember by means of it, or it itself remembers, or it is merely a remembering (*saraṇa*). Its characteristic is not floating away; its function is non-forgetfulness;

its manifestation is guarding, or its manifestation is being directed toward the object; its proximate cause is firm perception, or its proximate cause is the foundations of mindfulness such as the body.
Furthermore, because it is firmly established upon the object, it is like a pillar; and because it guards the doors of the eye and so forth—
And they should be regarded as being like a gatekeeper.

(466) One feels shame (*hiriyati*) because of bodily misconduct and so forth; thus it is *hirī*. This is a designation for modesty (*lajjā*). One feels dread of wrongdoing (*ottappati*) because of those very same things;
thus it is *ottappa*. This is a designation for the state of being agitated by evil. In this context, *hirī* has the characteristic of disgust toward evil.
Moral dread has the characteristic of causing alarm. Modesty has the function of not doing evil through a sense of shame; moral dread has the function of not doing evil through a sense of alarm.
Both have the manifestation of shrinking away from evil in the manner already described, and they have self-respect and respect for others as their proximate cause.
Through modesty, having held oneself in respect, one abandons evil like a well-bred lady; through moral dread, having held others in respect, one abandons evil.
One abandons evil like a courtesan. Furthermore, these two qualities should be regarded as guardians of the world.
467. Non-greed (*alobha*) is so called because one is not corrupted by that [object], or because one is not oneself corrupted, or because it is simply the state of being uncorrupted.

The same method applies to non-hatred (*adosa*) and non-delusion (*amoha*). Among them, non-greed has the characteristic of the mind’s lack of attachment toward an object, and the characteristic of the state of being unclinging.
Or it is like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Its characteristic of non-possessiveness is like that of a monk who has renounced all things;
its manifestation as a state of non-attachment is like a man who has fallen into filth.

(468) Non-hatred has the characteristic of absence of ferocity, or the characteristic of non-opposition, like a well-disposed friend; its function is the removal of resentment, or the removal of feverish heat, like sandalwood; its manifestation as a state of gentleness is like the full moon.
469. Non-delusion (amoha) has the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of things, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer;
its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp; it is manifested as non-confusion, like a guide who knows the way in the forest.
These three [roots] should be regarded as the foundation for all wholesome states.
470. Tranquility of the body is *kāyapassaddhi*. Tranquility of the mind is *cittapassaddhi*.

Here, "body" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). Taken together, both these forms of tranquility of body and mind have the characteristic of the subsiding of bodily and mental distress.
Their function is the crushing of bodily and mental distress. They are manifested as the state of non-agitation and coolness of body and mind.
They have body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as being the opposites of those defilements such as restlessness that prevent the subsiding of body and mind.
Lightness of body is bodily lightness; lightness of mind is mental lightness. Their characteristic is the subsiding of heaviness in body and mind;
their function is to crush heaviness in body and mind; they are manifested as the non-sluggishness of body and mind; they have body and mind as their proximate cause.
They should be understood as being the opposites of those defilements such as stiffness and torpor that cause heaviness of body and mind.
Softness of the body is bodily pliancy; softness of the mind is mental pliancy. Their characteristic is the subsiding of rigidity in body and mind;
their function is to crush bodily and mental stiffness; they are manifested as non-resistance; and their proximate cause is body and mind.
They should be regarded as being the antidotes to defilements such as views and conceit, which cause rigidity of body and mind.
The serviceability of the body is bodily pliancy (*kāyakammaññatā*); the serviceability of the mind is mental pliancy (*cittakammaññatā*).
These have the characteristic of calming the unserviceability of body and mind; their function is to crush the unserviceability of body and mind; [and they are] of body and mind...

They have the accomplishment of making an object as their manifestation; they have the body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be regarded as being like the purification of gold: they are the opposites of the remaining hindrances and so forth that cause unworkability in the body and mind;
they bring about confidence toward inspiring objects; and they bring about a state of fitness for application to beneficial activities.

The state of proficiency of the body is bodily proficiency (*kāya-pāguññatā*); the state of proficiency of the mind is mental proficiency (*citta-pāguññatā*). These [two] belong to the body and mind...

It has the characteristic of the state of being free from illness; its function is to crush physical and mental sickness; it is manifested as the absence of danger; its proximate cause is body and mind.
It should be regarded as the opposite of lack of faith and other factors that produce sickness of body and mind.
Rectitude of the body is bodily rectitude (*kāyujujatā*); rectitude of the mind is mental rectitude (*cittujujatā*). These have the characteristic of straightness of body and mind.
Its function is to crush crookedness of body and mind; its manifestation is straightness; its proximate cause is body and mind.
It should be regarded as the opposite of deceit, guile, and the like, which produce crookedness of body and mind.
(471) "Zeal" (*chanda*) is a designation for the desire to act; therefore, zeal has the characteristic of the desire to act.
Its function is the seeking of an object; its manifestation is the state of needing an object; and that same [seeking] is its proximate cause.
In the grasping of an object, it should be regarded as the stretching out of the mind’s hand.

472. Resolution (*adhimokkha*) is the act of resolving. Its characteristic is decisiveness; its function is non-wavering; its manifestation is certainty; and its proximate cause is the thing to be decided upon. It should be regarded as a city gate-post by way of its immovability with respect to the object.

473. *Kiriya* means making (*kāra*). "Making in the mind" is *manasikāra*. It is also called *manasikāra* because it makes the mind different from its previous state. This [mental engagement] is of three types: that which introduces the object, that which introduces the cognitive process (*vīthi*), and that which introduces the impulsion (*javana*).
Among these, "making in the mind" as the introducer of the object is *manasikāra*. Its characteristic is recollecting; its function is to yoke associated states to the object;
its manifestation is the state of being directed toward the object; its proximate cause is the object. It is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
It should be regarded as like a charioteer in its role of directing the associated mental states toward their object.

"Leading to the cognitive process" (*vīthipaṭipādaka*) is a designation for five-door adverting consciousness; "leading to the impulsion" (*javanapaṭipādaka*) is a designation for mind-door adverting consciousness.
Neither of these is intended here.
474. Equanimity toward those states is "equanimity as a specific neutrality" (*tatramajjhattatā*). It has the characteristic of keeping the mind and mental factors in balance;
its function is to prevent deficiency or excess, or alternatively, its function is to sever partiality; it is manifested as a state of neutrality.

It should be regarded as like a charioteer looking on with equanimity toward well-trained horses that are proceeding evenly, because it maintains a state of detached observation over the mind and mental factors as they proceed in equilibrium.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) should be understood in the same manner as described in the exposition of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). For the only difference is that those [two] reach absorption (*appanā*) and belong to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), whereas these [three] belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

Some, however, include loving-kindness (*mettā*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) among the indeterminate states; that should not be accepted. For in terms of meaning, loving-kindness is simply non-hatred (*adosa*), and equanimity is simply the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

475. Abstinence from bodily misconduct is "abstinence from bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccaritavirati*). This same method applies to the others as well. From the perspective of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), etc.:
These three also have the characteristic of non-transgression regarding the bases for bodily misconduct and so forth; what is meant is that they have the characteristic of not crushing [the mind].

Their function is to contract [the mind] from the bases of bodily misconduct and so forth. They are manifested as non-action. They have faith, moral shame, moral dread, fewness of desires, and other such qualities as their proximate cause.
They should be understood as being the state of the mind’s turning away from evil actions.

476. Thus, it should be understood that these same thirty-six formations enter into association with the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness. And just as they do with the first, so too with the second; the only difference here is the mere presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārabhāva*).
With the third, however, all are to be understood except for non-delusion (*amoha*). The same applies to the fourth; the only difference here is the mere presence of volitional effort.
With the fifth, all those mentioned in the first [consciousness] enter into association except for joy (*pīti*). Just as...
And with the fifth, and likewise with the sixth; here, the only distinction is the mere presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra-bhāva*).

With the seventh, however, one should understand the remaining factors, excluding non-delusion (*amoha*). The same applies to the eighth; here too, the only distinction is the mere presence of volitional effort.
Excluding the three abstinences from those mentioned in the first [jhāna], the rest are associated with the first of the fine-material-sphere wholesome states (*rūpāvacara-kusala*).

They proceed as follows: by the second [jhāna], those [wholesome states] excluding initial application (*vitakka*) from that [first jhāna]; by the third, those excluding sustained application (*vicāra*); by the fourth, those excluding zest (*pīti*);

by the fifth, those excluding both compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) from among the indeterminate states. These same [factors] apply to the four wholesome immaterial-sphere states (*arūpāvacara-kusala*).
For the distinction here consists solely in the state of being immaterial-sphere.

Regarding the supramundane (lokuttara) states: first, in the path-consciousness of the first jhāna, it should be understood according to the method already stated for the first fine-material-sphere consciousness;
in the various types beginning with the second jhāna, it should be understood by the same method as stated for the second fine-material-sphere consciousness and so forth.

However, there is this distinction here: the absence of compassion and appreciative joy, the nature of fixed abstinence, and the supramundane character. Thus, first of all, only wholesome formations are to be understood.

477. Among the unwholesome [states], first, regarding those associated with the unwholesome rooted in greed (*lobha*), there are seventeen: thirteen that have come down by their own specific names as "fixed" (*niyata*), and four that are "included" (*yevāpanaka*).

Therein, contact (*phassa*), volition (*cetanā*), applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), zest (*pīti*), energy (*vīriya*), life-faculty (*jīvita*), concentration (*samādhi*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*)—these are [the factors] by their own specific names.
Thirteen [factors] have arrived. These four—chanda (desire), adhimokkha (resolve), uddhacca (restlessness), and manasikāra (attention)—are the yevāpanaka (miscellaneous) factors.
In this context, one who does not feel shame is *ahirika*. The state of being *ahirika* is *ahirika*. One who does not feel dread of blame is *anottappa*.
Among these, *ahirika* has the characteristic of lacking disgust for bodily misconduct and so forth, or the characteristic of shamelessness. *Anottappa*...
It has the characteristic of lack of shame (*asārajja*) or the characteristic of lack of fear (*anuttāsa*). This is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, should be understood by way of the opposites of what has been said regarding moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).
479. It is called greed (*lobha*) because they are greedy by means of it, or it is itself greedy, or it is merely the state of being greedy. They are deluded...

Because of that, one is either deluded oneself, or the mere state of being deluded is the *taṇti*; thus it is delusion (*moha*). Among these, greed has the characteristic of grasping at an object, like the salivation of a monkey;
its function is clinging, like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan; it is manifested as non-renunciation, like the stain of oil and collyrium;
and its proximate cause is the perception of gratification in things that lead to fetters. By way of the river of craving—
It should be understood that, like a river with a swift current, as it increases, it goes only toward the great ocean of the states of loss (apāya). 480.

Delusion (moha) has the characteristic of blindness of the mind, or the characteristic of non-knowing; its function is non-penetration, or its function is the concealing of the true nature of the object;
it is manifested as wrong practice, or it is manifested as darkness; its proximate cause is improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra).
It should be understood as the root of all unwholesome states.
(481) It is wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) because by means of it they see wrongly, or because it itself sees wrongly, or because its essence is merely wrong seeing.
Its characteristic is irrational insistence; its function is misapprehension; it is manifested as wrong adherence.
The state of not wishing to see the Noble Ones and so forth is the proximate cause for these [defilements], which should be regarded as the supreme faults.
482. Restlessness (*uddhacca*) is the state of being agitated. Its characteristic is lack of tranquility, like water stirred by the impact of the wind;
its function is instability, like a banner or flag fluttering in the wind; its manifestation is wavering, like ashes tossed up by the impact of a stone.
Likewise, mental distraction should be understood as having improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) as its proximate cause for the lack of tranquility of the mind.

The remaining [factors] are to be understood in the same manner as described for the wholesome [states]. For their unwholesome nature itself constitutes their inferiority by way of being unwholesome; this is the distinction between them and those [other factors].
Thus, these seventeen formations enter into association with the first unwholesome consciousness.

They are to be understood. And just as with the first [hindrance], so it is with the second. However, the distinction here lies in the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) and the fact that sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) are not fixed [as to their timing].
In this context, *thīnanatā* is sloth (*thina*), and *middhanatā* is torpor (*middha*). It also refers to a lack of enthusiasm, a lack of firmness, and a failure of capability.
The meaning is as follows: *thina* (sloth) and *middha* (torpor) constitute *thinamiddha*. Therein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of exertion;
its function is the dispelling of energy; it is manifested as despondency. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness; its function is shrouding;
it is manifested as sluggishness, or alternatively, as drowsiness and sleep. Both have unwise attention regarding discontent, yawning, and so forth, as their proximate cause.
By the third [method], those remaining [factors] among those mentioned in the first [section], excluding wrong view, are to be understood. However, conceit (*māna*) here is indeterminate.

This is the distinction: it has the characteristic of puffing up, the function of grasping, the manifestation of desiring to be prominent, and its proximate cause is greed dissociated from views; it should be regarded as like madness.

In the second [jhāna], among those mentioned in the fourth [jhāna], one should understand that all remain except for wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*). Furthermore, in this case as well, conceit (*māna*) occurs among the indeterminate factors.

Among those mentioned in the first [jhāna], however, all remain except for joy (*pīti*), which associate with the fifth [jhāna]. And just as they associate with the fifth, so too do they associate with the sixth.
However, in this context, the state of being accompanied by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) belongs to sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

And the specific distinction is the state of being indeterminate (*aniyata*). By means of the seventh [category], one should understand the remaining factors among those mentioned in the fifth [category], excluding views (*diṭṭhi*).
However, conceit (*māna*) here is indeterminate. By means of the eighth [category], one should understand the remaining factors among those mentioned in the sixth [category], excluding views.
And here too, conceit is indeed included among the indeterminates.
484. Regarding the two [types of unwholesome consciousness] rooted in hatred (*dosa*), first, those associated with the primary [root] are eighteen:

eleven are fixed and listed by their own names, four are included factors (*yevāpanaka*), and three are indeterminate (*aniyata*). Among these, contact (*phassa*), volition (*cetanā*), applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), energy (*vīriya*), life-faculty (*jīvita*), concentration (*samādhi*), moral shamelessness (*ahirika*), moral recklessness (*anottappa*), hatred (*dosa*), and delusion (*moha*) are those listed by their own names.
Eleven [factors]. The four "included" (yevāpanaka) factors are: zeal (chanda), resolve (adhimokkha), restlessness (uddhacca), and attention (manasikāra).
The three "indefinite" (aniyata) factors are: envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), and worry (kukkucca). 485.

In this context, *dosa* is so called because one becomes corrupt (*dussanti*) by means of it, or because it itself is corrupt, or because it is merely the state of being corrupt. Its characteristic is ferocity (*caṇḍikka*).
It has the characteristic of being like a struck venomous snake, or like the spreading effect of a dose of poison, or like a forest fire whose nature is to burn its own support.

Its manifestation is that of a foe who has found an opening; its proximate cause is a basis for resentment; it should be regarded as like stale urine mixed with poison. (486) Envy (*issā*) is the act of envying.

It has the characteristic of being envious of the success of others. Its function is dissatisfaction with that very success. It manifests as turning away from it. Its proximate cause is the success of others; it should be regarded as a fetter.

487. *Maccharabhāva* (the state of being stingy) is *macchariya* (stinginess). It should be understood as having the characteristic of concealing one’s own prosperity—whether already acquired or yet to be acquired;
its function is the inability to endure others sharing that very prosperity; it is manifested as contraction, or alternatively, as harshness and rigidity;
its proximate cause is one’s own prosperity; and it should be seen as a deformity of the mind.
488. That which is done badly is *kukata*. The state of that is *kukkucca* (remorse). Its characteristic is subsequent regret;

its function is to sorrow over what has been done and left undone; it is manifested as remorse; its proximate cause is what has been done and left undone; it should be regarded like slavery. The remaining [factors] are of the same kind as already described.

Thus, these eighteen formations should be understood to associate with the first root of unwholesomeness (greed). And just as they associate with the first, so too with the second (hatred). However, the distinction lies in the presence of volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāratā*) and the occurrence of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) among the undetermined factors.

489. Among the two [types of consciousness] rooted in delusion (*moha*), first, in that associated with doubt (*vicikicchā-sampayutta*), there are eleven factors mentioned by their specific names: contact (*phassa*), volition (*cetanā*), applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), energy (*vīriya*), life-faculty (*jīvita*), mental stability (*cittatthiti*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), delusion (*moha*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*);
and two factors included in the "and-so-forth" category (*yevāpanaka*), namely restlessness (*uddhacca*) and attention (*manasikāra*), making thirteen in total.
490. Therein, "stability of mind" refers to weak concentration consisting merely of the persistence of the process [of consciousness].
"Vicikicchā" means the absence of investigation. It has the characteristic of doubt; its function is to waver; it is manifested as indecision or as the grasping of multiple alternatives;
its proximate cause is unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*); and it should be regarded as an obstacle to progress.
The remaining [factors] are of the same types as those already mentioned.
Among those stated in connection with restlessness-association and doubt-association, twelve remain after setting aside doubt itself.
However, because of the absence of doubt here, resolution (*adhimokkha*) arises; thus, with that included, there are thirteen, owing to the presence of resolution.
And concentration becomes stronger. As for the restlessness (*uddhacca*) here, it has come down in its own specific form.
"By way of the inclusion of resolve and attention" means that unwholesome formations (*akusala-saṅkhāra*) should be understood in this manner. 491.

Among the indeterminate (*abyākata*) states, those that are indeterminate as result (*vipāka-abyākata*) are first of two kinds: distinguished by being rootless (*ahetuka*) and having roots (*sahetuka*). Among these, those associated with rootless resultant consciousness (*ahetuka-vipāka-viññāṇa-sampayutta*)...
They are rootless (*ahetuka*). Therein, first, those associated with wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant eye-consciousness consist of five factors:

the four that come under their own names—contact (*phassa*), volition (*cetanā*), life-faculty (*jīvita*), and mental stability (*cittatthiti*)—plus attention (*manasikāra*), which is included among the "sometimes-mentioned" (*yevāpanaka*) factors. Those associated with ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness are likewise these same five.

In both types of resultant mind-element (*ubhayavipākamanodhātu*), there are eight: these same [five] plus initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), and resolution (*adhimokkha*). Likewise...

This applies to all three types of rootless mind-consciousness element (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*). Furthermore, it should be understood that where this [consciousness] is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), rapture (*pīti*) is additionally present.

However, those associated with resultant consciousness accompanied by roots (*sahetuka-vipāka-viññāṇa*) are themselves accompanied by roots. Among these, those associated with the eightfold sense-sphere resultant [consciousness]...
To that extent, they are exactly like the formations associated with the eight wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

However, as for those [mental factors] among the indeterminate (*aniyata*)—namely, compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*)—because they have sentient beings as their object, they do not exist among the results of kamma (*vipāka*). For the results of the sense-sphere are exclusively restricted to limited objects.

Not only are compassion and appreciative joy absent from the results, but the abstinences (*virati*) are also not found there. For it is said: "The five training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) are exclusively wholesome."
However, those associated with resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane are exactly similar to those associated with wholesome consciousness.
492. Functional indeterminate states are also twofold, distinguished as rootless and with roots. Among these, those associated with rootless functional consciousness are themselves rootless.
These are identical to those associated with the wholesome resultant mind-element and the two types of rootless mind-consciousness-elements. Regarding the two types of mind-consciousness-elements:
However, energy (*vīriya*) is predominant. Because of the presence of energy, concentration (*samādhi*) attains the state of power. This is the distinction here.
As for those associated with wholesome-with-root functional consciousnesses (*sahetuka-kiriya-viññāṇa*), they possess roots.

Among them, first, those associated with the eight sense-sphere wholesome-with-root functional consciousnesses—excluding the abstinences—are similar to the formations associated with the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses. Those associated with the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres...
Furthermore, in every respect, they are indeed similar to those associated with wholesome consciousness; thus, the indeterminate formations should also be understood in this way.
This concludes the introduction to the detailed exposition on the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
This, first of all, is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the aggregates according to the method of word-analysis (*padabhājaniya*) in the Abhidhamma.
493. Discourse on the Analysis of the Past and So Forth:
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle..."
Whether inferior or superior, far or near—having gathered all that together and condensed it into one—this is called the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).
Whatever feeling there is... whatever perception there is... whatever formations there are... whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present...
[as before] ...having condensed it, this is called the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*).”
Thus the aggregates have been explained in detail.
Therein, "whatever" (*yaṃkiñci*) is an exhaustive inclusion; "form" (*rūpa*) is a restriction to prevent over-extension.
Thus, by these two terms, the complete grasping of form is accomplished. Then, its classification according to the past and so forth is undertaken. For that—
Some are past, some are future, and so on according to their divisions.

This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. 494. In that regard, first, matter is called "past" in four ways: by way of extent (*addhā*), continuity (*santati*), period (*samaya*), and moment (*khaṇa*). Likewise for the future and the present. Therein, first, by way of extent:
for a single individual in one existence, what is prior to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is past; what is subsequent to death (*cuti*) is future; and what is between those two is present.
That which arises from a homogeneous temperature or nutriment within a single continuity, even while occurring in a temporal sequence of before and after, is "present.
That which arose previously from heterogeneous temperature or nutriment is "past," and that which will arise later is "future.

That which is mind-born, arising from a single cognitive series, a single impulsion, or a single attainment, is "present"; that which arose before it is "past," and that which will arise later is [future].
Regarding the future: for that which is produced by kamma, there is no distinction of past and so forth by way of a separate continuity;
rather, its status as past and so forth should be understood by way of its support for those very [material phenomena] produced by temperature, nutriment, and consciousness.

By way of time—occurring through a continuity during such periods as one muhutta, forenoon, afternoon, night, day, and so on—it is called "present" at that particular time; prior to that it is "past," and subsequent to that it is "future."
By way of moment, that which is included within the three moments of arising and so forth is the present; prior to that is the future; subsequent to that is the past.
Furthermore, that which has completed its function as a cause and condition is the past; that which has finished its causal function but whose conditional function is not yet finished is the present;
that which has not yet reached either function is the future. Or else, it is the present at the moment of performing its own function; from that...
What precedes is future; what follows is past. And herein, the discussion of moments (*khaṇa*) and so forth is in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*);

the rest are in the indirect sense (*sapariyāya*). 495. The distinction between internal and external is exactly as the method already stated. Furthermore, it should be understood that here "internal" refers to one's own internal [states], while "external" refers to those belonging to another person. The distinction between gross and subtle is also exactly as the method already stated.
496. The distinction between inferior and superior is twofold: in the indirect sense and in the direct sense. Therein, from the perspective of form, [it extends] up to the Akaniṭṭha [heaven].
The form of the Sudassī devas is inferior; that same form is superior compared to the form of the Sudassa devas.
Thus, the distinction between the inferior and the superior should be understood in this relative sense, extending down to the forms of beings in the hells.
However, in the absolute sense, wherever unwholesome kamma-result arises, that is inferior; wherever wholesome kamma-result arises, that is superior.
"Far and near"—this too is exactly as previously explained. Furthermore, here "far" and "near" should be understood in relation to one another according to their spatial location.

497. "Having gathered that together and condensed it": having made into a single heap by means of wisdom all that form which was specified separately by the terms "past" and so forth, within its single nature characterized by the quality of being subject to change (ruppana).

"It is called the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*)," this is the meaning here. By this, it is shown that all form (*rūpa*) is the "aggregate of form" by virtue of its arrival at the state of a heap within the characteristic of being afflicted (*ruppana*). For there is no such thing as an "aggregate of form" other than form itself.

And just as it is with form, so too are feeling and the others [aggregates] by virtue of their arrival at the state of a heap within the characteristics of being felt (*vedayita*), and so forth. For there are no such things as an "aggregate of feeling" and so on other than feeling and the rest themselves.

Regarding the classification into past and so forth herein, the state of feeling as past, future, and present should be understood by way of the continuity (*santati*) and by way of the moment (*khaṇa*), and so on.

Therein, by way of continuity, those feelings included within a single cognitive process (*vīthi*), a single impulsion (*javana*), or a single attainment (*samāpatti*), as well as those occurring in conjunction with the object of a single process, are "present";
those prior to them are "past," and those subsequent are "future. By way of the moment and so forth, those included within the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution] are [present].
Feeling that pertains to the past, the future, and the present, and which performs its own function, is "present"; prior to that it is "past," and subsequent to that it is "future.
The distinction between internal and external should be understood by way of one's own internal self (niyakajjhatta).
499. The distinction between the gross and the subtle is as follows: "Unwholesome feeling is gross; wholesome and indeterminate feeling is subtle," and so forth.

It should be understood according to the method stated in the *Vibhaṅga*, by way of genus (*jāti*), intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), person (*puggala*), mundane (*lokiya*), and supramundane (*lokuttara*).

First, by way of genus: unwholesome feeling is gross compared to wholesome feeling because it is the cause of blameworthy activity, because its mode is one of the fever of the defilements, and because its course is unpacified;
also because it involves active effort, exertion, and fruition, and because its mode is the fever of the defilements.

It is grosser than the indeterminate-without-result (kiriyābyākatā) because it is accompanied by fault (sāvajja), has a result (savipāka), involves the torment of the defilements (kilesasantāpa), and is associated with affliction (sabyābajjha).

Furthermore, it is grosser than the indeterminate-ineffective (kriyābyākatā) because it is accompanied by fault and has a result. Conversely, the wholesome-indeterminate (kusalābyākatā) is subtle compared to the unwholesome (akusalā) according to the opposite of what was stated above.
Both wholesome and unwholesome feelings are, as the case may be, characterized by activity (sabyāpāra), exertion (saussāha), and result (savipāka).
The two kinds of indeterminate [states] are gross; conversely, both kinds of indeterminate [states] are subtle in relation to those.
Thus, first of all, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of genus.
500. By way of intrinsic nature, however, painful feeling is gross because it is devoid of gratification, because it is expansive, and because it causes agitation.
The [first] two are grosser than the other two because they are terrifying and overwhelming;
however, the other two are subtler than the painful [feeling], as appropriate, because they are pleasant, peaceful, sublime, agreeable, and neutral.

Both pleasure and pain are grosser than the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling because they are expansive, agitating, and manifest; whereas that [neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling] is the opposite of what was stated [for the former two].
Therefore, they are subtle in both respects. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

Furthermore, by way of the person (*puggala*): the feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption (*asamāpanna*) is gross because it is distracted among various objects; conversely, the feeling of one who has attained absorption is subtle. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood by way of the person. By way of the mundane and the supramundane (*lokika-lokuttara*):
feeling associated with the taints (*sāsavā*) is mundane, because it is a cause for the arising of taints and because it is subject to the floods (*ogha*).

In terms of being subject to bondage, subject to the ties, subject to the hindrances, subject to clinging, subject to defilement, and shared by worldlings, they are gross with respect to the taintless state.
By way of the opposite, they are subtle with respect to that which is with-taints. Thus should grossness and subtlety be understood by way of the mundane and the supramundane.
502. In this context, the distinctions [between types of feeling] by way of birth and so forth must be avoided.

For feeling associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, although it is subtle due to its being indeterminate (*avyākata*) by way of birth, it is nevertheless gross by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and other such factors.

Indeed, this has been said: "Indeterminate feeling is subtle; painful feeling is gross. Feeling of one who has attained meditative absorption is subtle; [feeling] of one who has not attained absorption..."
“Feeling is gross; feeling associated with the taints (āsava) is gross; feeling dissociated from the taints is subtle.
Just as painful feeling is gross, so too pleasant feeling and the others are gross by way of their birth (jāti), while they are subtle by way of their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and so forth.
Therefore, the grossness and subtlety of feelings should be understood in such a way that there is no confusion regarding their birth and other such factors.
For example: by way of birth, the indeterminate (abyākatā) are subtler than the wholesome and unwholesome. In that regard, what is indeterminate? Is it painful? Is it pleasant?
Does it belong to one who has attained meditative absorption? Does it belong to one who has not attained absorption? Is it with taints (sāsavā)? Is it without taints (anāsavā)?
Thus, the distinction according to intrinsic nature and other such factors should not be misapprehended. This same method applies everywhere.
