Furthermore, according to the statement that "feeling should be regarded as gross or subtle relative to this or that particular feeling," even among unwholesome states and the like, feeling accompanied by greed (*lobha*) is gross because it burns its own support like a fire, whereas feeling accompanied by greed is subtle.
Feeling accompanied by hatred (*dosa*) is also gross when it is of fixed result (*niyata*), and subtle when it is of unfixed result (*aniyata*). Even among those of fixed result...

Those that endure for an eon (*kappaṭṭhitika*) are gross (*oḷārika*), while the others are subtle (*sukhuma*). Among those that endure for an eon, the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) are gross, while the others are subtle.
Furthermore, those accompanied by greed (*lobha*) and associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhi-sampayutta*) are gross, while the others are subtle.
Even among those, the fixed (*niyata*), eon-enduring, and unprompted are gross, while the others are subtle. And in general, unwholesome states (*akusala*) have abundant fruition (*vipāka*).
Those with little result are subtle. However, wholesome states with little result are gross, while those with much result are subtle.

Furthermore, wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are gross; those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are subtle; those of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) are subtler than those; and supramundane (*lokuttara*) states are subtler still.

Within the sense sphere, those consisting of giving (*dānamaya*) are gross; those consisting of virtue (*sīlamaya*) are subtle; and those consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*) are subtler than those. Even among those consisting of meditation, those with two roots are gross.

Those with three roots are gross; those with three roots are subtle. Even among those with three roots, those accompanied by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārika*) are gross, while those unaccompanied by volitional effort (*asaṅkhārika*) are subtle.
Those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) associated with the first jhāna are gross... [and so on] ...those associated with the fifth jhāna are subtle.

Those of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) associated with the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) are gross... [and so on] ...those associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) are indeed subtle.
Furthermore, supramundane feelings associated with the path of stream-entry are gross... [and so on] ...while those associated with the path of arahantship are subtle.

This same method applies to the resultant and functional feelings of each respective plane, and to the feelings described by way of being painful and so forth, non-attained and so forth, and with taints and so forth.
Also by way of location: in hell, painful feeling is gross; in the animal realm, it is subtle... [and so on] ...up to the gods who wield power over the creations of others.
Subtle. And just as with the painful, so too with the pleasant, it should be applied everywhere as appropriate.
Furthermore, by way of basis, any feeling that has an inferior basis is gross; that which has a superior basis is subtle.
Within the division of inferior and superior, that which is gross should be understood as inferior, and that which is subtle as superior.
503. As for the term "distant" (*dūrapada*), it is stated: "Unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings.
The term "near" (*santikapada*) is analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga* according to the method beginning with: "Unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling," and so forth.

Therefore, unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings by way of being of a different class (*visabhāga*), not being conjoined (*asaṃsaṭṭha*), and not being similar (*asarikkha*); likewise, [the others are distant from it].

Wholesome and indeterminate [states] arise from an unwholesome [state]. This same method applies to all sections. However, unwholesome feeling arises from an unwholesome [feeling] by way of its own kind (*sabhāga*) and by way of similarity (*sarikkha*).
This is the introduction to the detailed exposition regarding the classification of the aggregate of feeling into past and so forth.
It should be understood that the same applies to perception and the other [mental factors] associated with each respective feeling.
The Discourse on the Determination of the Sense-Spheres,
etc., 504. Having understood this, one should further [investigate] these very aggregates for the purpose of analyzing knowledge according to their order and their distinctions:
By way of neither deficiency nor excess, and likewise by way of simile,
and by way of the twofold aspect of what is to be seen, and because of the accomplishment of the goal for one who sees thus—
the method of determination should be correctly understood by the discerning person.
In this context, "order" (*kama*) refers to many kinds of order, such as the order of arising, the order of abandoning, the order of practice, the order of planes, and the order of teaching.
Among these, the "order of arising" is exemplified by such passages as: "First there is the *kalala*; from the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*.

The "order of abandoning" is exemplified by such passages as: "States to be abandoned by seeing; states to be abandoned by cultivation. The "order of practice" is exemplified by such passages as: "Purification of virtue..."

“Purification of mind,” and so forth, is the sequence of practice (*paṭipattikkamo*). “Belonging to the sense sphere, belonging to the fine-material sphere,” and so forth, is the sequence of planes (*bhūmikkamo*).
“The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors,” or “the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue,” and so forth, is the sequence of teaching (*desanākkamo*).
Among these, first of all, the sequence of arising (*uppattikkamo*) is not applicable here, as it is with the aggregates such as the *kalala* and so on.
It is not according to the sequence of arising, because they do not arise sequentially. It is not the sequence of abandoning, because the wholesome and the indeterminate are not to be abandoned.
It is not the sequence of practice, because the unwholesome are not to be practiced. It is not the sequence of planes, because feeling and the other [aggregates] are included within all four planes.
However, the sequence of teaching is appropriate.

For the Blessed One, desiring the welfare of those to be trained—who had fallen into the grasping for a self by viewing the five aggregates as an undifferentiated whole—wished to free them from that grasping by means of a vision that analyzes the compact mass.

Therefore, for the sake of easy comprehension for various individuals, he first taught the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), which is coarse and the objective domain of the eye and other senses. Following that, [he taught] that which experiences desirable and undesirable forms...
Feeling. Perception is that which grasps the mode of the object of feeling, according to the principle: "What one feels, that one perceives.
Formations are those that construct by way of perception. And consciousness is the support and the dominant factor for these [factors] beginning with feeling.
In this way, first of all, the method of analysis according to sequence should be understood.

505. "By way of distinction" means by way of the distinction between the aggregates (*khandhā*) and the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*). What, then, is their distinction? First, the aggregates are stated without distinction. The aggregates of clinging are distinguished by their state of being associated with taints (*sāsava*) and being subject to clinging (*upādāniya*).
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging;
listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever form, bhikkhus, whether past, future, or present... [and so forth].
Or near—at hand—this, monks, is called the aggregate of form. Whatever feeling... [as before] ...whatever consciousness...
[as before] ...or near—at hand—this, monks, is called the aggregate of consciousness. These, monks, are called the five aggregates. And what, monks, are the five aggregates subject to clinging?

Whatever form, monks... [as before] ...or near—at hand—[is the aggregate of form]. Whatsoever feeling... [as before] ...whatsoever consciousness... [as before] ...or near—at hand—this, monks, is called the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. These, monks, are called the five aggregates subject to clinging.

Or whatever feeling... [as before] ...or whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, that is accompanied by taints and subject to clinging—this, monks, is called the aggregate of clinging to form.
This, monks, is called the aggregate of clinging to feeling... [as before] ...this, monks, is called the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
These, monks, are called the five aggregates of clinging.”
And here, while there are such things as feeling and so forth that are untainted (*anāsava*), form is not like them.
However, because its status as an aggregate (*khandha*) is tenable in the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*), it is mentioned among the aggregates.

And because its status as a "clinging-aggregate" (*upādānakkhandha*) is tenable both in the sense of a heap and in the sense of being tainted, it is mentioned among the clinging-aggregates. Feeling and the others, however, are exclusively untainted.
They are called "aggregates" (*khandhā*) in general; they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*) when they are subject to taints (*sāsava*).

Herein, the meaning of "aggregates of clinging" should be understood as "those aggregates which are the domain of clinging. However, in this context, all of these taken together are intended by the term "aggregates."
506. Why did the Blessed One state that there are exactly five aggregates, neither fewer nor more?

It is because all conditioned phenomena are subsumed under a single homogeneous class; because this [classification] is the ultimate extent of the basis for grasping at a self or what belongs to a self;

and because all other [phenomena] are included within it. For when the variously differentiated conditioned phenomena are grouped according to their homogeneity, even form is included by way of its inclusion within the homogeneous class of form.
There is one aggregate. Feeling is one aggregate by way of being included within its own homogeneous class (*vedanā-sabhāga*).

This same method applies to perception (*saññā*) and the others. Therefore, because of their inclusion within their respective homogeneous classes among all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*), only five are mentioned.

Furthermore, this is the ultimate basis for the grasping of "self" and "belonging to self," namely, these five beginning with form (*rūpa*). For it has been said: "Bhikkhus, when form exists, depending on form, [clinging arises]..."
“By adhering [to it], this view arises: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
When there is feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, by clinging to consciousness and adhering to consciousness, this view arises:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Therefore, [it is the basis] for the grasping of a self and what belongs to a self.”

Even according to this ultimate reckoning, only five are stated. Furthermore, those other five aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandhas) mentioned, such as virtue and so forth, are included right here because they are comprised within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Therefore, since others are included therein, only five are stated;
in this way, the method of determination regarding neither deficiency nor excess should be understood.

507. Regarding the phrase "like a simile": here, the aggregate of clinging to form (*rūpupādānakkhandha*) is like a sickroom, because it is the place of residence for the aggregate of clinging to consciousness (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*), which is like a patient, by way of being its basis, door, and object. The aggregate of clinging to feeling (*vedanupādānakkhandha*) is like the illness itself, because it is afflictive.

The aggregate of clinging to perception (*saññupādānakkhandha*) is like the origin of the illness, because of the presence of feelings associated with lust and so forth, through such things as perceptions of sensual desire.
The aggregate of clinging to formations is like unwholesome food, because it is the cause of the ailment of feeling; for it is said: "They form formations for the sake of feeling.
Likewise: "Due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome kamma, resultant body-consciousness arises accompanied by suffering. The aggregate of clinging to consciousness is like a patient.

Because they are not free from the fever of feeling (*vedanā*). Furthermore, these should be understood through their method of determination by way of similes: as the simile of the prison, the executioner, the criminal, and the offender; and as the simile of the vessel, the food, the curry, the server, and the eater. 508.
"In two ways as to how it is to be regarded" means that here it is to be regarded in two ways: briefly and in detail. Thus it is in two ways as to how it is to be regarded.

The method of exposition should be understood. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are to be regarded, according to the method stated in the *Āsīvisa-upama Sutta* (Simile of the Venomous Snake), as an enemy with an upraised sword;
according to the *Bhāra Sutta* (Discourse on the Burden), as a burden; according to the *Khajjanīya-pariyāya* (Method of the Edible), as an eater;
and according to the *Yamaka Sutta* (Twin Discourse), as a murderer characterized by impermanence, suffering, non-self, and the conditioned. In detail, however, here—
Form should be viewed like a mass of foam because it cannot withstand being squeezed; feeling like a water bubble because it is delightful for only a moment;
perception like a mirage because it deceives; mental formations like the trunk of a plantain tree because they lack substance;
and consciousness like an illusion because it is deceptive. And specifically, even internal form, however beautiful it may be—
It should be seen as "the foul" (*asubha*). Feeling (*vedanā*) is "suffering" (*dukkha*) because it is not exempt from the three kinds of suffering.

Perception (*saññā*) and formations (*saṅkhārā*) are "non-self" (*anattā*) because they cannot be wielded at will. Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is "impermanent" (*anicca*) because its nature is to arise and pass away—this is how it should be seen.
509. "For one who sees thus, there is the accomplishment of the goal": this refers to seeing in two ways, by way of both brief summary and detailed exposition.
The method of analysis should be understood even from the accomplishment of this purpose. To explain:
in brief, one who views the five aggregates of clinging as being like an enemy with an upraised sword and so forth is not oppressed by the aggregates.
In detail, however, one who views form and the other aggregates as being like a lump of foam and so forth does not perceive a core in what is coreless.
And specifically, by seeing internal material form as foul, one fully understands physical nutriment,
abandons the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the foul, crosses the flood of sensual desire, becomes dissociated from the bond of sensual desire,
becomes free from the taint of sensual desire, breaks the bodily tie of covetousness, and does not cling to the clinging of sensual desire.
Seeing feeling as suffering, one fully understands the nutriment of contact; one abandons the perversion of regarding suffering as pleasure;
one crosses over the flood of existence; one becomes dissociated from the yoke of existence; one becomes free from the taint of existence; one breaks the bodily tie of ill-will;
and one does not cling to the clinging to rules and observances.
Seeing perception and mental formations as non-self, one fully understands the nutriment of mental volition; one abandons the perversion of regarding what is non-self as self;
one crosses over the flood of views; one becomes dissociated from the yoke of views;
one becomes free from the taint of views. One breaks the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence that "this is the truth," and one does not cling to the clinging to a self-theory.
One who contemplates consciousness as impermanent fully understands the nutriment of consciousness; one abandons the perversion that takes the impermanent to be permanent;

one crosses over the flood of ignorance; one becomes dissociated from the yoke of ignorance; one becomes free from the taint of ignorance; one breaks the bodily tie of clinging to rules and observances;
and one does not cling to the clinging to views.
Since seeing [the aggregates] as a murderer and so forth has such great benefit,
therefore a wise person should see the aggregates as a murderer and so forth.
Thus ends the Path of Purification composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Fourteenth Chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Aggregates," in the Section on the Development of Wisdom.
15. Exposition of the Bases and Elements:
Detailed Discussion of the Bases 510.

"Bases" refers to the twelve bases: the eye base, the visible-form base, the ear base, the sound base, [the nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the flavor base, the body base, the tangible-base, the mind base, and the mental-phenomena base].
The nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the flavor base, the body base, the tangible-object base, the mind base, and the mental-object base. Regarding these:
first, there are the characteristics, the number, the order, the summary, and the detailed exposition.
In this way, the exposition should be understood and known.
Therein, specifically: first, it is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) because it sees; the meaning is that it relishes and discerns visible form (*rūpa*).

It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is formed; the meaning is that, undergoing transformation of color, it manifests its state as being present before the heart. It is called "ear" (*sota*) because it hears.
*Sappaṭi* means sound; the meaning is that it is uttered. *Ghāyati* means the nose. *Gandhayati* means odor;
the meaning is that it indicates its own basis. *Jīvitaṃ avhayati* means the tongue. *Rasanti taṃ sattā* means taste;
the meaning is that beings relish it. *Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyo* means the body (*kāya*); *āyo* means the place of arising. *Phusiyati* means the tangible (*phoṭṭhabba*).
It is called *mano* because it "measures" (*munāti*). They are called *dhammā* because they "bear their own characteristics" (*lakkhaṇaṃ dhārenti*).

Furthermore, in general, it should be understood as an *āyatana* (base) because of its being a base (*āyatanato*), because of the stretching forth of what comes (*āyānaṃ tananato*), and because of leading that which has come (*āyatassa ca nayanato*).

For, in the case of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, the mental states and mental factors—such as consciousness and feeling—experience each [object] through their respective modes of experiencing and so on.
They "strive" (āyatanti) means they exert themselves, rise up, strive, and make an effort;
it is said that they "stretch out" these phenomena which have become their source (āya), meaning they expand them.
And this suffering of saṃsāra, which has proceeded through the beginningless cycle of existence and is exceedingly long, they "lead on"—meaning they cause it to proceed—until it ceases.

Thus, all these phenomena are called "bases" (*āyatana*) because they are a basis for the arrival [of consciousness], because they extend that which arrives, and because they lead that which has arrived.
Furthermore, a base should be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, a source, a meeting place, a region of birth, and a cause.
For instance, in common usage, one speaks of "the abode of Īśvara" (*issarāyatana*), "the abode of Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāyatana*), and so forth.
A place of residence is called an *āyatana*. In such expressions as “a gold mine (*suvaṇṇāyatana*)” or “a silver mine (*rajatāyatana*),” it means a source.

In the Dispensation (*sāsana*), however, in such passages as “birds frequent that delightful *āyatana*,” it means a meeting place. In such expressions as “the Southern Road (*dakkhiṇāpatho*) is the *āyatana* of cattle,” it means a region where something is born.
[And] when it is said, “In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization (*sakkhibhabbataṃ*)... [it refers to the sense-spheres].
In such passages as “when there is a sense-base,” it refers to the cause.

Furthermore, because those various states of consciousness and mental factors dwell within the eye and so forth—since their existence is dependent upon them—the eye and other faculties are the dwelling places of those states.
And within the eye and other faculties, they are crowded together because they are supported by them and take them as their object.
The eye and so forth are their source; the eye and so forth are their meeting place, because they meet there and there by way of the physical basis, the door, and the object.
The eye and so forth are their place of birth, because they arise right there through having those as their support and object.
The eye and so forth are their cause, because in their absence [the consciousnesses] are absent. Thus, in the sense of being a dwelling place...

These phenomena are called "bases" (āyatana) for the following reasons: in the sense of a mine, in the sense of a place of convergence, in the sense of a region of origin, and in the sense of a cause.

Therefore, according to the meaning already stated, it is called the "eye-base" because it is both the eye and a base; ... [and so on] ... it is called the "mental-object-base" because they are both mental objects and a base. Thus, first of all, the analysis should be understood here according to its meaning.

513. Regarding "characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*): here, the exposition should be understood by way of the characteristics of the eye and the other [senses]. And those characteristics of theirs are to be understood in the same manner as stated in the Exposition of the Aggregates (*Khandhaniddesa*).
Regarding "as far as their extent" (*tāvatvato*): this means "by way of their respective existence. This is what is meant: for even the eye and the rest are indeed phenomena (*dhammā*).

This being so, if one asks why they are called twelve bases (*āyatana*) instead of simply being called the "base of phenomena" (*dhammāyatana*), it is because of the determination of the doors, objects, and the arising of the groups of consciousness.
Here, these twelve are stated because they are defined by way of being the doors and the objects for the six groups of consciousness;

for the eye-base alone is the door of arising and the visible-object-base alone is the object for the group of consciousness included in the cognitive series of eye-consciousness, and likewise for the others in relation to their respective counterparts.
However, for the sixth [consciousness], only a portion of the mind-base (manāyatana) known as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is the door of arising, and the dhammāyatana alone is its specific object.
Thus, because the doors of arising and objects of the six groups of consciousness have been defined, twelve bases are stated;
this is how the analysis should be understood here by way of enumeration.
514. Regarding the phrase "in order of their arising" (*kamatoti*), here too, as in the cases previously mentioned, it is the order of the teaching (*desanākkamo*) that is appropriate.
For among the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*), the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) was taught first because its object is visible and impinging (*sanidassanasappaṭigha*), making it more manifest;

following that, the ear-base and the others were taught, as their objects are non-visible but impinging (*anidassanasappaṭigha*). Alternatively, it is due to their being the causes for the unsurpassed sight (*dassanānuttariya*) and the unsurpassed hearing (*savanānuttariya*).
Because they are of great assistance, among the internal bases, the eye-base and the ear-base are taught first;

after that, the three beginning with the nose-base; the mind-base is at the end because it is the objective domain for all five; and the external bases, beginning with the visible-form base, are placed between each of those respectively because they are the domains of the eye-base and so forth.
Furthermore, [the order is established] by way of defining the causes for the arising of consciousness.
This sequence should be understood for these [bases]. For it has been said: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises... pe...
dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. Thus, the exposition here should be understood according to this sequence.
515. As to brief and detailed: briefly, [this refers] to the mind base and to one portion of the mental-object base.

Since the remaining [ten] bases are comprised within "name" (nāma) by way of their designation and within "form" (rūpa) by way of their physical nature, all twelve bases are merely name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
In detail, first among the internal bases, the eye-base is merely the sensitivity of the eye by way of its genus;
however, it has infinite subdivisions according to the distinctions of conditions, destiny, category, and individual. The same applies to the four bases beginning with the ear-base.

The mind-base (manāyatana) is divided into eighty-nine types by way of the distinction between wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness, and into one hundred and twenty-one types.

Furthermore, it is of infinite variety when distinguished by way of its physical bases, modes of access, and so forth. The bases of visible form, sound, odor, and flavor are of infinite variety due to distinctions such as their heterogeneous conditions.
The tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana) is threefold by way of the earth element, the fire element, and the air element.

It has many divisions according to the distinctions of conditions and so forth. The sense-sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) has many divisions according to the distinctions in the specific characteristics and diversity of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as subtle matter and Nibbāna.
Thus the exposition should be understood both in brief and in detail. 516.
Regarding the phrase "to be seen": here, all conditioned bases (*āyatana*) are [to be seen] by way of neither coming nor going.
And they are to be seen thus: for these do not come from anywhere prior to their arising, nor do they go anywhere after their passing away;
rather, prior to their arising, they have not yet acquired their own nature, and after their passing away, their nature has been dissolved.
In the interval between the past and the future, they proceed dependent on conditions, having no independence. Therefore, because they do not come...
They should also be regarded as being without exit. Likewise, they are without effort and without activity.
For it does not occur to the eye, visible forms, and so forth, "O, may consciousness indeed arise through our combination!
Nor do they strive for the sake of producing consciousness by way of acting as a door, a basis, or an object; nor do they engage in any activity. Then...

This is indeed the natural law (*dhammatā*): that eye-consciousness and the rest arise from the coming together of the eye, visible forms, and so forth. Therefore, they should be regarded as inactive and devoid of effort.
Furthermore, the internal bases should be regarded as like an empty village, because they are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and a self-entity.
The external bases should be regarded as like the thieves who plunder that village, [for they assail] the internal bases.
Because they are subject to impact. For this has been said in detail: "The eye, bhikkhus, is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms," and so forth.
Furthermore, the internal [bases] should be regarded as like six creatures, and the external [bases] as their respective domains.
In this way, the analysis here should be understood from the perspective of how they are to be regarded.
This, then, is the section on the detailed exposition of the bases (*āyatana*).

Next, regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*): there are eighteen elements—the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, [the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue element, the flavor element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element].
The ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element;
the tongue element, the flavor element, the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element;
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. Therein—
By way of meaning, characteristics, and so forth, as well as by order, number, and enumeration;
then the conditions are to be seen, and the detailed exposition is to be understood.
Therein, "by way of meaning": it sees, thus it is the eye (*cakkhu*); it manifests form, thus it is form (*rūpa*); consciousness of the eye is eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
In this manner, by such a method, the analysis of the eye and the other [senses] should be understood according to their specific meanings.

However, in a general sense, it is called *dhātu* because it "lays out" (*vidahati*), "is laid out" (*dhīyate*), "is a laying out" (*vidhānaṃ*), "is laid out by means of this" (*vidhīyate etāya*), or "in this [element] is laid out" (*ettha vā dhīyati*).
For mundane elements, having been established as causal factors, [produce results] just as gold, silver, and other mineral ores produce gold, silver, and so forth.
They burn with manifold kinds of suffering in saṃsāra. They are borne, or maintained, by sentient beings like a burden by those who carry it—this is the meaning.
Moreover, they are merely the instruments of the infliction of suffering, because [beings] lack mastery over them.

And by means of these [aggregates], which function as instruments, the suffering of saṃsāra is experienced by sentient beings. Furthermore, that [suffering], being thus ordained, is borne and established in these very [aggregates].

This is the meaning. Thus, each individual phenomenon among the eye and the rest is called a "constituent" (*dhātu*) by way of its function—such as "it disposes" (*vidahati*) or "it is disposed" (*dhīyati*)—according to how it occurs.
Furthermore, just as the so-called "self" (*attā*) does not exist according to its own intrinsic nature for the heterodox teachers (*titthiya*), these [phenomena] are not like that;

rather, they are "constituents" because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Just as in the world various mineral components such as yellow orpiment and realgar are called "constituents" (*dhātu*).
They are called "elements" (dhātu) just as those [minerals] are elements; for these are the diverse components of that which is to be known by wisdom.

Or, just as the designation "element" is applied to the constituents of a whole—such as bile, blood, and so forth—which are parts of what is termed a "body" and are distinguished from one another by dissimilar characteristics, so too is the designation "element" applied to these [aggregates], which are the components of the personal existence termed the five aggregates.
They should be understood thus: for these, beginning with the eye, are demarcated by their mutually dissimilar characteristics.

Furthermore, "element" (*dhātu*) is a designation for that which is merely devoid of a soul (*nijjīva*). For it was for the purpose of uprooting the perception of a living soul that the Blessed One gave the teaching on the elements in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, this person consists of six elements."

Therefore, in the sense already stated, it is the eye and that element which is the eye-element … and so on … it is mind-consciousness and that element which is the mind-consciousness-element. Thus, first of all, the analysis here should be understood according to its meaning. 519. As to characteristic, etc.:

the analysis here should also be understood by way of the characteristics and so forth of the eye and the rest. And those characteristics and so forth of theirs should be understood in the same manner as explained in the *Niddesa* on the aggregates (*khandhaniddesa*).
As to order: here too, among the orders previously mentioned—such as the order of arising and so forth—it is the order of teaching (*desanākkama*) that is appropriate. And this [order] is as follows:

It is stated by way of the successive determination of cause and fruit. For this dyad—“eye-element” and “visible-object-element”—is the cause, while “eye-consciousness-element” is the fruit. It is thus in all instances.
(520) “By way of its extent” means by way of its limited nature. This is what is meant: for in various passages of the Suttas and the Abhidhamma...

“The light element, the beauty element, the base of infinite space element, the base of infinite consciousness element, the base of nothingness element, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception element, the cessation-of-perception-and-feeling element;
the sense-desire element, the ill-will element, the cruelty element, the renunciation element, the non-ill-will element, the non-cruelty element; the pleasure element, the pain element.”
the element of joy, the element of displeasure, the element of equanimity, the element of ignorance;
the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of perseverance; the inferior element, the intermediate element, the superior element;
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element; the conditioned element, the unconditioned element.
Other elements are also seen, such as “the world has many elements, various elements,” and so forth.
If this is so, why is the limit set at eighteen instead of making no distinction among all of them?
Because all elements that exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) are included within those eighteen.

For the light-element (*ābhā-dhātu*) is indeed the fine-material element (*rūpa-dhātu*), whereas the beautiful-element (*subha-dhātu*) is bound up with form and so forth. Why? Because it has the sign of the beautiful (*subha-nimitta*) as its characteristic.
For the beautiful-element is the sign of the beautiful; and that does not exist apart from form and the rest.

Alternatively, form and the rest themselves, when they are objects of wholesome kamma-resultant consciousness, are the beautiful-element; thus this [element] consists merely of form and the rest. In the case of the space-infinity-base element (*ākāsānañcāyatana-dhātu*) and the others, the mind...

The mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) alone [is included], while the remaining ones are the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*). However, the element of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu*) does not exist as a distinct intrinsic nature.
For it is merely the state of the cessation of those two elements.
Or, the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) is merely the mental-object element. As it is said: "In this context, what is the sense-sphere element? That which is associated with sensual desire..."
“Reasoning, applied thought, and wrong intention. Or else, there are eighteen elements. As it is said:
“Taking the Avīci hell as its lower limit and including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas above, whatever is within this interval—whether aggregates, elements, or bases;
whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—[is included therein].”
“This is called the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu).
The renunciation-element (nekkhammadhātu) is indeed the mental-object element (dhammadhātu), because of the statement: “All wholesome states (kusala-dhamma) are the renunciation-element”;

thus, the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is also included therein. The elements of ill-will, cruelty, non-ill-will, non-cruelty, pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, ignorance, initiative, exertion, and perseverance are also indeed the mental-object element.
The inferior, intermediate, and superior elements are merely eighteen elements. For the eye and so forth that are inferior are the inferior element;

those that are intermediate and superior are both the intermediate and superior elements. But in the absolute sense, the unwholesome mental-object element and mind-consciousness element are the inferior element;
the mundane wholesome and indeterminate elements, as well as both sets of the eye-element and so forth, are the intermediate element; and the supramundane [elements] are the superior element.
However, the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) are the sublime element (*paṇītadhātu*).

The earth, fire, and air elements are simply the tangible-object element (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*); the water element and the space element are simply the mental-object element. The consciousness element is merely a summary of the seven consciousness elements beginning with eye-consciousness.

Seventeen elements and a portion of the mental-object element are conditioned elements (*saṅkhatadhātu*), whereas the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatadhātu*) is only a portion of the mental-object element.

Furthermore, the world of manifold elements and diverse elements is merely a classification of eighteen elements. Thus, because all elements existing by way of their own nature are included therein, only eighteen are mentioned.
Moreover, even for the purpose of uprooting the perception of a "living soul" (jīva) in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing, only eighteen are taught.
It has been said. For there are beings who perceive a "living soul" (jīva) within consciousness (viññāṇa), whose intrinsic nature is knowing.

Desiring to eradicate their long-standing latent perception of a soul, the Blessed One—having demonstrated its manifoldness through the division into the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element, and having demonstrated its impermanence because it exists in dependence upon conditions such as the eye and visible forms—proclaimed the eighteen elements (dhātu). Furthermore, likewise...

And according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*). Furthermore, those beings who are to be trained by this teaching—which is neither too concise nor too prolix—are revealed as being exactly eighteenfold, according to their respective inclinations.
For, by way of both summary and detailed exposition, it is presented in various such manners.
He proclaims the Dhamma in whatever way is appropriate for each;
by the power of the True Dhamma, the darkness within the hearts of those beings who are ready to be trained is destroyed and vanishes in an instant.
Thus, first of all, the analysis here should be understood according to their number.
(522) As for "conditioned": first, the eye-element is reckoned as a single phenomenon by way of its genus, namely, the sensitivity of the eye;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible-form, sound, odor, and taste elements are so reckoned by way of the sensitivity of the ear and so forth; and the tangible-object element...
Furthermore, it is reckoned as three phenomena by way of earth, fire, and air. The eye-consciousness element is reckoned as two phenomena by way of wholesome and unwholesome resultants;

likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body-consciousness elements. The mind element, however, is reckoned as three phenomena by way of the five-door adverting consciousness, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the resultant receiving consciousness.

It is so designated. The element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*) is reckoned as twenty phenomena by way of the three immaterial aggregates, the sixteen subtle material phenomena, and the unconditioned element.
The mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) is reckoned as seventy-six phenomena by way of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousnesses.
Thus, herein the exposition should be understood in terms of the conditioned as well.

523. Regarding "condition" (*paccaya*): here, first of all, the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*) acts as a condition for the eye-consciousness-element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*) by way of six conditions—namely, dissociation, pre-existence, presence, non-disappearance, support, and faculty.
The visible-form element (*rūpadhātu*) acts as a condition for it by way of four conditions—namely, pre-existence, presence, non-disappearance, and object.
In the same way, the ear-consciousness-element and so forth [are related] to the ear-element, sound-element, and so forth.

Furthermore, among these five, the adverting mind-element (āvajjana-manodhātu) is a condition for the five [subsequent consciousnesses] by way of five conditions: proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), absence (natthi), disappearance (vigata), and decisive support (upanissaya).
And those same five are [conditions] for the receiving mind-element (sampaṭicchana-manodhātu).

Likewise, the receiving mind-element is a condition for the investigating mind-consciousness-element (santīraṇa-manoviññāṇadhātu), and that [investigating mind-consciousness-element] is a condition for the determining mind-consciousness-element (voṭṭhabbana-manoviññāṇadhātu), and the determining mind-consciousness-element...

And [it is a condition] for the impulsion mind-consciousness element. However, the impulsion mind-consciousness element is a condition for the immediately subsequent impulsion mind-consciousness element by way of those same five conditions and by way of the repetition condition (*āsevanapaccaya*);
thus, it is a condition by way of six conditions. This, first of all, is the method regarding the five doors.
Regarding the mind door, however, the life-continuum mind-consciousness element is a condition for the advertence mind-consciousness element; and the advertence mind-consciousness element...
Furthermore, the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) acts as a condition for itself through the first five types of conditions.

The mental-object element (dhammadhātu), however, acts as a condition for all seven consciousness elements in many ways, such as by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).
Moreover, the eye-element and so forth, as well as certain portions of the mental-object element, act as conditions for certain portions of the mind-consciousness element.

They also function as conditions by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and others. For the eye-consciousness element and the rest, it is not only the eye, visible forms, and so forth that serve as conditions;
rather, light and other factors do as well. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
"Eye-consciousness arises dependent upon the eye, visible forms, light, and attention. Ear-consciousness [arises] dependent upon the ear, sounds, an opening, and attention..."
“Dependent on the ear and sounds and the attention directed toward them, ear-consciousness arises. Dependent on the nose, odors, and the attention directed toward them, nose-consciousness arises.
Dependent on the tongue, tastes, and the attention directed toward them, tongue-consciousness arises.

Dependent on the body, tangibles, and the attention directed toward the earth element, body-consciousness arises. Dependent on the life-continuum, mental objects, and the attention directed toward them, mind-consciousness arises.”

This is the summary here. However, the detailed classification of conditions will be revealed in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Thus, the analysis should be understood here by way of conditionality.
524. "As to how they are to be seen": the meaning is that the analysis should be understood here also by way of how they are to be seen.

For all conditioned elements (*saṅkhata-dhātu*) are indeed to be seen as secluded from the past and the future, as empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood, and as existing in dependence upon conditions.
In particular, however, here the eye-element should be regarded as like the surface of a drum, the visible-object element as like the drumstick, and the eye-consciousness element as like the sound.
Likewise, the eye-element is like the surface of a mirror, the visible-object element like a face, and the eye-consciousness element like the reflection of the face.
Alternatively, the eye-element is like sugarcane or sesame seeds, and the axle of the machine-wheel is like the visible-object element.
The visible-object element is like [the lower fire-drill], the eye-consciousness element is like honey, sugar, and oil.

Likewise, the eye element is like the lower fire-drill, the visible-object element is like the upper fire-drill, and the eye-consciousness element is like the fire. This same method applies to the ear element and the others.
As for the mind element, it should be regarded as preceding and following the eye-consciousness element and the rest, according to how they arise.
Within the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) should be regarded as like a dart and like a stake.

The aggregates of perception (*saññā*) and formations (*saṅkhāra*) are like those afflicted by the application of the dart and stake of feeling; or, for worldlings (*puthujjana*), perception is like an empty fist because it generates the suffering of hope, and like a wild animal because it grasps signs that do not correspond to reality. Formations are so called because they cast one into rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Form should be viewed as being like charcoal embers to those who throw them at people; like a bandit pursued by royal guards because he is followed by suffering due to birth;

like seeds of a poisonous tree because they are the cause for the continuity of the aggregates which bring about all manner of harm; and like a wheel of razors because it is the sign of various kinds of calamities.
However, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) should be viewed as the deathless, as peace, and as security.
Why? Because it is the direct opposite of that which brings about all harm.
The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) is like a monkey in the forest because it lacks stability among its objects; like a wild colt because it is difficult to tame;
like a stick thrown into the air because it falls wherever it pleases; and because it is associated with the various manifestations of defilements such as greed, hatred, and so forth.
They should be regarded as like actors on a stage.
Thus ends the section on the Development of Wisdom in the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Fifteenth Chapter, titled "Exposition of the Bases and Elements. 16.
Exposition of the Faculties and Truths.
The Discourse on the Detailed Exposition of the Faculties (Indriyavitthārakathā) 525. Following the elements, the faculties were enumerated; these are the twenty-two faculties:
the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, and the male faculty.
The life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty, the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty,
the faith faculty, the energy faculty, the mindfulness faculty, the concentration faculty, the wisdom faculty, the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty,
the final-knowledge faculty, and the final-knower faculty. Therein—
One should understand the analysis [of these faculties] by way of meaning, characteristics, and so forth, as well as by way of order, classification and non-classification, function, and plane.
Therein, first, the meaning of the eye and the others is clarified by the method beginning with "it sees, therefore it is the eye" (*cakkhati iti cakkhu*). In the latter [faculties],...

However, among the three, the first is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) because it arises in one who has entered the practice in the prior stage with the thought, "I shall know the Deathless state or the Dhamma of the Four Truths which was previously unknown," and because it possesses the sense of a faculty.
The second is the faculty of "knowing" (*aññindriya*) because it arises from the act of knowing and possesses the sense of a faculty. The third belongs to one who has already known.

The faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya) arises because it occurs in one whose taints are destroyed and who has completed the task of knowledge regarding the four truths, and because it possesses the sense of a faculty.

What, then, is this so-called "sense of a faculty" (indriyattha)? It is the sense of a faculty in the sense of being a characteristic of a lord (indaliṅga). It is the sense of a faculty in the sense of being taught by a lord (indadesita).

It is the sense of a faculty in the sense of being seen by a lord (indadiṭṭha). It is the sense of a faculty in the sense of being permitted by a lord (indasiṭṭha). It is the sense of a faculty in the sense of being frequented by a lord (indajuṭṭha).
Thus, everything here is applicable according to its respective fitness. For the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the *Inda* (Lord) by virtue of his supreme state of sovereignty.
And wholesome and unwholesome karma is [the *Inda*] among karmas, because no one else possesses sovereignty over karmas.

Therefore, in this context, the faculties (*indriya*) produced by karma first indicate wholesome and unwholesome karma; and since they are established by that [karma], they are called "faculties" in the sense of being the marks of the Lord (*indaliṅga*).
They are called *indriyas* in the sense of being "ruled by a lord" (*indi-sittha*).

Furthermore, because all of these were proclaimed and fully awakened to by the Blessed One exactly as they truly are, they are *indriyas* in the sense of being "taught by the Lord" (*indi-desita*) and in the sense of being "seen by the Lord" (*indi-diṭṭha*).

For that very reason, since some of them were cultivated by the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, through the cultivation of the field of activity (*gocara-sevanā*) and others through the cultivation of meditation (*bhāvanā-sevanā*), they are also *indriyas* in the sense of being "adorned by the Lord" (*indi-juṭṭha*).
Furthermore, these are called "faculties" (indriya) also in the sense of sovereignty (issariyattha), which is defined as predominance (ādhipacca).

For the predominance of the eye and so forth is established in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and the rest; for when that [faculty] is keen, [the consciousness] is keen, and when it is dull, it is dull.
This, then, is the analysis of the meaning here.

"By means of the characteristics, etc. means that one should understand the analysis of the eye and the other [faculties] by way of their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), function (*rasa*), manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

Their respective characteristics and so forth have already been stated in the "Exposition of the Aggregates" (*Khandhaniddesa*). For the four beginning with the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) are, in actual fact, nothing other than non-delusion (*amoha*);
the remaining ones are presented there in their own essential form.

526. "In order" (*kamatoti*)—this too is merely a sequence of teaching. In this context, because the attainment of the noble plane occurs through the full understanding (*pariññā*) of internal phenomena, the faculties such as the eye, which are included within the personal existence (*attabhāva*), are taught first.
Furthermore, that personal existence is designated as "woman" or "man" depending upon certain factors; therefore, these [faculties] are taught first for the purpose of illustration.
Then, the female faculty and the male faculty. Then, for the purpose of making known that both of these two function in dependence upon the life-faculty, the life-faculty [is mentioned].

Then, for the purpose of making known that as long as that [life-faculty] continues to proceed, there is no cessation of these feelings, and that whatever is felt is all suffering, the faculties of pleasure and so forth [are mentioned]. For the purpose of the cessation of that [suffering]—
Next, the faculties beginning with faith are mentioned for the purpose of showing the practice, in the sense that "these states are to be developed.

Then, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) is mentioned for the purpose of showing the fruitfulness of that practice, in the sense that "by means of this practice, this state first becomes manifest within oneself.
Immediately following that, because it is the fruit of that very [faculty] and because it is to be developed next, the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) is mentioned.

Following that, the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) is taught at the end as the ultimate consolation, for the purpose of making it known that this [path] is attained through meditation and that once this has been attained, there is nothing further to be done. This is the sequence here. Regarding their classification and lack of classification:

here, there is a classification only of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). For that is twofold: the material life-faculty and the immaterial life-faculty. There is no classification of the remaining ones. Thus should one understand the determination here by way of classification and lack of classification.
527. As for "function": if it is asked what the function of the faculties is, first, regarding the eye-faculty:

because of the statement, "The eye-base is a condition by way of faculty-condition for eye-consciousness and for those states associated with it," that which is to be established by way of being a faculty-condition is the state of sharpness, dullness, and so forth, in eye-consciousness and the other states, reckoned as sharp, dull, and so on, [due to] its own state of sharpness, dullness, and so forth.
Causing those co-nascent states to conform to its own mode—this is the function. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
For the mind faculty (*manindriya*), however, it is the exercising of mastery over its co-nascent states. For the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*), it is the preservation of its co-nascent states.

For the female and male faculties (*itthindriya-purisindriya*), it is the conformity to the characteristics, signs, gestures, deportment, and physical forms of a woman or a man. For the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief...
It is the overcoming of co-arisen states and the bringing about of their respective coarse modes; the bringing about of the peaceful, sublime, and neutral mode for the faculty of equanimity;
the overcoming of the opposites of faith and the rest, and the bringing about of the state of clarity and so forth in the associated states;
and for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," it is both the abandoning of the three fetters and the causing of the associated states to be oriented toward that abandoning.

The function of the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) is both the attenuation and abandonment of sensual lust, ill will, and so forth, as well as the bringing of its co-nascent factors under its own control.

The function of the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is both the abandonment of exertion in all tasks and the state of being a condition for associated states to be directed toward the Deathless.
In this way, one should understand the analysis of these faculties by way of their functions.
528. Regarding the "planes" (bhūmi): here, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, masculinity, pleasure, pain, and grief belong exclusively to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

The faculty of mind (manindriya), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), the equanimity-faculty (upekkhindriya), and the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (saddhā-vīriya-sati-samādhi-paññindriyāni) are included within all four planes.
The faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) is included in three planes by way of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and the supramundane (lokuttara).
"At the end, three are supramundane alone"—thus one should understand the analysis here according to plane as well. For one who understands thus:
"The bhikkhu, full of spiritual urgency, established in the restraint of the faculties, having fully understood the faculties, will make an end of suffering."
This is the section on the detailed exposition of the faculties.
529. The detailed exposition of the truths follows immediately after that;
namely, the four noble truths: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering...
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Regarding these: [They are explained] by way of analysis, etymology, the distinctions of characteristic and so forth, the extraction of the meaning, and likewise by way of neither deficiency nor excess.
By way of sequence, by the determination of birth and so forth, by the function of knowledge,
by the inclusion of its various divisions, by way of similes, by way of the fourfold sets, by emptiness,
by the single-fold and so on, and by way of the similar and the dissimilar.
The exposition should be understood by the wise according to the sequence of the teaching.

Therein, "by way of analysis" means that four meanings each for suffering and the other [truths] have been analyzed—true, not false, and not otherwise—which are to be fully realized by those who are realizing suffering and the rest.
As it is said: "The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned..."
The meaning of burning, the meaning of change—these four are the meanings of suffering as suffering; they are such, not otherwise, and not different.
The meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, the meaning of impediment—these are the meanings of origin.

The meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, the meaning of the deathless—these are the meanings of cessation. The meaning of outlet, the meaning of cause, the meaning of seeing, the meaning of predominance—these are the meanings of the path.
"These four are the meaning of the path as the path; they are such, not otherwise, and not different. Likewise:
"The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization," and so forth.
Thus, suffering and the other [truths] are to be understood by way of these fourfold sets of meanings as thus analyzed. This, then, is the exposition here by way of analysis.
530. Regarding the phrase "by way of the distinctions of derivation, characteristic, and so forth":

here, first of all, as to derivation, the word *du* is seen in the sense of the contemptible (*kucchita*). For they say that a contemptible son is a "bad son" (*dupputto*). The word *kha*, however, refers to the void (*tuccha*).
For the void sky is called "space" (*kha*). And this First Truth is contemptible because it is the locus for manifold calamities.

It is empty because it is devoid of the state of being permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and a self as imagined by foolish people. Therefore, because it is base and empty, it is called "suffering" (*dukkha*).
Furthermore, this word *saṃ-* indicates conjunction, as in such phrases as "coming together" (*samāgama*) and "united" (*sameta*). This [word] *u-* [indicates] "arisen" (*uppanna*)...

In such passages as “arisen” (*udita*), [the suffix] indicates origination. The word *aya* signifies a cause. Furthermore, this second truth is the cause for the origination of suffering when there is the conjunction of the remaining conditions.
Thus, because it is the cause for the origination of suffering through its conjunction with suffering, it is called the "origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*).
As for the third truth, since the prefix *ni-* signifies non-existence and the word *rodha* signifies confinement, therefore it is non-existence...
Here, it is called the "cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodha*) because the prison of saṃsāra—which is characterized as suffering—is empty of all destinations;
or, when that [emptiness] is attained, there is an absence of the prison of saṃsāra characterized as suffering, because it is the opposite of that [suffering].
Alternatively, it is called the cessation of suffering because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering.

As for the fourth truth, it is called the "path leading to the cessation of suffering" because it proceeds toward that cessation by way of being its object—since it is directed toward it—and because it is the practice for the attainment of the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, because these truths are penetrated by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, they are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*).
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four Noble Truths. Which ones... [omitted] ...These, bhikkhus, are the Noble Truths."
“There are four noble truths. Noble ones penetrate these; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.
Furthermore, they are ‘noble truths’ because they are the truths of the Noble One (ariya). As it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas...
including humans, the Tathāgata is the Noble One; therefore they are called noble truths. Alternatively, they are so called because the Noble One has fully awakened to them.”
They are called "Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni) because they are established by the noble state (*ariyabhāva*). As it is said:
"Monks, because he has fully awakened to these four Noble Truths as they really are, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, is called 'Noble' (*ariya*).
Furthermore, they are "Noble Truths" in the sense that they are truths belonging to the Noble Ones (*ariyāni saccāni*). "Noble" means that they are suchness, not otherwise, and non-deceptive.
This is the meaning. As it has been said: “These, monks, are the four noble truths; they are such, not otherwise, not different; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.
In this way, the analysis [of the term] should be understood here according to its etymology. 532. How [should it be understood] according to the classification by characteristics and so forth?
For here, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppression (*bādhanalakkhaṇa*), and its function is tormenting (*santāpanarasa*).

The truth of suffering has the characteristic of occurrence; its function is to manifest; it is manifested as a burden. The truth of origin has the characteristic of source; its function is to cause non-interruption; it is manifested as an impediment.
The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace; its function is deathlessness; it is manifested as the signless.

The truth of the path has the characteristic of outlet; its function is the abandoning of defilements; it is manifested as emergence. Furthermore, they have the characteristics of occurring, causing occurrence, ceasing, and causing cessation.

In succession. Likewise, conditioned craving and the characteristics of seeing the unconditioned—thus should the analysis here be understood according to the distinctions of characteristics and so forth. 533.
"And by way of extracting the meaning from the meaning": herein, first, as to the meaning, what is the meaning of truth (*sacca*)? That which is seen by the eye of wisdom...
To those who investigate it, [the world] is not like an illusion—deceptive—or like a mirage—misleading—and it does not have the nature of being unfindable like the "self" (attā) of the sectarians;
rather, by way of its true, non-erroneous, and real state, characterized by affliction, origination, and the path of transcendence, it is indeed the objective domain of noble knowledge (ariyañāṇa).
This true, non-erroneous, and real state is like the characteristic of fire and like the natural order of the world.
It should be understood as "the true meaning" (*saccaṭṭho*). As it is said in detail: "Bhikkhus, 'this is suffering'—this is real, this is not unreal, this is not otherwise. Furthermore:
"Since suffering does not oppress [in any other way], and nothing other than suffering is oppressive..."
By way of the principle of sublation, this is considered the Truth.
Without that [craving], suffering does not arise from anything else, nor does it cease when that [craving] is absent.
By way of the principle of the cause of suffering, thus is "clinging" (visattikā) the Truth.
There is no peace other than Nibbāna, nor is that which is peaceful not it;
because it is established by the nature of peace, it is therefore considered the Truth.
There is no way of deliverance other than the Path, nor is that [Path] one that does not lead to deliverance.
Because it is not subject to being cut down, it is thus considered "truth" (sacca). Thus,

the wise have declared that the meaning of truth (saccaṭṭha) consists in its being undistorted, unperverted, and real across all four [noble truths], such as suffering and the rest, without distinction.
Thus should the analysis be understood according to its meaning.
534. How [is it understood] by way of extracting the meaning? Here, this word *sacca* (truth) is seen in many meanings.

For example, in such passages as "One should speak the truth and not be angry," it refers to verbal truth (*vācāsacca*). In such passages as "The recluses and brahmins are established in truth," it refers to...

Regarding "abstinence and truth" (*viratisacce*): in passages such as, "Why do those who speak of truths, proponents of various views, and those who declare what is skillful [speak differently]? it refers to the truth of views (*diṭṭhisacca*).
In passages such as, "For there is only one truth, not a second," it refers to the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), namely Nibbāna and the Path (*magga*).

In passages such as, "Of the four noble truths (*ariyasacca*), how many are wholesome? it refers to the noble truths. Since this [term *sacca*] here also applies to the noble truths, it is so used in this context.
The exposition should also be understood by way of the extraction of the meaning.
535. As for "neither less nor more": why are exactly four noble truths stated, neither fewer nor more?
Because nothing else is possible and because there is nothing among them that can be removed. Indeed, there is nothing else besides these, nor is there anything redundant.
Or, even one of these can be removed, as it were; for it has been said: “In this case, monks, should a recluse or a brahmin come and say, ‘This is not the noble truth of suffering;
there is another noble truth of suffering. Setting aside this noble truth of suffering, I shall proclaim another noble truth of suffering,’ such a possibility does not exist,” and so forth.
And as it is said: "Bhikkhus, it is impossible that any ascetic or brahmin should say:
'This which has been taught by the ascetic Gotama as the first noble truth of suffering is not suffering;
rejecting this first noble truth of suffering, I shall proclaim another as the first noble truth of suffering. And so forth.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One explained the process of existence (*pavatti*), he explained it with its cause; and when he explained cessation (*nivatti*), he explained it with its means.

Thus, at most, only four factors have been stated: existence, its cause, cessation, and its means. Likewise, this applies to that which is to be fully understood, that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be realized, and that which is to be developed;

to the basis for craving, craving itself, the cessation of craving, and the means for the cessation of craving; and to the attachment, delighting in attachment, the uprooting of attachment, and the means for the uprooting of attachment.
Since only four are mentioned even by way of their basis, the analysis here should be understood as being neither deficient nor redundant. 536.
As for "in order": this too refers to the sequence of the teaching.

And herein, because it is coarse and because it is common to all beings, the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) is stated first; immediately after that, for the purpose of showing its cause, [the truth of the origin is stated].

The truth of the origin [of suffering]. Then, for the purpose of making known that with the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of the fruit, the truth of cessation follows. Finally, for the purpose of showing the means to attain that [cessation], the truth of the path is taught.
Alternatively, suffering is mentioned first in order to generate a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in beings who are attached to the gratification of the pleasure of existence.
That [suffering] does not come unmade, nor does it arise from the creation of a Supreme Lord (*issara-nimmāna*) and so forth; rather, it arises from this [cause].
Immediately after that, origination is taught for the purpose of making it known.

Then, for those whose minds are agitated because they are overwhelmed by suffering accompanied by its cause, and who are seeking an escape from suffering, cessation is taught for the purpose of generating consolation through the vision of the escape. After that, the path—which brings about the attainment of cessation—is taught for the purpose of reaching that cessation.
Thus, the analysis of the sequence here should be understood.
537. Regarding the determination of birth and so forth: those noble truths which were demonstrated by the Blessed One as he taught, "Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering;
sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering;
separation from the pleasant is suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering."
In the description of suffering, there are twelve phenomena: "The five aggregates of clinging are suffering. In the description of the origin, there is threefold craving:

"That craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
[And] "the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishing, its abandoning..."
In the description of cessation (*nirodhaniddesa*), it is stated: "Liberation is non-attachment"; thus, in terms of its meaning, there is only one *nibbāna*.

In the description of the path (*magganiddesa*), it is stated: "What is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this very noble eightfold path. That is to say: right view... [and so on]... right concentration"; thus, there are eight factors.
Therefore, in the descriptions of the four truths, various phenomena such as birth and so forth have been mentioned.
The detailed exposition (vinicchaya) should also be understood here by way of the determination of birth and the other [links].
The Discussion on the Exposition of Suffering;
the Exposition of Birth.
For example, this word *jāti* has many meanings. Thus, in the passage, “one birth, two births,” it refers to existence (*bhava*).
In the passage, “There are, Visākhā, those called Nigaṇṭhas, a class of recluses,” it refers to a group (*nikāya*).
In the passage, “Birth is comprised within two aggregates,” it refers to a conditioned characteristic (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*). [And] in the passage, “That which first [enters] the mother’s womb...”
In the passage, "The mind has arisen, the first consciousness has appeared; based on that, there is his birth," it refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
In the passage, "The Bodhisatta was just born, Ānanda," it refers to physical birth (*pasūti*). In the passage, "Unassailed and unreviled by talk of birth," it refers to the family.
In the passage, "From the time I was born, sister, with noble birth," it refers to noble virtue (*ariyasīla*).

538. Here, for those born from a womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*), it should be understood that [the aggregates] refer to those occurring from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) until emergence from the mother’s womb; for others, they refer only to the aggregates at rebirth-linking.
Moreover, this is merely an explanatory discourse (*pariyāyakathā*). However, in the absolute sense (*nippariyāyato*), for beings being reborn here and there, whichever...
The aggregates manifest; their first manifestation in each respective case is called birth (*jāti*).

This, moreover, has the characteristic of being the initial production in this or that state of existence; its function is to deliver [one] over [to that state]; it is manifested as emerging here from a past existence, or it is manifested as the diversity of suffering.
Why is this suffering? Because it is the basis for many kinds of suffering. For there are indeed many sufferings.
That is to say: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, figurative suffering, and literal suffering.
Therein, bodily and mental painful feelings are called the "suffering of suffering" because they are suffering both by their intrinsic nature and by name.
Pleasant feeling is suffering through change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), because it is the cause for the arising of suffering through transformation.

Both equanimous feeling and the remaining formations (*saṅkhārā*) belonging to the three planes are suffering due to formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), because they are oppressed by arising and passing away.
Physical and mental afflictions—such as earaches, toothaches, and the fever born of lust or the fever born of hatred—having been asked about...

Because it must be known through inquiry and because its cause is not manifest, it is called "concealed suffering" (*paṭicchanna-dukkha*). It is also called "non-manifest suffering" (*apākaṭa-dukkha*).

Illness arising from the thirty-two types of judicial torture and so forth is called "unconcealed suffering" (*appaṭicchanna-dukkha*), because it must be known without inquiry and because its cause is manifest. It is also called "manifest suffering" (*pākaṭa-dukkha*).

Setting aside the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), all the rest—birth and so forth—as it appears in the analysis of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca-vibhaṅga*), is "suffering by way of metaphor" (*pariyāya-dukkha*) because it serves as the basis for various forms of suffering. However, the suffering of suffering is said to be "suffering in the primary sense" (*nippariyāya-dukkha*).

In this regard, birth is that suffering pertaining to the states of woe which was illustrated by the Blessed One through similes in such discourses as the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*, as well as the suffering that arises even in the happy realms within the human world, beginning with the descent into the womb.
It is suffering because it is its basis.
540. Herein, this suffering is divided into that rooted in the descent into the womb and so forth:
for when this being is being reborn in the mother’s womb, he is not reborn among blue, red, or white lotuses and the like; rather, he is below the stomach and above the intestines.

In the region of the belly, which is situated between the layers of the abdomen, the backbone, and the ribs— a place of extreme confinement, thick with darkness, pervaded by winds of most foul odor infused with the stench of various corpses,
and exceedingly loathsome— he is born there like a worm in putrid fish, putrid sour gruel, or a cesspool. Having been born there,
for ten months he is cooked as if by a process of steaming by the heat produced within the mother’s womb.
Being squeezed like a lump of dough, deprived of the ability to contract or extend its limbs, it experiences extreme suffering;
this, first of all, is the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb.
Furthermore, when that [embryo] is in the hands of a drunkard or a gambler, [it suffers] during the mother’s sudden stumbling, walking, sitting, rising, turning over, and so forth.

Like a goat in the hands of a snake-charmer, or like a young snake in the hands of a snake-charmer, he experiences excessive suffering through such treatments as being pulled back and forth, shaken, and tossed about.
Furthermore, when his mother drinks cold water, he is as if reborn in a cold hell;
when she swallows hot gruel, rice, and so forth, he is as if surrounded by a falling shower of glowing coals; and when she swallows salt, sour liquids, and the like—
Like one who has reached the place of execution for crimes such as receiving bribes, he experiences intense suffering; this is the suffering rooted in the maintenance of the womb.

Furthermore, when the mother’s pregnancy becomes obstructed, she is brought to a place of suffering where even friends, ministers, and kinsmen are not permitted to see her, and suffering arises through cutting, tearing, and so forth; this is the suffering rooted in the failure of the pregnancy.
And when the mother is giving birth, [the child] is turned by the winds born of karma into a state as utterly terrifying as a fall into hell.
As he is being expelled through the vaginal opening— which is extremely narrow like the hole of a palm-wood pestle—
the great being experiences suffering like that of a mahānāga elephant or a hell-being being crushed by colliding mountains;
this is the suffering rooted in birth.

Furthermore, when that newborn whose delicate body resembles a fresh wound experiences suffering— comparable to being pierced by needle points or split by razor edges— at the time of being grasped by the hand, bathed, washed, rubbed with cloth, and so forth,
this is the suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb.

The suffering that subsequently arises for one who, during the course of existence, inflicts injury upon oneself by engaging in the practice of self-mortification and austerity through such means as the naked ascetic’s observances,
or who abstains from food out of anger, or who hangs oneself— this is suffering rooted in one's own initiative (*attūpakkamamūlaka*).
