However, the suffering that arises for one who undergoes execution, imprisonment, and so forth at the hands of others— this is suffering rooted in the initiative of another (*parūpakkamamūlaka*).
Thus, for all this suffering, birth is indeed the basis.
Therefore, it is said:
"If a being were not to be born in the hells..."
"Would one not obtain suffering—such as being burned by a real fire—which is difficult to endure? Where, then, could it find a footing?
Thus did the Sage here say that birth is suffering.
In the animal realm, there is manifold suffering arising from the striking of whips, goads,
and sticks; how could one take birth in such a place?
In that realm, even birth itself is suffering.
Furthermore, among the hungry ghosts (petas), suffering is manifold, arising from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and so forth.
Because that which is unborn does not exist therein,
for this reason also the Sage called birth "suffering.
And in the intense darkness and the unbearable cold,
Whatever suffering exists among the asuras in other worlds does not exist there,
nor would there be birth for one who has gone thither;
yet even from that world, this birth is suffering.
And even as in the excrement-hell, so too in the mother’s womb,
the being dwells for a long time; and when emerging from there,
it encounters suffering that is exceedingly terrible— yet even this does not exist [for the enlightened].
"Without birth, indeed—this birth is suffering.
What is the use of much speaking?
Is there not, anywhere at all, some kind of suffering here at any time?"
"Since there is nothing at all that is free from birth,
the Great Sage declared at the very outset that 'birth is suffering.
This, then, is the analysis of birth.

542. "Aging is suffering": here aging is twofold—the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), which is recognized as decrepitude and so forth, and the state of the aggregates (*khandha*) having become worn out within a single continuity (*santati*) included in one existence;
it is this latter that is intended here. Furthermore, this aging has the characteristic of the maturation of the aggregates.

Its function is to bring about death; it is manifested as the destruction of youth. It is suffering both because it is of the nature of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and because it is a basis for suffering.

For whatever bodily and mental suffering arises—having as its conditions the loosening of limbs and joints, the disfigurement of the sense faculties, the destruction of youth, the impairment of strength, the loss of mindfulness and intelligence, and being despised by others—aging is the basis for that. Therefore, this is said:
“From the loosening of the limbs, from the transformation of the faculties,
from the destruction of youth, and from the impairment of strength;
from the separation of oneself from one’s virtuous qualities and from one’s children and wife.”
“Because it leads to being despised and because it brings about even greater foolishness,
the suffering that a mortal attains— both physical and mental—
all this has old age as its cause; therefore, old age is suffering.”
This is the analysis of aging.
543. Regarding the statement "death too is suffering," here too death is twofold: the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), with reference to which—

It is said: "Old age and death are comprised within two aggregates. That which is intended here is the interruption of the continuity of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) included within a single existence, with reference to which it was said:
"There is constant fear of death. Death conditioned by birth is also classified as that very same [death], namely:
death by violence, natural death, death through the exhaustion of the lifespan, and death through the exhaustion of merit.
This is its name. It has the characteristic of passing away, the function of dissociation, and it is manifested as departure from one’s place of existence.
Furthermore, it should be understood as "suffering" because it serves as the basis for suffering. Thus it is said:
"For one who contemplates evil as the sign of evil kamma and so forth..."
The mental suffering, without distinction, that arises for one who is being separated from beloved objects, or for one who is dying,
as well as the suffering of all beings arising from the severing of joints and bonds, and so forth— [all this is mental].
For those whose vital organs are being pierced, there arises bodily suffering that is unbearable and incurable. Since this is the source of such suffering,
death is therefore described as suffering itself.
This is the analysis of death. 544. Regarding the exposition of sorrow and the rest:
"Sorrow" (soka) refers to the burning of the mind in one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth. Although in its actual meaning...
There is only mental distress (*domanassa*). Even so, it is characterized by inward brooding, its function is to consume the mind, and it is manifested as constant grieving.
Furthermore, it is suffering both by way of the suffering of suffering and by way of being a basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
"Sorrow pierces the hearts of beings like a poisoned arrow."
Like a flame, it burns even more fiercely than a mass of fire;
and because it brings about the breaking up of disease, old age, and death,
as well as manifold suffering, it is therefore called "suffering."
This is the analysis of sorrow (*soka*). 545.
Lamentation (*parideva*):
Lamentation is the verbal outpouring of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and other such misfortunes. Its characteristic is wailing; its function is the proclaiming of virtues and faults.

It has the manifestation of agitation. It is suffering, however, because it is of the nature of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*) and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“That which, when one is struck by the dart of sorrow and lamenting, is difficult to endure due to the drying up of the throat, lips, and palate.”
"One attains even greater suffering;
therefore, the Blessed One called lamentation 'suffering.
This is the analysis of lamentation (*parideva*).

Suffering (dukkha) 546. What is called suffering is bodily suffering; it has the characteristic of afflicting the body, the function of producing mental distress in those lacking wisdom, and it is manifested as physical affliction.
It is called "suffering" because it is the suffering of suffering itself and because it brings about mental suffering. Therefore, this is said:—
“Because it oppresses this bodily suffering and, moreover, generates mental suffering,
for that reason it is specifically called ‘suffering.
This is the analysis of suffering.
547. *Domanassa* (mental grief) is mental suffering. It has the characteristic of oppressing the mind; its function is to afflict the mind; it is manifested as a mental ailment.
Furthermore, it is "suffering" by virtue of being the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*) and because it brings about bodily suffering.
For those possessed by mental suffering tear out their hair and weep; they beat their breasts, wring their hands, and roll back and forth;
they fall headlong, take up weapons, swallow poison, hang themselves with ropes, and enter fire—thus they experience that manifold suffering. Therefore this is said:
“Because it oppresses the mind and brings about oppression of the body, it is called ‘suffering’;
therefore, those who are free from mental distress have said [it is] ‘dejection.
This is the analysis of dejection (*domanassa*).
548. Despair (*upāyāsa*):
This is simply the corruption produced by excessive mental suffering in one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth.
Some say it is a single dhamma included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). Its characteristic is the burning of the mind; its function is sighing.

It has despondency as its manifestation. It is suffering, however, because of the nature of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkha*), because it burns the mind, and because it causes despondency of the body.
Therefore, this is said:
“Because of the excessive burning of the mind and the despondency of the body...”
“Whatever suffering despair produces, it is therefore called suffering.
This is the analysis of despair (*upāyāsa*).
And herein, sorrow (*soka*) is like cooking within a vessel over a mild fire; while [the suffering] of one being roasted by a fierce fire from the vessel...

Lamentation is like the act of going outside; despair (upāyāsa) is to be seen as like the cooking of what remains after one has gone outside—unable to escape because there is no more room—within the very vessel until it is completely consumed.
Association with the unpleasant...
549. Association with the unpleasant (*appiyasampayoga*) means the coming together with disagreeable beings and formations. Its characteristic is the coming together with what is undesired;
its function is to cause mental distress; it is manifested as the state of misfortune. It is suffering, however, by virtue of being the basis for suffering. Therefore, this is said:
“Even upon merely seeing the unpleasant, suffering first arises in the mind;”
Since the body is subject to affliction arising from the pursuit of those [objects],
therefore, by way of its basis, that meeting with the unpleasant was called "suffering" by the Great Seer,
as was the pair of sufferings [birth and aging]. Thus it should be understood.
This is the analysis of association with the unpleasant. 550.
Separation from the pleasant:
"Separation from the pleasant" means being deprived of agreeable beings and formations. Its characteristic is the dissociation from desired objects.
Its essence is the production of sorrow; its manifestation is calamity. But suffering is the basis for the suffering of sorrow. Therefore, this is said:
“Through separation from relatives, wealth, and so forth, people are pierced, being joined with the essence of sorrow.”
"Since from whatever cause it arises,
the separation from the beloved is considered suffering.
This is the analysis of separation from the beloved.
“Not obtaining what one desires”:

here, in such instances as “O, may we not be subject to birth,” the very desire for things that cannot be obtained is what is called “not obtaining what one desires,” and that too is stated to be suffering. Its characteristic is the longing for unobtainable objects.
They have the nature of seeking them and are manifested by the non-attainment of those [objects]. Furthermore, they are suffering by virtue of being the basis for suffering.
Therefore, this is said: “For beings who long for this or that, From the non-attainment of each and every one, Whatever suffering consisting of frustration arises here in this world.”
“For those things that cannot be obtained, yearning is the cause;
therefore the Victor declared suffering to be the non-attainment of what is desired.
This is the analysis regarding the non-attainment of what is desired.
552. "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering"— herein,
that suffering beginning with birth which was spoken of by the Tathāgata:
Whatever has been spoken [elsewhere] regarding all that, it does not exist apart from these.
Therefore, these aggregates of clinging have been briefly described as "suffering" by the Great Seer, the Teacher of the end of suffering.
For in this way, just as fire [afflicts] fuel, weapons [afflict] a target, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like [afflict] cattle, reapers [afflict] a field,
and village-robbers [afflict] a village, so too birth and the other [sufferings], afflicting the five aggregates of clinging in various ways, [reside] within those very aggregates of clinging—
just as grass, creepers, and the like [grow] upon the earth, or flowers, fruits, and shoots [grow] upon trees.
They arise. Furthermore, among the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), birth is suffering at the beginning, aging is suffering in the middle, and death is suffering at the end.
Due to the impact of the suffering of death, there is the suffering of burning anguish (*soka*); due to the inability to endure that, there is the suffering of lamentation (*parideva*);
and from that, through contact with undesirable tactile objects characterized by the disturbance of the elements, there is the suffering of physical affliction.
Suffering is the mental affliction of grief (*domanassa*), which arises as resistance in ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are oppressed by that [physical] suffering;
despair (*upāyāsa*) is the suffering of brooding produced by the dejection born from the increase of sorrow and so forth;

and the non-attainment of what is desired is the suffering of frustrated longing for those whose wishes have been thwarted. Thus, when examined in these various ways, they are nothing other than the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*).

"Regarding 'suffering': since it is impossible to describe this suffering in its entirety—even over many eons—by pointing to each individual instance as it is being spoken of, therefore, in order to show all that suffering by condensing it into any five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhas), just as the taste of the water of the entire ocean is contained within a single drop of water, [the Buddha said]: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging..."
“...are suffering,” said the Blessed One. This is the exposition regarding the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
This, then, is the method in the description of suffering. Now follows the discourse on the description of its origin (*samudaya*).
553. In the exposition of the origin (*samudaya-niddesa*), however: "That which is this craving" means that which is this craving. "Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobbhavikā*):

renewed existence (*punobbhava*) is the making of renewed existence; it is called "leading to renewed existence" because it has the nature of producing renewed existence. "Accompanied by the lust of delight" (*nandīrāga-sahagatā*): it is accompanied by the lust of delight;
what is meant is that it has reached a state of essential identity with the lust of delight. "Finding delight here and there" (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī*).
"Wherever a personal existence (*attabhāva*) is reborn, there it finds delight. The phrase "namely" (*seyyathidaṃ*) is a particle;

its meaning is "and what is that? Craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*), craving for existence (*bhavatanha*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatanha*) will be explained in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Here, however, all three of these are brought together as a unity in the sense of being the producer of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
It should be understood that [it] is stated as "the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
This is the method for the exposition of the origin. Now, the discourse on the exposition of cessation.
554. As for the description of the cessation of suffering, why is it that the cessation of the origin has been stated by way of the formula beginning with "that very craving"?
Because the cessation of suffering occurs through the cessation of the origin. Indeed, suffering ceases through the cessation of the origin, and not otherwise.
Therefore he said:
“Just as a tree that has been cut down will grow again if its root remains firm and undamaged, even so,
as long as the underlying tendency of craving has not been uprooted,”
“This suffering arises again and again.
Thus, because suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin, the Blessed One, when teaching the cessation of suffering, taught it precisely by means of the cessation of its origin.
For the Tathāgatas conduct themselves like lions; when they bring suffering to an end, they do so in this manner.

Those who teach the cessation of suffering apply themselves to the cause, not to the fruit. But the heretics, who live like dogs, when they seek to extinguish suffering and teach the cessation of suffering, apply themselves to the fruit through such things as teaching the practice of self-mortification, and not to the cause.
Thus, first of all, is the teaching on the cessation of suffering by way of the cessation of its origin.
The purpose should be understood.
555. But this is the meaning: "Of that very craving" refers to that craving which was described as "leading to renewed existence" and analyzed by way of sensual craving and so forth.
"Dispassion" (virāga) is said to be the Path; for it is said, "Through dispassion one is liberated. Through dispassion comes cessation.
The cessation through dispassion (*virāga-nirodha*). Because it is the eradication of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), it is the cessation through dispassion without remainder;

thus it is "cessation through dispassion without remainder. Alternatively, "dispassion" (*virāga*) is said to mean abandoning; therefore, the construction here should be understood as "the complete dispassion" and "the complete cessation.
In terms of meaning, however, all of these are synonyms for *nibbāna*. For in the ultimate sense, it is the cessation of suffering.
The Noble Truth is called Nibbāna. Because by resorting to it, craving both fades away and ceases, it is therefore called "fading away" (virāga) and "cessation" (nirodha).

And because by resorting to that very same state, there is the relinquishing and so forth of that craving, and because among the attachments to the strands of sensual pleasure there is not even a single attachment remaining, it is therefore called "relinquishment," "renunciation," "liberation," and "non-attachment."

556. This [Nibbāna] has the characteristic of peace, the essence of deathlessness, or the essence of providing consolation; it is manifested as signless, or manifested as the absence of proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
557. Discussion on Nibbāna:
If it is argued that Nibbāna does not exist at all because it is unapprehendable, like the horn of a hare, we say no, because it is apprehendable by means of the appropriate method.

For it is indeed apprehended by means of the appropriate method known as "practice in accordance with that," just as the supramundane mind of others is apprehended by the knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*);
therefore, one should not say, "it does not exist because it is not apprehended.
For it cannot be said that "whatever foolish worldlings do not apprehend does not exist."
Furthermore, it should not be said that "nibbāna does not exist. Why?

Because it would follow that the practice [of the path] would be fruitless. For if nibbāna did not exist, the right practice—comprising the three aggregates beginning with virtue and preceded by right view—would result in being barren.
Yet this practice is not barren, because it leads to the attainment of nibbāna. Thus, there is no falling into the error of the practice being fruitless.

If it is argued that [Nirvana] is the non-existence of evil, we say no; for even when past and future [phenomena] are non-existent, there is no attainment of Nirvana. If it is argued that the non-existence of present phenomena is Nirvana, we say no;
because such non-existence is impossible for them, and because if they were non-existent, they would necessarily cease to be present.
Furthermore, there is the fault that the element of Nirvana with residue (sopādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) could not arise at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa) which depends upon the present aggregates.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the defilements do not exist at that time, we say no; for this would result in the Noble Path being rendered purposeless.
For if this were so, since the defilements would not exist even prior to the moment of the Noble Path, it follows that the Noble Path is purposeless.
Therefore, this is not a valid reason.

559. If it is argued that "destruction is Nibbāna" because of the statement beginning, "That which, friend, is the destruction of lust," etc., we say no, because even Arahantship would result in being merely a destruction.
For that too is defined by way of the same method as "that which, friend, is the destruction of lust," etc.
Furthermore, this is so because Nibbāna would incur the fault of being temporary and so forth; for if that were the case, Nibbāna would be of limited duration.
It attains the state of being characterized by the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) and of being attainable without depending on right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).

Precisely because it possesses the characteristics of the conditioned, it is included within the conditioned (*saṅkhatapariyāpanna*); because it is included within the conditioned, it is ablaze with the fires of lust and so forth;
and because it is ablaze, it is also subject to suffering (*dukkha*). Since there is no further occurrence from the moment of its destruction onward, it possesses the nature of *nibbāna*.
If it is argued that this is not a fault, we say no; because such a "destruction" (khaya) does not exist.

Even if it did exist, it would not escape the aforementioned faults, and furthermore, it would entail that the Noble Path itself becomes Nibbāna. For the Noble Path destroys the defilements (dosa), and therefore it is called "destruction.
From that point onward, the defilements do not arise again.

However, because it is a remote support (*upanissaya*) for destruction—which is defined as the cessation of what has arisen—by way of a figurative expression, that which serves as its support is called "destruction" through a metaphorical designation.
If one asks why it is not stated in its own literal form, it is because of its extreme subtlety.
Its extreme subtlety is established by the fact that it brings about a state of non-concern for the Blessed One, and because it is to be seen with the noble eye (*ariya-cakkhu*).
560. This [Nibbāna] is unique because it is to be attained by one possessing the Path; it is without origin because it has no prior limit.
If it is argued that it is not "without origin" because it exists when the Path exists, we say no, because it is not something to be produced by the Path.

For this is only to be attained by the Path, not to be produced. Therefore, it is indeed without origin. Because it is without origin, it is ageless and deathless. Because of the absence of origin, aging, and death, it is permanent.
If it is argued that even atoms and the like would attain the status of permanence because of [their alleged similarity to] Nibbāna itself, we say no, because of the absence of a cause.

If it is argued that they are permanent because Nibbāna is permanent, we say no, because the characteristics of a cause are not applicable. If it is argued that they are permanent—like Nibbāna—due to the absence of arising and so forth, we say no, because atoms and the like are unestablished.
Furthermore, because it possesses the reasoning already stated, this very state is permanent; because it transcends the intrinsic nature of form, it is formless (arūpa).
Since there is no difference in the final goal (niṭṭhā) for the Buddhas and others, there is but one single goal.
Because it is designated by way of the subsiding of defilements and the remainder of substrate (upādisesa) attained through that cultivation, it is designated "with remainder" (saupādisesa).
Because, through the abandoning of the origin [of suffering], the karma that leads to future existence has been destroyed;

because the aggregates no longer arise after the final consciousness and those already arisen have vanished; and because there is an absence of any substrate of rebirth (*upādiśeṣa*)—it is called "without substrate" (*anupādisesa*) since it is defined by means of that very absence.

Because it is to be attained through a distinction of knowledge accomplished by unremitting effort, and because it is the word of the Omniscient One, Nibbāna is not non-existent in its own-being from the ultimate standpoint.
For this has been said: "There is, monks, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned.
This is the section on the exposition of the cessation of suffering.

562. Regarding the exposition of the way leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā*), although the eight factors mentioned therein have indeed already been explained by way of their meaning in the Exposition of the Aggregates (*khandhaniddesa*),
they are treated here for the purpose of clarifying their specific characteristics as they occur simultaneously in a single moment.

We say: In brief, for the yogi practicing for the penetration of the Four Truths, right view is the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu) which has Nibbāna as its object and eradicates the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya).
It has the characteristic of seeing correctly, the function of revealing the elements (dhātu), and the manifestation of destroying the darkness of ignorance.
For one whose view is thus perfected, there is the directing of the mind toward the state of Nibbāna, which destroys wrong intention associated with that [view].
Right intention: it has the characteristic of directing the mind correctly; its function is absorption; it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong intention.
For one who sees and reflects in this way, right speech—consisting of the abstinence from wrong speech that eradicates verbal misconduct—is associated with that [intention].
It has the characteristic of embracing; its function is refraining; it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong speech.
Likewise, for one who abstains, the abstinence from killing and so forth—which is associated with that [volition] and effects the eradication of wrong action—is called right action (*sammākammanta*).
Its characteristic is instigating; its function is abstaining; its manifestation is the abandoning of wrong action.
Furthermore, that which constitutes the purification of those [factors of] right speech and right action, and which is associated with them, is the cutting off of hypocrisy and the like.

Abstinence from wrong livelihood is what is called right livelihood. It has the characteristic of cleansing; its function is the occurrence of a livelihood in accordance with the True Way (ñāya); it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong livelihood.

Now, for one established on that plane of virtue consisting of right speech, right action, and right livelihood, the exertion of energy that arises in conformity with them, which is associated with them, and which cuts off indolence—this is called right effort. Its characteristic is uplifting.
Its essence is the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and so forth; it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong effort.

For one who exerts himself in this way, right mindfulness (*sammāsati*)—which is associated with that [right effort] and shakes off wrong mindfulness—is the non-forgetfulness of the mind. Its characteristic is establishing; its essence is non-forgetfulness;
it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong mindfulness. Thus, for one whose mind is guarded by such unsurpassed mindfulness...
Right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) associated with that [right view], which pierces through wrong concentration.

It has non-distraction as its characteristic, the state of being concentrated as its function, and the abandoning of wrong concentration as its manifestation. This is the method in the exposition of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, the analysis of birth and the other factors should be understood here.

563. As to the function of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca*): the exposition should be understood also by way of the function of the knowledge of the truths (*saccañāṇa*). For the knowledge of the truths is twofold:
the knowledge of conformity (*anubodhañāṇa*) and the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*).

Therein, the knowledge of conformity is mundane; it occurs with respect to cessation and the path by way of hearsay and so forth. The knowledge of penetration is supramundane; having made cessation its object, it performs four functions.

He penetrates the truths. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—all this should be stated.
Furthermore, that task of his will become manifest in the purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).
As for that which is mundane: therein, knowledge of suffering, by way of overcoming obsessions as it arises, turns back the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).

Knowledge of the origin turns back the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). Knowledge of cessation turns back the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). Knowledge of the path turns back the view of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*).

Alternatively, knowledge of suffering [turns back] the perception known as permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood with respect to the aggregates which are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood.
Knowledge of the fruit [corrects] the misconception regarding the fruit.

Knowledge of the origin [corrects] the misconception regarding the cause—that is, the misconception that takes what is not a cause to be a cause, such as the belief that the world proceeds from a Lord (Issara), a primal essence (Padhāna), time (Kāla), or inherent nature (Sabhāva). Knowledge of cessation [corrects] the misconception regarding cessation—that is, the grasping of non-liberation as liberation in regard to the formless realm (Arūpaloka), the World-Summit (Lokathūpika), and so forth.

Knowledge of the path [corrects] the misconceptions regarding the path, such as those consisting of devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure (Kāmasukhallika) and devotion to self-mortification (Attakilamatha).
It turns back the misapplication regarding the means that occurs by way of grasping at a path to purification when the path is actually impure. Therefore, this is said:
“As long as a person is deluded regarding the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the auspicious means thereto, so long does he not understand the truths.”
In this way, the exposition should also be understood here by way of the function of knowledge (ñāṇakicca).

564. Regarding the classification of those included [within the truths]: within the truth of suffering, with the exception of craving and untainted phenomena (anāsava-dhamma), all remaining phenomena are included.
Within the truth of the origin, there are thirty-six modes of the wandering of craving. The truth of cessation—

Unmixed: under the heading of right view within the truth of the path, there are the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena.
Under the heading of right intention, there are the three types of thoughts beginning with renunciation. Under the heading of right speech, there are the four kinds of verbal good conduct.
Under the heading of right action, there are the three kinds of bodily good conduct. Under the heading of right livelihood, there are fewness of wishes and contentment.
Or alternatively, because all these— right speech, right action, and right livelihood— are the virtue dear to the Noble Ones (*ariyakanta-sīla*),
and because virtue dear to the Noble Ones must be received with the hand of faith, there exist, due to their presence, the faculty of faith, the power of faith,
the basis of psychic power consisting of desire, the fourfold right striving, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the enlightenment factor of energy under the heading of right effort.

Under the heading of right mindfulness (sammāsati), there are included the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the mindfulness enlightenment factor.

Under the heading of right concentration (sammāsamādhi), the three types of concentration beginning with "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra), as well as mental concentration, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the concentration enlightenment factors of rapture, tranquility, and equanimity, are included.
Thus, the exposition should be understood here also by way of the classification of those factors that are so included.
565. Indeed, the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) should be viewed as a burden; the truth of origination (samudayasacca) as the taking up of the burden;
the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca) as the laying down of the burden; and the truth of the path (maggasacca) as the means for laying down the burden.
Furthermore, the truth of suffering is like a disease, the truth of origination like the cause of the disease, and the truth of cessation like the subsiding of the disease.
The truth of the path is like medicine. Alternatively, the truth of suffering is like a famine; the truth of the origin is like a drought; the truth of cessation is like a good harvest;
and the truth of the path is like a timely rain. Furthermore, [they may be compared] by way of the enemy, the root of enmity, the eradication of enmity, and the means for its eradication;

or by way of the poisonous tree, the root of the tree, the cutting off of the root, and the means for that cutting off; or by way of fear, the root of fear, fearlessness, and the means for attaining it.

Having applied these [terms] by way of analogy—namely, the near shore, the great flood, the far shore, and the effort that brings one to that [far shore]—these should be understood through their similes;
thus should the analysis here be understood by way of analogy.
566. As for "by way of fourfold": herein, there is suffering that is not a Noble Truth, and there is a Noble Truth that is not suffering.
There is that which is both suffering and a noble truth; there is that which is neither suffering nor a noble truth. This same method applies to the origin and the other truths.

In this context, the states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are suffering by way of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*), according to the statement "whatever is impermanent, that is suffering," yet they are not noble truths.
Cessation is a noble truth, but it is not suffering. As for the remainder...

However, two noble truths may be suffering from the perspective of impermanence, yet they are not such in their true nature (*tathattena*) for the sake of whose full comprehension the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
In every respect, however, the five aggregates of clinging—excluding craving—are both suffering and a noble truth.
The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are for the sake of the full comprehension of that [suffering] under the Blessed One.
The holy life is lived such that there is neither suffering nor the Noble Truth [of suffering].
Having applied this in the same way as appropriate to the origin and the other truths, the analysis here should be understood as being fourfold. 567.

Regarding "by way of emptiness, the singlefold, etc.": first, by way of emptiness, all truths indeed should be understood as empty in the ultimate sense because of the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who attains Nibbāna, or one who goes [to a further shore]. Therefore, this is said:
“There is only suffering, but no one who suffers;
there is no agent, but only action exists.
There is extinction, but no person who has attained extinction.”
“The path exists, but no traveler is found.
Alternatively:
“The first two [realms] are empty of permanence, beauty, and pleasure; the state of ‘mine’ is empty of even those two alone.”
The path is empty of a self characterized by permanence and bliss; thus, emptiness applies to these [three].

Alternatively, the three [truths] are empty of cessation, and cessation is empty of the other three. Or else, the cause here is empty of the fruit, because suffering is absent in the origin and cessation is absent in the path;
it does not contain the fruit within itself, unlike the "primordial nature" (*pakati*) asserted by those who propound a primal essence.
The fruit is empty of its cause because of the non-conjunction of the origin of suffering with its cessation and the path;
the fruit of a cause is not conjoined with its cause, unlike the proponents of conjunction who claim that dyads and so forth are so conjoined. Therefore, this is said:
“Herein, this cessation is empty of the three [factors]; by those three, even nibbāna is empty.”
“The cause is empty of its fruit, and the fruit is empty of that cause.
In this way, first of all, the exposition of emptiness should be understood.
This concludes the discussion on the exposition of the singlefold and so forth.
568. Regarding the phrase "of one kind, etc.": here, all suffering is of one kind in terms of its mode of occurrence (*pavatti*). It is of two kinds in terms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

It is of three kinds according to the distinction between the existence of rebirth in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms. It is of four kinds according to the distinction of the four nutriments (*āhāra*).
It is of five kinds according to the distinction of the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
Origination (*samudaya*) is also of one kind by way of its state as that which sets [existence] in motion. It is of two kinds by way of being associated with or dissociated from views.

It is of three kinds by way of the division into craving for sense-pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. It is of four kinds by way of being abandoned by the four paths. It is of five kinds by way of the division into delighting in form and so forth.
It is of six kinds by way of the division into the six groups of craving.

Cessation is also of one kind by virtue of being the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). But figuratively, it is of two kinds through the distinction between that with a residue remaining (*saupādisesa*) and that without a residue remaining (*anupādisesa*).

It is of three kinds through the subsiding of the three types of existence (*bhava*). It is of four kinds because it is to be attained by the four paths. It is of five kinds through the subsiding of the five forms of delight (*abhinandana*).
It is of six kinds through the destruction of the six groups of craving (*taṇhākāya*).
The path is also singlefold in terms of its being developed. It is twofold according to the distinction between serenity and insight, or according to the distinction between seeing and development.

It is threefold according to the distinction of the three aggregates; for, like a city which has a limited extent, this [path] is comprised by the three aggregates which are without such limitation. As it has been said:
“Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not included within the Noble Eightfold Path;
rather, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is included within the three aggregates.
And as for right speech, right action, and right livelihood, friend Visākha, these states are included within the aggregate of virtue.”
“Right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration.
Right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom.
For here, the three beginning with right speech are simply virtue; therefore, they are included in the aggregate of virtue by way of their own kind.
For although in the text the designation "aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*) is made using the locative case, the meaning should nevertheless be understood in the sense of the instrumental.
However, among the three beginning with right effort, concentration by its own nature is unable to settle upon the object with one-pointedness;
rather, it does so when energy performs the function of exertion and mindfulness performs the function of non-forgetfulness.
Having become one who has received assistance from her while she is practicing, he is able [to succeed].

Herein, this is the simile: just as when three friends have entered a park intending to play at the festival of the constellations (*nakkhatta*), one of them might see a *campaka* tree in full bloom, yet even if he raises his hand, he would not be able to grasp it.
Then a second person might bend down and offer his back; though he stood upon that man's back, he would still be unable to grasp [the flowers] because of his own trembling.

Then the other might offer him his shoulder. Standing on one man’s back and leaning against the other’s shoulder, he could pluck the flowers as he pleased, adorn himself with them, and enjoy the festival. This is how this matter should be understood.
For the three qualities beginning with right effort, which are born together, are like three companions who have entered a garden together.

The object is like a fully blossomed *campaka* flower. Concentration (*samādhi*) is like one who, though unable to grasp it even by raising his hand, is nonetheless unable—due to his own nature—to settle with one-pointedness upon the object.
The companion who leans forward, having given his back [in support], is like [the quality of] mindfulness.
Energy is like two companions; mindfulness is like a companion who stands by placing his shoulder against one's own.

Just as one of them, standing on the back of the other and leaning upon the other's shoulder, is able to gather flowers as he pleases, so too concentration, having received assistance from energy—which performs the function of exertion—and from mindfulness—which performs the function of non-forgetfulness—is able to achieve its task.

It is able to settle upon the object through one-pointedness. Therefore, it is concentration itself that is included here under the aggregate of concentration by way of its intrinsic nature (*sajātito*);
however, effort and mindfulness are included by way of their function (*kiriyato*).
As for right view and right intention, wisdom, by its own essential nature, takes as its object [the truths] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
He is unable to determine it. However, by repeatedly striking at the thoughts, he is able to do so.
How? Just as a money-changer, wishing to examine a coin on all sides while holding it in his hand, is not able to turn it over merely with the surface of his eye;
but by turning it over and over again with his fingers and joints, he is able to examine it from this side and that.
In the same way, wisdom is not able by its own nature to determine an object in terms of impermanence and so forth.

However, it is only when assisted by initial application (vitakka)—which has the characteristic of directing onto and the function of striking and threshing, as if hammering and turning over—that it is able to determine [the object] by taking it up again and again.
Therefore, in this context as well, it is right view alone that [is primary] by way of its own kind.
Right view, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are included within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*), whereas right intention is included by way of its functional activity.

Thus, the path is comprised of these three aggregates. Therefore it is said: "It is threefold according to the division into three aggregates. It is fourfold by way of the paths of stream-entry and so forth.
Furthermore, all the truths are of one kind because they are non-false, or because they are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*). They are twofold as mundane and supramundane.
Or [they are distinguished] by the conditioned and the unconditioned. They are threefold according to what is to be abandoned by seeing and development, and what is not to be abandoned.
They are fourfold according to the classification of the fully understood and so forth. Thus, the analysis here should be understood by way of these singlefold and other categories.
569. As for "by way of similarity and dissimilarity": all the truths are similar to one another because they are non-false, empty of self, and difficult to penetrate. As it has been said:
“What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult to do or more difficult to accomplish:
one who would shoot an arrow from afar through the fine hole of a palm-leaf so that it passes straight through, arrow after arrow, without missing;
or one who would pierce the tip of a hair split a hundredfold with the tip [of another hair]? This latter, venerable sir, is indeed more difficult to do.”
“And it is even more difficult to penetrate than that, Ānanda, for one who would pierce the tip of a hair split a hundredfold with the tip [of another hair].
Yet, Ānanda, those who penetrate this as it really is— ‘This is suffering’ … pe … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’— penetrate what is more difficult to penetrate.”

They are dissimilar by way of their definition through specific characteristics. The first two are similar in that they are difficult to fathom due to their profundity, being mundane and associated with the taints (*sāsava*).
They are dissimilar by way of the distinction between fruit and cause, and by way of what is to be fully understood and what is to be abandoned.
The last two are also similar in that they are difficult to fathom due to their profundity, being supramundane and free from the taints (*anāsava*). They are dissimilar...
[They are] similar by way of the distinction between object and subject, and by way of being realized and cultivated; and the first and third are also similar by way of being designated as fruits.
They are dissimilar by way of being conditioned and unconditioned. The second and fourth are also similar by way of being designated as causes;
they are dissimilar by way of being exclusively wholesome and unwholesome. The first and fourth are also similar by way of being conditioned; [they are] dissimilar...

By way of the mundane and the supramundane; and the second and third pairs are also similar because they consist of those who are neither-learner-nor-non-learner. They are dissimilar because one has an object and the other does not.
Thus, in such ways and by means of these methods, the wise one [should investigate].
"One should understand the noble truths as similar and dissimilar.
Thus ends the section on the Development of Wisdom in the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "Exposition of the Faculties and Truths. 17.
Exposition of the Grounds of Understanding.
The Discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādakathā).

570. Now, regarding those phenomena which constitute the ground for this wisdom—among those stated as "the phenomena classified as aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, and so forth"—since it is dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the others]...
The remaining dependently arisen phenomena have been included; therefore, the order for their explanation has now arrived.

In this regard, first, those phenomena beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*) should be understood as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what, monks, is dependent origination?
Monks, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*); conditioned by volitional formations..."
consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact;
with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging;
with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They come into being. Thus there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
This, monks, is called dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that aging, death, and so forth are dependently originated phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma*). For this was said by the Blessed One:

“And what, bhikkhus, are the dependently arisen phenomena? Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.

Birth, bhikkhus... existence... clinging... craving... feeling... contact... the six sense bases... name-and-form... [is likewise impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.]”

“Consciousness... volitional formations... ignorance, bhikkhus, are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. These, bhikkhus, are called dependently arisen phenomena. 571. This, moreover, is the summary here:

“Dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be understood as the phenomena that serve as conditions; “dependently arisen” (paṭiccasamuppanna) [refers to the phenomena resulting from those conditions].
“Dhammas” refers to phenomena produced by their respective conditions. If it is asked how this is to be known, it is by the word of the Blessed One.
For in the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma-desanā-sutta*, the Blessed One said:
“And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? Dependent on birth, bhikkhus, is aging-and-death; from arising...”
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed:
the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena, specific conditionality. A Tathāgata awakens to this and realizes it;
having awakened to and realized it, he declares it, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, makes it plain, saying: "Behold!"
And he said: "Monks, conditioned by birth, there is aging and death. Conditioned by becoming, monks, there is birth...
[etc] ...Conditioned by ignorance, monks, there are volitional formations. Whether Tathāgatas arise or not, this nature of things remains—this causal status, this causal sequence.

But the Tathāgata, monks, having realized and directly known it, proclaims it, reveals it, makes it known, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and elucidates it, saying: 'Behold! Thus, monks, that which therein is suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness..."
“Conditionality (idappaccayatā). This, monks, is called dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Thus, when teaching dependent origination, it is the very phenomena that serve as conditions which, by synonyms such as “suchness” (tathatā) and others, are stated to be dependent origination.
Therefore, dependent origination has the characteristic of being the condition for phenomena such as aging and death; its function is the continuous succession of suffering.
It should be understood as having the characteristic of appearing as a wrong path.
Furthermore, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*) because each respective phenomenon arises from its corresponding conditions neither deficiently nor redundantly;
and it is called "non-falsity" (*avitathatā*) because when the conditions have come together in harmony, there is no absence of the arising of the phenomena produced from them, even for a moment.
It is called "non-alterability" (*anaññathatā*) because other phenomena do not arise through conditions that are other than themselves;
or, it is called "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*) because of these aforementioned factors—such as aging and death—as their respective conditions or as a collection of conditions.

Regarding this, the etymological analysis (*vacanattha*) is as follows: the conditions for these [factors] are "specific conditions" (*idappaccayā*); the state of being specific conditions is "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*); or, the collection of specific conditions is "specific conditionality. As for the grammatical definition (*lakkhaṇa*) here, it should be sought from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).

574. However, some say that dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is merely arising—that is, an arising that is dependent and free from causes such as "primordial matter" (*pakati*) or "the primal person" (*purisa*) imagined by the heretics. This is not tenable. Why?
Because it lacks support in the Suttas, because it contradicts the Suttas, because the profound method is impossible [therein], and because of a discrepancy in terminology. "Merely arising..."

For there is no sutta that says, "dependent origination" [is the first abiding]. If one were to say that it is "dependent origination," it would result in a contradiction with the *Padesavihāra Sutta*.

How so? For, based on such statements as, "Then, during the first watch of the night, the Blessed One attended to dependent origination in forward and reverse order," the mental attention to dependent origination is the first abiding of the Fully Enlightened One.

And his dwelling was a partial dwelling, a dwelling in only one part of it. As it was said: "Bhikkhus, I dwelt in a portion of that very dwelling in which I dwelt when I had first attained full enlightenment.
And there he dwelt by seeing the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), not merely by seeing the arising [of phenomena].
As it was said: "He understands thus: 'Feeling conditioned by wrong view, and feeling conditioned by right view...'"

“Feeling also has wrong intention as its condition”—all this should be elaborated in full. Thus, for one who asserts that mere arising is “dependent origination,” there arises a contradiction with the *Padesavihāra Sutta*.
Likewise, there is a contradiction with the *Kaccāna Sutta*. For in the *Kaccāna Sutta* it is also said:
“Kaccāna, for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom...”

"That which is non-existence in the world does not exist"—thus, dependent origination in its forward order is explained as the "origin of the world" by way of worldly conditions for the purpose of uprooting the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*), and not merely as arising.

For the uprooting of the annihilationist view does not occur through the mere observation of arising; rather, it occurs through the observation of the non-cessation of conditions. When conditions cease...
“Because the fruit does not cease. Furthermore, for one who asserts that mere arising is “dependent origination,” there arises a contradiction with the *Kaccāna Sutta*.

Regarding the phrase “because of the impossibility of a profound method,” this was indeed stated by the Blessed One: “This dependent origination, Ānanda, is profound and appears profound. And profundity is fourfold; we shall explain that later.
That [arising] does not exist at the moment of arising. Furthermore, they describe this dependent origination as adorned with the fourfold method;
since that tetrad of methods also does not exist at the moment of arising, dependent origination is not merely arising because of the impossibility of such profound methods.
575. As for the analysis of words: this word *paṭicca* is used when the agent is the same and refers to a prior time.
It establishes a meaning, namely: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
However, when used here together with the word *uppāda* (arising) as a term denoting a state (*bhāvasādhana*), it undergoes a change in its verbal form because there is no common agent;
nor does it establish any meaning [in this context]. Thus, even from the perspective of the change in verbal form, mere arising (*uppādamatta*) is not dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
In this regard, it might be argued: "We shall connect it with the word 'exists' [to say], 'Dependent origination exists'.
That is not correct. Why? Because there is no grammatical connection (yoga), and because it would entail the fault of origination arising from origination.
[As the Buddha said: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination. And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?... This is called... [and so forth].
“...monks, this is dependent origination. For in these instances, the word *hoti* does not connect with even one [of the terms], nor is there an arising (*uppāda*).
If there were such an arising, it would follow that there would be an arising of arising itself.

Furthermore, those who think: “The state of having this as its condition is ‘conditionality’ (*idappaccayatā*), and a state is indeed a mode (*ākāra*) of ignorance and the rest,” [are also incorrect].

"It is the cause for the manifestation of volitional formations and so forth; and regarding that transformation of volitional formations, there is the designation 'dependent origination'"—this [position] of theirs is not tenable.
Why? Because ignorance and the other factors are stated to be causes. For the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging and death, namely birth... [and so on]."
“...of formations, namely ignorance”—thus it is stated that ignorance and the rest alone are the causes, not their transformation.
Therefore, that which was said—“Dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) should be understood as the phenomena that are conditions”—should be understood as having been rightly said. 577.

However, if the notion arises here from the mere shadow of the phrasing “dependent origination” that this refers only to arising, that should be dispelled by taking the meaning of this term in the following way. For the Blessed One [said]:
Since this term refers to a collection of phenomena (*dhammasamūha*) that exists in two ways,
it is therefore stated here by way of a metaphorical designation (*phalopacāra*) for its condition.
For this term "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) applies to that very collection of phenomena which exists as a state of being conditioned.
They maintain that it is twofold. For since, when it is understood, it leads to welfare and happiness, therefore the wise ought to comprehend it;
thus it is *paṭicca*. And as for its arising, it arises together and rightly, not singly, nor without a cause;
thus it is *samuppāda*. Therefore, being both *paṭicca* and *samuppāda*, it is *paṭiccasamuppāda*. Furthermore, it arises together (*saha uppajjati*).
Furthermore, it is *paṭiccasamuppāda* because it arises dependently, not having rejected the completeness of conditions.
And since this collection of causes is its condition (*paccaya*), it is also [called *paṭiccasamuppāda*] by virtue of being conditioned by that;

just as in the world molasses, being the condition for phlegm, is called "phlegm-molasses," and just as in the Teaching the arising of Buddhas, being a condition for happiness, is called "the happiness of the Buddhas."
Just as "arising" (uppāda) is so called, it should be understood that "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda) is likewise spoken of by way of the designation for the fruit.
Alternatively,
it is said that "paṭicca" refers to a collection of causes that have come together (paṭimukham ito).
"And it arises together"—thus is "co-arising" (samuppāda) defined.

For that collection of causes, which has been pointed out under the heading of individual causes such as ignorance for the manifestation of formations and so forth, is called "co-arising" in the sense of producing a common fruit and in the sense of being complete;
it refers to the factors of the assembly facing one another.

Because it has come from this, it is called "dependent" (*paṭicca*). Furthermore, since this [condition] produces phenomena that arise together in mutual inseparability, it is also called "arising together" (*samuppāda*).
Thus, it is "dependent arising" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) because it is both dependent and an arising.
579. Another method:
Because phenomena arise together and simultaneously in dependence upon one another,
this conditionality is therefore stated here by the Sage in this way.
For among the conditions specified under the heading of ignorance and so forth, those conditions which produce a phenomenon such as volitional formations—
They are not capable of arising when they do not depend on one another or when there is a deficiency of one another.
Therefore, this conditionality produces phenomena by depending [on them], simultaneously and not in part, nor in a sequence of before and after;
thus it was spoken here by the Sage, who is skilled in conventional terminology according to the meaning: "It is called dependent origination"—this is the meaning.
580. By speaking thus, the non-existence of the former [views] such as eternalism is shown by the first part, and the refutation of annihilationism and so forth is shown by the latter part;
thus the method is elucidated by both.
By the first word, "dependent" (*paṭicca*), which illuminates the completeness of conditions, the absence of eternalism and so forth—
namely, the doctrines of eternalism, causelessness, and the lack of control over causes— is illuminated,

because the occurrence of phenomena is dependent upon the completeness of conditions. For how could there be such things as eternalism, or occurrence by way of causelessness and so on, apart from the completeness of conditions?
And by the phrase "with the subsequent foot," which clarifies the arising of phenomena through the term "co-arising" (*samuppāda*),
the refutation of annihilationism and other errors is demonstrated, since phenomena arise when there is a completeness of conditions.
For when phenomena arise again and again by way of successive prior conditions, how could there be annihilation?

And [the views of] nihilism and non-action. By "by means of both" is meant that the entire teaching of dependent origination is the middle way, because various phenomena arise from their respective combinations of conditions without interrupting the continuity; it is the abandonment of the two doctrines:
"he who acts is he who experiences [the result]" and "one acts and another experiences [the result]."
“Non-adherence to local dialects and not overstepping common usage”—this is the method that has been elucidated.
This, first of all, is the meaning of the mere expression “dependent origination.
581. Furthermore, when the Blessed One was teaching dependent origination by saying, “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise],” and so forth...
The *tantra* has been set forth according to the method; while composing its commentary on the meaning, one should enter the circle of those who advocate analytical exposition (*vibhajjavāda*),
without misrepresenting the teachers, without overstepping our own system, without importing the systems of others, without contradicting the discourses (*sutta*),
in accordance with the discipline (*vinaya*), looking to the great authorities (*mahāpadesa*), and illuminating both the Dhamma and the meaning.
Since a commentary on the meaning must be composed by one who summarizes that very subject and demonstrates it through other modes of exposition as well—
and because a commentary on the meaning of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is inherently difficult even for those naturally gifted— so it has been said by the ancients:
"Truth, a being, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditions;..."
"The four things are hard to see, and they are very difficult to teach.
Therefore, having reflected that it is not easy to explain the meaning of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) except for those who have attained the scriptures and realization,
I now desire to speak the commentary on the mode of conditions (paccayākāra).
I find no foothold, as if plunged into the depths of the ocean.
Yet this teaching is manifold, adorned with the methods of exposition,
and the path of the ancient masters continues on without interruption.
Therefore, relying upon both of these, I shall undertake a commentary on the meaning of this work;
listen to it with concentrated minds.
For this was said by the ancient teachers:
“Whoever listens to me with earnest attention will obtain distinction between what precedes and what follows;
having obtained this distinction between what precedes and what follows,”
“May I go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Thus, regarding the formula “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” and so forth, the detailed exposition should be understood from the very beginning by way of:
the diversity of the teaching, the meaning, the characteristics, the various classifications, and the definition of the factors.
In this context, "by way of the different modes of teaching" refers to the fourfold teaching on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) by the Blessed One:
like four men carrying a creeper, it may proceed from the beginning or from the middle up to the end;
likewise, it may proceed from the end or from the middle up to the beginning. Thus, there are four ways of teaching dependent origination.
For just as among four men clearing away creepers, one first sees the very root of the creeper;
having cut it at the root, he pulls out the whole thing and brings it for use—so too, the Blessed One [taught], starting from the beginning and continuing to the end:
"Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations... [and so on] ...with birth as condition there are aging and death."
He teaches dependent origination.

Just as one among those men first sees the middle of the creeper, cuts it at the middle, pulls out and takes only the upper portion, and brings it to his work; even so, the Blessed One [teaches] regarding that person who delights in that feeling...
"For one who greets with approval and remains attached, delight arises. That delight in feelings is clinging. With that clinging as condition, there is becoming;
with becoming as condition, there is birth. Thus he taught starting from the middle up to the end.
And just as among those men, one who first sees the tip of the creeper takes hold of the tip and follows along it...
Just as one takes everything down to the very root and applies it to the work, so too the Blessed One said:
"It has been said, 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be. Now, monks, is it with birth as condition that aging-and-death comes to be, or not?
What do you think of this? "Bhante, it is with birth as condition that aging-and-death comes to be. This is how we understand it here: 'With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be.'"
"‘With existence as condition, birth... [and so on] ...with ignorance as condition, volitional formations’: thus it has been said.
But, monks, do volitional formations have ignorance as their condition or not? What is your view in this matter?
Thus he teaches dependent origination from the end back to the beginning.
Just as one among these men first sees the middle of the creeper, cuts it in the middle, and while descending, takes it down to its root and brings it for use; even so, the Blessed One [considered]:
"And, monks, what is the source of these four nutriments? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their provenance? These four nutriments have craving as their source..."
"From the arising of craving, from the birth of craving, from the origin of craving [arise these things]. Of what is craving the source?... feeling... contact...
the six sense bases... name-and-form... consciousness... formations? ... Formations have ignorance as their source... [and so on]... they originate from ignorance.
Thus he teaches, starting from the middle down to the beginning.
583. But why does he teach in this way? Because dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is all-encompassing and because the Blessed One himself has attained mastery in the art of teaching.
Dependent origination is indeed all-encompassing; it leads precisely to the penetration of the principle from every perspective.

And the Blessed One has attained mastery in the art of teaching through his possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) and the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), as well as by having reached a fourfold state of profundity. He...
Because he has attained mastery in the elegance of teaching, he teaches the Dhamma by means of various methods.
In particular, the progressive teaching (*anulomadesanā*) beginning from the outset is intended to demonstrate the process of occurrence according to its own respective causes,
and to demonstrate the order of their arising, for the sake of those disciples who are confused regarding the analysis of the causes of occurrence.

The sequence [of the teaching] should be understood as follows. That which is the reverse-order teaching starting from the conclusion—beginning with the method, “Alas, this world has fallen into hardship;

it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and reappears”—is according to the prior-stage penetration of one who surveys the world fallen into hardship, following upon each respective [link] such as aging-and-death.
It is for the purpose of demonstrating the causes of suffering as realized by oneself.

That [exposition] which proceeds from the middle back to the beginning is for the purpose of tracing it back through the sequence of cause and effect, starting again from the past, by means of the determination of nutriment and its origins.
However, that which proceeds from the middle to the end...

That [exposition] which occurs in the present time was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the future period, starting from its origination by causes in the future period. Among those [three expositions],

that which was stated as a teaching in direct order (anuloma-desanā) beginning from the start— for the purpose of demonstrating the occurrence according to their respective causes to those people to be trained who are confused about the cause of occurrence,
and for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of arising— should be understood as being set forth here.

584. But why is ignorance mentioned first here? Is it because, like the "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) of those who propound primordial nature, ignorance is also a root cause of the world that has no further cause?
It is not without a cause; for the cause of ignorance has been stated: "With the arising of the taints (*āsava*), there is the arising of ignorance.
However, there is a way in which it may be considered a root cause. What is that way? Its status as the head of the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
For when the Blessed One speaks on the discourse of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), he does so by making two things the head: either ignorance (*avijjā*) or craving. As it was said:
"Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is discerned such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist; then afterwards it came into being.
Even though this is said, bhikkhus, nevertheless ignorance is discerned as having this specific condition."
Or craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). As it has been said: "Monks, no prior limit of craving for existence is discerned, such that one could say:
'Before this, craving for existence did not exist; then afterwards it came into being.
Even though this is said, monks, nevertheless craving for existence is discerned as having this specific condition."
585. But why does the Blessed One, when teaching the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), teach by making these two factors the head?
Because they are the specific causes of karma that leads to happy and miserable destinies. For ignorance (*avijjā*) is the specific cause of karma leading to a miserable destiny.
Why? Because an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), overcome by ignorance, is like one overcome by the heat of fire, the blow of a club, or the distress of fatigue.
Just as a cow about to be slaughtered, out of weariness and distress, begins to drink hot water— which is tasteless and brings her no benefit—

so too does one begin various kinds of karma leading to miserable destinies, such as the taking of life, which is devoid of flavor due to the torment of the defilements and brings one no benefit because it causes a fall into a miserable rebirth.
However, craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is the specific cause of karma that leads to a happy destiny.

Why? Because the worldling, overcome by craving for existence, undertakes various kinds of action leading to a happy destination—such as abstaining from taking life—which, like that aforementioned cow’s drinking of cool water, possesses its own gratification and dispels his own exhaustion;

and which, through being free from the torment of the defilements, possesses its own gratification and dispels the exhaustion of suffering in miserable destinies by bringing about rebirth in a happy destination.

586. Furthermore, among these phenomena which form the head of the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), in some instances the Blessed One teaches a teaching rooted in a single phenomenon.
For example: "Thus, monks, with ignorance as its proximate cause (*upanisā*) are volitional formations; with volitional formations as their proximate cause is consciousness," and so forth. Likewise:
"Monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are subject to clinging..."
“Craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises,” and so forth. In some instances, it is rooted in both. For example:
“Bhikkhus, for the fool who is hindered by ignorance and associated with craving, this body has thus come to be.
Thus, this body and external name-and-form—this is the dyad. Dependent upon this dyad is contact, which consists of the six sense bases.”
“By whatever [contact] the fool experiences pleasure and pain,” and so forth.
Among those teachings, the statement “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise” should be understood here as a teaching based on a single factor by way of ignorance.
Thus, first, the exposition should be understood here according to the different modes of teaching.

587. *Atthato* means "according to the meaning" of the terms beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*). To illustrate: bodily misconduct and so forth are called "unfindable" (*avindiya*) in the sense that they are unfit to be fulfilled;
the meaning is that they cannot be attained. Ignorance is that which finds what is unfindable; thus it is ignorance. Conversely, bodily good conduct and so forth are called "findable" (*vindiya*);
ignorance is that which does not find what is findable; thus it is ignorance. The meaning of the aggregates (*khandha*) is "a heap."

Ignorance (avijjā) is so called because it makes unknown the sense-sphere-meaning of the sense-bases (āyatana), the emptiness-meaning of the elements (dhātu), the sovereignty-meaning of the faculties (indriya), and the suchness-meaning of the truths (sacca).
It is also ignorance because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning described in terms of the oppression and so forth of suffering and the rest.
[It functions] within the beginningless saṃsāra, amidst all the wombs, destinies, states of existence, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

It is called ignorance (*avijjā*) because it causes beings to run hither and thither. It is ignorance because it runs after things such as "woman" or "man" which do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), yet it does not run after things that do exist in the ultimate sense, such as the aggregates (*khandha*).

Furthermore, it is ignorance because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and so forth, as well as the phenomena of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently originated (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) states.
That depending upon which a fruit comes to be is the condition (*paccaya*). "Depending upon" (*paṭicca*) means not without [it], that is, not without having directly perceived it.
"Comes to be" (*eti*) means both arises and proceeds. Furthermore, the sense of being an auxiliary factor is the sense of "condition.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) and that which is a condition (*paccayo*) together constitute "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccayo*). Therefore: "with ignorance as condition."
They are called *saṅkhārā* because they construct the conditioned (*saṅkhata*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of *saṅkhārā*:

those that arise with ignorance as their condition (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), and those referred to by the term *saṅkhāra* itself. Among these, there are three—meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations (*abhisankhārā*)—and three—bodily, verbal, and mental formations.
These six are the formations conditioned by ignorance. All of them are merely mundane wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*).

Furthermore, there are these four types of formations conveyed by the term *saṅkhāra*: conditioned formation (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*), formed formation (*abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra*), forming formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra*), and functional formation (*payoga-abhisaṅkhāra*).

Among these, all conditioned phenomena (*dhammas*) with causes that are spoken of in such passages as "Impermanent, alas, are formations" are called conditioned formations. These include the material and immaterial phenomena of the three planes produced by kamma.

"Conditioned formations" (*abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhārā*) are mentioned in the commentaries; these too are included within the phrase "Impermanent indeed are formations" (*aniccā vata saṅkhārā*). No separate location for them is found.

However, wholesome and unwholesome volition belonging to the three planes is called the "formative formation" (*abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra*); regarding that, it is said: "Bhikkhus, this person, immersed in ignorance..."
The sense in which it occurs in such passages as, "One performs a meritorious volitional formation" (puññañceva saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti), is well known.
However, bodily and mental energy is called "volitional formation as application" (payogābhisaṅkhāra);
this is found in such passages as, "Having gone as far as the range of volitional formation extends, he stood as if struck by a pin."

And it is not only these; there are also many other formations (saṅkhāra) that have come down under the term "formation" in such passages as: "Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu enters the cessation of perception and feeling, first his verbal formation ceases, then his bodily formation, then his mental formation.
Among those, there is no such formation that exists apart from conditioned formations.

It would not be included [in the summary]. Hereafter, in such passages as "with formations as condition, consciousness," and so forth, what has already been stated should be understood according to the method already explained.
However, regarding what has not yet been stated: it cognizes, thus it is *viññāṇa* (consciousness). It bends, thus it is *nāma* (name). It is affected, thus it is *rūpa* (form).

It extends toward its source and leads that which is extended, thus it is *āyatana* (base). It touches, thus it is *phassa* (contact). It feels, thus it is *vedanā* (feeling). It is agitated, thus it is *taṇhā* (craving). It grasps, thus it is...
Grasping is *upādāna*. It exists and it causes [beings] to exist, thus it is *bhava* (existence). Birth is *jāti*. Aging is *jarā*. They die by means of this, thus it is *maraṇa* (death).
