Sorrowing is *soka* (sorrow). Lamenting is *parideva* (lamentation). It causes suffering, thus it is *dukkha* (suffering);

or alternatively, it is *dukkha* because it cuts [life] in two according to its arising and its persistence. A state of mental distress is *domanassa* (grief). Intense exertion is *upāyāsa* (despair).
“Arise” means they are produced. And this connection with the word “arise” (sambhavanti) should be made not only with sorrow and the rest, but with all the terms.
For otherwise, if it were merely stated that “with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations” (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), it would not be understood what they do;

however, when the connection is made as “they arise,” then ignorance is both itself and the condition, thus “ignorance-condition. Therefore, “with ignorance as condition... [the volitional formations arise].

The determination of conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena is thus made: "formations arise. This same method applies everywhere. The phrase "in this way" indicates the method already demonstrated.
By this, he shows that [formations arise] through causes such as ignorance alone, and not through the creation of a Lord (Issara-nimmāna) or other such factors.
"Of this" refers to what has been stated. "Of the whole" means unmixed, or complete. "Of the mass of suffering" (dukkha-kkhandha).
[It arises] from the mass of suffering, not from a being, nor from pleasure, beauty, and so forth. "Origin" (*samudaya*) means arising. "Occurs" (*hoti*) means comes into existence.
In this way, the analysis should be understood here according to its meaning.

588. "From the characteristics, etc. refers to the characteristics and so forth of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the other [factors]. That is to say: ignorance has the characteristic of non-knowing (*aññāṇa*).

Delusion has the characteristic of causing bewilderment; its manifestation is concealing; its proximate cause is the taints (*āsava*). Formations have the characteristic of volitional processing; their function is accumulating; they manifest as volition;
their proximate cause is ignorance. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing; its function is being the forerunner; it manifests as rebirth-linking;
its proximate cause is formations, or else it has the physical base and the object as its proximate cause. Bending is the characteristic of [name].
Name has the characteristic of bending toward an object, the function of association, the manifestation of inseparability, and consciousness as its proximate cause.
Matter has the characteristic of being affected (ruppana), the function of dispersing, the manifestation of the indeterminate (abyākata), and consciousness as its proximate cause.

The six sense bases have the characteristic of being a sense field (āyatana), the function of seeing and so forth, the manifestation of the state of being the physical basis and the door, and name-and-form as their proximate cause.
Contact has the characteristic of touching; its function is impingement; it is manifested as meeting;

its proximate cause is the sixfold base. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; its function is the enjoyment of the flavor of the object; it is manifested as pleasure and pain; its proximate cause is contact.
Craving has the characteristic of being the cause [of suffering]; its function is delighting; it is manifested as insatiability; its proximate cause is feeling.
Clinging has the characteristic of grasping; its function is non-relinquishing; it is manifested as intensified craving and views; its proximate cause is craving.

Becoming has the characteristic of action and the fruit of action; its function is the process of becoming and the state of being; it is manifested as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states; its proximate cause is clinging.
The characteristics and other attributes of birth and the rest should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Description of the Truths.
In this way, the exposition should be understood here also by way of its characteristics and so forth.
(589) Regarding "by way of the singlefold, etc.": herein, ignorance is singlefold by way of its nature as non-knowing, non-seeing, delusion, and so on.

It is twofold by way of non-practice and wrong practice; likewise, it is twofold by way of being with formations and without formations. It is threefold by way of association with the three kinds of feeling. It is [fourfold] by way of penetration of the Four Truths...
They are fourfold. They are fivefold by way of concealing the danger of the five destinations and so forth.
Furthermore, among all immaterial phenomena, their sixfold nature should be understood by way of the doors and objects.

Volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are singlefold by way of being states that are subject to taints (*āsava*) and subject to fruition (*vipāka-dhamma*), etc. They are twofold by way of being wholesome and unwholesome. Likewise...

[Volitional formations] are of three kinds according to whether they are limited, sublime, inferior, intermediate, fixed in wrongness, or unfixed. They are of three kinds by way of being formations of merit and so forth.
They are of four kinds because they lead to the four modes of birth. They are of five kinds because they lead to the five destinations.

Consciousness is of one kind by way of being mundane resultant and so forth. It is of two kinds by way of being with root-cause or without root-cause. [It is of three kinds] because it is included within the three realms of existence.

[Contact] is threefold by way of association with the three feelings, and also threefold by way of being rootless, doubly-rooted, or triply-rooted. It is fourfold and fivefold by way of birth-place (yoni) and destiny (gati).

Name-and-form is singlefold by way of its dependence on consciousness and its condition as kamma. It is twofold by way of having an object and not having an object. It is threefold by way of the past and so forth. It is fourfold and fivefold by way of birth-place and destiny.
The six sense bases are singlefold by way of being the place of birth and convergence. They are twofold by way of the primary elements, the sensitive organs, and consciousness.
It is threefold by way of the spheres of the fortunate, the unfortunate, and both; it is fourfold and fivefold by way of being included within the modes of birth (*yoni*) and destinations (*gati*).

Following this method, the singlefold and other classifications of contact (*phassa*) and the rest should also be understood. Thus, the exposition here should be understood according to its singlefold and other aspects.

(590) Furthermore, regarding the "definition of the factors": sorrow (*soka*) and the others are mentioned here for the purpose of showing the uninterrupted continuity of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).
For these [defilements] arise in the fool who is struck down by aging and death. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, when an uninstructed worldling is touched by bodily painful feeling, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
And as long as those [defilements] continue to occur, so long does ignorance persist; thus, once again—
The wheel of existence is indeed a continuous sequence, beginning with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
Therefore, by condensing those [factors] together with aging-and-death into a single group, it should be understood that there are exactly twelve factors of dependent origination.
Thus, the exposition of this matter should be understood here also from the perspective of the definition of its factors.
This, then, is the brief explanation here.
561. This, however, is the method of detailed exposition:
"Ignorance" (avijjā), according to the Sutta method, [refers] to the four bases beginning with suffering (dukkha).
Ignorance (aññāṇa), according to the Abhidhamma method, consists of eight types together with the past limit and so forth. For this has been said: "In that regard, what is ignorance?
It is ignorance regarding suffering... [and so on] ...ignorance regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering;

ignorance regarding the past limit, ignorance regarding the future limit, ignorance regarding both the past and future limits, and ignorance regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena."
In this context, although ignorance arises by way of an object in all remaining instances—setting aside the two supramundane truths—even so, it is intended here specifically by way of concealment.

For once arisen, it remains having concealed the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), not permitting the penetration of its characteristic as it actually is; likewise with the truth of origin (samudaya).

It stands concealing cessation, the path, the five aggregates of the past designated as the "prior limit," the five aggregates of the future designated as the "subsequent limit," both together designated as the "prior and subsequent limits," and the specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena designated as "specific conditionality" and "dependently arisen phenomena. This is ignorance.
“‘These are formations’—in this way, it does not allow one to penetrate the specific characteristic [of formations] as it truly is. Therefore, ignorance regarding suffering...
[and so on] ...is called ignorance regarding phenomena that have arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination. 592.
‘Formations’ refers to the three types of meritorious and other formations, and the three types beginning with bodily formations; thus they were previously stated in brief.”
Sixth: in detail, however, the volitional formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) here consists of thirteen types of volition:

namely, the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions that arise by way of giving, virtue, and so forth, together with the five wholesome fine-material-sphere volitions that arise by way of meditation (*bhāvanā*).

The volitional formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) consists of twelve unwholesome volitions that arise by way of killing living beings and so forth. The volitional formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*)...
The four wholesome volitions of the formless sphere that proceed by way of development alone—these three types of formations together constitute twenty-nine volitions.
As for the other three: bodily volition is the bodily formation, verbal volition is the verbal formation, and mental volition is the mental formation.
This triad is presented to show how the accumulations of merit and so forth proceed by way of the doors at the moment of kamma-accumulation.

It has been said. For the twenty volitions—namely, the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions and the twelve unwholesome volitions—which arise from the body door after having originated bodily intimation, are called the "bodily formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra).

Those same [volitions], when they arise from the speech door after having originated vocal intimation, are called the "verbal formation" (vacīsaṅkhāra). However, the volitions pertaining to direct higher knowledge (abhiññā) herein are [excluded] further on...

Because it does not serve as a condition for consciousness, it is not included. And just as with the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*), so too the volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*) does not exist [as such].
Therefore, that too must be excluded from being a condition for consciousness; however, all these [types of volition] do indeed exist as conditions through ignorance (*avijjā-paccaya*).
Furthermore, all twenty-nine types [of volition] that arise at the mind-door (*manodvāra*) without having produced either of the two forms of intimation (*viññatti*) are likewise [excluded].
“Volition is the mental formation. Thus, this triad enters into the preceding triad;
therefore, in terms of its meaning, the conditionality of ignorance should be understood solely by way of the formative activities of merit and so forth.
In this regard, it may be asked: “But how is it to be known that ‘these formations have ignorance as their condition’?”

Because [the formations] exist when ignorance exists. For one whose ignorance—known as non-knowing—regarding suffering and the rest has not been abandoned, he first grasps the suffering of saṃsāra through his non-knowing regarding suffering and regarding the past and so forth, taking it to be a perception of pleasure;

he then initiates the three kinds of formations which are the causes of that very [suffering]. Through his non-knowing regarding the origin, he [initiates] the requisites of craving, even though they are the causes of suffering.

Mistaking volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) for a cause of happiness, he exerts himself. However, due to ignorance regarding cessation and the path, he perceives certain specific states of existence—which are not actually the cessation of suffering—as the cessation of suffering;

and perceiving sacrifices, self-mortification, celibacy, and so forth—which are not actually the path to cessation—as the path to cessation, he aspires for the cessation of suffering by way of sacrifices, self-mortification, celibacy, and the like.
He undertakes the threefold volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Furthermore,

because of that non-abandonment of ignorance regarding the Four Truths, he— specifically failing to understand as suffering the suffering known as the fruit of merit, which is interspersed with manifold disadvantages such as birth,
aging, sickness, and death— engages in the various types of bodily, verbal, and mental volitional formations for its attainment.
One undertakes a meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra) like one desiring a celestial nymph who leaps into the abyss of Mount Meru.

And even though one does not perceive that at the end of that fruit of merit— which is considered happiness— there is the suffering of change (vipariṇāmadukkha) that produces great feverish distress and its lack of true satisfaction,
one nevertheless undertakes a meritorious formation of the aforementioned kind for the sake of that [fruit], like a moth [flying into a flame].
Like one greedy for a drop of honey who licks the edge of a blade smeared with honey,
he fails to see the danger in the indulgence of sensual pleasures and the like, which entail karmic results. Under the influence of the perception of pleasure and being overwhelmed by defilements,
he initiates unwholesome volitional formations even through the three doors of action— just as a child plays with excrement, or as one desiring death consumes poison.

Furthermore, even regarding the immaterial-sphere kamma-results, one who fails to understand the suffering inherent in the change of formations initiates the immovable formation—which is itself a mental formation—through the perversion of eternalism and so forth;
it is like a person lost on his way setting out on a path toward a city of demons.
Thus, since the state of being a formation exists only because of the presence of ignorance, and not due to its absence, this should be understood: "These..."

“Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition. And this has also been said: “Bhikkhus, one who is ignorant, possessed by ignorance, performs a meritorious volitional formation, performs a demeritorious volitional formation, and performs an imperturbable volitional formation.
But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned ignorance and knowledge has arisen in him, then, with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge...”
“...nor does one form a formation of merit.
[End of] Discourse on the Conditions in the *Paṭṭhāna*. 594.
Here it is said: Let us first accept that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations; however, this must be explained:
Of which formations is it a condition, and how does it act as a condition? Regarding this, it is said: by the Blessed One, indeed, [the twenty-four conditions were taught]:

the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*), the contiguity-condition (*samanantara-paccaya*), the co-nascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), the mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), the prenascence-condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), and the postnascence-condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).

The twenty-four conditions have been stated as follows: the condition of repetition, the condition of kamma, the condition of result, the condition of nutriment, the condition of faculty, the condition of jhāna, the condition of path,
the condition of association, the condition of dissociation, the condition of presence, the condition of absence,
the condition of disappearance, and the condition of non-disappearance.

In this context, that which is both a cause (*hetu*) and a condition (*paccaya*) is called the "cause-condition" (*hetupaccaya*). This means it is a condition by way of being a cause; that is to say, it is a condition through its state as a cause. The same principle applies to the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and the others. 595.

Herein, "cause" (*hetu*) is a designation for a member of a syllogism, a reason, and a root. For in common worldly usage, in such expressions as "the proposition (*paṭiññā*) and the reason (*hetu*)," the term "reason" refers to a member of a syllogism.
However, in the Teaching (*Sāsana*), in such passages as "those phenomena that arise from a cause" (*ye dhammā hetuppabhavā*), [it refers to the root].
Regarding the term *kāraṇa* (cause): in such passages as "three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots," the word *hetu* (root) is used to mean the fundamental cause;
that is what is intended here. As for the term *paccaya* (condition), its etymological meaning is this: it is called a *paccaya* because "it goes (*eti*) depending (*paṭicca*) upon it.
The sense is that it functions without rejecting that [other thing]. For whatever phenomenon exists or arises without rejecting another phenomenon, [that is a condition].
Or rather, it is said that "it is a condition for that. By way of its characteristic, however, a condition has the characteristic of being helpful (*upakāraka-lakkhaṇa*).
For whatever phenomenon (*dhamma*) is helpful for the persistence or the arising of another phenomenon, that is called its condition.
Condition (*paccaya*), cause (*hetu*), reason (*kāraṇa*), source (*nidāna*), origin (*sambhava*), and provenance (*pabhava*)—these are identical in meaning, though different in phrasing.

Knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Thus, in the sense of being a root it is a cause (*hetu*), and in the sense of being an assistant it is a condition (*paccaya*); briefly, a phenomenon that assists in the sense of being a root is a causal condition (*hetupaccaya*).

The teachers' intention is that, like the seeds of rice and so forth for rice and the like, or like the color and other qualities of a gem for the radiance of a gem, it establishes the state of being wholesome and so forth for the wholesome states and so forth.
But this being so, [how does it apply] to the material phenomena originated by those [mental states]?
The state of being a root-condition (hetupaccayatā) does not apply [to these]. For it does not establish their status as wholesome and so forth, yet it is not the case that they are not conditions.
Indeed, this has been stated: "Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for those states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated by them.
Furthermore, the indeterminate nature of rootless consciousnesses is established even without this [root-condition], and the same applies to those with roots.
Furthermore, the state of being wholesome and so forth is dependent upon appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and the like, not dependent upon associated causes.

If the state of being wholesome and so forth were due solely to its own intrinsic nature among the associated causes, then non-greed (*alobha*), being dependent on those associated causes, would have to be either wholesome or indeterminate.
Since, however, it is both ways, therefore, just as with the associated [factors],...
In the same way, the state of being wholesome and so forth should be sought among the causes as well.

However, if one does not take the meaning of "root" for the causes in the sense of establishing their status as wholesome and so on, but rather takes it in the sense of establishing their state of being well-established, nothing is contradicted.
For phenomena that have obtained causes and conditions are like trees whose roots have grown deep.
They are firm and well-established; those that are rootless, such as moss from sesame or grain seeds, are not well-established.
Thus, a phenomenon that is helpful by way of being a root—meaning it is helpful by accomplishing the state of being well-established—is to be understood as the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*). 596.
Among those that follow, a phenomenon that is helpful by way of being an object is the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). This [is exemplified by] the visible-base (*rūpāyatana*).

Even though it begins with the phrase "with the eye-consciousness element," it concludes by stating: "Whatever states, whether mental or mental concomitants, arise depending upon whatever state, those [latter] states are a condition for those [former] states by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Therefore, there is no state that does not exist [as an object]. For just as a weak man must lean on either a staff or a rope, [so too do all states depend on objects].
Just as a person both arises and stands, so too mental states (citta) and mental concomitants (cetasika) arise and persist only by taking objects such as visible forms as their basis.
Therefore, all phenomena that serve as the objects of mental states and mental concomitants should be understood as object-conditions (ārammaṇa-paccaya). 597.
A phenomenon that assists by way of being predominant is the predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya). It is twofold: by way of being co-nascent (sahajāta) and by way of being an object (ārammaṇa).

In this context, it should be understood that the four factors known as desire (*chanda*), energy (*viriya*), consciousness (*citta*), and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) are predominance conditions (*adhipatipaccaya*), according to such statements as: “Desire is a condition, by way of predominance condition, for states associated with desire and for the material phenomena originated thereby.
However, they do not function simultaneously. For when desire is predominant, when desire is the primary factor...
When the mind proceeds by making something its chief (jeṭṭhaka), then desire (chanda) alone is the predominance (adhipati), not the others.

This same method applies to the remaining [predominances] as well. Furthermore, whatever state (dhamma) immaterial states proceed by regarding as important, that is their object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati).
Therefore it was said: "Whatever states, whether mental or mental concomitants, arise by regarding whatever state as important..."
"Those respective states are conditions for those respective states by way of the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya).

598. A state that assists by way of immediate succession is the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). A state that assists by way of equal and immediate succession is the contiguity condition (samanantara-paccaya).
These two conditions are elaborated upon in many ways; however, this is the [essential] point here.

The essence is this: the fixed order of consciousness—such as "the mind-element immediately following eye-consciousness, and the mind-consciousness-element immediately following the mind-element," and so forth—is established only by way of each preceding consciousness and not otherwise.
Therefore, a state (dhamma) that has the capacity to produce its own corresponding succeeding state of consciousness immediately after itself is the proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*).

For this very reason it was said: “The ‘proximity condition’ (anantarapaccaya) means that the eye-consciousness element and the states associated with it are a condition for the mind-element and the states associated with it by way of proximity condition,” and so forth.

That which is the proximity condition is itself the contiguity condition (samanantarapaccaya). Herein, the difference is merely in the phrasing, just as in the case of accumulation and continuity, or in the pairs concerning designation and etymology.
And it is like that. In terms of meaning, however, there is no difference.

As for the opinion of some teachers that "the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*) is due to the absence of another object, while the immediate condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) is due to the absence of another moment," that [does not apply] to the wholesome consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) of one emerging from cessation, [which acts as the condition] for the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
This contradicts such statements as, "it is a condition by way of the immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapaccaya*).

As for what they say there—"the capacity of phenomena to arise does not diminish, but because it is obstructed by the power of meditation (*bhāvanābala*), the phenomena do not arise immediately following"—this too merely establishes the absence of immediate succession in time. For, in that case, by the power of meditation...
"There is no temporal succession"—this we also say. And because there is no temporal succession, the status of being a "contiguous condition" (*samanantara-paccaya*) is not tenable.
For their doctrine is that it is due to temporal succession that those [factors] constitute a contiguous condition.
Therefore, without forming a dogmatic attachment, one should understand that the distinction here lies merely in the phrasing, and not in the meaning.

In terms of meaning: how so? Because there is no interval (*antara*) between these, they are "immediate" (*anantara*). Because they are perfectly immediate due to the absence of any shape or form, they are "contiguous" (*samanantara*).
599. A phenomenon that, while arising itself, assists by way of the state of arising together is a "co-nascence condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*), like a lamp for light.
It is sixfold according to the immaterial aggregates and so forth. As it is said: "The four aggregates..."

Immaterial states are related to one another by way of the co-nascence condition. The four great elements are related to one another; at the moment of descent [into the womb], name-and-form are related to one another;
mental states and mental factors are related to mind-produced matter; the great elements are related to derived matter;
and material states are related to immaterial states by way of the co-nascence condition at certain times.
"At some times it is not a condition by way of co-nascence-condition. This was said specifically with reference to the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*).
600. A phenomenon that assists another by way of mutual production and support is a mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), like a tripod of three sticks supporting one another.
It is threefold, according to the immaterial aggregates and so forth. As it is said: "The four aggregates..."

“Immaterial states are related to one another by way of mutuality condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*). At the moment of descent [into the womb], the four great elements are related to mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*) by way of mutuality condition.

(601) A phenomenon that assists by way of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and by way of being a support (*nissaya*) is a support condition (*nissayapaccaya*), just as the earth is to trees and canvas is to paintings. This is stated thus:
“The four immaterial aggregates are related to one another by way of support condition.”
In this way, it should be understood according to the same method as stated for co-nascence (*sahajāta*). However, the sixth section here is as follows:
"The eye-base is a condition, by way of support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), for the eye-consciousness-element and for those states associated with it... the ear... the nose... the tongue...

the body-base is a condition, by way of support-condition, for the body-consciousness-element and for those states associated with it. Whatever material form depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed..."

"That form is a condition for the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and the mental states associated with them, by way of a support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*).
Thus it is analyzed. 602.
Regarding the "decisive support-condition" (*upanissayapaccaya*), first, this is the etymological meaning: because of its state of being dependent upon that [object], its own...
"Supported by a fruit, not rejected"—this is *nissaya*. Just as *upāyāsa* (distress) is an intense form of *āyāsa* (exertion), so too *upanissaya* (decisive support) is an intense form of *nissaya*;
it is a designation for a powerful cause. Therefore, a phenomenon that assists by way of being a powerful cause should be understood as the *upanissaya-paccaya* (decisive support condition).
Thus, the decisive support (upanissaya) is threefold: objective decisive support, immediate decisive support, and natural decisive support. Among these:
"Having given a gift, undertaken virtue, or performed the Uposatha duty, one esteems it and reviews it;
one esteems past well-performed deeds and reviews them; having emerged from jhāna, one esteems the jhāna and reviews it."
“Learners (sekkhā), esteeming the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), review it; esteeming purification (vodāna), they review it.
Learners, having emerged from the path, esteeming the path, review it.

In this manner, the object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) has been analyzed without making any distinction from the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati). In that context, regarding the object which is esteemed—
Mind and mental factors arise; among those objects, that which is necessarily the strongest object becomes the dominant condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*).

Thus, it should be understood that their distinction lies in this: in the sense of being merely worthy of esteem, it is the object-dominant condition; in the sense of being a powerful cause, it is the decisive support condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*).
The proximity-decisive support condition (*anantarūpanissaya*) is also [stated as]: "Preceding wholesome aggregates are [the condition] for succeeding wholesome [aggregates]."

It is analyzed according to the method beginning with, "The aggregates are a condition for [subsequent aggregates] by way of the decisive-support condition," without making any distinction from the proximity condition.
However, in the presentation of the matrix (mātikā), it is stated:
"The eye-consciousness element and the states associated with it are a condition for the mind-element and the states associated with it by way of the proximity condition," and so forth.

There is a distinction in the presentation [of these conditions], because the *anantara* (proximity) condition is taught according to the method of the immediately preceding, while the *upanissaya* (decisive support) condition is taught according to the method beginning with: "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for subsequent wholesome states by way of the decisive support condition.
Nevertheless, in terms of their actual meaning, they both arrive at the same state. Even so, immediately after each respective [condition]...
The state of being immediate (*anantaratā*) should be understood as the capacity for a corresponding arising of consciousness to proceed;
and the state of being an immediate decisive support (*anantarūpanissayatā*) is to be known by the power of the preceding consciousness in producing the subsequent consciousness.

For while consciousness may arise even without certain factors such as the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), there is no such thing as the arising of consciousness without an immediately preceding consciousness.

Therefore, it is a powerful condition (*balava-paccaya*). Thus, the "proximity condition" (*anantara-paccaya*) is so called by way of the arising of a corresponding consciousness immediately after its own [preceding] state, while the "proximity-strong-dependence" (*anantara-upanissaya*) is so called by way of being a powerful cause; in this way, their distinction should be understood.
As for the "natural strong-dependence" (*pakatūpanissaya*), it is a strong-dependence that is natural (*pakata*); "natural" means within one's own continuum (*santāna*).
It is either faith, virtue, and so forth that has been produced, or the season, food, and so forth that have been utilized;
or else, natural support is *pakatūpanissaya*, meaning it is unmixed with objective conditions (*ārammaṇa*) or immediate conditions (*anantara*). Regarding its natural support:
"Relying on faith, one gives a gift, undertakes virtue, performs the Uposatha rite, and arouses jhāna."
One arouses insight, arouses the path, arouses direct knowledge, and arouses meditative attainment.
Relying upon virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, one gives a gift... [and so on] ...one arouses meditative attainment.
Faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom are related to faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
The diversity [of this condition] is to be understood in many ways according to the method beginning with “condition” (*paccayo*).

Thus, these factors beginning with faith (*saddhā*) are called “natural decisive support” (*pakatūpanissaya*), because they are both natural conditions and possess the sense of being powerful causes. 603.
A state that arises earlier and assists by way of its continued presence is the “prenascence condition” (*purejātapaccaya*). That...
At the five doors, it is elevenfold by way of the bases, objects, and the heart-base. As it is said:
“The eye-base is a condition, by way of prenascence-condition, for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated therewith.
The ear... [and so on] ...the nose, tongue, and body-base; the visible-object, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible-object-base are [conditions] for the body-consciousness element...”

It is also a condition, by way of prenascence-condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), for those states associated with it. The spheres of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects are [conditions] for the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

Whatever material form depending upon which both the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) proceed—that material form is a condition, by way of prenascence-condition, for the mind-element and for those states associated with it.

It is a condition for the mind-consciousness element and its associated states at times by way of the pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), and at other times it is not a condition by way of the pre-arising condition. 604.
An immaterial state that assists material states that have arisen previously by way of providing support is the post-arising condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).

It is like the volition for the taste of food in the bodies of young vultures. Therefore it is said: "Mentally arisen states, both consciousness and mental factors, that arise later are a condition for this body that arose earlier by way of the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).
605. A state that assists subsequent states to become proficient and powerful in the sense of repetition is the repetition condition (*āsevana-paccaya*).
It is like the repeated application to learning and so forth. It is threefold by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and functional javanas.

As it is said: "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding wholesome states by way of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). Preceding unwholesome... [and] functional-ineffective states are [conditions] for succeeding..."
“It is a condition for subsequent functional-ineffective (kiriyābyākata) states by way of the relation of repetition.
606. A state that assists by way of the functional nature termed “mental application” (cittapayoga) is the kamma-condition.
It is twofold: by way of wholesome and unwholesome volition (cetanā) belonging to different moments, and by way of all co-nascent volition. As it has been said:
“Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for resultant aggregates and for kamma-produced matter by way of kamma-condition.
Volition is a condition for associated states and for matter originated by them by way of kamma-condition.
(607) A resultant state that assists in producing a state of quietude and lack of exertion through its own quality of quietude and lack of exertion is a resultant-condition (*vipāka-paccaya*).

Thus, during the course of existence, it is a condition for the material phenomena originating from that [consciousness], and at the moment of rebirth-linking, for the material phenomena produced by past deeds (*kaṭattā-rūpa*); and in all instances, it is a condition for the associated mental states.
As it is said: "One resultant indeterminate aggregate is a condition, by way of resultant condition, for three aggregates and for mind-originated material phenomena...
At the moment of rebirth-linking, one resultant indeterminate aggregate [is a condition] for three..."

“Aggregates are related to aggregates and to the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of resultant condition (vipāka-paccaya). Three aggregates are related to one aggregate; two aggregates are related to two aggregates and to the matter produced by kamma by way of resultant condition. Aggregates are related to the physical basis (vatthu) by way of resultant condition.
The four nutriments (āhāra), which assist both the material and immaterial realms by way of sustaining (upatthambhaka), are the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya). As it has been said:
“Edible food is a condition for this body by way of nutriment-condition.
Immaterial nutriments are a condition for associated states and for the matter produced by them by way of nutriment-condition. However, in the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions), it says:
“At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate nutriments are a condition for the associated aggregates and for the matter of the kamma-born [body] by way of nutriment-condition.”
It is also stated: “...condition. 609.

The twenty faculties, excluding the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the male faculty (*purisindriya*), are the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*) in the sense of being supportive as a predominance (*adhipati*).

Among these, the eye-faculty and the others are conditions for immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*) alone; the remaining ones are conditions for both material and immaterial phenomena. As it has been said:

“The eye-faculty is a condition, by way of faculty-condition, for the eye-consciousness-element and for those states associated with it; … [and so on] … the ear… the nose… the tongue… the body-faculty is a condition, by way of faculty-condition, for the body-consciousness-element and for those states associated with it. The material life-faculty is a condition, by way of faculty-condition, for kamma-produced matter.
The immaterial faculties are conditions, by way of faculty-condition, for their associated states and for the states originated by them.”

“Material phenomena are a condition for material phenomena by way of the faculty-condition. Furthermore, in the Section on Questions (Pañhāvāra), it is also stated: “At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate faculties are a condition for their associated aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of the faculty-condition.

610. Excluding those that assist in the sense of being objects of close contemplation, [the faculties] are conditions for the two pairs of feelings—pleasure and pain—within the two sets of fivefold consciousness.
All seven jhāna factors, distinguished as wholesome and so forth, are the jhāna condition. As it is said:

“The jhāna factors are a condition, by way of the jhāna condition, for the states associated with the jhāna and for the material phenomena originated thereby. However, in the *Pañhāvāra*, it is stated:

“At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate jhāna factors are a condition, by way of the jhāna condition, for the associated aggregates and for the material phenomena produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).”
It is also stated: “...is a condition.
611. In the sense of leading out from this or that [state], the twelve path-factors—classified as wholesome and so forth—are the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*).
As it is said: “The path-factors are a path-condition for those states associated with the path and for the material phenomena originated by them.”

Regarding the "condition" (paccaya): in the section on questions (pañhāvāra), it is further stated that "at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), resultant indeterminate path-factors (maggaṅga) are a condition, by way of the path-condition (maggapaccaya), for the associated aggregates (khandha) and for the materiality produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa).
However, it should be understood that both of these—jhāna-condition and path-condition—are not found in the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions or in rootless consciousnesses (ahetuka-citta).

612. Non-material phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) that provide assistance by way of the state of association—characterized by having a single basis (*ekavatthuka*), a single object (*ekārammaṇa*), a single arising (*ekuppāda*), and a single cessation (*ekanirodha*)—are the associated condition (*sampayuttapaccaya*).
As it is said: "The four non-material aggregates (*khandhā arūpino*) are a condition for one another by way of the associated condition.

613. Material phenomena (*rūpino dhammā*) that provide assistance by not failing to attain the state of having a single basis and so forth, as well as non-material phenomena, [provide assistance] to non-material phenomena...
The dissociation condition for material phenomena is threefold, by way of conascence, post-nascence, and pre-nascence. For it has been said:
“Conascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-produced matter by way of dissociation condition;
postnascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for this prenascent body by way of dissociation condition.”

Furthermore, in the analysis of co-nascence (*sahajāta-vibhaṅga*) regarding the indeterminate category (*abyākatapada*), it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-kkhaṇa*), resultant indeterminate aggregates (*vipākābyākatā khandhā*) are a condition for the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*).
Aggregates are [a condition] for the physical basis (*vatthu*); the physical basis is a condition for the aggregates by way of dissociation-condition.
However, the pre-nascent (*purejāta*) should be understood solely by way of the physical bases such as the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) and so forth. As it has been said:
“The pre-arisen eye-base is a condition for eye-consciousness … [and so on] … the body-base is a condition for body-consciousness by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*).

The physical basis (*vatthu*) is a condition for resultant-indefferent and functional-indefferent aggregates … [and so on] … the physical basis is a condition for wholesome aggregates … [and so on] … the physical basis is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of dissociation-condition.”
614. The presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) is a state that assists by way of supporting a similar state through its existence as a present characteristic.

Its matrix is set forth in seven ways, according to the immaterial aggregates, the great primaries, mind-and-matter, consciousness and mental factors, the great primaries, the bases, and the physical heart-base.
As it is said: “The four immaterial aggregates are mutually related by way of the presence condition...”
Condition: the four great elements; at the moment of conception, mind-and-matter are mutually related to one another. Mental states and mental factors are related to matter produced by mind.

The great elements are related to derived matter. The eye-base is related to the eye-consciousness element …pe… the body-base …pe… the visible-form base …pe… the tangible-object base is related to the body-consciousness element and to those [mental states] associated with it.

“Material phenomena are a condition for mental phenomena by way of presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*). The visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) … [and so on] … the tangible-object base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*) is a condition for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and for the states associated with it.

Whatever material form depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) proceed—that material form is a condition for the mind-element, for the mind-consciousness-element, and for the states associated with them, by way of presence-condition.”

In the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), however, having set forth conascence (*sahajāta*), prenascence (*purejāta*), postnascence (*pacchājāta*), nutriment (*āhāra*), and faculty (*indriya*), first, regarding conascence, the exposition is made according to the method beginning:
"One aggregate is a condition by way of presence for three aggregates and for the matter originated thereby.
Regarding prenascence, the exposition is made by way of the prenascent eye and so forth.
The exposition has been made thus: by way of being a condition for this body that has arisen earlier, there is the exposition of the mind and mental factors that have arisen later;
and among the nutriments and faculties, the exposition has been made thus: "Edible food is a condition for this body by way of presence-condition (atthipaccaya);
the material life-faculty is a condition for the matter produced by kamma by way of presence-condition."

615. Non-existent conditions (*natthipaccaya*) are those immediately preceding immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) that have ceased, which assist by providing a sphere for the occurrence of the immaterial phenomena arising immediately after them.
As it is said: “Consciousness and mental factors that have ceased immediately before are a condition, by way of non-existence, for consciousness and mental factors that are presently arisen.”

These same [states], by virtue of having passed away, are the *vigata-paccaya* (passed-away condition) because they provide assistance. As it is said: "Consciousness and mental factors that have just passed away are a condition for presently arisen consciousness and mental factors by way of the passed-away condition.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the very states which serve as the *atthi-paccaya* (existence condition) are the *avigata-paccaya* (not-passed-away condition) because they provide assistance by virtue of not having passed away.
However, this dyad was stated either as a stylistic feature of the teaching or to suit those disciples who were to be trained in that manner, following the dyad on rootless states (*ahetuka-duka*).
"Even though it has been stated, it is like the pair dissociated from cause.
Thus ends the detailed exposition of the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise].
Regarding these twenty-four conditions, this is ignorance.
"It is a condition for merits in two ways and also in many ways;
for others who follow, it is considered a condition in one way.
Therein, "in two ways for merits" means it is a condition in two ways: by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and by way of decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*).
It exists. For when one comprehends ignorance as subject to destruction and vanishing, it serves as the object-condition for the meritorious formations of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
When one knows a deluded mind with a mind of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), it serves as such for the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) formations.
Furthermore, for one who fulfills the bases of meritorious action of the sense-sphere, such as giving and so forth, for the purpose of transcending ignorance, [it serves as the condition].
And for one who arouses the fine-material-sphere jhānas, it serves as a condition for both of them by way of decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Likewise, for one who, being deluded by ignorance, aspires to the excellence of sense-sphere existence and fine-material existence and performs those very same meritorious deeds, it is a condition.
However, it is a condition for the formations of demerit (*apuñña-abhisaṅkhāra*) of others in many ways. How so? For this [ignorance]—

When greed and the other [defilements] arise with ignorance as their object, it is by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*); when they esteem and relish it, it is by way of the object-predominance, object-object-decisive-support, and object-strong-dependence conditions;
for one who, deluded by ignorance and failing to see the danger, commits acts such as killing, it is by way of the strong-dependence condition;
and for the second impulsion and subsequent moments, it is by way of the proximity, contiguity, proximity-strong-dependence, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions.
For one performing any unwholesome action, it serves as a condition in many ways—by way of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.

It is considered to be a condition for the subsequent [wholesome] ones in only one way; that is, it is considered to be a condition for the formations of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) solely by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) condition. Furthermore, its status as a decisive support should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
617. Here it may be asked: Is this ignorance alone the condition for the formations, or are there other conditions as well?
What follows from this? If it were ignorance alone, one would fall into the doctrine of a single cause.
But if there are others, then the statement of a single cause—“with ignorance as condition, formations arise”—would be untenable. It is not untenable. Why? Because:

Here, there is no single fruit from a single cause, nor is there a plurality of fruits from a plurality of causes; yet there is a purpose in illustrating the relationship between a single cause and its single fruit.
For here, from a single cause, there is neither any single fruit nor a plurality of fruits; nor indeed [is there a plurality of fruits] from multiple causes.
It is one. However, by means of many causes, it becomes manifold.

For instance, it is observed that when a fruit designated as a sprout arises, it is manifold—consisting of visible form, odor, taste, and so forth—due to many causes known as temperature, earth, seed, and water.

As for this demonstration of single cause and single effect, namely, "with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness," [it is intended to show the primary factor].
It has been said that there is a purpose and a motive therein.

For the Blessed One, in some instances, elucidates either the cause or the fruit alone—whether because it is the primary factor, because it is manifest, because it is unique, or in accordance with the Teacher’s skill in exposition and the disposition of those to be trained—as in the statement: "With contact as condition, feeling arises."
Indeed, because of its preeminence, [the text] mentions only one cause and one fruit. For contact is the preeminent cause of feeling, since feeling is defined according to the nature of the contact;
and feeling is the preeminent fruit of contact, since contact is defined according to the nature of the feeling.
Because it is evident that "diseases arise from phlegm," [the text] mentions only one cause; for in this case, the phlegm is evident, whereas karma and the rest are not.
“Bhikkhus, whatever unwholesome states there may be, they all have their root in improper attention (ayonisomanasikāra).

He stated this single cause because of its unique (asādhāraṇa) nature. For improper attention is the unique cause of unwholesome states, whereas the physical basis, the object, and so forth, are common (sādhāraṇa) causes.

Therefore, although other causes for volitional formations (saṅkhāra)—such as the physical basis, the object, and co-nascent phenomena—exist, it is this ignorance (avijjā) that is [the primary cause] here.

Because of the statements, “Craving increases for one who contemplates gratification,” and “With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints,” it is the cause of other causes of volitional formations such as craving;

because of its predominance as the cause of volitional formations; because of its manifest nature, as in the passage, “Bhikkhus, the ignorant person, immersed in ignorance, performs even a meritorious volitional formation”; and because of its uniqueness as the cause of volitional formations.

It should be understood that [the cause] has been illuminated. And by this very statement regarding the avoidance of explaining each individual cause and fruit, the purpose for explaining each individual cause and fruit in every instance should be understood. 618.
Here it is asked: Even if this is so, how can ignorance—which is exclusively undesirable in its fruit and is blameworthy—be a condition for the formative acts of merit and the imperturbable?
Is this logical? No, for sugarcane does not arise from a nimba seed. How is it not logical?
For in the world, the conditions of phenomena are established as being both contradictory and non-contradictory, as well as similar and dissimilar;
yet these [conditions] are not themselves karmic results.
For in the world, a condition—whether contradictory or non-contradictory—is established for phenomena by way of their location, intrinsic nature, function, and so forth.

A preceding consciousness is a condition for a subsequent consciousness that is contradictory in terms of location; likewise, prior training in crafts and the like is a condition for the performance of those same crafts occurring later.
Kamma is a condition for material form that is contradictory in terms of intrinsic nature, as are milk and other such substances for curds and the like.
Light is a condition for eye-consciousness that is contrary to its function; likewise, molasses and so forth are conditions for the taints and so on that are contrary to their functions.

However, the eye, visible objects, and so forth, are conditions for eye-consciousness and the rest that are neither contrary to their location nor contrary to their function. Similarly, preceding impulsions and so forth are conditions for succeeding impulsions and the rest that are neither contrary to their intrinsic nature nor contrary to their function.

Just as conditions are established as being either contrary or non-contrary, so too are they similar or dissimilar. For it is only that which is similar—namely, temperature and nutriment—that [acts as a condition].
Material form is a condition for material form, as are rice seeds and the like for rice fruits and the like.

Even dissimilar material form is a condition for immaterial phenomena, and immaterial phenomena are likewise conditions for material form; for example, cow-hair, sheep-hair, horns, curd, sesame flour, and so forth, are conditions for *dubbā*, *sara*, *bhūtiṇaka*, and other grasses.
Those phenomena for which these are conditions—whether they be opposed, non-opposed, similar, or dissimilar—are not necessarily the kamma-results of those phenomena.

Thus, this ignorance should be understood as having exclusively undesirable results by way of its maturation (*vipāka*), and as being blameworthy (*sāvajja*) by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

Furthermore, it should be understood as a condition for all these formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth, by way of being a condition that is either compatible or incompatible with their respective locations, functions, and natures, and by way of being a similar or dissimilar condition. And its state of being a condition is [expressed by the verse]: "For whom..."

For it has been stated in such a manner as follows: "When ignorance—defined as non-knowing—regarding suffering and the other [truths] has not been abandoned, one, through that non-knowing regarding suffering and regarding the past and so forth, grasps the suffering of saṃsāra with the perception of pleasure, and consequently initiates the three kinds of formations which serve as its cause. Thus it was said.
Furthermore, there is this other method:
He who is deluded regarding death and rebirth, regarding the cycle of existence,
regarding the characteristics of conditioned phenomena, and regarding those things that have arisen dependently.
"Since he conditions these threefold formations, ignorance is their condition for all three types.
But how is it that one who is deluded regarding these [aggregates] performs these threefold formations? First, by way of death:

Being confused regarding death, one who does not grasp that "death is the dissolution of the aggregates in all cases" conceptualizes such things as "a being dies" or "the transmigration of a being to another body.

Being confused regarding rebirth, one who does not grasp that "rebirth is the manifestation of the aggregates in all cases" conceptualizes such things as "a being is reborn" or "the manifestation of a new body for a being."
He who is deluded regarding this saṃsāra—
of which it is said: “The continuous, uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases is called ‘saṃsāra’”— is thus bewildered.

When saṃsāra has been described in this way, one who does not grasp it as such conceptualizes it thus: "This being goes from this world to the next world; from the next world he comes to this world," and so forth.

Being deluded regarding the characteristics of formations (saṅkhāras), and failing to grasp both their specific and general characteristics, one conceptualizes formations as self, as belonging to a self, as permanent, as pleasant, and as beautiful.
Being deluded regarding dependently arisen phenomena, and failing to grasp the occurrence of formations and the rest through ignorance and the other factors, one [conceptualizes]: "Self..."
Whether he knows or does not know, he himself acts and causes others to act. He is reborn at the moment of conception (*paṭisandhi*);
then atoms, the Lord (*Issara*), and so forth, fashion his body from the stage of the embryo (*kalala*) onwards and bring about the sense-faculties.
Endowed with these faculties, he touches, feels, craves, clings, and exerts effort. Thus, in another existence...
Or he conceptualizes that "all beings are transformed by destiny, chance, inherent nature, or evolution. Being blinded by ignorance,
while conceptualizing in this way, he— just as a blind man walking upon the earth might take a path or a non-path,
dry land or a low place, level ground or uneven ground— likewise engages in both merit and demerit.
"One also performs an immovable volitional formation.
Therefore this is said:
"Just as if a man born blind, without a guide..."
At one time he goes by the right path, and at another time even by the wrong path.
"Thus wandering in saṃsāra, the fool, being without a guide,
performs merit at one time and demerit at another."
“And when, having known the Dhamma, he realizes the truths, then,
with the subsiding of ignorance, he will live in peace.
This is the detailed explanation for the phrase “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.”

The Detailed Exposition of the Section on Consciousness with Formations as Condition (Saṅkhārapaccayāviññāṇapadavitthārakathā) 620. Regarding the phrase "consciousness with formations as condition": "Consciousness" refers to the sixfold [consciousness], beginning with eye-consciousness.
Therein, eye-consciousness is twofold: wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant. Likewise for ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness.

Mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa) is twenty-two-fold: the two mind-elements (manodhātu) which are wholesome and unwholesome resultants; the three rootless mental-consciousness-elements (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu);
the eight sense-sphere resultant cittas accompanied by roots (sahetuka-kāmāvacara-vipākacitta); the five fine-material-sphere [resultants]; and the four immaterial-sphere [resultants].
Thus, by means of these six types of consciousness, all thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses are accounted for.
They are included. However, those pertaining to the supramundane (*lokuttara*) are not included because they do not fit within the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).
Herein, it may be asked: "How is it to be known that this consciousness of the aforementioned kind has formations as its condition?
Because there is no result (*vipāka*) in the absence of accumulated karma. For this is a result, and a result does not occur in the absence of accumulated karma.
It arises. If it were to arise [indiscriminately], then all resultant consciousnesses would arise for everyone;
but since they do not so arise, it should be understood that this consciousness exists by way of the condition of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya*).

If it is asked, "By way of which specific volitional formations does which specific consciousness arise?"—first, by way of the volitional formation of meritorious kamma belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-puññābhisaṅkhāra*):

There are sixteen [types of consciousness] that are wholesome-resultants: the five beginning with eye-consciousness; in the case of mind-consciousness, one mind-element and two mind-consciousness-elements;
and the eight great sense-sphere resultants. As it is said:
"Due to the performance and accumulation of wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness has arisen..."
There arises ear-consciousness… nose-consciousness… tongue-consciousness… body-consciousness… resultant mind-element has arisen.

Mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy has arisen. Mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity has arisen. [Mind-consciousness-element] accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge.
[Mind-consciousness-element] accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and with volitional formation. Accompanied by joy...
“Dissociated from knowledge. Accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge with volitional effort. Accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge.

Accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge with volitional effort. Accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge. Accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge with volitional effort.”
But with the volitional formation of merit pertaining to the fine-material sphere as condition, there are five resultant states of the fine-material sphere. As it is said:

"Due to having performed and accumulated that very wholesome kamma of the fine-material sphere, he—secluded from sensual pleasures—enters and dwells in the first jhāna... [and so on] ...up to the fifth jhāna. Thus, with the volitional formation of merit as condition.
Consciousness is twenty-one-fold.

However, conditioned by unwholesome formative volitions (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), there is a sevenfold consciousness consisting of the five unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousnesses and so forth, one mind-element (*manodhātu*), and one mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). As it is said:

"Due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome kamma, resultant eye-consciousness arises... ear... nose... tongue... body-consciousness... resultant mind-element and resultant mind-consciousness-element arise."
But with the immovable formative action as condition, there are four types of immaterial resultant consciousness; thus, consciousness is fourfold. As it is said:

"Due to the performance and accumulation of that very wholesome kamma of the immaterial sphere, as its result, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, [there arises] consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space...
[the base of] infinite consciousness... [the base of] nothingness... [the base] accompanied by neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
“With the abandoning of both pleasure and pain, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Thus, having understood that consciousness arises with volitional formations as its condition, its mode of occurrence must now be understood:
for all this occurs in two ways, namely by way of the process of existence (*pavatti*) and by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Of these, there are two...
The five types of sensory consciousness, the two mind-elements, and the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—
these thirteen occur only during the course of existence (*pavatti*) within the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra-bhava*). The remaining nineteen occur, as appropriate,
both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) across all three realms of existence.
How so? First, regarding the five types of wholesome-resultant consciousness, such as eye-consciousness and the rest:

when a desirable or desirable-neutral object—such as a visible form and so forth—comes within the range of the eye and other faculties that have reached their respective stages of maturation in one who has been reborn through either wholesome or unwholesome kamma-result, [these consciousnesses] perform the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, supported by the sensitivity of the eye and other sense organs.
They proceed by accomplishing their respective functions. Likewise, there are five unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses]. For these have only an undesirable or undesirably-neutral object;
this alone is the distinction. Furthermore, all ten of these are fixed as to door, object, basis, and origin, and they possess fixed functions.

Immediately after the wholesome resultant eye-consciousnesses and so forth, the wholesome resultant mind-element arises, taking their very same object and depending on the heart-base, performing the function of receiving.
Likewise, immediately after the unwholesome resultants, the unwholesome resultant [mind-element] arises. Moreover, this pair has indeterminate doors and objects.
It has a fixed physical basis and a fixed function.
However, the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy, immediately following the wholesome resultant mind-element,
accomplishes the function of investigation by taking that same object, depending on the heart-basis, across the six sense doors.

In the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that when the object is powerful, for beings in the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is generally interrupted at the conclusion of the impulsion (*javana*) associated with greed;
then, with respect to the object grasped by that impulsion, the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) occurs once or twice.
However, in the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*, regarding the registration [consciousness]...
Two types of consciousness have arrived. This consciousness, however, receives two names: "registering consciousness" (*tadārammaṇa*) and "subsequent life-continuum" (*piṭṭhibhavanga*).
It has an indeterminate door and object, a determinate physical basis, and an indeterminate place and function.
Thus, it should be understood that these thirteen [types of consciousness] occur only during the course of existence within the five-aggregate realm.
In the remaining nineteen [types of consciousness], nothing fails to occur in accordance with their respective rebirth-linking.

However, during the course of existence (*pavatti*), first, the two rootless mind-consciousness elements (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*)—both wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant—perform the function of investigation (*santīraṇa-kicca*) immediately following wholesome and unwholesome resultant mind-elements at the five sense doors.
At the six doors, they perform the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa-kicca*) in the manner previously described. By themselves...
From the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, when there is no thought-moment to interrupt the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), these [resultants] proceed performing four functions:
the function of the life-continuum, and finally the function of death. Having fixed objects but with indeterminate doors, objects, locations, and functions, they operate.
The eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses accompanied by roots perform the function of registration (tadārammaṇa) at the six doors in the manner already described; by themselves...
From the moment of the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) provided by itself onwards, in the absence of a consciousness-moment that interrupts the life-continuum (bhavaṅga),

these [consciousnesses] proceed performing three functions— the function of the life-continuum, and finally the function of death— while having fixed bases, but with indeterminate doors, objects, locations, and functions.

This applies to the five fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) consciousnesses and the four immaterial-sphere (āruppa) consciousnesses from the moment of the rebirth-linking they themselves have provided onwards, in the absence of an interrupter of the life-continuum.
In the arising of consciousness, they proceed by accomplishing two functions: the function of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) at the beginning, and the function of death (*cuti*) at the end.
Among them, those of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) have fixed bases and objects but indeterminate places and functions;
the others have fixed bases and fixed objects but indeterminate places and functions. Thus, first of all, even the thirty-two-fold [consciousness]...
In the course of existence, consciousness proceeds with volitional formations as its condition;
therein, those various volitional formations serve as conditions for it by way of both kamma-condition and decisive-support-condition.
As for what was stated: "Regarding the remaining nineteen [types of rebirth-linking], none [proceeds] to a rebirth-linking corresponding to itself..."
“...does not proceed,” this is difficult to understand because it is too concise. Therefore, in order to show the method of exposition for this, it is said:
How many kinds of rebirth-linking are there? How many types of rebirth-linking consciousness are there? By what means and where does rebirth-linking occur?
What is the object of rebirth-linking?
There are twenty types of rebirth-linking, including that of non-percipient beings. There are nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness of the kinds already mentioned.
Among these, rebirth-linking in the woeful states occurs through the rootless mind-consciousness element of unwholesome-resultant type.

Rebirth-linking in the human world occurs through the wholesome-resultant type for those born blind, deaf from birth, insane from birth, mute, eunuchs, hermaphrodites, and so forth. [The remaining types occur] through the eight root-cause-accompanied sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses.
Rebirth-linking occurs for those possessing merit among the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and among human beings.

It occurs in the world of form (*rūpī-brahmaloka*) through the five types of fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) resultant consciousness, and in the formless world (*arūpaloka*) through the four types of immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) resultant consciousness.
That by which rebirth-linking occurs in a particular place is itself called its corresponding rebirth-linking. In brief, however, there are three kinds of objects for rebirth-linking.
They are past, present, and not-to-be-described (*navattabba*). The rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of non-perception is without an object.
Among those, for the rebirth-linkings of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the object is exclusively past.
For the ten sense-sphere [rebirth-linkings], it is either past or present. For the remainder, it is exclusively not-to-be-described. Thus, regarding the three types of objects:
Furthermore, as for the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) that occurs, it arises immediately after a death-consciousness (cuticitta) that has either a past object or an indeterminate object;

there is no such thing as a death-consciousness with a present object. Therefore, following a death with an object from either of those two [past or indeterminate] objects, the rebirth-linking occurs with an object from any one of the three [past, present, or future] objects.
The mode of occurrence by way of happy and miserable destinies should be understood.
For example, in the case of a person who has committed evil deeds and is situated in a happy destiny of the sense-sphere,
as he lies upon his deathbed, his accumulated evil karma— according to the statement beginning with "At that time, those [karmas] hang over him"— [manifests].
Or else, either a kamma or a sign of kamma comes into range at the mind-door.

Taking that as its object, immediately after the cognitive series of impulsions—which ends with the registration consciousness—has arisen, the death-consciousness arises, making the object of the life-continuum its own object.
When that has ceased, taking that same kamma or sign of kamma which had come into range as its object, [the rebirth-linking consciousness arises], impelled by the power of unabated defilements.
A rebirth-consciousness included within the miserable destinies arises. This is a rebirth with a past object immediately following a death with a past object.
In another case, at the time of death, by way of the aforementioned type of kamma, a sign of a miserable destiny—such as the color of a mass of flames in the hells and so forth—[appears].
When [an object] comes into the range of the mind-door, after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen and ceased twice, three process-minds arise:

one adverting consciousness (āvajjana) directed toward that object, five impulsion moments (javana)—because their momentum is weakened due to proximity to death—and two registration moments (tadārammaṇa). Thereafter, the object of the life-continuum...
Having passed through one death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*), eleven thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) have thus elapsed.

Then, within that same object which has a remaining lifespan of five thought-moments, the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*) arises for him. This is a rebirth-linking with a present object immediately following a death with a past object.
In another person, at the time of death, an inferior object—acting as a cause for lust and other defilements—enters the range of perception through one of the five doors.

As it arises in due order, following the stage of determining (voṭṭhabbana), because the force [of consciousness] has weakened due to the proximity of death, five impulsion moments (javana) and two registration moments (tadārammaṇa) arise. Thereafter, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) [takes over] its own object...
Taking that as its object, there is one death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). At this point, fifteen mind-moments have passed:

two life-continuum moments (*bhavaṅga*), adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, five impulsion moments (*javana*), two registration moments (*tadārammaṇa*), and one death-consciousness. Then, while that very same [object] still has the duration of one remaining mind-moment—

The rebirth-linking consciousness arises with that [past] object as its objective support. This, too, is a rebirth-linking with a present objective support immediately following a death with a past objective support.

Such, then, is the manner of occurrence of a rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination with an objective support of the past or the present, immediately following a death in a happy destination with a past objective support.

624. However, for one situated in an unhappy destination (duggati) who has accumulated blameless kamma, that blameless kamma or the sign of the kamma (kamma-nimitta) enters the avenue of the mind-door in the same manner already described.
Thus, setting aside the bright side (sukkapa-kkha) from the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), everything should be understood according to the previous method.
This [process] occurs immediately after a death in an unhappy destination whose object is past, and which has both past and present objects.
The mode of occurrence for rebirth-linking in a happy destination (sugati). Furthermore,

for one established in a happy destination who has accumulated blameless kamma, as stated in the passage beginning, “At that time they hang down before him,” the blameless kamma accumulated according to its nature,
or the sign of the kamma (kamma-nimitta), appears at the mind-door to the person lying on the deathbed.
It comes into the range of perception; and that occurs only for one who has accumulated blameless kamma pertaining to the sense-sphere.
However, for one who has accumulated sublime (mahaggata) kamma, only the sign of the kamma (kammanimitta) comes into the range of perception.

Taking that as its object, following a pure cognitive series (javanavīthi) that culminates in registration (tadārammaṇa), the death-consciousness (cuticitta) arises, making the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) its objective support.

When that [death-consciousness] has ceased, there arises a rebirth-linking consciousness included within the happy realms, directed toward that very same object— either the kamma or the sign of kamma— that has come into range, and which is impelled by the power of unabated defilements.
This is the rebirth-linking with either a past object or an indeterminable object immediately following a death-consciousness with a past object.
In another person, at the time of death, due to blameless karma of the sense-sphere, a sign of a happy destination— appearing as the color of a mother’s womb in the human world,
or as the color of gardens, celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth, in the deva world— comes into range at the mind-door.
Following the same sequence shown for the presentation of signs of an unhappy destination, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises immediately after the death-consciousness.
This is rebirth-linking with a present object immediately following a death-consciousness that had an past object.
In the case of another person, at the time of death, relatives might say, "Dear one, this offering to the Buddha is being made for your sake;
gladden your heart," and thus provide a visible object such as a garland of flowers or a banner, or a sound object such as the hearing of the Dhamma or the playing of musical instruments.
Or they present an object of smell through incense, perfumes, and so forth;
