or an object of taste by saying, "Father, please taste this, it is a gift to be given for your sake," such as honey, molasses, and so forth;

or an object of touch by saying, "Father, please feel this, it is a gift to be given for your sake," such as Chinese silk, Somāra cloth, and so forth—thus they present [objects] at the five sense doors.

When that object, such as a visible form, has come into range, following the sequence of the arisen five-door adverting consciousness, there arise five impulsion moments and two registration moments, because their momentum has weakened due to the proximity of death.

Then, taking the life-continuum’s own objective field as its object, one death-consciousness arises; at the conclusion of that, within that very same single mind-moment, [the rebirth-linking consciousness arises].
The rebirth-linking consciousness arises with that object. This too is a rebirth-linking with a present object immediately following a death with a past object.

However, for another person who has attained a sublime state by means of the earth-kasiṇa jhāna and so forth, and who is situated in a happy destination, at the time of death there appears either one of the wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, the sign of the kamma, or the sign of the destiny, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.

Or, when a sublime state of mind (mahaggata-citta) enters the range of the mind-door, or when a refined object that serves as a cause for the arising of wholesome states enters the range of either the eye or the ear,

five impulsive moments (javana) arise in due order at the conclusion of the arisen registration (voṭṭhapana), because their momentum has become weakened due to the proximity of death. This applies to those whose destiny is a sublime realm.

However, there is no registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) at that time; therefore, immediately after the impulsion, a single death-consciousness (cuticitta) arises, taking as its object the sphere of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

At the conclusion of that, a rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) arises, included within one of the fortunate realms—whether sense-sphere or sublime—and taking as its object whichever among the objects thus presented is appropriate. This [consciousness] has an indeterminate object.
Immediately after death in a happy destination (sugati), rebirth-linking occurs with an object that is either past, present, or inexpressible (navattabba), whichever is appropriate.

Following this same principle, rebirth-linking immediately after death in the formless realms (ārūpa) should also be understood. This is the mode of occurrence of rebirth-linking with a past or inexpressible object, following death in a happy destination with a past or inexpressible object. 627.
However, for one who has committed evil deeds and remains in an unhappy destination (duggati), that karma, according to the method already stated, becomes the sign of the deed (kamma-nimitta).

Or [it occurs] through the sign of destiny at the mind-door. Or else, when an unwholesome object that has become the cause for the arising of unwholesome states enters the range of the five doors, then, in due order, at the conclusion of the death-consciousness, a rebirth-linking consciousness arises having one of those objects as its object, included within the miserable destinies.
This [occurs] immediately after a death in a miserable destiny with a past object.
The mode of occurrence of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) which has past and present objects as its support.
Up to this point, the occurrence of all nineteen types of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking has been explained.
And all of this is thus.
While occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking, it proceeds in two ways by way of kamma;
and through divisions such as the mixed [kamma], the division [of rebirth] is of two kinds and so forth.
For this nineteenfold resultant consciousness, while occurring at rebirth-linking, proceeds in two ways by way of kamma.
It applies. For, in the case of a single person, one's own productive kamma acts as a condition both by way of asynchronous kamma-condition and by way of decisive-support condition.
For this has been said: "Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for its result by way of decisive-support condition.
Furthermore, regarding that which is thus occurring, its classification into two types and so forth should be understood through its divisions such as mixed and the rest.
To explain: although this [existence] occurs in a single way by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is twofold according to the distinction between being mixed or unmixed with form (*rūpa*).

It is threefold according to the distinction between the realms of sense-desire, fine-material, and immaterial existence (*bhava*). It is fourfold according to the classification of the modes of birth (*yoni*): egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously born (*opapātika*). It is fivefold according to the destinies (*gati*).
It is sevenfold according to the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*). And it is eightfold according to the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
629. Therein, the mixed [categories] are twofold according to the distinction of their nature; and therein, the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is also twofold:
either two or three decads, including the first [decad] with its sub-divisions.
"Mixed existence is twofold according to the distinction of states": this means that here, apart from the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), rebirth-consciousness arises mixed with form;
however, in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), because it arises without the states known as the female faculty and male faculty, it is "without state" (*abhāva*).

In the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), apart from the rebirth of those born as eunuchs (*jātipaṇḍaka*), because it arises together with such states, it is "with state" (*sabhāva*). Thus, it is twofold: with state and without state.

"And therein, by way of intrinsic nature, it is twofold": furthermore, that which possesses an intrinsic nature (sab-hāva) is exclusively twofold because it arises together with either the female or male state.

"Two or three decads from the beginning, together with that": herein, the material-mixed rebirth-consciousness—which is the first in the dyad of "mixed" and "unmixed"—is twofold by way of the decad of the physical basis and the body, or [threefold] by way of the decad of the physical basis, the body, and the sex.
Or, at minimum, three sets of ten arise; there is no reduction of form beyond this.

When arising at such a minimal measure, it arises having received the designation "kalala," with the size of a drop of clarified butter extracted by a single fiber from a spider's web, within two types of birth: those born from eggs and those born from moisture. Therein—
The diversity of origins (yoni) should be understood according to the modes of rebirth (gati).
For among these,
there are no origins in the hells, nor in the gods, with the exception of those belonging to the earth-dwellers (bhummaja).
There are three previous births (*purimikā*) [in the first three realms], and all four exist within the three destinies (*gatittaya*).

In that context, regarding the phrase "and among the gods" (*devesu ca*), by means of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that just as there are no three previous births among the hell-beings and among the gods excluding those on earth, so too there are none among the *nijjhāmataṇhika* hungry ghosts;
for they are exclusively of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). As for the remainder, however...

In the three realms consisting of animals, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and humans, as well as among the devas of the earth who were excluded previously, all four modes of birth (yoni) exist. Regarding this:
"In the nine [realms] of the fine-material beings, there are at most thirty-nine material forms."
In the moisture-born and spontaneously born [realms], or at least thirty;

among the material Brahmās who are spontaneously born, thirty-nine material phenomena arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness, by way of four groups: the eye-decad, the ear-decad, the base-decad, and the life-nonad.

However, excluding the material Brahmās, among the other moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, there are at most seventy [material phenomena], by way of the decads consisting of the bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

And these are always present among the devas. Therein, the aggregate of material form measuring ten units—consisting of color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, the four primary elements, visual sensitivity, and vitality—is called the "eye decad."

The rest should be understood in the same way. At the minimum, however, thirty material phenomena arise for one who is blind from birth, deaf, noseless, and asexual, by way of the tongue-decad, the body-decad, and the base-decad.
Between the maximum and the minimum, the appropriate variations should be understood accordingly.
Having understood this, again—

The distinction between the difference and non-difference of death and rebirth-linking—by way of aggregates, objects, destinations, roots, feelings, raptures, applied thought, and sustained thought—is to be fully understood. The meaning is this:

that distinction between difference and non-difference of these two—the rebirth-linking which is of two kinds (mixed and unmixed) and the death that immediately precedes it—must be known by means of these factors beginning with the aggregates.

How so? Sometimes, immediately after a death-consciousness (cuti) in the formless realm consisting of four aggregates, there arises a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) also consisting of four aggregates, having an object that is non-distinct [from the previous one].
Sometimes, following a death-consciousness with a sublime (mahaggata) and internal object, there arises a rebirth-linking with an object that is not sublime and is external.
This, first of all, is the method regarding the formless planes themselves. However, sometimes, immediately after a death-consciousness in the formless realm consisting of four aggregates...

The five aggregates [constitute] rebirth-linking in the sense sphere. Sometimes, immediately after a five-aggregate death in the sense sphere or a death in the fine-material sphere, there is a four-aggregate rebirth-linking in the immaterial sphere.
Thus, there is rebirth-linking with a present object following a death with a past object;
rebirth-linking in certain happy realms following a death in certain miserable realms; and rebirth-linking with roots following a rootless death.
From a death with two roots, there is a rebirth-linking with three roots. From a death accompanied by equanimity, there is a rebirth-linking accompanied by joy.

From a death without rapture, there is a rebirth-linking with rapture. From a death without applied thought, there is a rebirth-linking with applied thought. From a death without sustained thought, there is a rebirth-linking with sustained thought.
From a death without applied or sustained thought, there is a rebirth-linking with both applied and sustained thought—thus, for each respective case...
And the opposite should be applied accordingly.
"Having obtained conditions"—this is a mere phenomenon (dhamma) that passes into another state;
it does not transmigrate from there, nor does it exist without a cause from there.
Thus, this mere collection of material and immaterial phenomena, arising when the necessary conditions are met, is said to "enter another existence";
it is not a "being" (satta), nor a "life-principle" (jīva). Nor does there exist any transmigration (saṅkanti) of that [collection] from a past existence to this one;
nor is there its manifestation here without a cause. We shall illustrate this by means of the manifest process of human death and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
For in a past existence, when death was imminent due to either a violent assault or a natural calamity,

he was unable to endure the onset of the lethal weapons of death-pain— which sever all the joints and bonds of the limbs and members— and while his body gradually withered like a green palm leaf laid out in the heat,
his sense-faculties such as the eye ceased, and they remained established only in the heart-base.
In the case of the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, and the life-faculty, consciousness— which at that moment is supported by the remaining heart-base—
proceeds by taking as its object either (1) a kamma characterized as a residual formation whose conditions have been obtained due to its being weighty,
habitually practiced, proximate, or previously performed; or (2) the objective field presented by that [kamma], known as the sign of the kamma or the sign of the destination.
Thus, as this process occurs, because craving and ignorance have not been abandoned, craving impels one toward that object whose dangers are concealed by ignorance;

the co-nascent formations then project it. Being thus impelled by craving and projected by the formations, following the continuity of the stream, it is like one who has crossed a dyke while clutching a rope tied to a tree on the near bank, and [clinging] to what was before...
It abandons its support; furthermore, whether it relishes or does not relish the support arisen from kamma, it proceeds by means of conditions such as the object alone.
In this context, the former is called "falling away" (cuti) because of falling away, and the latter is called "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) because of linking to another existence.
It is said: "This [consciousness] has not come here from a previous existence, nor has it appeared there without the causes such as kamma, volitional formations, or objects.
There may be illustrations for this, such as echoes and the like.
Due to the continuity of the stream, there is neither identity nor difference.

In this regard, if this consciousness does not come here from a previous existence, then for its arising—conditioned by causes included within the past existence—there would be illustrative examples such as an echo, a lamp, a seal, and a reflection. Just as:
For indeed, echoes, lamps, shadows, and hand-signs have sounds and so forth as their causes; they do not go elsewhere [to produce their effects]. In the same way, this mind [functions].
And herein, due to the continuity of the stream (*saṃtāna*), there is neither identity nor difference.

For if, despite the existence of a continuous stream, there were absolute identity, curd would not arise from milk. On the other hand, if there were absolute difference, [the curd] would not be dependent upon the milk.
It might be curd. This same principle applies to all things produced by causes and conditions. And if this were the case, there would be an abolition of all worldly conventions, which is undesirable.
Therefore, in this matter, one should not adhere exclusively to either identity or difference.
634. Here it is asked: "If, in this way, there is manifestation without transmigration, then as for those aggregates that exist in this human existence—"

Because those [kamma-formations] have ceased, and because the kamma that serves as the condition for the fruit does not go there, that fruit would either belong to one thing from another, or else, in the absence of an experiencer, to whom would that fruit belong? Therefore, this formulation is not tenable.
On this point, it is said:
This fruit arises within a single continuum; it does not belong to another, nor does it arise from another.
The conditioning of seeds is the proof of this point.
For when a fruit arises within a single continuum, absolute identity and absolute difference are both excluded therein.
It is not that [the result] comes from something else or from another source. Furthermore, the formative activity (*abhisaṅkhāra*) of seeds is the means of accomplishing this matter.

For when formative activities have been performed upon mango seeds and the like, a specific fruit arising at a later time—having obtained its conditions within the continuity (*santāna*) of that seed—does not arise from other seeds, nor does it arise from other formative activities as its condition. It is not...
And just as those seeds or volitional formations reach the place where the fruit is produced, so too should this matter be understood.

This meaning should also be understood by way of knowledge, medicinal herbs, and so forth, which, when applied to the body of a child, yield their fruit at a later time in the body of an adult and so on.
Regarding what was said, "If there were no experiencer, to whom would that fruit belong?"—in this regard:
The designation "experiencer" is established precisely through the arising of the fruit;
Just as the designation "it bears fruit" applies to a tree by virtue of the production of fruit.
Just as a tree is said to "bear fruit" or to have "borne fruit" simply through the arising of a tree-fruit,
which is a single part of those phenomena designated as a "tree," so too a god or a human [is so called] simply through the arising of the fruit of pleasure and pain,
designated as experience, which is a single part of the aggregates designated as "god" or "human."
Or one who experiences it, or one who is happy, or one who is suffering is spoken of. Therefore, there is no other entity here called an "experiencer. 635.
Even if one were to say: "Even if this were so, these formations must either exist as conditions for the fruit, or..."
"Whether they do not exist or if they do exist, their result ought to occur at the very moment of their occurrence;
or else, if they do not exist, they would have to bring forth a fruit constantly, both before and after their occurrence. To him, one should say:
"These [results] arise because of conditions having been performed; they do not bring forth a fruit constantly."
In this context, examples such as surety and so forth should be understood.
For volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) become conditions for their own fruit precisely because they have been performed, not because they exist [at that time], nor because they do not exist.
As it is said: "Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma belonging to the sense sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness [arises]."
"...has arisen," and so forth. Having served as conditions for their respective fruits, they do not again bring about those fruits because they have already matured (vipāka).
To clarify this meaning, the following examples, such as a guarantor, should be understood.
For instance, in the world, when someone acts as a guarantor (*pāṭibhoga*) for the delivery of a certain object, or purchases goods, [they do not have to pay again once the debt is settled].
Or, when one takes a loan, for that person the mere performance of the act serves as the condition for the repayment of the debt and so forth;
it is neither the actual existence nor the non-existence of the action [at that later time] that matters. Furthermore, after the repayment of the debt and so on, he is no longer the debtor.

Why? Because the repayment and other acts have been completed. In the same way, because they have been performed, the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) also [serve as conditions] for their own fruit.
They act as conditions, yet they do not bring about further results beyond the giving of their respective fruits.
To this extent, the occurrence of rebirth-linking consciousness—which functions in two ways, both mixed and unmixed—with volitional formations as its condition has been illustrated.
Now, for the purpose of dispelling confusion regarding all those thirty-two resultant consciousnesses:
By way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence,
these formations in the realms of existence and so forth should be understood, as well as their conditions. Therein,
there are three realms of existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings.

These are called existence and so forth. The meaning is that among these—existence and the rest—one should understand for which resultant consciousnesses these [formations] are conditions during rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, and in what manner they serve as conditions.

In that regard, first, concerning meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), the meritorious formation consists specifically of the eight types of volition belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Unspecified, however, it is...
In the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), within a happy destination (*sugati*), there are two ways in which the nine resultant consciousnesses act as conditions for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*):

by way of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānakkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*) and by way of decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*). The volitional formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), consisting of the various types of wholesome volition of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), acts as a condition for the five [resultant consciousnesses] at rebirth-linking alone in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*).

Furthermore, the sense-sphere consciousness of the aforementioned classification acts as a condition in two ways during the course of existence (*pavatta*), but not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for seven limited resultant consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity and devoid of roots, within a happy destination in the sense-sphere existence.
That same [consciousness] likewise acts as a condition during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking, for five resultant consciousnesses in the fine-material existence.

In the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), however, in the case of the miserable destinies (*duggati*), all eight types of limited resultant consciousness (*parittavipākaviññāṇa*) function as conditions in the course of existence (*pavatta*) in the same manner, but not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
In that regard, in hell—as seen in the Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s wanderings through the hells and similar instances—that condition exists when there is contact with a desirable object;
furthermore, among animals and among hungry ghosts possessing great psychic power (*mahiddhika*), a desirable object is indeed obtainable.

In the same way, in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) within the happy destinies (*sugati*), that wholesome formative action (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) is likewise a condition for all sixteen wholesome resultant consciousnesses,

both during the course of existence (*pavatta*) and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Without distinction, however, in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), the wholesome formative action is likewise a condition for ten resultant consciousnesses, both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.

The formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), consisting of the twelve types of unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*), is a condition for one consciousness in a state of woe within the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) during rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), but not during the course of existence (*pavatta*). It is a condition for six [consciousnesses] during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking.
It is a condition for all seven unwholesome resultant consciousnesses both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.

In the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*), however, within the happy destinies (*sugati*), these same seven [types of consciousness] function as conditions in the course of existence (*pavatta*) in that very way, but not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
In the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*), they function as conditions for the four resultant consciousnesses in the course of existence in that very way, but not at rebirth-linking.
Moreover, this occurs in the sense-sphere realm by way of seeing undesirable forms and hearing undesirable sounds; however, in the Brahma-world, there are no undesirable forms and so forth.
Likewise in the world of the sense-sphere devas.

The immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) is likewise a condition for the four resultant consciousnesses in the formless existence, both during the course of existence (*pavatta*) and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Thus, first of all, with respect to the rebirth-linking and the course of existence within the various states of existence (*bhava*), these formations should be understood as to which things they are conditions for and how they function as conditions. By this same method, they should also be understood in relation to the modes of birth (*yoni*) and so forth.

637. Herein, this is the brief explanation starting from the beginning: For among these formations, first of all, the meritorious formation, having given rebirth-linking in two types of existence, produces its entire fruit of ripening.

Likewise, it does so in the four modes of origin, such as the egg-born; in the two destinations, namely gods and humans; and in the various classes of beings reckoned as those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, those with diverse bodies and unified perceptions, those with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, and those with unified bodies and unified perceptions.
In the four stations of consciousness, however, he forms only material form in the abode of non-percipient beings;
thus, having given rebirth-linking within these four stations of beings alone, he produces all his own kamma-result.

Therefore, in these two types of existence, four modes of birth, two destinations, four stations of consciousness, and four stations of beings— [He] produces [it]. Therefore, in these two types of existence, four modes of birth, two destinations, four stations of consciousness, and four stations of beings...

And the unwholesome volitional formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) is a condition for twenty-one resultant consciousnesses— according to the method already stated— in rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, as far as possible.
For it is only in a single sensual existence (kāmabhava), among the four modes of birth (yoni), in the remaining three destinations (gati),
and in one station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) known as "diversity of body and unity of perception," and in such a single [station], that it occurs.
It ripens by way of rebirth-linking in the abodes of beings; therefore, in a single existence, across the four modes of birth,
the three destinations, one station of consciousness, and one abode of beings, it is a condition for the seven resultant consciousnesses in the manner already described,
both at the moment of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.
As for the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), because it ripens by way of rebirth-linking only in a single existence, namely the formless existence;

in a single mode of birth, namely the spontaneous birth (*opapātika*); in a single destiny, namely the divine destiny; in three stations of consciousness, namely the base of infinite space and so forth;
and in four abodes of beings, namely the base of infinite space and so forth—therefore, this [formation] pertains to a single existence, a single mode of birth, and so on.
In one destiny, in three stations of consciousness, and in four abodes of beings, it is a condition for the four types of consciousness—

both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence— in the manner already described. Thus, by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence, these [are the conditions] in the realms of existence and so forth.
The formations are to be understood, as well as their conditions.
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase "with formations as condition, consciousness.
Now follows the detailed exposition on the phrase "with consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality."
638. Regarding the phrase "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form":

the exposition of name-and-form should be understood through their analysis according to the occurrence [of the factors] in the states of existence and so forth, and through their synthesis according to the method of conditions.
Regarding the phrase "the analysis of name-and-form": here, "name" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling, so called because they bend toward the object;
"form" refers to the four great elements and the derived form dependent upon those four great elements.
Their analysis has already been stated in the Exposition of the Aggregates (*Khandhaniddesa*). Thus, first, the exposition concerning the analysis of name-and-form should be understood.

Regarding the phrase "occurring among the states of existence" (*bhava*): here, *nāma* (mentality) occurs in all states of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and remaining abodes of beings, with the exception of one abode of beings.
*Rūpa* (materiality), however, occurs in two states of existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, the first four stations of consciousness, and five abodes of beings.
And while this name-and-form is thus occurring, because at the moment of rebirth-linking for those who are non-percipient, born from the womb, or born from an egg,
two series-heads of materiality arise by way of the tenfold materiality of the physical basis and the body,
along with the three immaterial aggregates, therefore, in detail, twenty states arise as materiality and the three immaterial aggregates; thus, these are twenty-three.
It should be understood that mental phenomena (dhammā) conditioned by consciousness (viññāṇa) constitute name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

By the method of "taking what has not been taken," if one excludes nine material phenomena from a single stream-head, there remain fourteen. By adding the sex-decad (bhāvadasaka) of intrinsic-nature phenomena, there are thirty-three;
and by the same method of "taking what has not been taken," if one excludes eighteen material phenomena from two stream-heads, there remain fifteen.
And because, among spontaneously born beings (opapātika-satta), at the moment of rebirth-linking for those such as the deities of the Brahma-world,
four continuities of material form arise by way of the decads of eye, ear, and base, and the nonad of the life-faculty, as well as three immaterial aggregates; therefore, in detail,
for them there are forty-nine states consisting of both material and immaterial form, and three immaterial [aggregates].
Regarding the "aggregates" (khandhā): these forty-six factors, conditioned by consciousness, should be understood as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
By taking what has not yet been included, and excluding twenty-seven factors from the three heads of the continuum, there remain fifteen.

However, in the sensual realm (kāmabhava), for the remaining types of spontaneous birth (opapātika) or moisture-born beings (saṃsedaja) whose sense bases are naturally complete, [the situation is as follows].
At the moment of rebirth-linking, seven heads of the material continuity and the three immaterial aggregates become manifest;
therefore, in detail, seventy material phenomena and the three immaterial aggregates—these seventy-three phenomena should be understood as "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.
However, by taking what has not yet been taken from the six heads of the material continuity...
Having excluded fifty-four factors, there remain nineteen; this is the maximum.

However, by way of the minimum, for those lacking the head of this or that particular continuity of material form, one should understand the designation of "name-and-form" conditioned by consciousness at rebirth-linking—both briefly and in detail—by successively omitting each respective factor.

In the case of non-material beings, there are only the three non-material aggregates. In the case of non-percipient beings, from the perspective of materiality, there is only the life-faculty ennead. This, first of all, is the method regarding rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

However, in the course of existence (pavatta), in every place where materiality occurs, at the moment of the subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the temperature-originated pure octad arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness, originating from the heat that functions simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness. As for the rebirth-linking consciousness itself...

It does not originate matter. For just as a man who has fallen over a precipice is unable to serve as a condition for another, so too, due to its weakness resulting from the weakness of the physical basis (*vatthu*), it is unable to originate matter.

However, after the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), starting from the first life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) onwards, there is the pure octad originated by consciousness; at the time of the manifestation of sound—

From the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, there exists the sound-nonad arising from both the physical heat and the consciousness. However, as for those womb-born beings who subsist on edible food, [it is said]:
"Whatever food, drink, and nourishment her mother eats..."
"By that he sustains himself there, the man while still in the mother's womb"— according to this statement,
when the body has been sustained by the food swallowed by the mother, at the moment of swallowing the saliva first present in one's own mouth,
there arises the "pure octad produced by nutriment" (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna-suddha-aṭṭhaka*). This is [the example] of that which is produced by nutriment.
Pure octad, and the temperature-born and consciousness-born [octads]—at most, by way of two nonads, there are twenty-six kinds;
and the kamma-born [nonads], which were previously stated to arise three times in each moment of consciousness, amount to seventy kinds.
Thus, there are ninety-six kinds of material phenomena. Together with the three immaterial aggregates, there are, in brief, ninety-nine states (dhammas). Since—

The word "or" (*vā*) is indefinite because it manifests only at certain times; therefore, having set aside both of those [alternatives], it should be understood that these ninety-seven states, as they occur, constitute name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by consciousness for all sentient beings.
For even when they are sleeping, heedless, eating, or drinking—by day or by night—these [states] exist with consciousness as their condition.
They proceed. And we shall explain later how these [nutriments] function as conditions for consciousness.

Now, as for the materiality born of kamma that arises here, although it establishes itself first of all within the realms of existence, the modes of birth, the destinations, the stations, and the abodes of beings, it cannot maintain its stability unless supported by materiality originated by the three [other causes];
nor can the materiality originated by the three [other causes] [maintain its stability] without it.

They were not supported by one another. Rather, like bundles of reeds propped up against each other from the four directions when buffeted by the wind, or like a wrecked ship that has found some foothold in the great ocean when struck by the force of the waves, these beings remained standing together, not falling down, for one year, two years... [and so on] ...even for a hundred years, until those beings...

"Or until the exhaustion of the life-span or the exhaustion of merit, they continue to proceed. In this way, the exposition regarding the occurrence within existence (*bhava*) and so forth should be understood here.

639. Regarding "compendium": herein, that which consists of name alone—conditioned by consciousness—in the occurrence and rebirth-linking of the immaterial realm, as well as in the occurrence of the five-aggregate existence;
and that which occurs everywhere among non-percipient beings, as well as in the occurrence of the five-aggregate existence.
Material form conditioned by consciousness alone, as well as the name-and-form conditioned by consciousness everywhere in the five-aggregate existence—
all that name and all that form are subsumed under the term "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) by means of the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (retaining one from among similar things). Thus,
it should be understood that there is "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness."
If it is argued that [the statement] is incorrect because consciousness is absent among the non-percipient beings, it is not incorrect. For this too has been stated:
"That which is the cause of name-and-form, consciousness, is considered to be twofold:
resultant and non-resultant; therefore, this is indeed correct."
For that consciousness which is the cause of name-and-form is considered to be twofold, by way of the distinction between resultant and non-resultant.
And this [matter] among the non-percipient beings is matter produced by kamma, because it arises from the condition of volitional consciousness occurring in the five-aggregate existence.

Likewise, it is entirely logical that during the course of existence in the five-aggregate realm, at the moments of wholesome and other types of consciousness, there is matter produced by kamma. Thus...
The exposition here should be understood by way of grouping.
Regarding the method of conditions: herein, for name, the resultant consciousness is a condition in nine ways.
The materiality of the physical basis [the heart-base] conditions materiality in nine ways;
the remaining types of materiality condition it in eight ways. Volitional consciousness conditions materiality in one way;
as for other types of consciousness, they condition their respective objects as appropriate.
Whatever name— reckoned as resultant— that exists at rebirth-linking or during the course of existence, whether mixed with matter or unmixed,

whether it be the rebirth-linking consciousness itself or another resultant consciousness, serves as a condition in nine ways for that [name] by way of the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, association, resultant, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance.

At the moment of rebirth-linking, the materiality of the physical basis (vatthurūpa) is a condition for [the mental aggregates] in nine ways: by way of the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

However, excluding the materiality of the physical basis itself, the remaining materiality is a condition for the rest of the materiality through these same nine conditions, with the exception of the mutuality condition;
thus, it acts as a condition by way of the remaining eight conditions.

Furthermore, from the perspective of the Suttanta method, the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) is a condition for the matter of non-percipient beings or for kamma-born matter in the five-aggregate existence in one way only,

namely, by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). It should be understood that all remaining consciousness, beginning from the first life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), is a condition for its respective name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as appropriate.
However, if its mode of conditions were to be shown in detail, the entire exposition of the *Paṭṭhāna* would have to be set forth;
therefore, we do not undertake it here.
In this regard, one might ask: "How is it to be known that rebirth-linking mentality-materiality has consciousness as its condition?"

From both scripture and reasoning. For in the Sutta, by way of the method beginning with "states that follow upon consciousness," the fact that feeling and the other [mental aggregates] have consciousness as their condition is established in many ways. As for reasoning:
here, it is established by what is seen, namely, that material form is born of consciousness.
"Even for matter that has not been seen, consciousness is a condition.
For when the mind is either pleased or displeased, the corresponding types of matter arising therefrom are seen.
And since there is inference of the unseen from the seen, by means of this "seen" matter born of mind, even the "unseen" matter of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi-rūpa) [is understood].

It should be understood that consciousness is a condition. For even in the case of that [materiality] originated by kamma, its status as being conditioned by consciousness is established in the *Paṭṭhāna* just as it is for that originated by mind.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood from the perspective of the method of conditions.
This concludes the detailed exposition on the phrase "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form."

The Detailed Exposition of the Section on the Six Bases with Name-and-Form as Condition (Nāmarūpapaccayā Saḷāyatanapadavitthārakathā) 641. Regarding the section on the six bases with name-and-form as condition:
"Name" is considered to be the three aggregates; "form" is considered to be the primary elements, the sense-bases, and so forth.
That remainder of the catechism is a condition for that very same [result].
For as regards this name-and-form which serves as the condition for the sixfold base (*saḷāyatana*), therein "name" refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling,
while "form" refers invariably to the four primary elements, the six bases, and the life-faculty included within one's own continuity.

In this way, it should be understood that the "ground of being" (bhūtavatthu) and so forth are considered [as such]. Furthermore, it should be understood that "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)—formed by the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) compound of "name" (*nāma*) and "form" (*rūpa*)—is the condition for the "sixfold base" (*saḷāyatana*), which is likewise formed by the *ekasesa* compound of the six bases. Why?
Because in the formless realm (*ārūpa*), name alone is the condition, and that is the condition specifically for the sixth base.
It is not for anything else. For it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: “The sixth base has name as its condition.
Herein, one might ask: how is it to be known that “name-and-form is the condition for the six bases”?
It is because they exist when name-and-form exists. For when this or that name and form exist, the corresponding base comes to be, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, that cultivation of this state will become manifest precisely within the method of conditions. Therefore:
"Whether in rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, whatever is a condition for whatever, and in whatever way it is a condition—that should be understood by one who discerns."
Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning:
In the immaterial plane, during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence, name alone is the condition;
it is sevenfold and sixfold, according to the minimum.

How so? First, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), name is a condition for the sixth base in seven ways by way of the co-nascent, mutuality, support, association, resultant, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
However, some of these act as a condition here by way of the root condition and some by way of the nutriment condition;
thus it is a condition in other ways as well, and its maximum and minimum strength should be understood accordingly.
In the course of occurrence (*pavatta*), resultant [consciousness] is a condition in the manner already stated;

however, the other [resultant consciousness] is, at minimum, a condition by way of six conditions—excluding the resultant-condition—from among the types of conditions mentioned. Yet, some of these act as a condition through the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), and some through the nutriment-condition (*āhārapaccaya*);
thus it acts as a condition in other ways as well, and the maximum and minimum [of its conditioning role] should be understood according to that.
In other existences as well, name is likewise [a condition] for rebirth-linking;
for the sixth [consciousness], and for the others, it is a condition in six ways.
For even in the five-aggregate existence other than the formless realm, that resultant name, acting as an associate to the heart-base, [is a condition].
As has been stated regarding the formless realm (*ārūpa*) for the sixth mind-base (*manāyatana*), it likewise serves as a condition in seven ways at minimum.

However, for the other five—the eye-base and so forth—it serves as a condition in six ways by way of being conascent, a support, a result, dissociated, present, and non-disappeared, acting as an assistant to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, some among these act as a root-condition (*hetupaccaya*), while others act as a nutriment-condition (*āhārapaccaya*). Thus...
The condition is also otherwise; by way of that, the superior and inferior grades are to be understood.
It is likewise in the course of existence: the resultant is a condition for the resultant;
the non-resultant is a condition for the non-resultant; and in six ways, it is a condition for the sixth.

For even in the course of existence within the five-aggregate plane, just as in the case of rebirth-linking, resultant name is a condition for resultant sixth base in seven ways by way of its capacity.
Non-resultant [name], however, is a condition for non-resultant sixth base in six ways, excluding the resultant condition from those seven.
In this context, according to the method already stated:
The maximum and minimum [number of conditions] should be understood.

In that very same way, for the remaining five [types of consciousness], the resultant [consciousness] is a condition in four ways; likewise, the non-resultant [consciousness] is explained in the same manner.

For within that very process, the remaining five bases—such as the eye-base and so forth—are also a fourfold condition for the other resultant-namings (vipāka-nāma) by way of the conditions of postnascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, just like the eye-sensitivity and the rest.

And just as this was explained regarding the resultant, it is likewise explained for the non-resultant as well. Therefore, even those [namings] distinguished as wholesome and so forth are a fourfold condition for them.

It should be understood that [it] "becomes. Thus, first of all, it should be understood which base (āyatana) serves as a condition for whichever [base] during rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, and in what manner it serves as a condition.
However, in this context, matter (rūpa) becomes a condition within the immaterial realm (ārūpa-bhava).
Not even for a single base (*ekāyatana*), but rather within the existence of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*).
At the linking of rebirth (*sandhi*), the physical basis (*vatthu*) is a condition for the sixth [consciousness] in six ways;
the primary elements (*bhūtāni*) are a condition for the five [senses] in four ways without distinction.

For, in terms of material form (*rūpa*), at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the basis-materiality (*vatthurūpa*) is a condition for the sixth sense-base, the mind-base (*manāyatana*), in six ways:

by way of the conditions of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*). Furthermore, the four primary elements (*bhūta*), both generally at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence (*pavatta*), act as conditions—by way of the conditions of co-nascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance—for whichever of the five bases, such as the eye-base, arises.
The conditions are fourfold.
For these [five aggregates], life-faculty is threefold and nutriment is threefold during the course of existence;
for the sixth [consciousness-element], those same two are sixfold, and its object-base is fivefold.

Furthermore, for these five—beginning with the eye—the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvita*) serves as a condition in three ways by way of presence and non-disappearance, both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.
Food also serves as a condition in three ways by way of presence and non-disappearance;
however, this occurs only during the course of existence in the bodies of those beings who subsist on food, and not at rebirth-linking.

Furthermore, those five bases, beginning with the eye-base, act as conditions for the sixth base—the mind-base (manāyatana)—which consists of eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, in six ways during the course of existence (pavatta): by way of support (nissaya), prenascence (purejāta), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata).
However, this does not apply at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Excluding the five types of sense-consciousness, for that same remaining mind-base...
Basis-materiality is a condition in five ways— by way of support, prenascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—

but only during the course of existence (pavatta), not at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Thus, it should be understood exactly how and for which sense base materiality serves as a condition, whether at rebirth-linking or during the course of existence.
But as for both name-and-form, it is that which becomes the condition for whatever [it conditions];
and how this is so in all cases must be understood by one who is discerning. To illustrate:
first, in the case of rebirth-linking in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), [name-and-form] consists of the three aggregates and the bodily form of the physical base.
Name-and-form is a condition for the sixth sense-base by way of such conditions as co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.
This is merely an outline here; however, since it is possible to apply all [the details] according to the method already stated, no further elaboration is given here.
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase “with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base.
642. The detailed exposition on the phrase “with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact”: In the phrase “with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact”:
In brief, there are only six types of contact, beginning with eye-contact and so forth;
in detail, they become thirty-two, just like consciousness.
For, in brief, it is said that "with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact," namely: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, [tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact].
Tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—these six contacts, beginning with eye-contact, thus come to be.

In detail, however, there are ten: five wholesome-resultants and five unwholesome-resultants (eye-contact and so forth), and the remaining twenty-two associated with mundane resultant consciousness; thus, all these are conditioned by formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya*).
There are thirty-two [types of contact], just as consciousness was stated [above].
As for the sixfold base (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which is the condition for these thirty-two kinds of contact:
therein, together with the sixth, the internal [bases] such as the eye and so forth, along with the external ones.
The wise maintain that there are six sense bases together with the six [consciousnesses].

In this regard, those who explain that "this is a discourse on the occurrence of what is appropriated" (upādiṇṇaka-pavatti-kathā) and thus point only to conditions and conditionally arisen states included within one's own continuity,
do so— following the canonical text— "contact has the sixth base as its condition" in the case of the formless realm.

Because the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) and the six bases (*saḷāyatana*)—which include all [bases] elsewhere—are conditions for contact, they maintain that "the internal six bases," such as the eye and so forth, together with the sixth, constitute the six bases; this is done by applying the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpekasesa* (retaining one member of a group where members are similar in part).
For that which is both the sixth base and the six bases comes to be designated simply as "the six bases."
However, those who maintain that only what has arisen through conditions is included within a single continuity, while the condition itself may belong to a different continuity,
include everything that serves as a condition for contact— whether internal or external— in their definition. Thus, by encompassing even external factors,
they assert that the "sixfold base" (*saḷāyatana*) consists of the six bases together with the internal and external sense-bases of form and so forth, including the sixth.
For even that [sixth base] and the six bases—when the term "six bases" is formed by retaining only one from among these—the designation "six bases" alone is applied.
Here it may be asked: "Contact does not arise from all the bases together, nor do all contacts arise from a single base;
yet this contact is spoken of as being 'one' with the condition of the six bases. Why is that? To this, the answer is as follows:
This is true: from all [bases], one does not arise; nor from one, do all arise. However, from many, one does arise.

Just as visual contact arises from the eye-base, the visible-form base, the mind-base—which is reckoned as eye-consciousness—and the remaining associated mental-object bases, so too should this be applied accordingly in all instances. Therefore, indeed:
It is demonstrated by the Tathāgata that "this contact arises from many bases" by means of the singular designation.

By the phrase "by means of the singular designation," the meaning is this: by this singular designation, "contact conditioned by the six bases," it is shown by the Tathāgata that there is one contact arising from many bases. Furthermore, regarding the bases:
One should analyze how these [bases] function as conditions for this [contact] in six ways, five ways, one way, nine ways, and six external ways, according to their possibility.
Herein, this is the analysis: first, the five bases beginning with the eye-base function in five ways by way of the division into eye-contact and so forth.
Contact has six modes of conditionality: by way of support, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

Following that, one resultant mind-base is a condition in nine ways for the various types of resultant mind-contact: by way of conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance.
Among external phenomena, however, the visible-object base is a condition for eye-contact by way of object, prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.
The condition is fourfold. Likewise, the sound-base and so forth are conditions for ear-contact and so forth.

For mind-contact, however, those [bases] and the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana) act as such by way of being merely object-conditions; thus, one should understand how these six external bases function as its conditions according to their respective possibilities.
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase, “With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
643. The detailed exposition on the phrase, “With contact as condition, feeling arises”:
In the phrase, “With contact as condition, feeling arises”—
Feeling is stated according to its doors as that born of eye-contact and so forth;
these six, when divided in detail, are considered to be eighty-nine.
Regarding this term, in its analysis (*vibhaṅga*), it is said: "feeling born of eye-contact; [feeling] born of ear... nose... tongue... body... mind-contact."

Thus, by way of the doors, only six kinds of feeling have been mentioned; yet, by way of their classification, they are considered to be eighty-nine, because they are associated with eighty-nine types of consciousness.
Among these feelings, thirty-two are relevant here.
It is stated that only those associated with resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) are intended here.
Among them, in the five doors, there are eight ways in which the condition for the five [sensory] consciousnesses arises;
for the remaining [mental states], it is one way, namely contact (phassa), and it is the same in the mind door as well.
For there, in the case of the five doors, contact such as eye-contact is an eightfold condition for the five feelings based on the sensitive matter of the eye and so forth—
by way of being conascent, mutuality, support, resultant, nutriment, associated, presence, and non-disappearance. However,
for the remaining [mental states] that occur at each door by way of reception, investigation, and registration:
That contact, beginning with eye-contact, is a condition in one way—as a decisive support (upanissaya)—for the resultant feelings of the sense-sphere.

It is the same in the mind-door as well; for in the mind-door too, that contact known as "conascent mind-contact" is likewise a condition in eight ways for the resultant feelings of the sense-sphere that occur by way of object-representation (tadārammaṇa), through the modes of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
This also applies to the resultant feelings of the three planes that have arisen. As for those sense-sphere feelings that arise in the mind-door by way of registration (tadārammaṇa),
the mental contact associated with the mind-door adverting consciousness is a condition for them in one way only, namely, as a decisive support (upanissaya).
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase "with contact as condition, feeling arises.
644. Regarding the phrase "with feeling as condition, craving arises":
In this context, six types of craving are explained here through their divisions, such as craving for form and so forth.
Each of these is considered to be threefold according to its mode of occurrence.
For in this term, just as a son is designated by his father’s name as "the merchant’s son" or "the brahmin’s son," [craving] is likewise designated as "craving for form."
In the Vibhaṅga, craving is explained by way of its objects and its names as sixfold: “craving for sounds... for odors... for tastes... for tangibles... for mental phenomena.

Furthermore, among those cravings, each individual craving is considered to be threefold according to its mode of occurrence: craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
For when craving for form itself takes a visible object that has come within the range of the eye and, by way of relishing it, [clings to it]...
When it proceeds by relishing [the object], then it is called craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*).

When that same object proceeds together with the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), which occurs [thinking] "it is permanent, it is eternal," then it is called craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*); for passion accompanied by the view of eternalism is termed craving for existence.
However, when that same object proceeds [with the thought] "it is cut off, it perishes" ...

When it occurs together with the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), it is called craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*). For lust accompanied by the annihilationist view is termed craving for non-existence.
This same method applies to craving for sound and the others as well. These constitute eighteen types of craving.
These eighteen [types] directed toward internal forms and so forth, and eighteen directed toward external [objects], make thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six past [cravings].
There are thirty-six types of craving regarding the future and thirty-six regarding the present; thus, there are one hundred and eight kinds of craving.
When these are further condensed, they should be understood as six, by way of their objects such as visible forms and so forth, or simply as three, by way of craving for sensual pleasure and so on.

Furthermore, because these beings, having relished a son, possess a sense of "mine-ness" toward that son—just as a nurse does toward a child—they [cling] to objects such as visible forms and so forth.

Relishing the feeling as it arises, and through attachment to that feeling, people pay great honor to those who provide the objects of experience such as forms—namely, painters, musicians, perfumers, cooks, weavers, formulators of elixirs, physicians, and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that all these [feelings] have craving as their condition.
Moreover, it is specifically the feeling of resultant pleasure (*vipāka-sukha-vedanā*) that is intended here.
This [craving] is of one kind alone; therefore, it is a condition for craving.
"Of one kind" means it is a condition solely by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). Or else:
"The suffering person longs for pleasure; the happy person desires even more."
But because equanimity is peaceful, it is described simply as "pleasure.
Therefore, through craving as a condition, all three kinds of feeling arise;
and with feeling as a condition, craving arises—thus it was said by the Great Seer.
"And because feeling does not exist without a latent tendency,
therefore that [feeling] does not exist for a brahmin who is possessed of virtue.
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase "with feeling as condition, craving arises."
The detailed explanation of the phrase "with craving as condition, clinging":
Regarding the phrase "with craving as condition, clinging," there are four kinds of clinging; these are [to be understood] according to their analysis of meaning.
One should explain the phenomena both briefly and in detail, and according to their sequence.

Herein, this is the detailed exposition: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self—these, first of all, are the four kinds of clinging here.
This is the analysis of their meaning: sensual pleasure, which is reckoned as the objective base...

It is called *kāmupādāna* because one clings (*upādiyati*) to sensual pleasures; it is also *kāmupādāna* because it is both sensual pleasure (*kāma*) and clinging (*upādāna*). "Clinging" (*upādāna*) means firm grasping;
here the prefix *upa-* has the sense of "firmness," as in words such as *upāyāsa* (distress) and *upakaṭṭha* (near). Likewise, it is *diṭṭhupādāna* because it is both a view (*diṭṭhi*) and clinging;
or, it is *diṭṭhupādāna* because one clings to a view. This refers to [views] such as, "The self and the world are eternal."
For one clings to a later view by means of a prior view. Likewise, because one clings to virtue and observance (*sīlabbata*), it is called the clinging to virtue and observance (*sīlabbatupādāna*).

Alternatively, it is the clinging that consists of virtue and observance; thus it is the clinging to virtue and observance. Indeed, practices such as the cow-virtue and cow-observance are themselves forms of clinging due to the dogmatic insistence (*abhinivesa*) that "purity comes through this.
Furthermore, it is called a "doctrine" (*vāda*) because they speak by means of it; it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because they cling by means of it.
What do they say, or what do they cling to? They cling to a self (*atta*). Or, clinging to the doctrine of a self is the "clinging to the doctrine of a self" (*attavādupādāna*).

Alternatively, it is called "clinging to the doctrine of a self" because by means of this, they cling to the mere doctrine of a self as being a "self. This, first of all, is the analysis of its meaning.

Regarding the summary and detailed exposition of the phenomena (*dhamma*), first, as for sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*): "In that regard, what is sensual clinging? That which, among sensual pleasures..."

Because it is stated: "Sensual desire, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, and sensual cleaving—this is called clinging to sense pleasures (*kāmupādāna*)," it is, in brief, called the intensification of craving.

The intensification of craving is simply subsequent craving that has become strengthened by way of its relation as a decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for preceding craving. However, some say it is the longing for objects not yet attained.
Craving is like a thief reaching out his hand in the darkness; grasping at the objects encountered is clinging (*upādāna*), which is like that very thief seizing the goods.
Furthermore, these two states are the opposites of fewness of wishes and contentment. Likewise, they are rooted in the suffering of seeking and guarding.
As for the remaining three types of clinging, they consist, in brief, of mere views alone.
In detail, however, *kāmupādāna* (clinging to sense pleasures) is the firm state of craving (*taṇhā*), which—as previously stated regarding form and so forth—has eight hundred divisions.
*Diṭṭhupādāna* (clinging to views) is wrong view with ten bases. As it is said: "In this context, what is clinging to views?
It is such a view as: 'There is no giving, there is no sacrifice... [etc. ...they declare having realized for themselves'—such a view... [etc. ...a perverted grasp."
“This is called clinging to views. Clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), however, is the misapprehension that purification comes through rules and observances.

As it is said: “In this context, what is clinging to rules and observances? It is the view, and so forth... the inverted grasp, that purification comes through virtue, purification comes through observance, and purification comes through both virtue and observance. This is called clinging to rules and observances.”
The embodiment-view consisting of twenty bases is the clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*). As it is said: "In this context, what is the clinging to a doctrine of self?
Here, an uninstructed worldling... [omitted] ...untrained in the Dhamma of the true men, regards form as self...
[omitted] ...this perverted grasping is called the clinging to a doctrine of self. This is the summary and detailed exposition of the teaching herein.
Regarding the term "order" (*kama*) here, there are three kinds of order: the order of arising, the order of abandoning, and the order of teaching.

Among these, because it is impossible to say that there was a first arising of these defilements in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the order of arising is not spoken of in an absolute sense.
However, in a figurative sense, in most cases within a single existence, the adherence to eternalism or annihilationism is preceded by the grasping of a self.
Then, for one who grasps "this self is eternal," there is the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) for the sake of purifying the self;

for one who grasps "it is annihilated" and is indifferent to the next world, there is the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Thus, first comes the clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*), followed by the clingings to views, rules and observances, and sense-pleasures—this is the order of their arising within a single existence.

Among these, the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and the others are abandoned first, because they are to be eliminated by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). Clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is abandoned later, because it is to be eliminated by the path of arhatship (*arahatta-magga*); such is their order of abandonment.
However, among these, clinging to sense-pleasures is taught first because its scope is vast and it is more manifest.

It has a vast scope because it is associated with eight types of consciousness, whereas the others have a narrow scope as they are associated with only four types of consciousness; furthermore, for the most part, beings delight in attachment (*ālaya-rāma*).
Clinging to sense pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is evident among the people, but not the others. Or, for the sake of attaining sense pleasures, one is full of curiosity, auspicious rites, and so forth;

that is his "view" (*diṭṭhi*), and thus immediately following that comes clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). When that is divided, it becomes twofold by way of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
Among those two, even when seeing the practice of cows or the practice of dogs, it is to be understood as gross (*oḷārika*).

The clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) was taught first. Because it is subtle, the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*) is placed at the end; such is the sequence of their teaching.
Herein, craving (*taṇhā*) is a condition for the former [clinging] in one way;
for the remaining three, it is a condition in seven or eight ways.

And here, when this fourfold clinging has been thus taught, craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) is a condition for the first type of clinging, that of sense-pleasures, in one way alone by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), because it arises toward objects that are relished through craving.

However, for the remaining three types of clinging, it is a condition in seven ways—by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root—or in eight ways when including decisive support. And when it [craving] acts as a decisive support...
When it is a condition, it is then necessarily non-coexistent.
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase "with craving as condition, clinging arises.
Now follows the detailed exposition on the phrase "with clinging as condition, existence arises."
646. Regarding the section on existence conditioned by clinging:
its meaning, its phenomena, its purpose, its classification, its grouping, what is the condition for what—all these determinations are to be understood.
In this context, "it comes to be" (*bhavati*) is "existence" (*bhava*). That is twofold: existence as kamma (*kammabhava*) and existence as rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
As it has been said: "Existence is twofold: there is existence as kamma, and there is existence as rebirth. Herein, kamma itself is existence, thus "existence as kamma";
likewise, rebirth itself is existence, thus "existence as rebirth. And herein, rebirth comes to be, thus it is "existence."

But as for kamma, just as it is called "the arising of Buddhas is blissful" because it is a cause of happiness, so too it should be understood as "existence" (bhava) by way of the designation of its fruit, because it is a cause of existence.
Thus, first, the analysis here should be understood according to the meaning. 647.
As for the analysis according to the phenomena (dhamma), kamma-existence (kammabhava) consists, in brief, of volition itself and the covetousness and other factors associated with volition.

Phenomena classified as kamma. As it is said: “In this context, what is kamma-existence (*kammabhava*)? The volitional formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), the volitional formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), and the volitional formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), whether belonging to the limited plane or the great plane—this is called kamma-existence.
Furthermore, all kamma that leads to existence is kamma-existence. Herein, the volitional formation of merit refers to the thirteen types of volition. The volitional formation of demerit refers to...

"Twelve. "Imperturbable volitional formations" refers to the four types of volition (*cetanā*). By the phrase "whether belonging to the limited plane or the great plane," the weak or strong ripening of those very same volitions is expressed.
By the phrase "all karma leading to existence," however, covetousness and so forth associated with volition are expressed.
Rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), however, consists in brief of the aggregates produced by karma; in detail, it is of nine kinds.

As it is said: "In this context, what is rebirth-existence? It is existence in the sense-sphere (*kāma-bhava*), existence in the fine-material sphere (*rūpa-bhava*), existence in the immaterial sphere (*arūpa-bhava*), existence with perception (*saññā-bhava*), existence without perception (*asaññā-bhava*), existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññā-bhava*), existence with one constituent (*ekavokāra-bhava*), existence with four constituents (*catuvokāra-bhava*), and existence with five constituents (*pañcavokāra-bhava*)."

“This is called rebirth-existence (upapattibhava). In this context, existence consisting of sense-desire is “sense-desire existence” (kāmabhava). The same method applies to fine-material existence (rūpabhava) and immaterial existence (arūpabhava).
Existence belonging to those possessed of perception, or existence in which perception exists, is “perception existence” (saññābhava).

By contrast, there is “non-perception existence” (asaññābhava). Because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception in this existence, it is “neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence” (nevasaññānāsaññābhava).
Existence mixed with one aggregate of form is "existence with one constituent" (*ekavokārabhava*). Or, because that existence has one constituent, it is called "existence with one constituent.

This same method applies to existence with four constituents and existence with five constituents. Therein, sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) consists of the five aggregates acquired by clinging (*upādiṇṇakkhandha*).

So too does fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*). Immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) consists of four; perception-existence (*saññābhava*) consists of five; non-perception-existence (*asaññābhava*) consists of one aggregate acquired by clinging.

The state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consists of four [aggregates]. The one-aggregate existence and so forth consist of one, four, or five aggregates respectively, by way of the appropriated aggregates.

Thus, the analysis here should be understood according to the nature of the phenomena (*dhamma*). 648. As for "according to the purpose" (*sātthato*): just as it was in the exposition of existence (*bhava*), so too in the exposition of formations (*saṅkhāra*), it is certainly the meritorious formations and so forth that are intended.

Although this has already been stated, this repetition is indeed purposeful: while the former [formations] serve as conditions for rebirth-linking here through the influence of past karma, these [volitions] serve as conditions for future rebirth-linking through the influence of present karma.

Alternatively, previously it was stated that "volition itself is formations" by way of such methods as: "In this context, what is the formation of merit? It is wholesome volition of the sense-sphere. Thus, volition alone is the formations.
[The formations] have been explained. Here, however, because of the statement, "All karma leading to existence [is included]," they include those associated with volition (*cetanā*) as well.
Previously, only karma that serves as a condition for consciousness was called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*); now, even that which produces the non-percipient realm (*asaññā-bhava*) is included.

Or rather, what need is there for much? In the context of "with ignorance as condition, formations arise," it is only the meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhārā*) and so forth—both wholesome and unwholesome—that are intended.

“States” were mentioned [previously]. However, here, because even the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is included in the phrase “with clinging as condition, existence,” states that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate are mentioned. Therefore, this repetition is in every respect purposeful;
thus, the analysis should be understood here also by way of its purposefulness.
649. "By way of division and inclusion" means by way of both the division and the inclusion of existence (*bhava*) conditioned by clinging (*upādāna*).

For when karma that produces sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is performed with sense-sphere clinging as its condition, that is "karma-existence. The aggregates produced therefrom are "rebirth-existence" (*upapattibhava*).

This same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial existences. Thus, conditioned by sense-sphere clinging, there are two types of sense-sphere existence, as well as the perception-existence (*saññābhava*) and the five-constituent existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) included therein.

There are two fine-material existences (*rūpa-bhava*), which include the existence of perception (*saññā-bhava*), the existence of non-perception (*asaññā-bhava*), the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*), and the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*);

there are two immaterial existences (*arūpa-bhava*), which include the existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññā-bhava*) and the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*).

Thus, together with those included therein, there are six existences. And just as, with those included therein, there are six [existences] conditioned by clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna-paccaya*)...
Thus there are twenty-four types of existence (*bhava*) according to the classification by way of the condition of clinging (*upādāna*), including those included within them.

However, when grouped together—taking both kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) as one—there is one sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) with sense-sphere clinging as its condition, including those included within it.

Likewise, there are three existences: fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) and immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*). Similarly, there are [other] existences with the remaining types of clinging as their conditions.
Rapture (*pīti*). Thus, from the perspective of inclusion, there are twelve existences (*bhava*) together with those included therein, conditioned by clinging (*upādāna-paccaya*).

Furthermore, generally speaking, the karma that leads to sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is "kamma-existence" (*kammabhava*); the aggregates produced by that [karma] are "rebirth-existence" (*upapattibhava*).
This same method applies to fine-material and immaterial existences. Thus, from the perspective of inclusion, there are two sense-sphere existences conditioned by clinging.
By another way of grouping, there are six existences: two as form-existence (*rūpa-bhava*) and two as formless-existence (*arūpa-bhava*).

Alternatively, without including the distinction between kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), there are three existences by way of sense-sphere-existence (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth, together with what is included therein.

Or, without including the distinction of sense-sphere-existence and so forth, there are two existences by way of kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. And even without including the distinction between kamma and rebirth...
Without approaching [the next life], "with clinging as condition, there is becoming"—thus, by way of becoming, there is only a single becoming.
In this way, the analysis of the condition of clinging should also be understood here through its classification according to the divisions of becoming. 650.
"Whatever is the condition for whatever": furthermore, it should be understood from this as well which clinging serves as the condition for what.
The meaning is "determination. But here, what is the condition for what? Whatever serves as a condition for anything whatsoever indeed does so.
