For the worldling is like one who is insane; without investigating whether this is appropriate or that is inappropriate, he performs whatever action he wills, having aspired to whatever state of existence by means of whatever clinging.
Therefore, when some say that through clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) there are no rebirths in the fine-material or immaterial realms, that should not be accepted.
Rather, it should be accepted that [rebirth] occurs in its entirety.
For example: here, someone—either by way of hearsay or by following a particular view—[thinks], "These sensual pleasures in the human world..."

Having thought, "They are indeed prosperous among the great aristocratic kṣatriya families and so forth, and in the six celestial worlds of the sense-sphere," one is deceived by listening to false doctrine and other such means for the sake of attaining those [states].
Thinking, "By this action, sensual pleasures will be accomplished," one commits bodily misconduct and the like through the grasping of sensual desire (*kāmupādāna*).
Due to the fulfillment of that misconduct, one is reborn in the woeful states.

Alternatively, one who aspires to sense-pleasures visible here and now, and who guards those already obtained, commits bodily misconduct and so forth by way of clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
Through the fulfillment of such misconduct, he is reborn in the woeful states. Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for his rebirth is *kammabhava*.
The aggregates produced from that karma are *upapattibhava*. The *saññābhava* and *pañcavokārabhava*, however, are included within these very categories.

Furthermore, another person whose knowledge has been nourished by hearing the true Dhamma and so forth, thinking "by this action, sensual pleasures will be accomplished," performs bodily good conduct and the like through the influence of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Through the fulfillment of that good conduct, he is reborn among gods or humans.
Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for his rebirth is *kammabhava*. That which is produced from that karma...

The aggregates constitute existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*). However, the existence of perception (*saññābhava*) and five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) are included within that very same category. Thus, clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is the condition for sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), which includes its own subdivisions and their respective contents.
Furthermore, having heard or imagined that "sense-pleasures are more abundant in the fine-material and immaterial existences," one acts through the influence of clinging to sense-pleasures alone.
Having produced the form and formless attainments (*samāpatti*), one is reborn in the fine-material and immaterial Brahma-worlds through the power of those attainments.

Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for that rebirth is *kammabhava*. The aggregates (*khandha*) produced by that karma are *upapattibhava*. Furthermore, the perceptions, non-perceptions, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception realms, as well as the one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences, are included within these very categories.
Thus, clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is a condition for both the fine-material and immaterial existences, along with their respective subdivisions and what is included therein.

Another, holding the view of annihilationism—thinking, "When this so-called self is cut off in either a fortunate existence in the sense-sphere realm or in one of the form or formless realms, it is utterly annihilated"—performs karma leading to that state;
for him, that karma is *kammabhava*. The aggregates produced from that karma are *upapattibhava*. Furthermore, the states of perception (*saññābhava*) and so forth...

They are indeed included therein. Thus, the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is a condition for all three types of existence—sensual, fine-material, and immaterial—along with their subdivisions and their respective inclusions.

Furthermore, by means of clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*), thinking, "This so-called self is happy and free from feverish distress in either a fortunate rebirth in the sensual sphere or in one of the fine-material or immaterial existences," one performs karma that leads to such states; for him, that...
Kamma is *kammabhava*. The aggregates produced by that are *upapattibhava*. The states of perception (*saññābhava*) and so forth are indeed included within those.
Thus, the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*) is the condition for the three types of existence (*bhava*), along with their subdivisions and their respective inclusions.

Another [teacher] says: "This so-called virtue-and-observance (*sīlabbata*) [clinging] pertains either to the fortunate existence of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-sampatti-bhava*) or to one of the form or formless existences (*rūpa-arūpa-bhava*)."
"For one who fulfills [the precepts], happiness reaches fulfillment. Thus, by way of the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), one performs karma leading to that [existence];
for such a person, that karma is *kammabhava*. The aggregates (*khandhā*) produced from that are *upapattibhava*.

Furthermore, the existence of perception (*saññābhava*) and the others are indeed included within those [three]. Thus, the clinging to rules and observances is the cause for the three types of existence (*bhava*) along with their subdivisions and what is included therein.
It is a condition. Thus, herein, the analysis should be understood according to what serves as the condition for what.

But if it is asked: "In this context, how does what serve as a condition for which existence?"—it is clinging that serves as the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for both the material and immaterial existences.
It should be understood that this [clinging] applies to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) by way of co-nascence and the other conditions as well.

For these four kinds of clinging are a condition in only one way—by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)—for the existence of form and the formless (*rūpārūpabhava*), for wholesome kamma within the kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) included in the sense-sphere existence, and for the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). Regarding the sense-sphere existence...

It acts as a condition for the unwholesome kamma-existence associated with itself by way of the various types of conditions—conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root—and by way of conascence and so forth.
However, for that which is dissociated from it, it acts as a condition only by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
This is the detailed exposition on the phrase "with clinging as condition, existence."

651. The detailed exposition of birth and the rest, beginning with “With existence as condition, birth,” etc., should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Niddesa of the Truths*.
Here, however, by “existence” (*bhava*) is intended only *kamma-bhava* (existence as kamma), for that is the condition for birth, not *upapatti-bhava* (existence as rebirth).
Furthermore, that condition is twofold by way of the condition of kamma and the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
In this regard, one might ask: "How is it to be known that existence (*bhava*) is a condition for birth (*jāti*)?

It is because even when external conditions are equal, differences such as inferiority or superiority are observed. For, among external conditions—such as the father, mother, semen, blood, food, and so forth—[the result varies].
Even among beings who are twins, differences such as inferiority or superiority are observed.
This is not without cause, because it does not exist at all times for all beings;

nor is it caused by anything other than kamma, because there is no other cause within the internal continuum of those beings produced by it. Thus, it has kamma as its cause. For kamma is [the cause] of beings...
It is the cause for the distinction between the inferior and the superior. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Kamma divides beings, that is to say, according to their inferiority and superiority.
Consequently, it should be understood that "existence is a condition for birth.
Furthermore, because when there is no birth, there is no such thing as aging-and-death, nor do the states beginning with sorrow exist; but when there is birth...

When there is birth, there is both aging-and-death, and for the foolish person touched by the painful phenomena designated as aging-and-death, there arise states such as sorrow—either through their connection with aging-and-death or through their lack of connection with those various touched painful phenomena.
Therefore, it should be understood that this birth is also a condition for both aging-and-death and for sorrow and the rest. Furthermore, that [birth]...
By way of the decisive support (upanissaya), it is a condition in a single way.
This concludes the detailed exposition on such passages as "with existence as condition, birth [arises]" and so forth. The Discourse on the Wheel of Existence (Bhavacakka).

652. But because sorrow and the rest are mentioned here at the end, therefore that which was stated at the beginning of this wheel of existence as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]"—that ignorance is established by means of sorrow and the rest. Thus, this wheel of existence has an unknown beginning;
it is devoid of an agent or an experiencer, and it is empty of the twelvefold emptiness.
It should be understood that it proceeds constantly and continuously.
But how, in this context, is ignorance established by means of sorrow and the rest; how is this wheel of existence beginningless and endless;
how is it devoid of an agent and an experiencer; and how is it empty of the twelvefold emptiness? For herein, sorrow, lamentation, and despair—
Since lamentation belongs to one who is deluded, and since those [other factors] are already established, ignorance (*avijjā*) is thereby established as well.
Furthermore, it is said: "With the arising of the taints (*āsava*), there is the arising of ignorance. And these states beginning with sorrow arise from the arising of the taints. How so?
First, in the case of separation from the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), sorrow arises from the arising of the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*). As it has been said:
“If those desires elude a person who longs for them and has conceived a craving for them, he suffers as if pierced by an arrow.
And as it is said: “From desire arises sorrow.”
All these, moreover, originate from the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). As it is said:
"For one who dwells obsessed with the thought 'I am form' or 'form is mine,' sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise due to the change and alteration of form.
And just as they originate from the taint of views, so too do they originate from the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*). As it is said:
“Even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abounding in happiness, and dwell for long periods in lofty celestial mansions—
even they, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, fall into fear, terror, and a sense of spiritual urgency.
This is like the gods who, having seen the five portents, were struck with alarm by the fear of death.
And just as there is the arising from the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), so too is there the arising from the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*). As it is said:
"That fool, monks, experiences threefold suffering and mental distress even here and now.
Thus, because these states arise from the taints, when they are being accomplished, they have ignorance as their cause.
They accomplish the taints (*āsava*). And when the taints are accomplished, ignorance (*avijjā*) is also necessarily accomplished by virtue of its existence as a condition for them.
Thus, first of all, it should be understood that ignorance is established here through sorrow and the rest.
Furthermore, since ignorance has been established in this way by virtue of its existence as a condition, [it follows that] "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) arise."
"Conditioned by volitional formations (saṅkhāra), consciousness (viññāṇa)"—thus, there is no end to this succession of cause and effect.
Therefore, it is established that the twelvefold wheel of existence (bhavacakra), which proceeds by way of the connection between cause and effect, is "unknown at the beginning" (aviditādi).
If it is argued that this contradicts the statement of the mere beginning, namely, "conditioned by ignorance (avijjā), volitional formations arise," this is not so.

This is a statement regarding the beginning. However, this is a statement concerning the primary factor (*padhānadhamma*). For among the three rounds (*vaṭṭa*), ignorance (*avijjā*) is the primary factor.

By the inclusion of ignorance, the remaining round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) as well as karma and the rest obstruct the fool, just as grasping the head of a snake obstructs the rest of its body and the arm.
But when ignorance is completely severed, liberation from them occurs, just as [liberation occurs] upon cutting off the head of the snake.

It is like the release of the arms that were bound by a fetter. As it is said: "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations," and so forth.

Thus, this is a statement concerning that primary factor through the grasping of which there is bondage and through the relinquishing of which there is liberation; it is not merely a statement about the beginning.
In this way, this wheel of existence should be understood as being "unknown" and so on.
Since the occurrence of volitional formations and so forth proceeds by means of causes such as ignorance and the rest, therefore,
[the world] does not proceed from anything other than those— neither from a creator such as Brahmā or Mahābrahmā, who is imagined to be "the best, the creator,
the ruler," nor from a self imagined in the manner of "this self of mine is the speaker and the feeler" as the cause of pleasure and pain within saṃsāra.
It is devoid of an experiencer. Thus, it should be understood as being devoid of both an agent and an experiencer.
Furthermore, because ignorance here possesses the nature of arising and passing away, it is devoid of permanence; because it is defiled and subject to defilement, it is devoid of beauty;
because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, it is devoid of pleasure; and because its existence is dependent on conditions, it is devoid of mastery.

And it is empty of a self-entity (*attabhāva*). Likewise, the factors beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are also [empty]. Or rather, because ignorance is not a self, does not belong to a self, is not within a self, and does not possess a self;
likewise, the factors beginning with volitional formations are also [empty]. Therefore, this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) should be understood as being empty of twelvefold emptiness.
653. Having understood this, [one sees that] its roots are ignorance and craving, and its times are the three: past and so forth.
Within these, the factors are two, eight, and two respectively according to their specific forms.
Furthermore, it should be understood that for this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*), two factors—ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*)—are the roots. This [wheel] is twofold:

from the perspective of bringing in the past, it has ignorance as its root and ends with feeling (*vedanā*); from the perspective of the continuity of the future, it has craving as its root and ends with aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Therein, the former is stated according to the temperament of views (*diṭṭhicarita*), while the latter...
This is by way of the temperament of craving. For ignorance is the leader of the cycle of existence for those of speculative temperament, while craving is the leader for those of craving-temperament.
Alternatively, the first [truth] is for the eradication of the view of annihilationism, because it demonstrates the non-interruption of causes for the arising of results;
the second is for the eradication of the view of eternalism, because it demonstrates aging and death for those already arisen. This is with reference to those born from a womb.
The former [formula] is used because it illustrates successive occurrence, while the latter, by way of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), illustrates simultaneous arising.

Furthermore, there are three times: past, present, and future. Among these, according to how they appear explicitly in the text, two factors—ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*)—belong to the past time.
The eight factors beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and ending with existence (*bhava*) belong to the present time.
Birth and aging-and-death should be understood as two factors belonging to the future time.
Furthermore:
"This [dependent origination] comprises four divisions: those preceded by cause and fruit, and those preceded by cause and cause, and the three links. 654.
"It whirls with twenty spokes, three folds, and is unstable"—
thus it should be understood. Therein,
between the formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*), there is one junction of cause and fruit, which is feeling (*vedanā*).

Between craving (*taṇhā*) and becoming (*bhava*), there is one called the "junction of fruit and cause" (*phala-hetu-sandhi*). Between becoming and birth (*jāti*), there is one "junction of cause and fruit" (*hetu-phala-sandhi*).
Thus, this should be understood as a junction consisting of fruit, cause, and cause preceded by fruit.
Furthermore, its four groupings are established according to its beginning and end. They are as follows: ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*).
There is one grouping: consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute the second. Craving, clinging, and becoming constitute the third.
Birth, aging, and death constitute the fourth. Thus, this should be understood as the fourfold grouping.
In the past there were five causes; now there is the pentad of results.
Now, there are five causes and five fruits in the future.
By means of these twenty spokes, which consist of twenty aspects, it should be understood as "the wheel with twenty aspects.

Therein, regarding "five causes in the past," first, ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*)—these two have already been mentioned. For it is one who is ignorant who becomes agitated.
Being agitated, one clings; with clinging as condition, there is becoming (*bhava*). Therefore, craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming are also included.

Thus he said: "In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance (*avijjā*), the accumulation [of kamma] is volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), attachment is craving, the approaching is clinging, and volition is becoming—these five factors in the previous kamma-existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking here."
In that context, "in the previous kamma-existence" means in the prior kamma-existence; the meaning is: while the kamma-existence of a past birth was being performed.
Ignorance is *avijjā*: that which is ignorance regarding suffering and so forth at that time, by which one who is deluded performs kamma—that is *avijjā*.
Accumulation is *saṅkhāra*: those prior volitions of one performing that kamma, such as the thought, "I shall give a gift."
The volitions that have arisen while one is preparing the requisites for giving for even a month or a year are called "prior volitions.
However, the volition of one who actually places the offering into the hands of the recipients is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Alternatively, among the six types of wholesome impulsive consciousnesses (*javana*) that belong to a single cognitive process, the volition is termed "effort," "accumulation," or "formations" (*saṅkhāra*); in the seventh [consciousness], it is "existence. Or, any volition whatsoever [may be so designated].

Existence (*bhava*). The volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are the associated efforts. Craving (*taṇhā*) is attachment; that longing and aspiration for the fruit—the state of rebirth—by one performing karma is called craving. Grasping (*upādāna*) is the approaching;

that which serves as the condition for the existence of karma, such as thinking, "Having done this, I will enjoy sensual pleasures in such-and-such a place" or "I will cut off [the world]," and so forth.
Approaching, grasping, and clutching that which proceeds by way of the [four] modes—this is called clinging (*upādāna*). Intention (*cetanā*) is "existence" (*bhava*);
the meaning should be understood as follows: intention is said to be existence at the conclusion of the stage of accumulation (*āyūhana*).
Now, regarding the "fivefold fruit," beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, it has already appeared in the Canon itself. As it was said: "Herein, rebirth-linking..."
“Consciousness, descent [into the womb], mind-and-body, the sense bases as clarity, contact as what is touched, and feeling as what is felt—
these five phenomena here in the existence of rebirth have as their condition karma performed in the past. In that context,
“rebirth-linking consciousness” refers to that which is called “rebirth-linking” because it arises by way of linking to another state of existence.
Consciousness (*viññāṇa*). "Descent is name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): that descent of material and immaterial phenomena into the womb, like arriving and entering, is this "name-and-form.
"The sensitive organ is the sense-base" (*āyatana*): this is stated by way of the five sense-bases beginning with the eye. "That which is touched is contact" (*phassa*):
that which has arisen having touched or is touching an object is this "contact. "That which is felt is feeling" (*vedanā*): that which...
The meaning should be understood as follows: "That feeling which arises together with rebirth-linking consciousness, or with contact conditioned by the six sense bases—that is feeling.
Now, regarding the phrase "the five causes," these are craving and so forth mentioned in the text: craving, clinging, and becoming. However, when becoming is included...
The formations associated with that [craving] are already included in its prior stage.

And by the inclusion of craving and clinging, ignorance—which is either associated with them or that through which one, being deluded, performs kamma—is also already included. Thus there are five. Therefore he said:
"Here, because the sense-bases have matured, delusion is ignorance; the exertion is formations; the attachment is craving."
“Approaching, grasping, volition, and becoming—these five factors here are the conditions for rebirth-linking in the future within this kamma-process existence.
In this context, by the phrase “because the sense bases have matured here,” the delusion at the time of performing the kamma by one whose sense bases are matured is shown.
The rest is of plain meaning.
"The five fruits in the future" refers to the five beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*). These are stated by way of their inclusion in birth (*jāti*).

Aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), however, is the aging-and-death of those very same factors. Therefore he said: "In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent [into the womb] is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the sensitivity is the sense base (*āyatana*);
the touched is contact (*phassa*); the felt is feeling (*vedanā*). These five things, in the future existence of rebirth..."
“...due to karma performed here. Thus, this consists of twenty modes.

Regarding the statement “it revolves as a threefold cycle that does not stand still”: herein, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) constitute the cycle of kamma; ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), and clinging (*upādāna*) constitute the cycle of defilements (*kilesa*);

and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) constitute the cycle of result (*vipāka*). It is by means of these three cycles [that it revolves].

This wheel of existence (bhavacakra) with its three revolutions should be understood as revolving indeed, because it turns again and again and remains unstable so long as the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) is not cut off, owing to the conditions for its arising being unsevered. 655.
While it is thus revolving, [it proceeds as follows:]
It should be understood, as appropriate, by way of its origin, its function, its prevention, through similes, and through the distinctions of its profound methods. In this regard,
since it is stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga* that wholesome and unwholesome kamma, without distinction, constitutes the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).
Therefore, regarding "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise": volitional formations originate from the second truth (the origin of suffering) by means of ignorance.
Consciousness originates from the first truth (suffering) by means of volitional formations.
Name-and-form and the subsequent factors, up to resultant feeling, originate from the first truth by means of consciousness and the rest. Craving originates from the first truth by means of feeling.
The second truth. Grasping arises from craving; thus, the second truth originates from the second truth. Existence arises from grasping;
thus, the first and second truths originate from the second truth. Birth arises from existence; thus, the first truth originates from the second truth.
Aging-and-death arises from birth; thus, the first truth originates from the first truth. Thus, in this way...
This should be understood according to the truth as it applies to each case.
For herein, ignorance deludes beings regarding the bases and serves as the condition for the manifestation of volitional formations;
likewise, volitional formations construct the conditioned and serve as conditions for consciousness.
Consciousness discerns both the physical basis and its object, and it serves as a condition for mind-and-body (nāmarūpa).

Mind-and-body mutually support one another, and they serve as a condition for the six sense bases (saḷāyatana). The six sense bases operate within their respective domains, and they serve as a condition for contact (phassa).
Contact touches upon the objective field, and it serves as a condition for feeling (vedanā).
Feeling also experiences the flavor of the object and serves as a condition for craving.
Craving also lusts after phenomena that are lustful and serves as a condition for clinging. Clinging also clings to phenomena that are subject to clinging and serves as a condition for becoming.
Becoming also disperses into various destinies and serves as a condition for birth.
Birth also produces the aggregates because it functions as their manifestation, and it is a condition for aging-and-death.

Aging-and-death also presides over the maturation and dissolution of the aggregates, and it is a condition for the appearance of another existence because it serves as the basis for sorrow and the rest.
Therefore, in all these instances, this should be understood accordingly according to its twofold functional activity.
657. And herein, "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations" is a negation of the view that there is an agent.

"With volitional formations as condition, consciousness" is a negation of the view that there is a transmigration of a self. "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form" is a negation of the perception of a solid mass, because it demonstrates the differentiation of the basis for what is merely imagined as a "self.
"With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," and so forth, [negates the views] that "the self sees... [and so on]... cognizes."
It prevents such views as "one touches," "one feels," "one thirsts," "one clings," "one comes to be," "one is born," "one ages," and "one dies.
Therefore, this wheel of existence (bhavacakra) should be understood accordingly as a prevention of wrong view (*micchā-dassana*). 658.
Furthermore, because one does not see phenomena here according to their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*), one is like a blind man.
Ignorance (*avijjā*). Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), like a blind man’s stumbling.

Conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*viññāṇa*), like the fall of one who has stumbled. Conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), like the appearance of a boil on one who has fallen.

Conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), like the pustules arising from the bursting of the boil. Conditioned by the six sense bases is [contact], like the rubbing of the boil and the pustules.

Contact (*phassa*). Just as there is pain from impact, so conditioned by contact arises feeling (*vedanā*); just as there is a desire for a remedy for that pain, so conditioned by feeling arises craving (*taṇhā*).
Just as there is the grasping of what is unsuitable through the desire for a remedy, so conditioned by craving arises clinging (*upādāna*).

Just as there is the application of an unsuitable ointment to what has been grasped, so conditioned by clinging arises becoming (*bhava*). Through the application of an unsuitable ointment, the manifestation of an abscess occurs.

Birth [arises] from existence as a condition, like the bursting of an abscess from its swelling. Aging-and-death [arises] from birth as a condition, like the bursting of an abscess from its transformation.
Or rather, because here ignorance overcomes beings by way of non-comprehension and wrong comprehension, just as a film [overcomes] the eyes;
and being thus overcome, the fool envelops himself with volitional formations leading to renewed existence, like a silkworm in its cocoon.

[It is] as if [by means of] the sheaths of the sheath-sections. Consciousness, when embraced by volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), gains a footing in the realms of existence (*gati*), just as a prince gains a kingdom when embraced by a counselor.
By way of imagining the sign of rebirth, consciousness produces manifold name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), just as a magician produces an illusion.
Established in name-and-form, the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) attain growth...
Established upon good ground, it reaches growth and abundance like a forest thicket.

From the contact of the sense bases, contact arises, like fire from the friction of kindling sticks. For one touched by contact, feeling becomes manifest, like the burning sensation of one touched by fire.
For one experiencing feeling, craving increases, like thirst in one drinking salt water.
Like one who is thirsty, he forms a longing for states of existence as if he were parched for water. That is his clinging (*upādāna*);
through clinging, he grasps at existence (*bhava*), just as a fish greedy for bait seizes the hook. When there is existence, there is birth, like a sprout when there is a seed.
For one who is born, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are inevitable, like the falling of a tree that has grown. Therefore:
Thus, this wheel of existence (bhavacakra) should be understood through these similes as appropriate.
Furthermore, because the Blessed One, with reference to its profundity in meaning, in nature, in teaching, and in realization, said:
"Ānanda, this dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is profound and appears profound. 659.
Therefore, the wheel of existence (bhavacakra), endowed with its profound divisions, should be understood according to what is appropriate. In this regard,
because aging and death do not exist apart from birth, nor do they arise from anything other than birth,
but rather emerge precisely through birth— thus, because the meaning of "arising conditioned by birth" is difficult to comprehend for aging and death—
The meaning of being produced and brought about with birth as a condition is profound. Likewise, the meaning of being produced and brought about with existence as a condition for birth...
[and so on] ...the meaning of being produced and brought about with ignorance as a condition for volitional formations is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence is "profound in meaning.
This, then, is its profundity of meaning (*atthagambhīratā*). For "meaning" (*attha*) is said to be cause and fruit. As it is said: "In cause and fruit..."
“Knowledge is the analytical knowledge of meaning.

However, because the manner and the state in which ignorance acts as a condition for those various formations is difficult to comprehend, the meaning of ignorance as a condition for formations is profound. Likewise, [the meaning of] formations... [and so on].
The meaning of birth as a condition for aging-and-death is profound; therefore, this wheel of existence is "profound in its nature" (*dhammagambhīra*).

This is what is meant here by "profundity in nature. For "nature" (*dhamma*) is a name for a cause, as it is said: "Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
Furthermore, because it must be set forth in various ways according to those respective reasons, the teaching (*desanā*) itself is also profound. It is not...
In this regard, knowledge other than omniscience finds its foundation therein. For it is found in some suttas in direct order,
in some in reverse order, in some in both direct and reverse order, in some starting from the middle in either direct or reverse order,
in some as the three links and four groups, and in some as the two links and three groups.
In some places it is taught as having one link and two groups; therefore, this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) is profound in its teaching—this is its profundity of teaching.

Furthermore, because herein that intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest, by the penetration of which ignorance and the others are correctly understood according to their specific characteristics, [is revealed].
They have been penetrated; because it is difficult to master, it is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) is profound in terms of penetration.

Likewise, herein, the meaning of ignorance (*avijjā*) as non-knowing, non-seeing, and non-penetration of the truths is profound; the meaning of volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) as the act of forming, accumulating, and being with or without lust;

the meaning of consciousness (*viññāṇa*) as emptiness, lack of agency, and the manifestation of rebirth-linking without transmigration; and the meaning of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as simultaneous arising, the analysis and non-analysis of the mental and the material, and the bending and deformation [of the mind].

The meaning of the six sense bases is that of being the sovereign, the door to the world, the field, and the objective domain; the meaning of contact is that of touching, impinging, conjunction, and collocation;
the meaning of feeling is that of experiencing the flavor of the object, and the state of being felt as pleasure, pain, or neutrality, which constitutes the life-principle.

The meaning of craving is that of delighting in, clinging to, streaming, creeping, and being like a river, a creeper, or the ocean of craving that is difficult to fill; the meaning of clinging is that of grasping, seizing, adhering, misapprehending, and being difficult to transcend.
The meaning of existence (*bhava*) as the act of accumulating, the formation of kamma, and the casting into a source, destiny, station, and abode;

the meaning of birth (*jāti*) as being born, coming-to-be, descent [into the womb], production, and manifestation; and the meaning of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) as exhaustion, passing away, breaking up, and transformation—this is the profundity of penetration here.

660. Since there are four methods of meaning here—namely, the method of identity (*ekattanaya*), the method of diversity (*nānattanaya*), the method of non-agency (*abyāpāranaya*), and the method of suchness (*evaṃdhammatānaya*)—therefore, this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) should be understood according to its appropriate classification by way of these methods.

In that regard, the sequence "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises" is called the method of identity because it represents the uninterrupted continuity of the stream, just as a seed attains the state of a tree through the stages of the sprout and so forth. One who sees this correctly [perceives] the connection between cause and fruit...

Through the realization of the non-interruption of the continuum, one abandons the view of annihilationism. Seeing wrongly, one clings to the view of eternalism by grasping at a unity in the non-interruption of the continuum as it proceeds through the connection of cause and fruit.
However, the defining of ignorance and the other factors according to their respective characteristics is called the method of diversity (*nānattanaya*). Seeing correctly—
One abandons the eternalist view by seeing the arising of ever-new [phenomena].
Seeing incorrectly, one clings to the annihilationist view because of grasping at diversity in what belongs to a single continuum as if it were different continua.
There is an absence of such activities as "formations must be produced by me" or "consciousness [must be produced] by us from formations," and so forth.
This is called the method of non-agency (*abyāpāranaya*). Seeing correctly, one abandons the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*) through the realization of the absence of an agent.

Seeing incorrectly, because one fails to grasp that causal status which is established by the inherent nature and necessity of ignorance and the other factors even in the absence of agency, one clings to the view of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*).
However, the arising of formations and so forth occurs only from causes such as ignorance, just as curds arise from milk and so forth, and not from anything else;

this is called the principle of "suchness of nature" (*evam-dhammatā-naya*). Seeing this correctly, one abandons the view of causelessness (*ahetuka-diṭṭhi*) and the view of non-action (*akiriya-diṭṭhi*) through the realization of the fruit according to its conditions. Seeing it incorrectly, [one fails to understand] the occurrence of the fruit in accordance with its conditions.
Because it grasps at anything whatsoever from wherever it may come, and because it grasps at what is impossible for anyone, it adopts both the view of causelessness and the doctrine of fatalism;
thus is this wheel of existence [described] by way of the arising of the truths, by way of functions, and by way of the prohibitions and similes.
And the distinctions of its profound methods should be understood according to what is appropriate.
For this [Dhamma] is unfathomable due to its extreme profundity; it is difficult to cross because of the density of its various methods.
Having shattered the wheel of existence with the well-sharpened sword of knowledge upon the excellent stone of concentration—like a thunderbolt wheel that constantly grinds down all things;
There is no one, even in a dream, who has transcended the fear of saṃsāra.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "This dependent origination, Ānanda, is deep and appears deep.
And because of the lack of realization and penetration of this Dhamma, Ānanda, this generation has become like a tangled skein."
“Born from the knot of the family, become like the *muñja* grass and the *pabbaja* grass, one does not transcend the states of loss, the miserable destination, the abyss, and saṃsāra. Therefore,
one who is practicing for the benefit and happiness of oneself or others, having abandoned all other duties,
is wise here in the profound analysis of the mode of conditions.
"Just as one would seek a firm footing, so should one always apply oneself to the good.
Thus ends the section on the Development of Wisdom in the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Plane of Wisdom. 18.
The Description of Purification of View.
The Discourse on the Comprehension of Mind-and-Matter (Nāmarūpa-pariggaha-kathā) 662. Now, it was said:

"Having cultivated familiarity with knowledge by means of learning and interrogation regarding these states that constitute the ground, one should accomplish the two fundamental purifications, namely, purification of virtue and purification of mind."
Therein, "purification of virtue" refers to the fourfold virtue beginning with restraint by the Pātimokkha, which is perfectly pure;
this has already been explained in detail in the Description of Virtue. "Purification of mind" refers to the eight attainments together with their preliminary stages;

these too have been explained in every aspect in the Description of Concentration, which was stated under the heading of "mind. Therefore, they should be understood according to the method explained therein.
As for what was stated— "Purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path,
purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision: these five purifications constitute the body"— therein,
the seeing of name-and-form as they truly are is called purification of view.

663. One who desires to achieve that by means of serenity as a vehicle should first emerge from any one of the remaining fine-material or immaterial-sphere jhānas—excluding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—and then discern the jhāna factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*), etc., along with the states associated with them, by way of their characteristics, functions, and so forth.
Having so discerned them, all of this [should be understood] in the sense of "bending" (*namana*), because it bends toward the object.
The name must be defined.

Then, just as a man who sees a snake inside his house and follows it might see its lair, even so this practitioner of yoga, while examining that name, [asks]: "Upon what does this name depend for its occurrence?"
Seeking its support, he sees the heart-base (*hadayarūpa*).
Then he discerns matter by way of the remaining derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) which is supported by the primary elements and which itself supports the primary elements.

He defines all of this as "matter" because of its quality of being molested (*ruppana*). Thereafter, he [discerns] in brief: "Name has the characteristic of bending (*namana*); matter has the characteristic of being molested."
He defines name-and-form.
However, one who takes pure insight as his vehicle, or this same person who takes serenity as his vehicle,
[proceeds] either briefly or in detail by means of any one of the methods for discerning the elements that were explained in the "Definition of the Four Elements."

He discerns the four elements. Then, when the elements have become manifest to him by way of their actual individual characteristics, first, regarding the hair produced by kamma, there are ten material phenomena by way of the "body decad" (*kāyadasaka*), namely:
the four elements, color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, life-faculty, and body-sensitivity.
In that very same place, because of the presence of the state [of being], there is also the "state decad" (*bhāvadasaka*).
In that same place, there is the nutritive-essence octad produced by nutriment, as well as those produced by temperature and mind;
thus there are another twenty-four. In this way, among the twenty-four groups within the fourfold origination, there are forty-four material phenomena for each.
However, regarding these four—sweat, tears, spittle, and snot—which are produced by both temperature and mind, there are two...
By way of the eightfold nutritive essence (*oja*), there are sixteen material phenomena for each of these;
and for the four temperature-originated [phenomena]—namely, bile, phlegm, pus, and urine—it is by way of the eightfold nutritive essence alone that eight material phenomena become manifest for each.
This, then, is the method regarding the thirty-two aspects.
Furthermore, when these thirty-two aspects have become manifest, ten other aspects also become manifest.

Therein, first, in the portion of fire born of karma that ripens food and so forth, there are nine material phenomena: the octad of nutritive essence (*ojā-aṭṭhamaka*) together with life-faculty (*jīvita*). Likewise, in the portion of air born of consciousness consisting of inhalation and exhalation, there are nine:
the octad of nutritive essence together with sound. In the remaining [portions] arisen from the four causes, there are...
In the eight [sets], the life-nonad and the three nutritive-essence-octads— thus thirty-three material phenomena become manifest.
When these derived matter and primary elements have thus become manifest in detail by way of forty-two modes,
there are another sixty material phenomena consisting of the five decads beginning with the eye-decad, and the heart-basis decad, according to the basis and door.
They become evident. Having unified all of them by means of the characteristic of being subject to deformation (*ruppana-lakkhaṇa*), he sees: "This is form.
For one who has thus discerned form, the immaterial states (*arūpa-dhamma*) become evident by way of the doors. Namely:

the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses, the three mind-elements (*manodhātu*), and the sixty-eight mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—that is, the eighty-one mundane types of consciousness—in general.
And born together with those consciousnesses are contact, feeling, perception, volition, life-faculty, mental stability, and attention—these seven are the mental concomitants (cetasika).
However, supramundane consciousnesses do not come within the range of discernment for either one who practices pure insight or one whose vehicle is serenity, because they have not yet been attained.
He [discerns] all those immaterial phenomena by means of the characteristic of bending (namana).
Having grouped them together, he sees, "This is called that. In this way, one person defines name-and-form in detail by means of the analysis of the four elements.
Another does so by means of the eighteen elements. How? Here, a bhikkhu [reflects]: "In this personal existence there is the eye-element... [and so on]..."
Having adverted to the elements known as the mind-consciousness element,
he does not take as "the eye" that lump of flesh which the world perceives as the eye— variegated with white and black circles, long and wide, and bound to the sockets by a string of sinews;
rather, in the exposition of the aggregates, he defines as the "eye element" the sensitivity of the eye described among the derived material phenomena.

Furthermore, there are nine co-nascent material phenomena (*sahajāta-rūpa*): the four elements that serve as its support, the four surrounding material qualities of color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence (*ojā*), and the sustaining life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

In that same location, there are twenty kamma-born material phenomena (*kammaja-rūpa*) consisting of the body-decad and the sex-decad; and twenty-four [material phenomena] consisting of the three sets of eight with nutritive essence as the eighth, produced by nutriment and so forth.
"Non-appropriated material phenomena" refers to the remaining fifty-three types of material phenomena; one does not define them as the "eye-element.
This same method applies to the ear-element and the others as well. However, in the case of the body-element, there are forty-three remaining material phenomena.
Some, however, state that there are forty-five by adding nine each—consisting of those produced by temperature and mind—together with sound.
Thus, these five translucent elements (pasāda) and their five respective objects—visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible object—constitute ten types of matter and ten elements.
All remaining types of matter are included solely within the element of mental data (dhammadhātu).

Furthermore, the consciousness that arises depending on the eye and having visible form as its object is called the eye-consciousness-element; in this way, the two sets of five consciousnesses constitute the five consciousness-elements.

There are three mind-element consciousnesses (*manodhātu-citta*) which constitute one mind-element (*manodhātu*), and sixty-eight mind-consciousness-element consciousnesses (*manoviññāṇadhātu-citta*) which constitute the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

Thus, all eighty-one mundane consciousnesses (*lokiya-citta*) are the seven consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*). The contact and other mental factors associated with them are the mental-object-element (*dhammadhātu*).
In this way, there are ten and a half elements that are form (*rūpa*), and seven and a half elements that are name (*nāma*); thus, by way of the eighteen elements, there is one [set].
He defines name-and-form.

666. Another way is by means of the twelve bases. How? Having set aside the fifty-three types of form in the same manner as described for the eye element, he defines the mere sensitivity of the eye as the "eye base. And in the same manner as described therein—
The elements of the ear, nose, tongue, and body are called the "bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five phenomena that serve as their respective objects are called the "bases of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

The seven mundane consciousness elements are called the "mind base," while the mental factors associated with them—contact and so forth—as well as the remaining material phenomena, are called the "mental-object base. Thus, there are nine and a half bases here.
"Form" and "the one and a half bases" are "name"—thus one person defines name-and-form by way of the twelve bases.
Another defines it more concisely than that by way of the aggregates. How? Here, a bhikkhu [considers]:
"In this body there are four elements originating from the four causes; dependent on them are color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and the sensitive eye-faculties, etc."
The five types of sensitivity, the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa), sex (bhāva), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and sound produced by two causes—
these seventeen kinds of form are "form that has reached comprehension" (sammasanupaga) and are "produced forms" (nipphanna-rūpa). However, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, the space element,
the lightness, malleability, wieldiness, integration, continuity, aging, and impermanence of form— these [nine]...
The ten kinds of materiality are not subject to comprehension; they are merely the delimitation of shape, change, and internal boundaries.

They are not produced materiality, nor are they primary materiality. Nevertheless, because they consist merely of the delimitation of shape, change, and internal boundaries among material phenomena, they are designated as "materiality.
Thus, all these twenty-seven kinds of materiality constitute the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha) with respect to the eighty-one mundane types of consciousness.
The feeling that arises together [with contact] is the aggregate of feeling; the perception associated with it is the aggregate of perception; the mental formations are the aggregate of formations;
and consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness. Thus, the aggregate of form is "form," and the four immaterial aggregates are "name.
In this way, one defines name-and-form by means of the five aggregates.

668. Another, having thus comprehended the form within this personal existence in brief—“Whatever form there is, all that form consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements”—and likewise having comprehended the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and a portion of the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*) as name (*nāma*), [reflects]: “Thus, this is name and this is form; this is called...”
Thus, he defines name-and-form in brief as "name-and-form.

However, if, while defining form through various approaches, the immaterial (arūpa) does not appear to him because of its subtlety when he attempts to define it, he should not abandon his effort; rather, he should continue to contemplate form again and again.

It must be brought to mind, grasped, and defined. For in whatever way form becomes well-washed, stripped of its tangles, and thoroughly purified, in that very same way the immaterial states that have it as their object become manifest of themselves.
Just as for a man with good eyesight looking at the reflection of his face in an unpurified mirror, the reflection—
When the reflection does not appear, he does not discard the mirror thinking, "The reflection does not appear," but rather polishes it again and again.
When the mirror is completely clean, the reflection becomes manifest of its own accord.
And just as one who needs oil, having poured sesame paste into a trough and sprinkled it with water, [obtains the oil] by pressing it once or twice;

When the sesame oil does not come out, one does not discard the sesame paste; rather, one repeatedly sprinkles it with warm water, kneads it, and presses it. While doing this, clear sesame oil comes forth.
Or again, just as one desiring to clarify water takes a *kataka* nut, inserts the hand into the jar, and by merely rubbing it once or twice—
When water is not clear, one does not throw away the soap-nut fruit; rather, one rubs it again and again.
As he does so, the mud and silt settle down, and the water becomes transparent and clear.
In the same way, that bhikkhu, without laying down his burden, must repeatedly comprehend and attend to form alone.
It should be grasped and defined.
For in whatever way that material form becomes well-washed, free from tangles, and perfectly pure, in that same way the defilements opposed to it subside;
the mind becomes serene like water on top of mud. The immaterial phenomena that have that as their object—
They become evident by themselves. In this way, this matter should also be illustrated by other similes such as those of sugarcane, thieves, cattle, curd, and fish.
670. Discourse on the Mode of Appearance of Immaterial Phenomena:
For one who has thus thoroughly purified the discernment of material form, the immaterial phenomena appear in three ways.
Either by way of contact (*phassa*), or by way of feeling (*vedanā*), or by way of consciousness (*viññāṇa*). How so?
First, for one who discerns the elements (*dhātu*) according to the method beginning with "the earth element has the characteristic of hardness," the initial impact is contact;

the feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*); the perception is the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*); and together with contact, volition (*cetanā*) [is the aggregate of formations].
The aggregate of formations appears as such, and the mind appears as the aggregate of consciousness. Likewise, regarding the hair: "The earth element in the hair has the characteristic of hardness...
[and so on] ...the earth element in the in-breaths and out-breaths has the characteristic of hardness.

Here, the initial impact is contact; the feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the mind appears as the aggregate of consciousness. Thus, immaterial phenomena appear by way of contact.
To one person, it appears thus: “The earth element has the characteristic of hardness”; the feeling that experiences the flavor of that object is the feeling aggregate;
the perception associated with it is the perception aggregate; the contact and volition associated with it are the formations aggregate;
and the consciousness associated with them is the consciousness aggregate. Likewise, [it appears] regarding the hair: “The earth element in the hair has the characteristic of hardness.”

"...pe... in the case of inhalation and exhalation, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness"—thus the feeling that experiences the taste of that object is the aggregate of feeling; "...pe...
the consciousness associated with that is the aggregate of consciousness. In this way, immaterial phenomena appear by way of feeling.
To another, it appears thus: "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness"—the consciousness that discerns this object is the consciousness aggregate;
the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; the perception is the perception aggregate; and contact and volition are the formations aggregate. Likewise, [it appears thus]:
"In the head hairs, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness... [and so on] ...in the in-breaths and out-breaths, the earth element..."
"Hardness is its characteristic"—thus consciousness, which cognizes the object, is the consciousness aggregate;
the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate; and contact and volition are the formations aggregate—this is how it appears.
In this way, immaterial phenomena appear by way of consciousness.

By this same method, one should apply the analysis following all its various divisions— by way of four elements each among the forty-two sets of elements beginning with "In hair produced by kamma, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness," and so forth,
as well as in the remaining modes of discerning material form such as the eye-element and others.

671. And because the immaterial phenomena become evident in three ways only to one who has thus thoroughly purified the discernment of material form, therefore the application for the discernment of the immaterial should be undertaken by means of the thorough purification of material form alone, and not by any other means.
For if, when one or two material phenomena have appeared, one abandons material form and begins the discernment of the immaterial, [the result will be failure].
The meditation subject declines, like a mountain cow described in the context of the earth-kasiṇa meditation.
However, for one who has thoroughly mastered the perception of form and applies himself to the mastery of the formless, the meditation subject reaches growth,
increase, and fullness.
Thus, he defines as "name" the four immaterial aggregates that appear by way of contact and so forth;
as "form," he defines the four great elements which have become their object, and the derived form based upon those four great elements.
In this way, all phenomena belonging to the three planes—namely the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates—he [cuts] with a sword...
As if opening a chest or splitting an almond kernel, one defines name-and-form in two ways.
One reaches the conclusion that beyond mere name-and-form there is no other being, person, deva, or Brahmā.
This is the synthesis of many suttas.

672. Thus, having defined name-and-form according to its true nature, for the purpose of abandoning the worldly convention of "a being" or "a person," for the purpose of transcending delusion regarding a being, and for the purpose of establishing the mind on the plane of non-delusion, one should, by means of many discourses, [contemplate]: "This is merely name-and-form; there is no being, no..."
Having correlated this meaning with the statement, "The person exists," he defines it. For this has been said:
"Just as when the parts are assembled, there is the designation 'chariot,' so too, when the aggregates exist, there is the conventional designation 'being.'"
Furthermore, it has been said: "Just as, friends, space enclosed by wood, creepers, clay, and grass comes to be designated as a 'house,' even so,
friends, space [enclosed] by bone, sinew, flesh, and skin..."
“Surrounded by it, indeed, it goes by the designation ‘form.
Furthermore, it has been said:
“Only suffering arises; suffering stands and passes away.”
“Nothing other than suffering arises; nothing other than suffering ceases.
Thus, by means of hundreds of discourses, it is only name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that is illuminated, not a being (satta) nor a person (puggala). Therefore...
Just as when the various parts and components such as the axle, wheels, and fender are arranged in a particular way,
there is the mere conventional designation "chariot," yet in the ultimate sense, when each individual part is examined, there is no such thing as a "chariot";
and just as when the building materials such as timber are arranged so as to enclose space in a particular way, there is the mere conventional designation "house."

In the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), there is no such thing as a "house. Just as when the fingers, the thumb, and so forth are arranged in a certain manner, there is the mere conventional designation (*vohāramatta*) of a "fist";

or as there is the designation of a "lute" in the case of the sounding board, strings, and so forth; or a "army" in the case of elephants, horses, and so forth; or a "city" in the case of walls, houses, gate-towers, and so forth;
so too, when the trunk, branches, foliage, and so forth are arranged in a certain manner, there is the mere conventional designation of a "tree."
When each individual component is examined from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), there is no such thing as a "tree.
In the same way, while the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandha*) exist, the expressions "being" or "person" (*puggala*) are merely conventional designations (*vohāramatta*).

When each individual phenomenon (*dhamma*) is examined from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no such thing as a "being" that serves as the basis for the grasping [of the notions] "I am" or "I am this."
In the ultimate sense, however, there exists only name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). For one who sees in this way, that vision is indeed called "seeing things as they really are" (*yathābhūtadassana*).
But whoever, abandoning this seeing of things as they really are, grasps at the notion that "a being exists," must admit either its destruction or its non-destruction.
If he admits its non-destruction, he falls into eternalism (*sassata*); if he admits its destruction, he falls into annihilationism (*uccheda*).
It falls away. Why? Because there is no other [entity] following it, just as there is no curd following the milk from which it arose.
One who grasps that "the being is eternal" is said to lag behind; one who grasps that "it is annihilated" is said to overreach. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, obsessed by two types of views, some among gods and humans lag behind, while others overreach; but those with vision see."
“And how, bhikkhus, do some shrink back? Deva and humans, bhikkhus, delight in existence, rejoice in existence, and find their origin in existence.
When the Dhamma is being taught for the cessation of existence, their minds do not leap forward, do not become confident, do not settle, and do not resolve.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that some shrink back.”
“And how, bhikkhus, do some overreach? Some, being terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by existence itself, delight in non-existence, thinking:
‘Indeed, sirs, when this self is cut off and perishes with the breakup of the body, and does not exist after death—this is peaceful, this is sublime, this is the true state. Thus...”
“Monks, some go too far.
And how, monks, do those with vision see? Here, monks, a monk sees what has come to be as it really is;
having seen what has come to be as it really is, he practices for disenchantment with, for the fading away of passion for, and for the cessation of what has come to be.”
"Thus indeed, monks, do those with eyes see. 675.
Therefore, just as a wooden machine is empty, soulless, and devoid of effort, yet it moves and stands by virtue of the combination of wood and strings;
and though it appears as if it were possessed of effort and activity, even so this name-and-form is empty.
It is soulless and devoid of effort; nevertheless, through the power of their mutual conjunction, it moves and stands as well.
It should be understood that it appears as if possessing effort and activity. Thus said the ancients:
"Name and form exist here in truth..."
“Herein, no being or person is found;
this is empty, conditioned like a machine,
a mere heap of suffering resembling grass and wood.”
This should not be understood through the simile of the wooden machine alone; it should also be clarified by other similes such as the bundle of reeds.

For just as when two bundles of reeds are set up leaning against one another, each serves as a support for the other, and when one falls, the other also falls—in the same way, name-and-form in the five-aggregate existence depend upon one another.
It proceeds by depending [on the other]; each one is a support for the other. By way of death, when one falls, the other also falls.
Therefore the ancients said:
"Name-and-form are like a pair, both dependent upon one another."
“When one [condition] breaks up, both conditions break up.
(676) And just as when a sound occurs in dependence on a drum struck by a stick, the drum is one thing and the sound another;
the drum and the sound are unmixed, the drum is empty of the sound, and the sound is empty of the drum—exactly so it is with that which is termed the basis, the door, and the object.
When name proceeds dependent on form, form is one thing and name is another; name and form are unmixed.
Name is empty of form, and form is empty of name. Nevertheless, name proceeds dependent on form, just as sound proceeds dependent on a drum.
Thus have the ancients said:
“Contact and its four companions do not arise from the eye,
nor from forms, nor from both together;
conditioned phenomena come into being dependent upon a cause.”
Just as the sound from a struck drum—“Contact and the other [factors] do not arise from the ear, nor from the sound, nor from between the two... [etc. —so too.
“Contact and its four companions do not arise from the nose, nor from odors, nor from between the two... [etc. ...
Contact and its four companions do not arise from the tongue.”
“Not from taste, nor from both together… [as before]… ‘The five aggregates,
with contact as the fifth, do not arise from the body,
nor from contact, nor from both together… [as before]…’”
“Conditioned phenomena do not arise from the materiality of the physical base,
nor do they emerge from the sense-sphere bases;
conditioned phenomena arise dependent upon a cause.”
"Just as the sound of a beaten drum.
Furthermore, here, name (nāma) being devoid of energy cannot proceed by its own power;
it does not eat, does not drink, does not speak, and does not assume postures. Form (rūpa), too, being devoid of energy, cannot proceed by its own power.
It is able [to do so]. For it has no desire to eat, nor desire to drink, nor desire to speak, nor desire to assume a posture;
rather, name proceeds dependent on form, and form proceeds dependent on name, due to the name’s desire to eat, desire to drink, desire to speak, and desire to assume a posture.
When there is existence, form eats, drinks, speaks, and performs postures.
To illustrate this point, they cite this simile: Suppose a man blind from birth and a cripple both desired to travel to a certain direction;
the man blind from birth said to the cripple, "I am indeed able, my friend..."
“I can perform with my feet what is to be done by the feet, but I have no eyes with which I might see the level and the uneven.
And the cripple said to the one born blind: “I, sir, can perform with my eyes what is to be done by the eyes, but I have no feet with which I might go forward or back. He was thrilled and overjoyed.
A man blind from birth placed a cripple on his shoulder. Seated upon the shoulder of the blind man, the cripple said:
"Let go of the left, take hold of the right; let go of the right, take hold of the left.
In this matter, the blind man—lacking power and weak—cannot go by his own power or his own strength; and the cripple, too, is lacking power and weak.
It does not move by its own radiance or by its own power, nor does its movement fail to proceed in dependence upon one another;
even so, name (nāma), being devoid of radiance, does not arise by its own radiance, nor does it engage in various activities.
Form (rūpa), too, being devoid of radiance, does not arise by its own radiance, nor does it engage in various activities. Nor...
And there is no arising or persistence of these things by depending upon one another. Therefore this is said:
“They are not born by their own power, nor do they persist by their own power.”
Those who follow after the influence of another's nature are born conditioned and weak in themselves;
they are born from external conditions.
They arise from external objects;
they are brought about by external conditions and by other phenomena.
“Just as people cross over the great ocean by means of a boat,
even so the mental body proceeds depending upon form.
And just as a boat moves across the ocean depending upon people,”
In the same way, depending upon name, the form-body proceeds.
“Just as both men and a boat proceed together upon the great ocean,
so too do name and form both depend upon one another.”
Thus, for one who defines name-and-form through various methods, the vision of name-and-form as it really is—
which stands upon the ground of non-delusion having overcome the perception of a "being"— should be understood as purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).
"The definition of name-and-form" and "the delimitation of formations" are also synonyms for this very same thing.
Thus ends the exposition on Purification of View, titled the "Path of Purification" (Visuddhimagga), composed for the delight of good people, within the section on the Development of Understanding.
The Eighteenth Chapter.
19. The Exposition of Purification by Overcoming Doubt:
The Discussion on the Comprehension of Conditions.

678. Furthermore, the knowledge established by dispelling doubt regarding the three periods of time through the discernment of the conditions for this very same name-and-form is called purification by overcoming doubt.
A bhikkhu desiring to accomplish that is like a skilled physician who, having seen a disease, searches for its origin;
or like a compassionate man who [examines] a young, weak infant lying on its back.
Seeing someone lying on a chariot track, he directs his attention to that person’s parents, thinking, "Whose child is this?
In the same way, he embarks upon an investigation into the causes and conditions of that name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
From the very beginning, he reflects thus: "To begin with, this name-and-form is not without cause; at all times and in all places..."

And because all things attain a state of being identical to one another, [the world] is not caused by a Lord (Īśvara) and so forth, since beyond name-and-form (nāmarūpa), there is no existence of a Lord or the like.
Even for those who claim that name-and-form alone constitutes the Lord and so forth, it follows that the name-and-form designated as "Lord" and so on would be without a cause.
Therefore, this [world] must have causes and conditions; what, then, are they?
679. Thus, having adverted to the causal condition for name-and-form, he first discerns the causal condition for this very physical body as follows:

"When this body is produced, it is not produced within the interior of blue, red, white, or fragrant lotuses, nor within gems, pearls, necklaces, and so forth; rather, it is produced between the stomach and the intestines."

Having placed the abdominal membrane behind and the spinal column in front, and being surrounded by the internal organs and the intestines, it itself—foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive—is produced within that same most cramped space which is foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive, like a worm in putrid fish, putrid sour gruel, a cesspool, a latrine, and so forth.
As it is thus being produced, [it arises] from these: ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma.
"Four factors are 'roots' (hetu) because they produce; nutriment (āhāra) is a 'condition' (paccaya) because it sustains. Thus, these five factors constitute the root-conditions.
Among them, the three beginning with ignorance (avijjā) serve as the supporting basis for this body, like a mother to a child.
Kamma is the progenitor, like a father to a son. Nutriment is the sustainer, like a nurse to a child."

Having thus analyzed the conditions for the material body, he further analyzes the conditions for the mental body according to the method beginning with, "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.

Having seen the occurrence of name-and-form from its conditions in this way, he reflects: "Just as it occurs through conditions now, so too did it occur through conditions in the past, and it will occur through conditions in the future."
680. For one who thus reflects, there arises that fivefold [speculation] concerning the past:
"Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?"
Doubt has been described; that which refers to the future limit:
"Shall I exist in the future time? Shall I not exist in the future time? What shall I be in the future time?
How shall I be in the future time? Having been what, what shall I become in the future time?"
Fivefold doubt has been described; furthermore, there is that which concerns the present, such as:
"Now, regarding the present time, one is inwardly full of perplexity: 'Do I exist? Or do I not exist? What am I? How am I?
From where has this being come? Where will it go? Thus it is sixfold.
Doubt has been mentioned; all of that is abandoned. 681.
Another [meditator] sees the condition for mentality (nāma) as twofold, by way of common and uncommon;
and for materiality (rūpa), as fourfold, by way of kamma and so forth. For the condition of mentality is indeed twofold: common and uncommon. In this regard, the eye and so forth...

The six doors and the six objects, such as visible forms, are common conditions for consciousness, because it proceeds from them in all its modes, including the distinction between the wholesome and so forth.
Attention and the rest are uncommon conditions. For wise attention, hearing the true Dhamma, and so forth, belong only to the wholesome;
their opposites belong to the unwholesome; kamma and so forth belong to resultant consciousness; and the life-continuum and so forth belong to functional consciousness.
Furthermore, for material form (*rūpa*), there are these four kinds of conditions beginning with karma: karma, consciousness (*citta*), temperature (*utu*), and nutriment (*āhāra*).
Among these, only past karma is the condition for material form originated by karma. Consciousness is the condition for material form originated by consciousness at the moment it arises.
Temperature and nutriment are the conditions for material form originated by temperature and nutriment respectively at the moment of their persistence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). Thus, each one...
He discerns the conditionality of name-and-form.

Having thus seen the occurrence of name-and-form by way of conditions, he reflects: "Just as this occurs by way of conditions now, so too it occurred by way of conditions in the past, and it will occur by way of conditions in the future. To him who thus...
For one who contemplates in the manner just described, doubt regarding all three time periods is abandoned.
Furthermore, another person, having seen the onset of aging in those very formations termed name-and-form, and the dissolution of what has grown old, realizes:
"This so-called aging and death of formations occurs when there is birth; birth occurs when there is becoming; and becoming [occurs when there is clinging]."
When there is clinging, it is because of craving; when there is craving, it is because of feeling; when there is feeling, it is because of contact;

when there is contact, it is because of the six sense bases; when there are the six sense bases, it is because of name-and-form; when there is name-and-form, it is because of consciousness; when there is consciousness, it is because of volitional formations;
when there are volitional formations, it is because of ignorance. Thus, by way of dependent origination in reverse order, one discerns the conditions for name-and-form.
He does so. Then, in the manner already described, his doubt is abandoned. 683.

Another, having first expanded upon the statement, “Thus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” investigates the conditions for name-and-form by means of the forward order of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) alone. Then, in the manner already described, his perplexity is abandoned.
684. Another [investigates] thus: “In the previous kamma-existence, delusion was ignorance; the exertion was volitional formations; the attachment was craving; the approaching was...”
Grasping (*upādāna*), volition (*cetanā*), and becoming (*bhava*)—these five factors in the previous kamma-existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking here.

Here, rebirth-linking is consciousness (*viññāṇa*); descent [into the womb] is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the sensitivity [of the sense bases] is the sense base (*āyatana*); what is touched is contact (*phassa*);
and what is felt is feeling (*vedanā*)—these five factors in this present existence-of-arising are the conditions for the previously performed kamma.
"Here, because the sense bases have matured, delusion is ignorance... [as before] ...volition is becoming;

these five states are the conditions here for rebirth-linking in the future within this kamma-process existence. In this way, he discerns the conditions for name-and-form by way of the round of kamma and the round of result.

685. Therein, action (kamma) is fourfold: to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya), to be experienced in the next rebirth (upapajjavedanīya), to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya), and inoperative action (ahosikamma).
Among these, the first impulsion volition—whether wholesome or unwholesome—within the seven consciousnesses of a single impulsion-process is called "action to be experienced in the present life.
It yields its result in this very existence. If it is unable to do so, [it becomes action to be experienced in the next rebirth].
Furthermore, "past karma" (*ahosikamma*) is so called by way of this triad: "the result of that karma did not exist, the result of that karma will not exist, the result of that karma does not exist.
However, the seventh impulsion volition that accomplishes the purpose is called "karma to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīyakamma*).
It yields its result in the immediately following existence. That which is unable to do so...

In the same manner as described, there is what is called "kamma that has been" (ahosikamma). Between these two, the five impulsion volitions are called "kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (aparāpariyavedanīyakamma);
