when it finds an opportunity in the future, it then yields its result. As long as the round of existence continues, there is no such thing as "kamma that has been."

686. Furthermore, there are four kinds of kamma: that which is weighty (*garuka*), that which is habitual (*bahula*), that which is proximate (*āsanna*), and also the kamma of what has been stored up (*kaṭattā*).

Among these, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, among the weighty and non-weighty, that which is weighty—such as the kamma of matricide and so forth, or sublime kamma—that alone ripens first. The same applies to the habitual and non-habitual.
Whichever is most abundant—whether it be good conduct or misconduct—that very thing ripens first.
That which is called "proximate" is the karma recollected at the time of death; for whatever one is able to recollect when death is near, by that very [karma] one is reborn.
Apart from these three, there is karma that has been repeatedly practiced, or karma that has been performed.
When those [other conditions] are absent, it draws that rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) toward itself.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of kamma: productive (janaka), supportive (upatthambhaka), obstructive (upapīḷaka), and destructive (upaghātaka).

Among these, the "productive" is both wholesome and unwholesome; it produces resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandha), both material and immaterial, during both the rebirth-linking and the course of existence (pavatta).
It produces [a rebirth]. However, it is not able to produce a supporting (upatthambhaka) kamma-result;
rather, once the rebirth-linking has been produced by another kamma and the kamma-result has arisen, it supports the pleasure and pain occurring therein and causes them to persist for a duration.
An obstructing (upapīḷaka) kamma, on the other hand, oppresses the pleasure and pain occurring when the kamma-result has been produced by the rebirth-linking given by another kamma.
It obstructs, not allowing the [kamma] to proceed for its course.
However, that which is obstructive—whether itself wholesome or unwholesome—destroys another weak kamma, wards off its result, and creates an opportunity for its own result.
When the opportunity has thus been made by that kamma, that result is said to have arisen.

Thus, among these twelve types of kamma, both the distinction between one kamma and another, and the distinction between their respective results, become manifest in their true nature only to the Buddhas through their knowledge of the maturation of kamma;
this is not shared by disciples. However, a practitioner of insight (vipassaka) should understand the distinction between kamma and its result at least in part.
Therefore, this specific classification of kamma has been explained here merely by way of illustration.

688. Having thus included these twelve kinds of kamma within the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa), he analyzes the conditionality of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) by way of the round of kamma and the round of its result (vipākavaṭṭa).

Having seen the occurrence of name-and-form through conditions by way of the round of kamma and the round of its result, he understands: "Just as it is now, so too in the past period, by way of the round of kamma and the round of its result..."
It has proceeded by way of conditions; in the future too, it will proceed by way of conditions precisely through the round of kamma and the round of kamma-result.
Thus: both kamma and the result of kamma; the round of kamma and the round of result; the process of kamma and the process of result;
the continuity of kamma and the continuity of result; and functional activity and the fruit of functional activity.
“Kamma and its result proceed; result is born from kamma;
through kamma there is renewed existence; thus the world revolves.”—Thus he contemplates.
As he contemplates in this way, regarding the past and so forth, [the thought arises]: “Did I exist? and so on.
By this method, the sixteenfold doubt that has been described is entirely abandoned.
In all states of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations, and abodes, there appears only name-and-form proceeding by way of the connection between cause and fruit.
One sees no agent beyond the cause, nor any experiencer of the result beyond the occurrence of the result. However, regarding the cause...
When there is a "doer," and when there is the occurrence of kamma-result, the wise describe it by the mere conventional designation "experiencer";
thus, this is well-seen with right wisdom.
Regarding this, the ancients said:
“There is no doer of karma, nor is there an experiencer of its ripening;
purely phenomena proceed—this is the right vision.
Thus, while karma and its ripening proceed with their causes,”
Just as the prior limit of seed-trees and the like is not known,
so too in the future *saṃsāra*, no point of non-occurrence is seen.
Not understanding this matter, the sectarians lack self-mastery.
Having grasped the perception of a self,
those who view things through the lens of eternalism or annihilationism adopt the sixty-two views, which are mutually contradictory.
Bound by the fetters of views, they are carried away by the current of craving.
Carried away by the stream of craving, they are not released from suffering.
Having directly known this, the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha penetrates the profound, subtle, and empty conditionality.
“Kamma exists not in its ripening, nor is ripening found in kamma;
both are empty of one another, yet there is no fruit without kamma.
Just as there is no fire in the sun, nor in a gem, nor in cow dung...”
It does not exist outside of them, yet it arises from the constituent factors.
Likewise, the result of karma is not found within the karma;
nor is it outside of the karma, for karma itself is not present there.
“That karma is empty of fruit, and the fruit does not exist within the karma;
yet, depending upon karma, the fruit is produced from it.
Herein, neither a deva nor a Brahmā is the creator of the cycle of existence.”
“Pure phenomena proceed by way of the conditions of the accumulation of causes.
(690) Having thus analyzed the conditions for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) by way of the round of kamma and the round of its result,
one who has abandoned doubt regarding the three periods of time perceives all past, future, and present phenomena by way of death and rebirth-linking.
These are known; this constitutes his full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).
He understands thus: "Those aggregates that arose in the past conditioned by karma have ceased right there.
However, other [aggregates] have arisen in this present existence conditioned by past karma; one has come from a past existence to this existence."

There is not even a single dhamma that passes from this state of existence to another; for although the aggregates produced by the condition of karma will cease in this very life, other [aggregates] will be produced in a future existence, and not even a single dhamma goes from this existence to a future existence.
Furthermore, it is just as when the recitation from the teacher’s mouth does not enter the mouth of the pupil, yet because of that [recitation], [the pupil’s recitation arises].
Recitation does not proceed from his mouth; the protective water (*mantodaka*) drunk by a messenger does not enter the stomach of the patient, nor does his illness subside because of it;
the application of ornaments on the face does not reflect the image of the face in mirrors and such, nor is that application of ornaments unperceived therein because of it. Nor...
Just as the flame of a lamp passes from one wick to another, yet the flame does not fail to arise there because of that [transition], even so,
no phenomenon whatsoever passes from a past existence to this present existence, nor from this present existence to a future existence;
yet, conditioned by the aggregates, bases, and elements in the past existence, they arise here, and conditioned by the aggregates, bases, and elements here, they arise there.
Furthermore, the aggregates, bases, and elements do not arise in a future existence.
Just as visual consciousness [does not arise] immediately after the mind-element—
neither having arrived nor being produced immediately after it— so too is this case.
In the same way, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the continuum of consciousness proceeds:
the preceding consciousness ceases, and immediately thereafter the subsequent one arises.
There is no interval between them; no gap exists between them.
"Nothing goes from here, yet rebirth arises.
(691) Thus, for one who has understood all phenomena by way of death and rebirth-linking, the knowledge that discerns the conditions of name-and-form in every aspect becomes firm;
the sixteen kinds of doubt are thoroughly abandoned. And not only that, but also regarding the Teacher...
In this way, even the eightfold doubt that occurs in the manner beginning with “he doubts” is abandoned, and the sixty-two types of speculative views are suppressed.

Thus, knowledge established by having crossed over doubt regarding the three periods of time through the discernment of the conditions for name-and-form by means of various methods should be understood as purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi). It is also called “knowledge of the stability of phenomena” (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).
“Knowledge of things as they really are” (*yathābhūtañāṇa*) and “right seeing” (*sammādassana*) are synonyms for this very thing.

For it has been said: “Ignorance is a condition; volitional formations are conditionally arisen. The wisdom that, in grasping the conditions, understands: ‘Both these phenomena are conditionally arisen,’ is knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
When one attends to [phenomena] as impermanent, what phenomena does one know and see as they really are? How is there right seeing?
How, by following that [contemplation], are all conditioned phenomena clearly seen as impermanent? Wherein is doubt abandoned?
When attending to them as suffering... pe ...as non-self, what phenomena does one know and see as they truly are?
... pe ... wherein is doubt abandoned?
“By attending to [the sign] as impermanent, one knows and sees the sign as it really is; therefore, it is called ‘right seeing.
In this way, by following that sequence, all formations are well-seen as impermanent. Herein, doubt is abandoned.
By attending to the process as suffering, one knows and sees the occurrence as it really is... pe ...by attending to it as non-self, one knows and sees the sign and...”
One knows and sees the process as it really is; therefore, it is called right vision.
In this way, by following that [insight], all phenomena are clearly seen as non-self. Herein, doubt is abandoned.
"The knowledge of things as they really are, the right vision, and the overcoming of doubt—these states are not different in meaning..."
"Are these things identical in meaning and different only in phrasing, or are they identical in meaning while the phrasing is indeed different?

That which is knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*), that which is right vision (*sammādassana*), and that which is the overcoming of doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇā*)—these states are identical in meaning; only the phrasing is different.

One who possesses this knowledge, a practitioner of insight (*vipassaka*) within the Buddha’s teaching, has found relief, found a firm footing, and is of certain destiny; he is called a "Lesser Stream-enterer" (*cūḷasotāpanna*).
"Therefore, a bhikkhu who is always mindful,
desiring to transcend doubt, should thoroughly comprehend the conditions for name-and-form.
Thus ends the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Purification by Overcoming Doubt," in the Section on the Development of Wisdom.
20. The Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is the Path and What Is Not the Path; The Discussion of Knowledge of Comprehension. 692.

Knowledge that stands having thus understood what is the path and what is not the path—namely, "This is the path" and "This is not the path"—is called purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.
One who desires to achieve that must first apply themselves to the method of insight (vipassanā) known as "comprehension by groups" (kalāpa-sammasana).

Why? Because for one who has begun insight practice, the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇa) arises when illumination and the other signs have appeared; and comprehension by groups is the beginning of insight practice.
Therefore, this [knowledge] is taught immediately after the overcoming of doubt. Moreover,

since the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇa*) arises when the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) is proceeding, and since the full understanding by scrutinization follows immediately upon the full understanding by having known (*ñātapariññā*),
one who desires to accomplish that purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path should first apply himself to the comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana*).

693. Herein, this is the analysis: there are three mundane thorough knowledges (*pariññā*), namely, thorough knowledge as the known (*ñāta-pariññā*), thorough knowledge as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and thorough knowledge as abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*).
With reference to these it was said: "The wisdom of direct knowledge is knowledge in the sense of the known; the wisdom of thorough knowledge is knowledge in the sense of investigating;
the wisdom of abandoning is knowledge in the sense of relinquishing. Therein, "matter has the characteristic of being molested (*ruppana*); feeling has the characteristic of being felt..."
Wisdom that proceeds by way of discerning the individual characteristics of various phenomena,

such as "feeling," is called the full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*). Wisdom that proceeds by superimposing the general characteristics upon those very same phenomena according to the method of "form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent," etc.,
is insight-wisdom having characteristics as its object (*lakkhaṇārammaṇika-vipassanā-paññā*), which is the full understanding through scrutiny (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).

Furthermore, the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) that occurs by way of abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth regarding those very same phenomena is called "full understanding as abandonment" (pahāna-pariññā).

In this context, the stage for full understanding through knowledge (ñāta-pariññā) extends from the delimitation of formations (saṅkhāra-pariccheda) up to the discernment of conditions (paccaya-pariggaha). Within this...
For within this interval, there is the predominance of the penetration of the specific characteristics (*paccatta-lakkhaṇa*) of phenomena alone.

From the stage of "comprehension by groups" (*kalāpa-sammasana*) up to the contemplation of rise and fall (*udaya-bbaya-anupassanā*), however, is the plane of full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*); for within this interval, there is the predominance of the penetration of the general characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*) alone.
Beginning with the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅga-anupassanā*), it is the plane of full understanding through abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). From that point onward...
For, by contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence; by contemplating as suffering, the perception of pleasure; by contemplating as non-self, the perception of self;
by becoming disenchanted, delight; by becoming dispassionate, lust; by causing cessation, origination; and by relinquishing, grasping—one abandons them.
Thus, [this refers to] the seven contemplations which accomplish the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth.

Sovereignty. Thus, because the delimitation of formations and the discernment of conditions have been accomplished within these three kinds of full understanding, this practitioner has attained the full understanding by knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), while the others are yet to be attained.

Therefore it was said: "Because the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path arises when the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) is proceeding, [this is] the full understanding by scrutinization..."

And because it immediately follows full understanding through knowledge, one who wishes to accomplish that purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path should first apply himself to the comprehension of groups. 694.
Here is the canonical text on this:
“How is it that wisdom in defining past, future, and present states by way of synthesis is knowledge of comprehension?
Whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or... [as before] ...whether far or near—all form he defines as impermanent:
this is one kind of comprehension. He defines it as suffering: this is one [kind of comprehension].”

Comprehension: He defines [it] as non-self; this is one kind of comprehension. Whatever feeling... pe... whatever consciousness... pe... he defines as non-self; this is one kind of comprehension. "He defines the eye... pe...
aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, as impermanent; this is one kind of comprehension. He defines it as suffering and as non-self; this is one kind of comprehension."

“Wisdom in defining, by way of summary, that ‘form—past, future, and present—is impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness,’ is knowledge of comprehension.
[The same applies to] feeling... consciousness... the eye... pe... aging-and-death... pe... this is knowledge of comprehension.
‘Form—past, future, and present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, and subject to destruction.’”
Wisdom in defining [feeling] by summarizing it as "subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation" is knowledge of comprehension. Wisdom in defining feeling...
consciousness... the eye... aging-and-death—whether past, future, or present—as "impermanent, conditioned...
subject to cessation," by summarizing them in this way, is knowledge of comprehension.
“With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be; in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death.
Wisdom in the concise determination of this is knowledge of comprehension. “In the past period too, with birth as condition, aging-and-death came to be;
in the absence of birth, there was no aging-and-death. Wisdom in the concise determination of this is knowledge of comprehension. “With becoming as condition...”
Wisdom that defines by way of summary—“With birth... [and so on] ...with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations;

when there is no ignorance, there are no volitional formations”—is knowledge of comprehension. Wisdom that defines by way of summary—“In the past time, too, with ignorance as condition there were volitional formations; when there was no ignorance, there were no volitional formations,” and “In the future time, too, with ignorance as condition there will be volitional formations;
when there is no ignorance, there will be no volitional formations”—is knowledge of comprehension.

“Knowledge is so called in the sense of knowing; wisdom is so called in the sense of understanding. Therefore it is said: ‘Wisdom regarding the defining of past, future, and present phenomena by way of synthesis is knowledge of comprehension.
And here, by this abbreviated formula beginning with ‘the eye’ … down to ‘aging-and-death,’ [are included] the phenomena occurring at the doors together with the doors and their objects:

the five aggregates, the six doors, the six objects, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, the six [feelings], the six perceptions, the six volitions, the six elements, the six bases, the six groups of craving, the seven stations of consciousness, the nine abodes of beings, the ten bases, and the twelve bases.”
the six feelings, the six perceptions, the six volitions, the six cravings, the six thoughts, the six investigations, the six elements, the ten kasiṇas,
the thirty-two parts of the body, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements,
the twenty-two faculties, the three realms, the nine states of existence, the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four attainments.
The twelve factors of dependent origination—these should be understood as the condensed heaps of phenomena.
For it is said in the *Abhiññeyyaniddesa*:
“Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known. And what, bhikkhus, is everything that is to be directly known? The eye, bhikkhus...”
It is to be directly known. Forms... eye-consciousness... eye-contact...
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is to be directly known. The ear... [and so on]...
and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact... [is to be directly known].
Or, that too is to be directly known.
“Form... consciousness... the eye... the mind... forms... mental objects... eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness... eye-contact... mind-contact...
feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact... perception of form... perception of mental objects. [Thus it is to be directly known.]

Volition regarding form... [and so on] ...volition regarding mental phenomena; craving for form... [and so on] ...craving for mental phenomena; applied thought regarding form... [and so on] ...applied thought regarding mental phenomena;
sustained thought regarding form... [and so on] ...sustained thought regarding mental phenomena.
The earth element... [and so on] ...the consciousness element; the earth kasiṇa... [and so on] ...the consciousness kasiṇa; head hairs... [and so on] ...urine; brain matter.
“The eye-base … [and so on] … the mind-object-base; the eye-element … [and so on] … the mind-consciousness-element; the eye-faculty … [and so on] … the faculty of one who has final knowledge.

The sense-sphere element … the fine-material element … the immaterial element; sense-sphere existence … fine-material existence … immaterial existence; perception-existence … non-perception-existence … neither-perception-nor-non-perception-existence;

one-aggregate existence … four-aggregate existence … five-aggregate existence. The first jhāna … [and so on] … the fourth jhāna; the liberation of mind through loving-kindness … [and so on] … the liberation of mind through equanimity; the attainment of the base of infinite space … [and so on].”
“The attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... ignorance is to be directly known... [and so on] ...aging-and-death is to be directly known.
Since this has been stated there in such detail, it is here abbreviated by way of a formula (*peyyāla*).

However, among those things included here in this abbreviated form, those states that are supramundane (*lokuttara*) should not be taken up in this context, as they do not come within the scope of comprehension (*asammasanupagatta*).
Furthermore, among those things that come within the range of comprehension, one should begin the investigation with whichever are most evident and can be easily grasped.
695. In this regard, the application of the method for beginning the investigation by way of the aggregates is as follows: "Whatever form there is... all form."
He defines it as impermanent: this is one mode of comprehension. He defines it as painful and as non-self: this is another mode of comprehension.

At this point, this bhikkhu—having delimited all material form, which was indicated without restriction by the phrase "whatever material form," through eleven spheres consisting of the past triad and the four dyads beginning with the internal—[comprehends] all material form as impermanent.
He defines it and comprehends it as impermanent.
How? By the method stated above. For this has been said: “Material form—past, future, and present—is impermanent in the sense of destruction.
Therefore, whatever material form is past, that has already perished in the past and has not reached this existence; thus it is impermanent in the sense of destruction.

That which is yet to come and will arise in the immediately succeeding existence will also perish right there; it will not go to a further existence—thus it is impermanent in the sense of destruction.
That material form which is present also perishes right here and does not go from here—thus it is impermanent in the sense of destruction.
That which is internal also perishes only internally and does not go to an external state—thus it is impermanent in the sense of destruction.

Whatever is external... coarse... subtle... inferior... superior... far... or near—that too is exhausted right there; it does not go to a state of distance. Thus one comprehends: "It is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion.

All of this constitutes a single mode of comprehension by way of the phrase "impermanent in the sense of exhaustion. However, in terms of its divisions, it is elevenfold. And all of that is suffering in the sense of terror.
"In the sense of terror" means because of being fearful. For whatever is impermanent... [is suffering].
That is terrifying, as in the Sīhupama Sutta, like [the fear felt by] the devas.
Thus, this is one way of comprehending (sammasana) by way of the phrase "suffering in the sense of terror. However, when analyzed, it is elevenfold.
And just as it is suffering, so too is all that non-self in the sense of being coreless (asāraka). By "in the sense of being coreless" is meant: "The self is the resident..."
This is because of the absence of a self-essence imagined in such ways as "one who acts, one who feels, one who is self-dependent.
For whatever is impermanent and suffering cannot prevent even a self from being impermanent or from being afflicted by arising and passing away;
how much less, then, can it possess the status of an agent and so forth? Therefore he said: "Bhikkhus, if this form were the self... and so on.
“Form would lead to affliction,” and so forth. Thus, this too is one mode of comprehension by way of the phrase, “It is non-self in the sense of being without core.
However, in terms of its divisions, it is elevenfold. This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates.
Now, since whatever is impermanent is necessarily characterized by such divisions as the conditioned and so on, [the following is] for the purpose of showing its synonyms:
Alternatively, the text is stated again as “Form— past, future, and present— is impermanent, conditioned,
dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation,” for the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention in various modes.
This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates.
The Discourse on the Contemplation of the Forty Modes (Cattārīsākāra-anupassanā-kathā) 697.
For the purpose of stabilizing that very comprehension of the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, [the Buddha said]:
"By which forty modes does one obtain the conformable acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*)? By which..."
In the analysis of the statement, "One enters the certainty of rightness through forty modes," it says:
"The five aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as an arrow, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as an epidemic,
as a misfortune, as a terror, as a trouble, as fickle, as perishable, as unstable..."
As providing no protection, no refuge, no shelter; as empty, vain, void, and non-self; as fraught with danger, subject to change, and devoid of essence;
as the root of evil, a murderer, and a source of destruction; as associated with taints, conditioned, and the bait of Māra;
as subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, subject to lamentation, and subject to despair.
“From defiled phenomena”—by way of forty modes, according to the method beginning with:

“One who sees the five aggregates as impermanent acquires conformity-acceptance; one who sees the cessation of the five aggregates as the permanent Nibbāna enters the certainty of rightness,” and so forth.

By one analyzing knowledge in conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), the comprehension of impermanence and so forth has been stated according to its divisions. By means of that as well, he comprehends these five aggregates. 698. How?
For he comprehends each individual aggregate as impermanent because of its non-eternality and because it has a beginning and an end;

as suffering because of its oppression by arising and passing away and because it is the basis for suffering; and [as a disease] because it is maintained by conditions and because it is the root of disease.

And it is like a disease because it is associated with the sting of suffering, because it drips with the impurity of the defilements, and because it is swollen, ripened, and burst by arising, aging, and dissolution.
It is like an abscess because it produces affliction, because it pierces inwardly, and because it is difficult to extract.

It is like a dart because it is censurable, because it brings about non-prosperity, and because it is the basis for misfortune. It is like a calamity because it produces a state of lack of mastery and because it is the proximate cause of illness.
And as "affliction" (*ābādha*) because it is subject to illness; as "subjection to others" (*parato*) because of its lack of autonomy and lack of control;
as "dissolution" (*paloka*) because of its disintegration through disease, aging, and death; as "calamity" (*īti*) because it brings about manifold misfortunes;
as "misfortune" (*upaddava*) because it brings about vast unknown evils and serves as the basis for all calamities; and as the "source of all fears," [the cessation of suffering is the opposite].

It is viewed as fear because it is the opposite of supreme consolation; as an affliction because it is beset by manifold misfortunes, is permeated by hatred, and—like an external calamity—is unfit to be endured;
and as unstable because it is shaken by disease, aging, and death, as well as by the worldly conditions such as gain and loss;
and because its nature is to pass away through both external violence and its own inherent essence.
It is impermanent because it is subject to dissolution; it is unstable because it lacks a state of permanence due to falling upon every possible occasion;

it is without refuge because it provides no protection and because security cannot be found therein; it is without shelter because it is unfit for taking refuge in, and because even for those who have taken refuge in it, it fails to perform the function of a shelter;

it is without a resort because it lacks the quality of being a source of relief for those who depend on it; [it is so] with respect to its nature as permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and a self, as they are merely conceptualized.
As empty (*rittata*) because it is empty. It is void (*tucchata*) because it is empty, or because it is slight; for even that which is slight is called "void" in the world.
It is empty (*suññata*) because it is devoid of a master, an inhabitant, an agent, an experiencer, or a controller. It is non-self (*anattata*) because it itself lacks ownership and so forth.

It is a danger (*ādīnava*) because of the suffering inherent in its occurrence and because of the perilous nature of suffering; or alternatively, it is a danger because it brings about decline (*ādīna*).

"It goes" and "it proceeds"—this is the disadvantage (*ādīnava*); it is a designation for a wretched person, and since the aggregates (*khandhā*) are likewise wretched, they are called "disadvantageous" due to their similarity to that disadvantage.
They are "subject to change" (*vipariṇāmadhamma*) because they have a dual nature of transformation through both aging and death.
They are "insubstantial" (*asāraka*) because of their weakness and because they are easily broken like pithless wood. They are [called suffering] because they are a cause of misfortune (*agha*).

From the root of evil; from being a murderer due to betraying trust, like a friend with a treacherous face; from non-existence, both because of the disappearance of existence and because it arises from the absence of wealth;
from being subject to taints because it is the footing for the taints; from being conditioned because it is constructed by causes and conditions;
from being the bait of Māra because it serves as the material lure for the Māra of death and the Māra of defilements; and because it has birth, aging, sickness, and death as its inherent nature.
He comprehends by means of the comprehension of impermanence and so forth, as explained according to their classifications: as being subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death;

as being subject to sorrow, lamentation, and despair because they are the causes of sorrow, lamentation, and despair; and as being subject to defilement because they are the objective sphere for the defilements of craving, views, and misconduct.

For here, by taking ten aspects for each aggregate— namely, as impermanent, as disintegrating, as unstable, as fragile, as non-enduring, as subject to change, as coreless, as perishable, as conditioned, and as subject to death— there are fifty contemplations on impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
Furthermore, by taking [ten aspects] for each aggregate— namely, as alien, as empty, as vain, as void, and as non-self...

By taking five [aspects] for each of the five aggregates, there are twenty-five contemplations on non-self (*anattā*). As for the remaining [contemplations], such as those on suffering (*dukkha*), disease (*roga*), and so forth, by taking twenty-five for each aggregate, there are one hundred and twenty-five contemplations on suffering.

Thus, for one who contemplates the five aggregates through this method of comprehension consisting of two hundred divisions beginning with impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth, that is known as "insight according to the method" (*nayavipassanā*).
The comprehension of impermanence, suffering, and non-self becomes firm. This, firstly, is the method for beginning the practice of comprehension according to the sequence of the texts. 699.
However, for one who applies himself to this practice of insight according to the method, yet for whom that method-insight does not succeed, [the following applies]:
By this means, "the faculties become sharp in nine ways: he sees only the destruction of arisen formations;

and therein he accomplishes through careful performance, he accomplishes through constant performance, he accomplishes through appropriate performance, and by grasping the sign of concentration, by the non-cessation of the factors of enlightenment, and in regard to the body..."
“and he maintains indifference toward life, overcoming that through renunciation and by not becoming despondent in the interval”—
by means of these nine aspects thus described, having sharpened his faculties,

avoiding the seven unsuitable things and cultivating the seven suitable things according to the method stated in the description of the earth-kasiṇa, he should at the proper time contemplate material form.
By time, it is formless. One who contemplates form must see the arising of form.
Discourse on the Mode of Seeing the Arising of Form (700):
That is to say—this so-called form arises by way of four causes, beginning with kamma. Therein:

For all beings, when form is being produced, it is first produced from kamma. Indeed, at the very moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for those born from a womb, thirty types of material phenomena—comprising the decads of the physical basis, the body, and the sex—are produced by way of three successive moments;
and these occur precisely at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness. And just as they arise at the moment of arising, [so too do they persist].
The same applies at the moment of its stationing and at the moment of its dissolution.
In this regard, matter has a slow cessation and a heavy revolution, whereas consciousness has a quick cessation and a light revolution. Therefore he said:
"Bhikkhus, I do not see any other single thing that revolves so quickly as this."
“Monks, it is the mind,” [he said]. For while the material form persists, the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) arises and ceases sixteen times.
The moment of arising, the moment of presence, and the moment of dissolution of the mind are all identical. However, the moments of arising and dissolution of material form are brief;
they are similar to those [moments of the mind]. But the moment of presence is great, lasting as long as sixteen consciousnesses arise and cease.

Thus it proceeds. At the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the second life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises supported by the pre-nascent (purejāta) physical basis that has arisen and reached its functional state.

Supported by the pre-nascent physical basis that has arisen and reached its functional state along with that [second bhavaṅga], the third life-continuum arises. In this manner, the flow of consciousness continues for as long as the lifespan lasts.
[These] should be understood. However, for one whose death is imminent, sixteen types of consciousness arise depending on a single pre-arisen material basis that has reached its [final] stage.
The matter that arose at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases together with the sixteenth consciousness subsequent to the rebirth-linking consciousness.
That which arose at the moment of its presence ceases together with the arising-moment of the seventeenth.
It ceases. At the moment of dissolution, having reached the seventeenth moment of its arising, it ceases.

As long as there is so-called "occurrence," it continues to occur in this very manner. In the case of beings of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) as well, seventy material phenomena continue to occur in this same way by way of the continuity of the sevenfold being.

701. In this regard, the classification should be understood as follows: [matter that is] kamma, matter originated by kamma, matter conditioned by kamma, matter originated by consciousness conditioned by kamma, matter originated by nutriment conditioned by kamma, and matter originated by temperature conditioned by kamma.
Therein, "kamma" refers to wholesome and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*). "Matter originated by kamma" refers to the resultant aggregates (*vipākakkhandhā*) and the eye-decad (*cakkhudasaka*), etc.
And the form of the seventy-three [types of consciousness]. What is called the kamma-condition is that very same kamma;
for kamma is also a supporting condition for the matter originated by kamma. Matter originated by consciousness with kamma as its condition is matter originated by resultant consciousness.

Matter originated by nutriment with kamma as its condition refers to the nutritive essence (*ojā*) present within matter originated by kamma, which, having reached maturity, originates another octad of nutritive essence; therein too—
Having reached its proper place, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) connects with another [octad]—thus it links four or five occurrences.
What is called "kamma-conditioned temperature-originated" means that the kamma-born heat element, having reached its proper place, originates an octad of nutritive essence originated by temperature;
therein, the temperature also originates another octad of nutritive essence—thus it links four or five occurrences. This, first of all, is the case for kamma-born materiality.
The arising [of material phenomena] is to be seen. 702.

Among those born of consciousness, this distinction is to be understood: consciousness itself, that which is originated by consciousness, that which is conditioned by consciousness, that which is originated by nutriment conditioned by consciousness, and that which is originated by temperature conditioned by consciousness. In this context, "consciousness" refers to the eighty-nine types of consciousness.
Among these, there are thirty-two, twenty-six, and nineteen; [thus they are classified].
Sixteen types of consciousness are considered to be the generators of material form, postures, and intimation.

For thirty-two types of consciousness—namely, the eight wholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), the twelve unwholesome states, the ten functional states excluding the mind-element (manodhātu), and the two types of super-knowledge (abhiññā) consciousness from among the wholesome functionals—generate material form, posture, and intimation. These exclude the resultant (vipāka) states.

Twenty-six types of consciousness—namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome states, the twelve sense-sphere unwholesome states, the ten sense-sphere resultant states, the eight fine-material-sphere states, the eight immaterial-sphere states, and the eight supramundane states—produce bodily form and the modes of deportment, but not intimation.

Nineteen types of consciousness produce neither: the ten life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousnesses of the sense sphere, the five of the fine-material sphere, the three mind-elements, and the one resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy.
Minds produce only material form (*rūpa*), not postures (*iriyāpatha*), nor intimation (*viññatti*).

Sixteen minds—namely, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) of all beings, the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), and the four immaterial-sphere resultants (*āruppavipāka*)—produce neither material form, nor postures, nor intimation. As for those among these that do produce material form, they...
Not at the moment of its persistence or at the moment of its dissolution, for at those times the mind is weak. However, at the moment of its arising it is powerful;
therefore, at that time, depending upon the pre-arisen physical basis (*vatthu*), it produces matter.
What is called "mind-produced" consists of the three immaterial aggregates, the sound-nonad, bodily intimation, and verbal intimation.
And the seventeenfold materiality consisting of the space element, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, integration, and continuity.

That which is called "conditioned by consciousness" refers to the fourfold-originated materiality described as: "The states of consciousness and mental factors that arise later are conditions for this body that arose earlier.
That which is called "nutriment-originated conditioned by consciousness" [is found] among the types of materiality originated by consciousness.
Nutritive essence that has reached its peak generates another octad of nutritive essence; thus it links two or three occurrences together.
That which is called "temperature-originated by mind-condition" means that temperature originated by mind, having reached its peak, generates another octad of nutritive essence;
thus it links two or three occurrences together. In this way, the production of matter born of mind should be understood.

703. Regarding those [material phenomena] born of nutriment (*āhāraja*), this classification should be understood: nutriment-born, nutriment-originated, conditioned by nutriment, conditioned by nutriment and originated by nutriment, and conditioned by nutriment and originated by temperature (*utu*).
In this context, "nutriment" refers to physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*).
"Nutriment-originated" refers to appropriated matter born of kamma that, having obtained a condition and being established therein, [arises].

The fourteenfold materiality consisting of the octad of nutritive essence produced by nutritive essence that has reached its proper state, the space element, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, integration, and continuity.

What is called the nutriment condition is the fourfold-originated materiality described thus: "Edible food is a condition for this body by way of the nutriment condition. This is the nutriment-originated [materiality] under the nutriment condition.

In the case of material phenomena produced by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that has reached its functional state produces another octad of nutritive essence; therein, too, the nutritive essence produces yet another.
In this way, it connects the process for ten or twelve times. Food consumed on a single day provides support for as long as seven days.
However, divine nutritive essence (*dibbā ojā*) provides support for even a month or two. This is also true of the food consumed by one's mother.
Having pervaded the body of the child, it produces material form. Even the food smeared upon the body produces material form. This is called nutriment-born derived (upādiṇṇaka) nutriment.
When that too reaches its proper place, it produces material form; therein, too, the nutritive essence (ojā) produces another.
In this way, one connects four or five occurrences [of production]. This is the nutriment-condition arising from temperature (utu).
The fire element produced by nutriment, having reached its proper state, produces the octad of nutritive essence produced by temperature.

In this context, this nutriment acts as a condition for those things produced by nutriment by being their producer; for the others, it acts as a condition by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance.
Thus should the arising of matter born of nutriment be understood.

704. Regarding temperature (*utu*) as well, this classification should be understood as follows: temperature itself, that which is temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*), that which is conditioned by temperature (*utupaccaya*), that which is conditioned by temperature and temperature-originated, and that which is conditioned by temperature and nutriment-originated (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*).
In this context, "temperature" refers to the fire element (*tejodhātu*) originated from the four [causes]. It is, moreover, twofold: namely, hot temperature and cold temperature.
"Temperature-originated" refers to the fourfold-originated temperature that takes the clung-to (*upādiṇṇaka*) as its condition.
Having obtained [the necessary conditions], it reaches its station and produces material form within the body. That consists of fifteen kinds:
the ninefold sound, the space element, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, integration, and continuity.

The condition known as temperature (utu-paccaya) is the condition for the occurrence and the destruction of material phenomena produced by the four [great] elements. This is temperature-produced matter conditioned by temperature.

In the case of what is called "nutriment-originated" [matter] produced by temperature-conditioned nutriment, the temperature-originated fire element, having reached its proper state, produces another octad of nutritive essence;
therein too, the temperature is distinct. Thus, even for a very long duration, that which is originated by temperature continues to occur while remaining on the side of the non-clung-to (anupādiṇṇa).

As for what is called "nutriment-originated" produced by the condition of temperature, the nutritive essence, having reached its proper state through the temperature-condition, [produces] another octad of nutritive essence.
It originates [matter]; there too, nutriment is distinct [from temperature]. In this way, one connects the process through ten or twelve stages.

In that context, temperature is a condition for temperature-originated matter by acting as its generator; for the remaining types of matter, it is a condition by way of presence (*atthi*) and non-disappearance (*avigata*).
Thus should the production of temperature-born matter be seen. For one who sees the production of matter in this manner, it is said that they "comprehend matter in time."

705. Just as the arising of material form must be seen by one who comprehends material form, so too must the arising of the immaterial be seen by one who comprehends the immaterial. And that [arising] occurs solely by way of the eighty-one types of mundane consciousness-arisings. To explain:
this so-called "immaterial" arises at rebirth-linking first of all through the power of kamma accumulated in a previous existence.

It arises as a classification of nineteen types of consciousness. Its mode of arising, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

That very [consciousness] functions as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) starting from the moment immediately following the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*), and as the death-consciousness (*cuti*) at the end of the lifespan.
Among those, that which pertains to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) functions as the registration-consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) when there is a strong object at the six doors.

In the course of its occurrence, however, because the eye is unimpaired and forms have come into its range, visual consciousness—dependent on light and caused by attention—is produced together with its associated mental states.

For at the very moment of the subsistence-phase (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) of the sensitive eye-organ, a form that has reached the state of subsistence strikes the eye. When it has been struck, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) arises twice; and then...
It ceases. Then, upon that very same object, the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) arises, performing the function of adverting.
Immediately after that, there arises either wholesome-resultant or unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, seeing that very same form.
After that, there arises the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*), receiving that very same form. After that, [there arises the investigating consciousness] examining that very same form.
The resultant rootless mind-consciousness element. Then, determining that same form, there is the functional rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity.

Following that, among the sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses, there is either one rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity, or five or seven impulsion moments. Then, among the eleven registration consciousnesses of sense-sphere beings...
"Whatever [object] is appropriate for the impulsion, that is its object. This same method applies to the remaining doors as well; however, in the mind-door, sublime consciousnesses also arise.
In this way, the arising of the immaterial should be seen in the six doors.
For one who sees the arising of the immaterial in this manner is said to "comprehend the immaterial at the proper time."
Thus, having contemplated both the material and the immaterial at their respective times and applied the three characteristics, one who practices in due order accomplishes the development of wisdom.
706. Another contemplates formations by applying the three characteristics by way of the sevenfold materiality and the sevenfold immateriality.

In this context, one who practices comprehension by applying [the analysis] through these aspects— namely, from the perspective of taking up and laying down, from the perspective of the passing away of youth and the arrival of old age, from the perspective of being composed of nutriment, from the perspective of being composed of temperature,
from the perspective of being born of kamma, from the perspective of being mind-originated, and from the perspective of natural materiality—
is said to practice comprehension by applying it according to the "sevenfold materiality. Thus say the ancients:
“One should contemplate the seven [types of] materiality in detail: from the perspective of taking up and laying down;
from the perspective of passing through youth and old age; and from the perspectives of nutriment, temperature, kamma, consciousness, and natural materiality.”
In this context, "taking up" (*ādāna*) refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and "putting down" (*nikkhepana*) refers to death (*cuti*).

Thus, the practitioner of yoga, delimiting a single hundred-year period by means of these two—taking up and putting down—superimposes the three characteristics upon conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). How so?

All conditioned phenomena within this interval are impermanent. Why? Because they possess the nature of arising and passing away, because they are subject to change, because they are merely temporary, and because they are the negation of permanence.
Furthermore, because arisen formations reach a state of stability, and in that state they are worn out by aging, and having reached aging they inevitably break up;
therefore, they are suffering because they are constantly oppressed, because they are painful, because they are the basis of suffering, and because they are the opposite of happiness.
And because [one thinks]: "May arisen formations not reach stability; having reached that state..."
In these three instances—"May they not grow old," "May those who have reached old age not break up"—there is no state of mastery for anyone;
it is empty of that mode of exercising mastery. Therefore, because it is empty, ownerless, devoid of mastery, and a negation of a self, it is "non-self" (anattā).
Thus, having applied the three characteristics to material form as delimited by a hundred years, by way of its taking up and laying down, [one proceeds] from there...

He applies [the three characteristics] by means of the cessation of growth through age. In this context, "cessation of growth through age" means the cessation of material form that has grown and increased by way of age. The meaning is that he applies the three characteristics by means of that. How so?
He [examines] that very hundred years by way of the three stages of life: the first stage, the middle stage, and the final stage.
He delimits it. Therein, the first period of life consists of thirty-three years from the beginning; the middle period consists of thirty-four years thereafter;
and the final period consists of thirty-three years thereafter. Having delimited it by these three periods of life, he reflects:
"Materiality that occurs in the first period of life ceases right there without reaching the middle period; therefore, it is impermanent. That which is impermanent..."
That is suffering. Whatever is suffering is non-self. Even the material form occurring in middle age ceases right there without reaching old age;

therefore, that too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Even the material form occurring for thirty-three years in old age is not capable of going beyond death; therefore, that too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.”
He applies the three characteristics.
Having thus applied the three characteristics by way of the passing away of youth, maturity, and old age through the divisions of the first stage of life and so forth, he further [considers]:
"the decade of dullness, the decade of playfulness, the decade of beauty, the decade of strength, the decade of wisdom, the decade of decline, the decade of stooping," and so on.

By means of these ten decades— the decade of crookedness, the decade of extreme delusion, and the decade of lying down— one applies the three characteristics [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self] based on the decline of youth and the onset of old age.
Regarding those decades, first, for a person living for a hundred years, the initial ten years constitute the "decade of slowness" (*mandadasaka*).
Next, there are ten years called the "Childhood Decade," for at that time he is dull and fickle.
Following that are ten years called the "Playful Decade," for at that time he is full of delight in play.

Following that are ten years called the "Complexion Decade," for at that time his sphere of physical beauty reaches its fullness. Following that are ten years called the "Strength Decade," for at that time his strength...
He attains strength and fullness. Following that is the next ten-year period called the "decade of wisdom" (*paññā-dasaka*);
for at that time, his wisdom becomes well-established. It is said that even for one who is naturally of weak intellect, a small measure of wisdom certainly arises during that period.
Following that is the next ten-year period called the "decade of decline" (*hāni-dasaka*); for at that time, his playfulness, delight, complexion, strength, and wisdom—
They decline. Following that are ten stages called the "Ten of the Forward Slope" (*pabbhāra-dasaka*); for at that time, his physical form begins to slope forward.
Following those are ten stages called the "Ten of the Crookedness" (*vaṅka-dasaka*); for at that time, his physical form becomes as crooked as the tip of a plough.
Following those are ten stages called the "Ten of the Utter Delusion" (*momūha-dasaka*); for at that time he becomes utterly deluded and forgets everything he has done.
Beyond that are ten decades called the "decade of lying down," for one who is a hundred years old lies down much.
Therein, this yogi, in order to apply the three characteristics to the passing away of youth and old age by way of these decades, reflects thus:
"The materiality occurring in the first decade, without reaching the second decade, right there..."

It ceases; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. In the second decad... [and so on] ...in the ninth decad, the matter occurring there ceases right there before reaching the tenth decad.
The matter occurring in the tenth decad ceases right here without reaching a new existence;
therefore, that too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self—thus he applies the three characteristics.

709. Thus, having applied the three characteristics by way of decades through the disappearance of youth and the increase of age, he again divides that same hundred years into twenty parts of five years each and applies the three characteristics by way of the disappearance of youth and the increase of age. How so?
He reflects thus: "The materiality occurring during the first five-year period [ceases] in the second five-year period..."
Without reaching [the next period], it ceases right there; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

The material form that occurred during the second five-year period... [and so on] ...the material form that occurred during the nineteenth five-year period ceases right there without reaching the twentieth five-year period.
The material form that occurred during the twentieth five-year period is not capable of proceeding beyond death.
“there is no self; therefore, that too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

Thus, having applied the three characteristics by way of the twenty sections according to the passing away of youth and maturity, he again divides them into twenty-five sections and applies them according to groups of four years. Then, [he applies them] by way of thirty-three sections...

Having divided [the lifespan] into three-year units, he applies the three characteristics to that form which marks the decline of youth and the onset of old age according to each of the three seasons— rainy, winter, and summer— by dividing it into fifty parts according to two-year units, into one hundred parts according to single-year units, and then by dividing a single year into three parts according to each season.
"How so? 'The material form that occurs during the four months of the rains ceases right there before reaching winter;
the material form that occurs in winter ceases right there before reaching summer; the material form that occurs in summer ceases right there before reaching the rains again.
Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Having thus applied [this reasoning], once more—"
Having divided one year into six parts: "The materiality that arises during the two months of the rainy season ceases right there before reaching autumn.
The materiality that arises in autumn [ceases] in winter. The materiality that arises in winter [ceases] in the cool season. The materiality that arises in the cool season [ceases] in spring.
The materiality that arises in spring [ceases] in summer. The materiality that arises in summer ceases right there before reaching the rains again."
“It has ceased; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. In this way, he applies the three characteristics to that material form which undergoes decline and dissolution through aging.

Having applied them thus, he then applies the three characteristics by way of the dark and bright fortnights: “The material form occurring during the dark fortnight ceases right there without reaching the bright fortnight; the material form occurring during the bright fortnight ceases right there without reaching the dark fortnight;
therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Thus he applies the three characteristics.
Then, by way of night and day, he applies the three characteristics thus: “The materiality occurring at night ceases right there without reaching the day;
the materiality occurring during the day also ceases right there without reaching the night; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Then, having divided that same night and day into six parts by way of the morning and so forth, he applies them as follows:
—“Form occurring in the morning ceases right there without reaching midday. Form occurring at midday [ceases] at evening.
Form occurring at evening [ceases] at the first watch. Form occurring in the first watch [ceases] at the middle watch.
Form occurring in the middle watch ceases right there without reaching the last watch. Form occurring in the last watch [ceases] again at the morning.”
“Without reaching [its destination], it ceases right there; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Thus he applies the three characteristics.
Having applied them in this way, he again considers that same material form by way of advancing, retreating, looking forward, looking around, contracting, and extending:
“The material form occurring during advancing ceases right there without reaching the act of retreating. The material form occurring during retreating...”
Looking is [materiality]. The materiality occurring in looking is gazing. The materiality occurring in gazing is contraction.
The materiality occurring in contraction ceases right there without reaching extension. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self—thus he applies the three characteristics.
Then, by way of lifting up, drawing forward, drawing aside, letting go, setting down, and pressing down, he divides the foot into six parts.
Therein, "lifting up" means raising the foot from the ground. "Drawing forward" means moving it toward the front.
"Drawing aside" means, upon seeing something such as a stump, a thorn, or a long snake, shifting the foot here and there.
"Lowering" means setting the foot down below [the surface]. "Placing" means setting it upon the surface of the earth.
"Pressing" means the pressing together of the foot with the earth at the time of lifting the foot again.
In that process, during the lifting, two elements—the earth element and the water element—are diminished and weak; the other two [elements] are strong.

In the processes of drawing together and spreading out, likewise, the fire element and the air element are slight and weak, while the other two elements are predominant and powerful. It is the same in the processes of laying down and pressing down.
Having thus divided the body into six parts, he applies the three characteristics to that material form which undergoes decline, growth, and dissolution by means of those parts.

How? He reflects thus: "Those elements that occur in lifting up, and those derived material phenomena that depend upon them—all these states cease right there without reaching the act of carrying across; therefore they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Likewise, those occurring in carrying across lead to carrying back and forth. Those occurring in carrying back and forth lead to letting go. Those occurring in letting go..."
As for the laying down: those [factors] occurring during the laying down cease right there without reaching the state of suppression.

Thus, having arisen here and there, without reaching their respective other components, they become segment by segment, joint by joint, and mass by mass right where they arose—crackling like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan.
“Formations break up; therefore they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. As he thus contemplates formations step by step through insight, his comprehension of form becomes subtle.
And regarding this subtlety, there is this simile:
It is said that there was once a man well-practiced in making fire with wood, grass, and so forth, who had never before seen a lamp.
A border-dweller, having come to the city and seeing a lamp burning in the marketplace, asked a man:
"Sir, what is this that is so pleasing? He said to him: "What is pleasing here? This is called a lamp;
when the oil is exhausted and the wick is spent, even its path will not be known. Another said this to him:
“This is coarse; for as this wick burns away gradually, the flames will cease at every third part without reaching one another’s location. Then another said to him: “This too is coarse;
for within every finger-breadth, within every half-finger-breadth, in every thread and in every fiber...”
“The flame will cease without even reaching the wick. But without emitting a flame, it is impossible to define the wick.

In this context, just as the man’s knowledge that “with the exhaustion of the oil and the exhaustion of the wick, even the path traversed by the lamp will not be discerned,” so too for the yogi is the application of the three characteristics to form limited by a hundred years, from its acquisition to its relinquishment.

Just as a man might have the knowledge that "at every third part of a bamboo pole, the flame will cease without reaching the next adjacent section," so too does the yogi apply the three characteristics to the material form that marks the transition from youth to old age, delimited by every hundredth part of a century.
Just as a man [might know] that "between each finger's breadth, the flame will cease without reaching the next adjacent section," so too...
Just as a man’s knowledge [of a firebrand] is the application of the three characteristics to a form delimited by ten years, five years, four years, three years, two years,

or one year; so too, for the yogi, by means of each single season, is one year divided into three parts and six parts— just like the man’s knowledge that "the flames, separated by half-a-finger or half-an-inch intervals, will cease without reaching one another."
The superimposition of the three characteristics upon form delimited by four months or two months; and,
like a man’s knowledge that “in each and every thread the flames will cease without reaching one another,” the superimposition of the three characteristics upon form delimited by black and white,
by night and day, and by dividing a single night and day into six parts such as the morning and so forth, according to the yogi.

"Just as a man’s knowledge that ‘in each and every ray, the flames will cease without reaching one another,’ so too is the application of the three characteristics to form delimited by each individual factor— such as the forward movement and so forth, or the lifting up and so forth—
by means of the meditator’s practice."

712. Thus, having applied the three characteristics to material form in its various modes of arising and passing away through the stages of youth and old age, he again analyzes that same material form into four portions—namely, those consisting of nutriment and so forth—and applies the three characteristics to each individual portion.
Among these, the material form consisting of nutriment becomes evident to him by way of hunger and satiety; it is that which arises at the time of hunger.
For the material form becomes withered and exhausted; it is discolored and misshapen, like a charred stump or like a crow perched in a pan of glowing embers.
At the time of being well-fed, the blood is arisen, nourished, plump, soft, moist, and possessed of pleasant contact.
Having discerned this, he reflects: "The material form occurring at the time of hunger ceases right here, without reaching the time of being well-fed."
"Even though it arises during a time of plenty, it ceases right there without reaching a time of famine; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
In this way, he applies the three characteristics to it.
(713) That which consists of the seasons is evident by way of cold and heat. For matter that has arisen during a time of heat becomes parched.
It is exhausted and discolored. Matter arisen during the cold season becomes heated, plump, and glossy.
Having discerned this, he reflects: "Matter occurring during the hot season ceases right here without reaching the cold season;
matter occurring during the cold season ceases right here without reaching the hot season. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
In this way, he applies the three characteristics there.

(714) That which is born of kamma becomes manifest by way of the sense bases and doors. For in the eye door, there are thirty kamma-born material phenomena by way of the decads of the eye, body, and sex;
and their twenty-four supporting [phenomena] are those originated by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.

There are fifty-four [material phenomena] in each of the doors of the ear, nose, and tongue. In the door of the body, there are forty-four by way of the body-constituent decad (*kāyabhāvadasaka*) and by way of those originating from temperature (*utusamuṭṭhāna*), and so forth.
In the mind-door (*manodvāra*), there are likewise fifty-four by way of the heart-basis decad (*hadayavatthu-kāyabhāvadasaka*) and by way of those originating from temperature, and so forth.
Thus, having discerned all that form: "The form occurring at the eye-door ceases right there without reaching the ear-door.
The form occurring at the ear-door [ceases] at the nose-door. The form occurring at the nose-door [ceases] at the tongue-door.
The form occurring at the tongue-door [ceases] at the body-door. The form occurring at the body-door ceases right there without reaching the mind-door."
"It ceases; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus he applies the three characteristics to that object.
(715) Matter originated by mind becomes evident through the states of joy and dejection;
for matter arisen at a time of joy is glossy, soft, plump, and possesses a pleasant touch. Matter arisen at a time of dejection...
It quickly becomes exhausted and discolored. Having observed this, he superimposes the three characteristics upon it in this way:
"The materiality occurring at the time of joy ceases right here without reaching the time of grief;
the materiality occurring at the time of grief ceases right here without reaching the time of joy. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
When he has thus discerned the material form originated by that mind and applies the three characteristics to it, this meaning becomes clear:
"Life and the physical personality, and all pleasure and pain, are joined with a single moment of consciousness; the fleeting instant passes away."
Even the eighty-four thousand deities who remain for an eon do not endure when they are possessed by two conflicting thoughts.
Those [thoughts] that have ceased in one who is dying or even living here [in this world], [do not persist].
All aggregates are alike, having passed away without reconnection.
Those that have perished immediately, those that will perish in the future,
and those that have ceased in the interval between— there is no difference in their characteristic.
Not born by what is yet unarisen, he lives by what is present;
when the mind dissolves, the world is dead—this is the ultimate designation.
Gone beyond storage, broken apart, there is no heap remaining in the future.
Even those things that have arisen and persist are like a mustard seed on the point of an awl.
For all phenomena that have arisen, their destruction stands foremost;
though subject to disintegration, they persist unmixed with what was before.
“They come from non-seeing, and having broken [through] they go to seeing;
like the arising of light in the sky, they arise and pass away.

(716) Having thus applied the three characteristics to those things consisting of nutriment and so forth, he again applies the three characteristics to the materiality of the natural order (*dhammatārūpa*).

The "natural form" (*dhammatārūpa*) refers to external matter not bound to the sense faculties, consisting of various types such as iron, copper, tin, lead, gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, crystal, quartz, coral, ruby, emerald, earth, stone, mountains, grass, trees, creepers, and so forth;
it is the matter that arises from the beginning of the eon of world-expansion (*vivaṭṭakappa*). This becomes evident through the case of the *asoka* sprout and others.
For the *asoka* sprout is initially thin and red; after two or three days have passed, it becomes thick and red; and again, after another two or three days have passed...
It becomes the color of a mandārava flower; then the color of a young sprout; then the color of a mature sprout;

then the color of a green leaf; then the color of a dark blue leaf. From the time it has the color of a dark blue leaf, continuing the stream of similar material form for about a year, it turns yellowish-white and falls, severed from its stalk.
Thus, having comprehended that: "The material form occurring during the time of slight redness ceases before reaching the time of dense redness.

The material form occurring during the time of dense redness [ceases] at the time of pale redness. The material form occurring during the time of pale redness [ceases] at the time of the color of young shoots.
The material form occurring during the time of the color of young shoots [ceases] at the time of the color of matured shoots. At the time of the color of matured shoots..."
"The time when it has appeared as the color of green leaves. The time when it has appeared as the color of green leaves ceases at the time of the color of blue leaves.

The time when it has appeared as the color of blue leaves ceases at the time of the yellowing leaf. The time when it has appeared as the yellowing leaf ceases before even reaching the point of falling after being severed from its stalk;
therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus he applies the three characteristics. In this way...
There, having applied the three characteristics by this method, one comprehends all materiality consisting of the "signs of phenomena" (dhammatārūpa).
Thus, first of all, one comprehends formations by applying the three characteristics by way of the sevenfold materiality.
The Discourse on the Comprehension of the Sevenfold Immateriality.

717. As for what was said, "by way of the seven immaterial groups," here is the matrix (*mātikā*): by way of aggregates (*kalāpa*), by way of pairs (*yamaka*), by way of moments (*khaṇika*), by way of sequence (*paṭipāṭi*), by way of the eradication of views (*diṭṭhi-ugghāṭana*), by way of the eradication of conceit (*māna-samugghāṭana*), and by way of the exhaustion of craving (*nikanti-pariyādāna*).
In that regard, "by way of aggregates" refers to the phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth.

How does one comprehend by way of aggregates? Here, a bhikkhu reflects thus: "These things—hair of the head—which have arisen during the comprehension [of them] as 'impermanent, suffering, and non-self,' consist of contact as the fifth..."
“Dhammas—those dhammas consisting of contact as the fifth factor that arise during the comprehension [of the body] as ‘hair... pe ...
brain are impermanent, suffering, and non-self’—all these, without reaching one another, having become separate and distinct, perish with a crackling sound like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan;
therefore they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. This, first of all, is the method according to the *Visuddhimagga*.

In the *Ariyavaṃsa-kathā*, however, it is stated: "Regarding the seven instances in the preceding section on the 'Sevenfold Group of Matter,' the mind that has proceeded by [contemplating] ‘matter is impermanent, suffering, and non-self’ contemplates with a subsequent mind as ‘impermanent, suffering, and non-self’;
this is called ‘contemplating by groups. That is more appropriate. Therefore, we shall analyze the remaining cases according to that same method.

718. Regarding "the yamaka" (pairing): here, a bhikkhu, having comprehended the material form of seizing and laying down as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," then comprehends that very consciousness with a subsequent consciousness as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

He comprehends material form subject to decay, growth, and dissolution—as well as nutriment-born, temperature-born, kamma-born, consciousness-originated, and natural material form—as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
Having comprehended that mind as well, he comprehends it with a subsequent mind as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
This is what is called "comprehending by way of pairs.
719. Regarding "momentary": here, a bhikkhu, having comprehended the material form of taking up and laying down as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self,"...
He comprehends that first consciousness with the second consciousness, the second with the third, the third with the fourth, and the fourth with the fifth, thinking:
"This too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Having comprehended materiality—whether it be that which is subject to decay, growth, and dissolution;
that which is derived from nutriment, from temperature, born of karma, mind-produced, or natural materiality—as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," he comprehends it.
He comprehends that first consciousness with the second, the second with the third, the third with the fourth, and the fourth with the fifth, reflecting:

"This too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Thus, by comprehending four consciousnesses at a time starting from the consciousness that discerns material form, he is said to comprehend by way of moments.

720. "Successively" means that after comprehending the materiality of assuming and laying down as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," one comprehends that first consciousness with the second consciousness, the second with the third, the third with the fourth... [and so on] ...the tenth with the eleventh, thinking: "This too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
[One likewise comprehends] materiality subject to decay, aging, and dissolution; materiality consisting of nutriment; and materiality consisting of temperature.
