Having comprehended that which is born of kamma, mind-originated, and natural materiality as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," one contemplates that first consciousness with the second consciousness, the second with the third, the third with the fourth... and so on up to the tenth with the eleventh, thinking, "This too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
In this manner, through the sequence of insight, one continues for the entire duration of the day.

It would be appropriate to contemplate [them] together. However, until the contemplation of the tenth consciousness, both the material meditation subject (*rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) and the immaterial meditation subject (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) become proficient.
Therefore, it is said that one should stop at the tenth [consciousness] itself. Contemplating in this manner is called "contemplating in serial order.
721. Regarding these three—removal of views, removal of conceit, and the exhaustion of craving—there is a separate method of contemplation for each.
There is no such thing as a "being. When one discerns that which was previously categorized as form and here as the formless, one sees no being other than these forms and formless states.
From the moment the being is no longer seen, the perception of a being is abolished.
For one who discerns formations with a mind from which the perception of a being has been abolished, wrong view does not arise.
When wrong view does not arise, it is said that wrong view has been eradicated. When one comprehends formations with a mind from which wrong view has been eradicated, conceit does not arise.
When conceit does not arise, it is said that conceit has been uprooted.
When one comprehends formations with a mind from which conceit has been uprooted, craving does not arise. When craving does not arise, attachment is exhausted.
“That it is called [‘insight’]” is what was stated in the *Visuddhikathā*.

However, in the *Ariyavaṃsakathā*, after establishing the matrix (mātikā) thus: “From the uprooting of views, from the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am,’ and from the exhaustion of craving,” this method is shown:
for one who grasps at the thought, “I am practicing insight; this is my insight,” there is no such thing as the uprooting of views. [Rather,] only formations...

When one grasps [the thought], "I am seeing formations with insight, I am comprehending them, defining them, discerning them, and delimiting them," it is called the removal of views (*diṭṭhi-ugghāṭana*).
However, for one who grasps [the thought], "I see well;
I see agreeably," it is not called the removal of conceit (*māna-samugghāṭa*). [It is only when one realizes], "Formations alone..."
For one who grasps [the thought], "I am seeing, comprehending, defining, discerning, and delimiting formations," there occurs what is called the uprooting of the mind.
However, for one who relishes insight with the thought, "I am able to see clearly," there is no exhaustion of attachment. "Formations alone..."
When one contemplates, comprehends, defines, grasps, and delimits formations, there occurs what is called the exhaustion of attachment for one who so grasps them.
If formations were the self, it would be appropriate to grasp them as "self"; however, they are non-self, yet they have been grasped as "self."

Therefore, for one who sees that these formations are non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, impermanent in the sense of existing and then ceasing, and suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, there occurs what is called the "uprooting of views.
If formations were permanent, it would be appropriate to grasp them as permanent; however, they are impermanent and yet [wrongly] taken to be permanent.

Because they have been grasped, they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence; they are suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away; and they are non-self in the sense of being beyond one's control.
For one who sees them thus, there occurs what is called the uprooting of the mind.
If conditioned phenomena were pleasant, it would be appropriate to grasp them as "pleasant"; however, since they are suffering, [to grasp them] as "pleasant" [is a misconception].
Because they are grasped, they are suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away; they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been;
and they are non-self in the sense of lack of mastery. For one who sees them thus, there is the exhaustion of attachment.
For one who sees formations as non-self in this way, there is the uprooting of views. For one who sees them as impermanent—
It is called the eradication of the mental [defilements]. For one who sees [them] as suffering, there is the exhaustion of craving.
Thus, this insight remains in its own respective place.

In this way, having applied the three characteristics even by means of the immaterial septad, one comprehends formations. At this point, however, both his material meditation subject and his immaterial meditation subject have become proficient.

722. Thus, when one has become proficient in the meditation subjects of both the material and immaterial, and while still in this very stage penetrating a portion of those eighteen great insights— which are to be attained in all their aspects through the full understanding by abandoning starting from the subsequent contemplation of dissolution—
one abandons the states that are their opposites.
The eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*) refer to the wisdom beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).

Among these, by cultivating the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence; by cultivating the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), one abandons the perception of pleasure;

by cultivating the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*), one abandons the perception of self; by cultivating the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*), one abandons delight; by cultivating the contemplation of dispassion (*virāgānupassanā*)...
By developing the contemplation of fading away, one abandons lust; by developing the contemplation of cessation, one abandons origination;
by developing the contemplation of relinquishment, one abandons grasping; by developing the contemplation of destruction, one abandons the perception of solidity;

by developing the contemplation of vanishing, one abandons accumulation; by developing the contemplation of change, one abandons the perception of permanence; [and] by developing the contemplation of the signless...

By developing [the perception of] the sign, one abandons the sign; by developing the contemplation of the wishless, one abandons wishing; by developing the contemplation of emptiness, one abandons adherence;
by developing higher wisdom and insight into phenomena, one abandons adherence to grasping at a core;
by developing knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, one abandons adherence to delusion; [and by developing] the contemplation of danger...
By developing [insight], one abandons adherence to the storehouse; by developing contemplation of reflection, one abandons non-reflection;
by developing contemplation of turning away, one abandons adherence to bondage.
Since formations have been seen by means of this triad of characteristics—impermanence and so forth—it is therefore the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
They have been penetrated. And because it is said: "The contemplation of impermanence and the contemplation of the signless—these states are one in meaning, differing only in expression.

Likewise: "The contemplation of suffering and the contemplation of the desireless—these states are one in meaning, differing only in expression. "The contemplation of non-self and the contemplation of emptiness—"
It is said: "These states have the same meaning; only the phrasing is different. Therefore, those [two] are also penetrated.

However, all insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) is simply insight (*vipassanā*). The knowledge and vision of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is included within the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*) alone.
Thus, this pair is also indeed penetrated. Among the remaining types of insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*), some...
Some have been penetrated and some have not; we shall explain their distinction later.

For it was with reference to that which has been penetrated that this was said: "In this way, for one whose subject of meditation on the beautiful (rūpa) and the un-beautiful (arūpa) is well-mastered, the eighteen [qualities] which are to be attained in every aspect by means of the full understanding through abandonment—starting from the subsequent contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā)—[are to be understood]."
This is great insight (*mahāvipassanā*). By penetrating even a portion of these right here, one abandons the states that are their opposites.
Thus ends the discourse on the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbayañāṇa). 723.
Having thus purified his knowledge by abandoning the perceptions of permanence and so forth, which are the opposites of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, he—

Having reached the culmination of comprehension-knowledge (*sammasana-ñāṇa*), he begins the practice for the attainment of that which was described as "the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall" (*udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa*)—which occurs immediately after comprehension-knowledge and is defined as "wisdom in contemplating the transformation of presently arisen phenomena.
And while beginning it, he begins first in brief. Herein, this is the text:
“How is it that wisdom regarding the contemplation of the change of present phenomena is knowledge of the contemplation of rise and fall?
Form that has arisen is present; its characteristic of being produced is ‘rise,’ and its characteristic of changing is ‘fall.
Contemplation is knowledge. Feeling that has arisen... perception... formations... consciousness... the eye that has arisen... [and so on] ... becoming that has arisen.”
“The present; its characteristic of arising is *udaya* (rise), its characteristic of change is *vaya* (fall), and the contemplation thereof is knowledge.

Following this scriptural method, he contemplates the characteristic of arising—namely, birth, production, and the novel mode of being—of the name-and-form that has been born as “rise,” and he contemplates its characteristic of change—namely, destruction and dissolution—as “fall. He understands it thus:
“Prior to the arising of this name-and-form, there was no mass or accumulation; even as it arises, there is no coming from a mass or an accumulation;
even as it ceases, there is no going to any direction or intermediate direction;
and once it has ceased, there is no remaining in any one place as a mass, an accumulation, or a hoard.”
Just as, when a lute is being played, the sound that arises has no accumulation prior to its arising,
nor does it come from an accumulation while it is arising, nor is there any going to the cardinal or intermediate directions while it is ceasing,
nor does it remain accumulated anywhere once it has ceased; rather, it depends upon the lute, the strings, and the appropriate effort of the person.

“Dependent on effort, it comes to be without having been; having been, it passes away. In this way, all phenomena, both material and immaterial, come to be without having been, and having been, they pass away.
Having thus performed the attention to rise and fall in brief, one should further [consider] those [points] which are in the analysis of that very knowledge of rise and fall:
“With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form”: thus one sees the arising of the aggregate of form in the sense of the arising of conditions.
“With the arising of craving... with the arising of kamma... with the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form”:
thus one sees the arising of the aggregate of form in the sense of the arising of conditions. Even when seeing the characteristic of generation, one sees the arising of the aggregate of form.
He sees. Seeing the arising of the aggregate of form, he sees these five characteristics:
"With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form"—thus he sees the fall of the aggregate of form in the sense of the cessation of conditions.

"With the cessation of craving... with the cessation of karma... with the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form"—thus [he sees the fall of the aggregate of form] in the sense of the cessation of conditions.
“He sees the fall. Even when seeing the characteristic of change, he sees the fall of the aggregate of form. Even when seeing the fall of the aggregate of form, he sees these five characteristics.
Likewise: “With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling; thus, in the sense of the arising of conditions, he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling.”

He sees it. He sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions: "From the arising of craving... from the arising of kamma... from the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling.
Even when seeing the characteristic of production, he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling.
Seeing the arising of the aggregate of feeling, he sees these five characteristics.

“With the cessation of ignorance... with the cessation of craving... with the cessation of kamma... with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling. Thus, in the sense of the cessation of conditions, he sees the fall of the aggregate of feeling.
Seeing the characteristic of change, he also sees the fall of the aggregate of feeling.
Seeing the fall of the aggregate of feeling, he sees these five characteristics.

And as with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness. However, this is the distinction: in place of "contact" for the aggregate of consciousness, it says, "With the arising of name-and-form, with the cessation of name-and-form.
Thus, by showing the rise and fall of each aggregate individually, fifty characteristics are stated—ten for each.
By means of these, it is shown: "In this way there is the rise of material form; in this way there is the fall of material form; in this way material form arises; in this way..."
He attends in detail to form by way of its conditions and by way of its momentary nature.
As he attends in this way, his knowledge becomes clearer: "Indeed, these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish.
Thus, as he sees both the arising and the passing away in two ways—by way of conditions and by way of moments—his insight becomes more refined.
The distinctions regarding the method and characteristics of dependent origination according to truth become manifest.

For when he sees that with the arising of ignorance and the other factors there is the arising of the aggregates, and with the cessation of ignorance and the other factors there is the cessation of the aggregates—this is his vision of rise and fall from the standpoint of conditions. Furthermore, [he sees] the characteristic of production and the characteristic of change.
Contemplating, he sees the arising and passing away of the aggregates; this is his seeing of arising and passing away from the perspective of moments.
For at the very moment of arising, there is the characteristic of production, and at the moment of dissolution, there is the characteristic of change.
Thus, as he sees arising and passing away in these two ways—from the perspective of conditions and from the perspective of moments—by means of seeing the arising from the perspective of conditions...

The truth of the origin becomes evident through the realization of its producer; the truth of suffering becomes evident through the vision of arising at every moment, owing to the realization of the suffering of birth;

the truth of cessation becomes evident through the vision of passing away by way of conditions, owing to the realization that what possesses conditions cannot arise when those conditions do not arise;
and through the vision of passing away at every moment, it is precisely the truth of suffering [that becomes evident].

It becomes evident through the realization of the suffering of death. Furthermore, because it dispels delusion regarding the view of its arising and passing away, the truth of the path becomes evident as "this is the mundane path.
By seeing its arising through its conditions, the forward order of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) becomes evident: "In this... [728]
Through the realization that "this being, that comes to be," dependent origination in its forward order becomes clear through the vision of arising from conditions;
through the realization that "with the cessation of this, that ceases," it becomes clear through the vision of passing away.

Furthermore, through the vision of rise and fall in terms of moments, dependently originated phenomena become clear through the realization of the characteristics of the conditioned. These possess rise and fall.
For these are conditioned, and they are dependently arisen.

By seeing their arising through the lens of conditions, the method of unity (*ekattanaya*) becomes evident, because one realizes that the continuum is uninterrupted due to the connection between cause and fruit.
Thus, one more effectively abandons the view of annihilationism. By seeing arising through the lens of moments (*khaṇa*),...
The method of diversity becomes evident through the realization of the arising of ever-new phenomena; then one abandons the view of eternalism even more effectively.
Through the vision of rise and fall by way of conditions, the method of non-agency becomes evident through the realization that phenomena are not subject to one's own mastery;
then one abandons the view of self even more effectively. Furthermore, through the vision of rise by way of conditions...
Thus the principle of natural law (*dhammatānaya*) becomes evident through the realization that a fruit arises in accordance with its conditions.
Consequently, he abandons the view of non-action even more thoroughly.

Furthermore, by seeing the arising [of phenomena] from their conditions, the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) becomes evident to him, because he realizes that phenomena are devoid of agency and exist dependent upon conditions.

Through the vision of rise and fall by way of moments, the characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest, owing to the realization that what has come to be does not exist [afterwards], and owing to the realization of the seclusion from the past and future limits.
The characteristic of suffering also becomes manifest, owing to the realization of oppression by rise and fall.

The characteristic of individual essence also becomes manifest, owing to the realization of being delimited by rise and fall. Within the characteristic of individual essence, the characteristic of the conditioned...
Even their momentariness becomes evident through the realization that there is no arising at the moment of fall, and no fall at the moment of arising. 731.
For one who has thus made manifest the method and characteristics of dependent origination and the truths, the formations (saṅkhāra), being ever-new, appear as:
"In this way, indeed, these phenomena arise having never arisen before; once arisen, they cease."

They appear [to the mind]. And not only are they ever-new, but at the rising of the sun they appear to last only briefly—like a drop of dew, like a bubble on water, like a line drawn with a stick on water, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl, and like a flash of lightning.

Furthermore, they appear to be without substance and devoid of essence, like an illusion, a mirage, the end of a dream, a circle of fire from a whirling torch, a city of the Gandharvas, a mass of foam, a plantain tree, and so forth.
To this extent, by penetrating the fifty characteristics in this manner— "Only that which is subject to fall arises, and what has arisen meets with fall"—

he has attained the knowledge of nascent insight called "contemplation of rise and fall," through the attainment of which he comes to be reckoned as one who has begun insight practice (*āraddhavipassaka*).
The Discourse on the Impurities of Insight (Vipassanupakkilesakathā) 732.
Then, for this practitioner who has begun insight through this nascent insight, ten impurities of insight arise.
For these impurities of insight arise both for the noble disciple who has attained penetration and for one who has fallen into wrong practice.
They do not arise in a lazy person who has laid aside his meditation subject.
However, they certainly do arise in a clansman who is practicing rightly, who is devotedly engaged, and who has initiated insight.
What, then, are those ten imperfections? They are: illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, bliss, resolve, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and attachment. For this has been said:
“How is the mind seized by agitation regarding the Dhamma? When one attends to [the object] as impermanent, a radiance arises.
One adverts to the radiance, thinking, ‘Radiance is the Dhamma. From that comes distraction and agitation.

With a mind seized by that agitation, one does not understand the appearance of things as they really are as impermanent. One does not understand the appearance of things as they really are as suffering... as non-self.”
Likewise, “When one attends to [the object] as impermanent, knowledge arises... pe ...rapture... tranquility... pleasure... resolution... exertion... establishment...
equanimity... attachment arises. One adverts to that attachment, thinking, ‘This is an attached state.
From that, there is distraction and restlessness. With a mind agitated by that restlessness, one does not see the appearance of impermanence as it truly is.”
“He does not understand it as it really is. He does not understand its appearance as suffering... as non-self as it really is.
(733) Therein, “illumination” refers to the illumination of insight (*vipassan-obhāsa*). When that has arisen, the practitioner thinks: “Indeed, no such illumination has ever arisen for me before;
surely I have attained the Path, I have attained the Fruit. Thus, he takes what is not the Path to be the “Path.”

And he takes what is fruitless as "fruit. For one who thus takes what is not the path to be "the path" and what is fruitless to be "fruit," the course of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) is said to have been interrupted.
Having abandoned his own original meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he sits enjoying only the illumination (obhāsa).
Now, this illumination arises for some bhikkhu illuminating only the area where he is sitting cross-legged.
For some, it illuminated the inner chamber; for some, even the outer chamber; for some, the entire monastery, or a *gāvuta*, half a *yojana*, one *yojana*, two *yojanas*, three *yojanas*...
and so on, up to some for whom it created a single expanse of light from the surface of the earth as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world.
But for the Blessed One, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world-system.
This is the story concerning such diversity: it is said that on Cittala Mountain, two elders were sitting inside a house with double walls.
On that day, it was the Uposatha of the dark fortnight; the quarters were shrouded by masses of clouds, and during the night, a darkness endowed with four characteristics prevailed.
Then one elder said: "Venerable sir, right now in the courtyard of the Cetiya..."
“Five-colored flowers are seen on the lion throne. The other said to him: “Friend, you speak of what is not wonderful;
but now, in the great ocean, fish and turtles are seen for a distance of a league.

This, however, is a defilement of insight (vipassanūpakilesa) that generally arises in those who have attained both serenity (samatha) and insight. It [arises] regarding those [objects] suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti).
One arouses the thought, "I am an arahant," due to the non-occurrence of defilements, as did the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Uccavālika,
the Elder Mahādatta who dwelt at Haṃkanaka, and the Elder Cūḷasumana who dwelt in the Niṅkapeṇṇaka meditation hall on Cittala Mountain.

Herein, this is the illustration by way of a single incident: There was once a certain Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), whose taints were utterly destroyed, and who served as the instructor for a great community of monks. One day, while sitting in his own daytime resting place, he thought:
"What indeed is the duty of the ascetic life for our teacher, the Elder Mahānāga, the resident of Uccavālika?"

Reflecting, "Has he reached the summit? No," and seeing that he was still in the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), and knowing, "If I do not go, he will surely die as an ordinary person," he rose into the air by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), descended near the Elder who was sitting in his daytime resting place, paid homage, performed the customary duties, and sat down to one side. "Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an improper time? [he asked.]
When he was asked, "Have you come? he replied, "Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question. Then, when it was said, "Ask, friend;
knowing, we shall explain," he asked a thousand questions.
The Elder answered each question as it was asked without any hesitation. Thereupon [the other monk] said, "Venerable sir, your knowledge is exceedingly sharp."
When he asked, "At what time was this Dhamma realized by you?", he replied, "Sixty years ago, friend.

[The other monk said,] "Venerable sir, please employ your concentration as well. [The elder replied,] "This is not difficult, friend. [The other said,] "In that case, venerable sir, manifest an elephant.
The elder manifested a completely white elephant. [The other said,] "Now, venerable sir, let this elephant have its ears pricked up..."
"Stretching out his hind leg and thrusting his trunk into his mouth, he approaches you while letting out a terrifying trumpeting cry;
act in such a manner! The Elder did as instructed. Seeing the terrifying appearance of the elephant rushing toward him with great speed, he rose and began to flee.
Then the Elder who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) reached out his hand and—
Taking hold of the corner of his robe, he said, "Venerable sir, does one whose taints are destroyed experience timidity?

At that moment, realizing his own state as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), he said, "Friend Dhammadinna, be my support," and sat down on his heels at the master's feet. "Venerable sir, it was with the very thought, 'I shall be your support,' that I came here."

"Do not worry," he said, and taught him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Having taken up the meditation subject, the Elder ascended the walking path (*caṅkama*) and attained the supreme fruit of *arahantship* at the third step. It is said that the Elder was of a temperament prone to hatred (*dosacarita*).
Monks of such a disposition are shaken by supernatural manifestations (*obhāsa*).

734. "Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). It is said that as one weighs and examines material and immaterial phenomena, there arises a knowledge that is sharp, keen, and exceedingly clear, with an unimpeded force like a released thunderbolt.

"Rapture" (pīti) refers to the rapture of insight. It is said that at that time, this fivefold rapture—namely, minor rapture, momentary rapture, showering rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture—arises filling the entire body.

"Tranquility" refers to the tranquility of insight (*vipassanā-passaddhi*). It is said that at that time, for him as he sits in his night-quarters or day-quarters, there is neither distress nor rigidity, neither harshness nor unwieldiness, nor sickness, nor crookedness in body and mind;
rather, his body and mind are tranquil, light, and pliant.

They become workable, very clear, and indeed straight. At that time, with his body and mind assisted by these factors beginning with tranquility, he experiences a delight called "superhuman. With reference to this, it was said:
"For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty place, whose mind is peaceful..."
“Supernatural delight arises for one who clearly sees the Dhamma with right insight.
In whatever way one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and joy; that is the deathless for one who understands.”
Thus, as he accomplishes this superhuman delight, tranquility associated with lightness and the other [mental factors] arises.
"Bliss" refers to the bliss of insight (vipassanā). It is said that at that time, an exceedingly refined bliss arises, flooding his entire body.
"Resolution" refers to faith (saddhā). For at that moment, there arises a powerful faith, which is an extraordinary clarity of mind and mental factors associated with insight.
“Exertion” is energy (*vīriya*). For in him there arises energy that is well-exerted—neither lax nor over-exerted—which is indeed associated with insight (*vipassanā*).

“Establishment” is mindfulness (*sati*). For in him there arises mindfulness that is well-established, firmly grounded, planted, immovable, and like the king of mountains; it is indeed associated with insight. Whatever object he adverts to or attends to...
He attends to and reviews it; having leaped upon and leaped into each respective state, it stands established through mindfulness as if the other world were before the divine eye.
"Equanimity" refers both to the equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*) and the equanimity of adverting (*āvajjanupekkhā*). For at that time, regarding all conditioned phenomena...
Equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*), having become balanced, also arises powerfully; so too does the equanimity of adverting at the mind-door (*manodvāra*).
For as he adverts to this or that object, it proceeds for him with sharp intensity, like a loose thunderbolt or like a red-hot iron arrow cast into a leaf-bowl.

"Craving" (*nikanti*) here refers to craving for insight (*vipassanā-nikanti*). Thus, as he forms an attachment to that insight adorned with the aura and so forth, there arises a subtle, peaceful form of craving that cannot even be identified as a defilement (*kilesa*).
And just as with the aura, when any one of these has arisen, the practitioner thinks:
"Indeed, never before has such knowledge, such rapture, such tranquility, such bliss, such resolution, or such exertion arisen in me."

He takes what is merely not the path to be "the path" and what is merely not the fruit to be "the fruit," thinking: "Attainment has occurred; equanimity has arisen; attachment has arisen before; indeed, I have reached the path and reached the fruit.

For one who thus takes what is not the path to be "the path" and what is not the fruit to be "the fruit," the course of insight is said to have gone astray. Having abandoned his own original meditation subject, he...
"He sits relishing attachment itself.
Herein, the illumination and so forth are called "defilements" by virtue of being the basis for defilement, not because they are unwholesome.
Attachment, however, is both a defilement and the basis for defilement. And these ten are [counted] as ten only by way of their bases, not by way of their modes of grasping.
But there are thirty. How so? For one who grasps [the light] thinking, "A radiance has arisen for me," there is a grasp of views;
for one who grasps it thinking, "Ah, what a pleasing radiance has arisen," there is a grasp of conceit; and for one who relishes the radiance, there is a grasp of craving.
Thus, with respect to the radiance, there are three grasps—by way of view, conceit, and craving. The same applies to the remaining [objects]. Thus, by way of these grasps, there are thirty.
These are the defilements. Under their influence, the unskilled and incompetent practitioner wavers and is distracted by the aura and the other signs.
He regards each of these—the aura and so forth—with the thought: "This is mine, this am I, this is my self. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"He wavers in respect of the aura, knowledge, and rapture;..."
“Because of serenity and pleasure, the mind trembles;
it wavers in resolution, exertion, and establishment;
and in the adverting of equanimity and in attachment to equanimity.”
The Discourse on the Determination of the Path and the Non-Path (Maggāmaggavavatthānakathā) 736.
But when illumination and the other signs have arisen, the skilled, wise, competent, intelligent practitioner of yoga reflects:
"This illumination has indeed arisen for me; however, it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, and subject to destruction."
Or he delimits and examines it with wisdom, thinking: "It is subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.
Or else, this thought occurs to him: "If light were self, it would be fit to be grasped as 'self.
But this is non-self, yet it is grasped as 'self. Therefore, in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery, it is non-self; and in the sense of ceasing to exist after having come to be..."
“It is impermanent; it is suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away”—all this should be elaborated in detail according to the method stated in the *Arūpasattaka*.
And just as with the light, so it is with the rest.
Having investigated in this way, he regards the light thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.”
He regards knowledge... [and so on] ...down to... attachment as “this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Regarding it thus, he does not waver or tremble regarding the aura and the other signs. Therefore the ancients said:
“These ten points are thoroughly mastered by his wisdom;”
“He is skilled in the agitation regarding phenomena (dhammuddhacca) and does not fall into distraction.
Thus, not falling into distraction, he disentangles that thicket of thirty kinds of defilements (*upakkilesa*).

Then, [realizing] that states such as the illumination (*obhāsa*) are not the path, but rather that insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*)—which is free from defilements and has entered the right course—is the path, he discerns both the path and...

And he defines what is not the path. Thus, when knowledge has become established by knowing both the path and the non-path in the manner of "this is the path" and "this is not the path," it should be understood as the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).
At this point, however, the definition of three truths has been accomplished by him. How so? In the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*)...
Thus, by means of the definition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the definition of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is accomplished.

By means of the discernment of conditions (*paccaya-pariggahaṇa*) within the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*), the definition of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is accomplished.

And here, in this purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi*), the definition of the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) is accomplished through the determination of the right path. Thus, first, by means of the mundane [path] alone...
Thus the defining of the three truths has been accomplished by means of knowledge.
Thus ends the section on the Development of Understanding in the *Visuddhimagga* composed for the delight of the virtuous.
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and Is Not the Path. 21.
The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way.

737. Insight that has reached its culmination by means of eight knowledges, together with the ninth knowledge which conforms to the truths—this is called purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).
And here, "eight" refers to the knowledge free from imperfections, which is termed insight that has entered the right path.

The eight knowledges to be understood are: knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, knowledge of appearance as terror, knowledge of contemplation of danger, knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment, knowledge of desire for deliverance, knowledge of reflective contemplation, and knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
The ninth is "knowledge in conformity with the truths," which is a designation for conformity (anuloma).
Therefore, one who wishes to achieve that should apply himself to these knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall which is free from the defilements.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of applying oneself again to the knowledge of rise and fall?", the answer is: for the purpose of discerning the characteristics.
For the knowledge of rise and fall, having previously been defiled by the ten imperfections, was unable to discern the three characteristics according to their actual nature.
He was unable [to see it]. But he is able to see it when it is freed from its imperfections. Therefore, one must again apply oneself here to the discernment of the characteristics.
739. Now, due to the non-attention to what and because of being concealed by what do the characteristics fail to appear?
First, the characteristic of impermanence does not appear because of the non-attention to arising and falling away, and because it is concealed by continuity. The characteristic of suffering...
The characteristic of non-self does not appear because of a lack of attention to constant oppression and because it is concealed by the postures.
The characteristic of impermanence appears according to its true nature once continuity has been disrupted by discerning rise and fall. Constant oppression, however, [does not appear].
When one has brought this to mind and suspended the postures, the characteristic of suffering becomes manifest according to its true nature.
Having analyzed the various elements and performed the analysis of the compact mass, the characteristic of non-self becomes manifest according to its true nature.
And herein, there is the impermanent, the characteristic of impermanence; the painful, the characteristic of pain; and the non-self, the characteristic of non-self.
This distinction should be understood. In this context, "impermanent" refers to the five aggregates. Why?

Because they possess the nature of arising, passing away, and change, or because they cease to exist after having come to be. Arising, passing away, and change constitute the characteristic of impermanence; alternatively, it is the transformation of state characterized by non-existence after having existed.

Furthermore, according to the statement, "That which is impermanent is suffering," that same fivefold aggregate is suffering. Why? Because it is constantly oppressed; the mode of being constantly oppressed is the characteristic of suffering.

Furthermore, because of the statement, “That which is suffering is non-self,” that same pentad of aggregates is non-self. Why? Because it does not exercise mastery; the mode of not exercising mastery is the characteristic of non-self.

This practitioner observes all of this according to its actual nature by means of the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall, known as insight that has entered the path and is liberated from imperfections.
The knowledge of rise and fall liberated from imperfections is completed.
741. Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution:
As he thus observes and repeatedly weighs and examines both material and immaterial phenomena as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," that knowledge proceeds with sharpness;
formations appear swiftly, and while the knowledge is sharp—
As the formations flow swiftly while appearing, one does not reach their arising, nor their station, nor their occurrence, nor their sign.
Mindfulness remains fixed only upon their exhaustion, destruction, breaking-up, and cessation.
For one who sees at this stage that "having arisen in such a way, the course of formations ceases in such a manner," there is what is called the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*).
Insight-knowledge arises. With reference to this it was said:
"How is it that wisdom consisting in the reflection on the object during the contemplation of dissolution is knowledge of insight?
Having arisen with a material form as its object, the consciousness breaks up; reflecting upon that object, one contemplates the dissolution of that consciousness."
"He contemplates": how does he contemplate? He contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent; he contemplates as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates as non-self, not as self; he becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not impassioned;
he causes cessation, not origination; he relinquishes, not grasps.

“Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence. Contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure. Contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self.
Becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight. Becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust. Bringing about cessation, one abandons arising. Relinquishing, one abandons grasping.”

“With feeling as object… perception as object… formations as object… consciousness as object… the eye as object… [and so on] … with aging-and-death as object, the mind arises and breaks up… By relinquishing, one abandons grasping.
“The shifting of the basis and the turning away through wisdom,
The power of adverting, and reflective insight.”
“By way of the sequence of the object, there is a single determination for both;
the state of being intent upon cessation is insight into the characteristic of vanishing.
One reflects upon the object and contemplates its dissolution.”
The appearance as empty is insight with higher wisdom.
“Skilled in the three contemplations and in the four insights,
skilled in the three modes of appearance, he does not waver amidst various views.”

“In the sense of knowing, it is knowledge; in the sense of understanding, it is wisdom. Therefore it is said: ‘The reflection upon the object and the contemplation of dissolution are wisdom in insight and knowledge.
(742) Therein, “reflection upon the object” means having reflected upon and known whatever object there may be, seeing it as subject to destruction and vanishing.
“Wisdom in the contemplation of dissolution” refers to that [wisdom] which, having reflected upon the object as subject to destruction and vanishing...
The wisdom that consists in contemplating the dissolution of arisen knowledge is called "knowledge of insight.

How does this come about? This is first the meaning of the question asked out of a desire to explain it. Then, in order to show how it comes about, the passage beginning with “having form as its object” was stated.
In this context, "consciousness arises and breaks up having visible form as its object" means that consciousness arises and breaks up with visible form as its objective support (*ārammaṇa*).
Alternatively, the meaning is: "consciousness arises and breaks up in the state of having visible form as its object.
"He reflects upon that object" means that having reflected upon—that is, having known—that object consisting of visible form, he sees it in terms of its destruction and its fall away.

“He contemplates the dissolution of that consciousness” means: with another consciousness, he contemplates the dissolution of that very consciousness by which that material object was seen as subject to destruction and vanishing. Therefore, the ancients said:
“He clearly sees both the known object and the knowing consciousness.”

And here, "he contemplates" (*anupassati*) means he sees repeatedly, seeing again and again in many ways; thus it is said: "He contemplates: how does he contemplate? He contemplates as impermanent," and so forth.

In that context, since dissolution (*bhaṅga*) is the ultimate limit of impermanence, the practitioner who contemplates dissolution contemplates every conditioned thing as impermanent, not as permanent. Then, because what is impermanent is suffering, and because what is suffering is...
And because it is non-self, one contemplates that very same thing as suffering, not as pleasure; one contemplates it as non-self, not as self.

Since whatever is impermanent, suffering, and non-self is not to be delighted in, and since what is not to be delighted in is not to be clung to with passion, therefore, by following this contemplation of dissolution, one [contemplates] it as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self."
One becomes disenchanted with the seen conditioned phenomena; one does not delight in them. One becomes dispassionate; one does not become impassioned.
Thus, by means of mundane knowledge alone, one ceases passion and does not cause it to arise. The meaning is that one does not create its origination.
Alternatively, just as one is dispassionate toward the conditioned phenomena seen, so too is one toward those not yet seen, by way of inferential knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*).
He causes cessation, not arising; he attends only to cessation. The meaning is that he sees only cessation, not arising.
Practicing in this way, he relinquishes and does not grasp. What is meant?

This contemplation of impermanence and so forth also, by means of "overcoming through substitution" (*tadaṅga*), involves the complete abandoning of defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates, through seeing the fault in the conditioned.
And because of its inclination toward Nibbāna, which is the opposite of that [suffering], there is both a relinquishment through renunciation and a relinquishment through leaping forward;
thus it is called "relinquishment by leaping forward. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this [faith] abandons the defilements in the manner already described and leaps forward into Nibbāna.
Furthermore, he does not take up the defilements by way of their production, nor does he do so by way of seeing them as unlovely.
It has conditioned phenomena as its object. Therefore it is said: "He relinquishes, he does not grasp.
Now, in order to show by means of those knowledges which phenomena are abandoned, it is said: "Contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence," and so forth.
Therein, "delight" (nandi) is craving accompanied by rapture. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

744. In the verses, however, "transitioning to another object" means that after seeing the dissolution of material form, one again sees the dissolution of the very mind by which that dissolution was seen;
thus, there is a transition from the previous object to another object by way of seeing its dissolution.

"Turning away through wisdom" means establishing oneself in the passing away [of formations] after abandoning their arising. And "the power of adverting" refers to [adverting] after having seen the dissolution of material form.
Furthermore, immediately after this, there is the capacity for adverting in order to see the dissolution of the mind that has dissolution as its object.
This is called "contemplation of reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhā-vipassanā*), which is the contemplation of the dissolution through reflection upon the object.
(745) "By means of the continuity of the object, both are determined as one": by means of the continuity of the object that has been seen directly.

The meaning is: by way of following [the sequence], one establishes both [past and future] as having the same essential nature, thinking, "Just as this [present conditioned state] has perished, so too did the category of formations perish in the past, and so too will it perish in the future.
And this was said by the ancients:
“With pure vision regarding what is presently existing,
he leads [the mind] accordingly toward the past and the future.
All conditioned things are subject to decay.”
"Like a dewdrop when the sun has risen.
"Devotion to cessation" means that, having thus established a single determination through the dissolution of both [the aggregates and the defilements],
there is devotion, earnestness, inclination, leaning toward, and biasing toward that very cessation known as dissolution.
The meaning is as follows: "Insight into the characteristic of vanishing" means that this is what is called "insight into the characteristic of vanishing.
(746) "And reflects upon the object" means having known the preceding object, such as form and so forth.

"And contemplates its dissolution" means having seen the dissolution of that object, one contemplates the dissolution of the consciousness that had that object. [He contemplates it] as empty (*suññato*).

And as for "establishment": for one who thus contemplates dissolution in this way, establishment through emptiness succeeds, [realizing] that "it is only formations that break up; their breakup is death; there is nothing else whatsoever.
Thus said the ancients:
“The aggregates cease, and there is nothing else;
the dissolution of the aggregates is called death.
One who is heedful perceives their destruction.”
“Like piercing a gem with a diamond, one should do so thoroughly.

Regarding “insight into higher wisdom” (*adhipaññā-vipassanā*): it is said that the reflection upon the object, the contemplation of dissolution, and the manifestation as empty—this is what is called insight into higher wisdom.
“Skilled in the three contemplations” means a bhikkhu who is expert in the three, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence. And the four...
"In insight" means in the four types of insight, beginning with disenchantment (*nibbidā*). "Skilled in the three modes of appearance" means through skill in these three modes of appearance:

as destruction, as vanishing, and as emptiness. "Does not waver among various views" means he does not tremble before the various kinds of views, such as the view of eternalism (*sassataditthi*) and so forth.
748. Thus, not wavering in this way, one whose attention is directed toward the fact that "only what has not ceased ceases;

only what has not broken breaks," having abandoned the signs of the arising, persistence, and occurrence of all conditioned phenomena—which are like a fragile vessel breaking, like fine dust scattering, or like sesame seeds being crushed—[contemplates] only their dissolution.

He sees them. Just as a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a lotus pond or a river, might see large water bubbles arising one after another and bursting very quickly as the rain falls in heavy drops, even so he sees:
"All conditioned phenomena are breaking up, they are breaking up."
He sees. For it was with reference to such a practitioner that the Blessed One said:
"As one might see a bubble, as one might see a mirage, so the King of Death does not see him who contemplates the world in this way."

749. For one who thus constantly sees that "all formations break up, they break up," the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution reaches its full strength, accompanied by eight benefits. These eight benefits are:
the abandoning of the view of existence, the relinquishing of attachment to life, constant application and exertion, purity of livelihood, the abandoning of striving, and freedom from fear.
The attainment of patience and gentleness, and the endurance of both the unpleasant and the pleasant.
Thus the ancients have said:
"These eight supreme qualities..."
Having seen it there, the sage contemplates it again and again,
like one whose head and clothes are on fire,
observing its dissolution for the attainment of the Deathless.
The knowledge of contemplation of dissolution is finished.
750. The Discussion of the Knowledge of the Appearance as Terror:
As he thus cultivates the contemplation of dissolution, which has as its object the destruction, fall, breakup, and cessation of all formations, [the knowledge of the appearance as terror arises].

For one who develops and cultivates this, the formations that differentiate all states of existence, wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes of beings appear as a great terror—like lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, jackals, ogres, fierce bulls, fierce dogs, rutting mad elephants, dreadful venomous snakes, assassins, discuses, charnel grounds, battlefields, and pits of glowing embers—to that timid person who desires to live in safety.
To him, it becomes clear: "Past formations have ceased; present ones are ceasing."
As he sees that even the formations that will arise in the future will cease in exactly this same way, at this point the knowledge called "the appearance of terror" arises.
Here is an illustration: it is said that a certain woman had three sons who were offenders against the king, and the king ordered their execution by beheading.
She went with her sons to the place of execution. Then, having severed the head of her eldest son—

They began to cut the middle one. Seeing that the eldest’s head had been cut off and the middle one was being cut, she abandoned her attachment to the youngest, thinking, "He too will become just like these.
In this context, that woman’s seeing the eldest son’s head cut off is like the meditator’s seeing the cessation of past formations.
The vision of the cessation of present phenomena is like seeing the head of the middle son being cut off;

the vision of the cessation of future phenomena is like relinquishing attachment to the youngest son with the thought, "He too will become just like these," thinking, "In the future, too, the formations that would arise will perish.
As he sees in this way, at this point there arises...
The knowledge of the appearance as terror.
There is another simile: it is said that a woman of putrid offspring gave birth to ten children. Of these, nine died;
one was dying in her hands, and another was still in her womb. Seeing the nine children dead and the tenth dying, she [looked at] the one in her womb...
She released her attachment [to the fetus], thinking, "This one too will be just like those.
In this context, for the practitioner, the vision of the cessation of past formations is like that woman’s recollection of the death of her nine children;
the vision of the cessation of present formations is like seeing the state of dying in one who has come into her hands; and the relinquishing of attachment to what is in the womb is...
It is like seeing the cessation of things yet to come. As he sees in this way, at that moment there arises the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*).
Now, does the knowledge of the appearance as terror feel fear or not? It does not feel fear.
For it is merely an investigation [of the fact] that past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and future ones will cease.
Therefore, just as a man with good eyesight, looking at three pits of glowing embers at a city gate, does not fear them himself, but merely observes them, thinking:
"Whoever falls into these will all experience no small amount of suffering";
or just as a man with good eyesight [sees] a stake of acacia wood, an iron stake, and a golden stake—
Just as one who gazes upon three spears set out in a row does not fear them personally,

but merely observes that "whosoever falls upon these spears will all experience no small suffering," even so the knowledge of the appearance of terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*) does not itself fear; for it merely observes those things which resemble the three spears in a pit of glowing coals.
In the three kinds of existence, which are similar to the three similes of the arrow, there is merely an investigation that "past formations have ceased,
present ones are ceasing, and future ones will cease. However, because all formations included within every state of existence,
womb, destiny, station, and abode appear to him as fearful— having fallen into calamity and being fraught with danger— it is therefore called the "appearance as fear" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*).

As for its presentation as fear, this is the text: "When one attends to [the body] as impermanent, what presents itself as fear? Suffering. When one attends to it as non-self, what presents itself as fear?
When attending to it as impermanent, the sign presents itself as fear. When attending to it as suffering..."
The occurrence appears as fear. For one who attends to [them] as non-self, both the sign and the occurrence appear as fear.
In this context, “the sign” refers to the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*). This is a designation specifically for past, future, and present formations.
For one who attends to them as impermanent sees only the death of formations; therefore, the sign appears as fear to him.

It appears. The occurrence of existence in the realms of form and the formless occurs. For one who attends to it as suffering, even that occurrence which is conventionally regarded as pleasant appears only as a state of constant oppression; thus, for him, occurrence appears as terror.
But for one who attends to it as non-self, both of these appear like an empty village, or like a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, and so forth.
And he sees it as if empty, vain, void, ownerless, and without a leader.
Therefore, both its sign (nimitta) and its occurrence (pavatta) appear to him as fearful.
Knowledge of the appearance as fear is completed.

752. For one who cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices that knowledge of the appearance as terror, no refuge, no shelter, no resort, and no protection is perceived within any state of existence, womb, destiny, station, or abode of beings.
Among all those states of existence, wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes...

Among formations (*saṅkhāra*), there is no aspiration for even a single formation, nor is there any clinging (*parāmāsa*). The three realms of existence (*bhava*) are like charcoal pits filled with glowing embers;
the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are like fierce venomous snakes; the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) are like executioners with raised swords;
the six internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) are like an empty village; and the six external bases (*bāhirāyatana*) are like the village-destroying thieves.
The seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of beings appear as if set ablaze, burning fiercely, and glowing with flames by means of the eleven fires;
and all conditioned phenomena appear like boils, like diseases, like arrows, like calamities, and like afflictions—
devoid of gratification, devoid of essence, and having become a great mass of danger.
How so? To a timid person who desires to live in comfort, even a forest thicket appearing beautiful is like one filled with tigers;
a cave is like one containing leopards; water is like one infested with crocodiles and *rakkhasas*;
enemies are like those with upraised swords; food is like that mixed with poison; a road is like one beset by robbers; a house is like one on fire; and an army is like one set for battle.

It is like a battlefield. For just as that man, having approached these thickets of reeds, forests, and so forth, becomes afraid, agitated, and his hair stands on end, seeing only danger on all sides;

even so this practitioner of yoga, through the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*), sees all conditioned phenomena as fearful, and perceives only their worthlessness, lack of sustenance, and danger on every side.
As he sees in this way, the knowledge called "knowledge of danger" arises. With reference to this it was said:
"How is it that wisdom in the appearance as terror is knowledge of danger? 'Arising is terror'—wisdom in the appearance as terror is knowledge of danger.
'Occurrence is terror'... 'The sign is terror'... 'Accumulation is terror'... 'Rebirth-linking is terror'..."
Existence is fearful... becoming is fearful... rebirth is fearful... arising is fearful... birth is fearful... aging is fearful... sickness is fearful...
death is fearful... sorrow is fearful... lamentation is fearful... despair is fearful.
Wisdom regarding the manifestation of fear is knowledge of danger. The non-arising [of these] is security; this is knowledge of the state of peace.

The knowledge of the state of peace that "non-arising is security" is knowledge of the state of peace. The knowledge that "arising is fear, non-arising is security" is knowledge of the state of peace.
The knowledge that "occurrence is fear, non-occurrence is security" is knowledge of the state of peace.

"The knowledge that 'arising is suffering' is wisdom regarding the presence of fear; it is knowledge of danger. [The same applies to] occurrence... [and so on]... The knowledge that 'despair is suffering'..."
Wisdom regarding the appearance as terror is knowledge of danger. "Non-arising is happiness": this is knowledge of the state of peace.
"Non-occurrence" ... pe ... "non-despair is happiness": this is knowledge of the state of peace. "Arising is suffering; non-arising is happiness":
this is knowledge of the state of peace. "Occurrence" ... pe ... "despair is suffering; non-despair is happiness": this is knowledge of the state of peace.

“Absence of despair is Nibbāna”: this is knowledge of the state of peace. “Arising is formations, non-arising is Nibbāna”:
this is knowledge of the state of peace. “Occurrence... [and so on] ... despair is formations, absence of despair is Nibbāna”: this is knowledge of the state of peace.
“One sees arising and occurrence, and the sign as suffering;”
This is the knowledge regarding danger: accumulation and rebirth-linking.
And this is the knowledge regarding the state of peace: non-arising, non-occurrence, signlessness, and happiness; non-accumulation and non-rebirth-linking.
“This knowledge of danger arises in five ways;
in five ways, one understands the state of peace through ten knowledges;
through proficiency in these two knowledges, one is unshaken by various views.”
“It is knowledge in the sense of having known; it is wisdom in the sense of understanding. Therefore it is said: ‘Wisdom regarding the appearance as terror is knowledge of danger. 753.
Therein, ‘arising’ is the occurrence here due to past kamma as a condition. ‘Occurrence’ is the continued process of what has thus arisen.
‘Sign’ refers to the sign of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). ‘Accumulation’ is that which serves as the cause for rebirth-linking in the future.”

Kamma is the cause. Rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is arising in the future. Destination (*gati*) is the state of existence by which that rebirth-linking occurs. Generation (*nibbatti*) is the production of the aggregates.
Re-appearance (*upapatti*) refers to the occurrence of result (*vipāka*), as described in the phrase "of one who has entered [a meditative attainment] or of one who has been reborn.
Birth (*jāti*) is birth conditioned by becoming, which serves as the condition for aging and the rest. Aging, death, and so forth are well known.

Thus it is. And here, exactly five factors—arising and so forth—are stated by way of being the objects for the knowledge of danger (*ādīnava-ñāṇa*). The remaining ones are synonyms for them. "Origination" (*nibbatti*) and "birth" (*jāti*):

this pair is a synonym for both arising (*uppāda*) and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Destination" (*gati*) and "reappearance" (*upapatti*): this pair refers to the process of existence (*pavatta*).
"Aging" (*jarā*) and so forth refer to the sign (*nimitta*). Therefore he said:
“He sees arising, occurrence, and the sign as suffering;
accumulation and rebirth-linking—this is knowledge regarding danger.
And: “This knowledge regarding danger arises in five instances.”

The passage beginning with "Non-arising is security; this is knowledge of the state of peace" is stated for the purpose of showing the knowledge that is the antidote to the knowledge of danger (*ādīnava-ñāṇa*).

Alternatively, it is stated for the purpose of producing consolation in those whose hearts are agitated after seeing danger through the manifestation of fear (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*), so that they may think:
"There is indeed fearlessness, there is security, free from danger. Or else, because its arising and so forth are [regarded] as fearsome...

They are well-established; his mind tends toward their opposites. Therefore, it should be understood that this is stated for the purpose of showing the benefit of the knowledge of danger, which is established by way of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*).

And herein, whatever is fear is necessarily suffering. That [suffering] arises from the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmisā*), the bait of the world (*lokāmisā*), and the bait of the defilements (*kilesāmisā*).
Because it is not free from attachment, it is indeed "with the material" (*sāmisam*); and that which is "with the material" is merely a conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*). Therefore, it is said:
"The wisdom that establishes fear through the thought 'arising is suffering' is knowledge of danger," and so forth.

Even though this is so, the diversity here should be understood as being solely by way of its mode of occurrence, according to the diversity of its aspects—namely, as the aspect of fear, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of the material.

“He understands ten kinds of knowledge” means that while understanding the knowledge of danger (*ādīnavañāṇa*), he understands, penetrates, and realizes ten kinds of knowledge: five having origination, etc., as their basis, and five having non-origination, etc., as their basis.
“Skill in two kinds of knowledge” means through skill in these two: namely, the knowledge of danger and the knowledge of the state of peace (*santipadañāṇa*). Regarding various views...
"It does not shake" means that it does not waver amidst views occurring through such things as the supreme Nibbāna in this very life. The rest here is self-evident.
The knowledge of contemplation of danger is finished.
Now begins the discussion on the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment.

754. Thus, seeing all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as fraught with danger, he becomes disenchanted, weary, and finds no delight in the entire range of conditioned states—including all states of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings—along with their various divisions.

Just as a golden royal swan, delighting in the foothills of Mount Cittakūṭa, finds no pleasure in the foul cesspool at the gate of a village of outcasts, but delights only in the seven great lakes; even so, this royal swan of a yogi, having clearly seen the danger, [finds no pleasure therein].

He does not delight in conditioned phenomena that are subject to disintegration. However, because he possesses a delight in meditation through his fondness for cultivation, he delights only in the seven contemplations.
And just as the lion, the king of beasts, cast into a golden cage does not find pleasure, so too [he does not delight] in that which extends over three thousand yojanas.
But he delights only in the Himalayas; likewise, this lion among yogis does not delight even in the three types of happy rebirths, but delights only in the three contemplations (anupassanā).
And just as the all-white, seven-footed, powerful, sky-faring, six-tusked king of elephants [delights] in the middle of the city...
He does not delight [in anything else], but delights only in the dense forest of the Chaddanta Lake in the Himālayas;

likewise, this elephant-like preeminent yogi does not delight in any conditioned state whatsoever, but delights only in the state of peace (santipada) seen through such methods as "non-arising is security," and his mind becomes inclined toward, slanted toward, and bent toward that.
The knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment is finished.
Furthermore, this is identical in meaning to the two preceding knowledges. Therefore the ancients said:
"The appearance as terror is one and the same, though it receives three names. One sees all formations as terrifying; thus it is called 'the appearance as terror.'"
The name "contemplation of danger" (ādīnavānupassanā) arose because it produces the perception of danger regarding those very same formations.
The name "contemplation of disenchantment" (nibbidānupassanā) arose because it arises as that which becomes disenchanted with those very same formations.
It is also said in the Pāḷi: "The wisdom in the manifestation of fear, the knowledge of danger, and disenchantment—these states have the same meaning; only the phrasing is different."
The Discourse on the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance (Muñcitukamyatāñāṇakathā) 756.
Now, by means of this knowledge of disenchantment, as this clansman becomes disenchanted, dissatisfied, and finds no delight in all formations— whether they pertain to any state of existence,
womb, destination, station of consciousness, or abode of beings, including all their various divisions— not even in a single formation...
The mind does not cling, does not adhere, and is not bound; it desires to be liberated from and to escape from all conditioned phenomena.

How so? Just as, for example, a fish caught in a net, a frog that has entered the mouth of a snake, a wild fowl confined in a cage, a deer fallen under the power of a strong snare, a snake held in the hand of a snake-charmer, or one who has plunged into a great mire.
Just as an elephant, a king of serpents who has entered the mouth of a garuḍa, the moon that has entered the mouth of Rāhu, or a man surrounded by enemies—
all such beings desire to be released from and wish to escape from their respective situations— so too,

the mind of that yogi desires to be released from and wishes to escape from the entire realm of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra). Then, for him who is thus devoid of attachment to all conditioned things...
For one who desires to be liberated from all conditioned things, there arises the knowledge of the desire for liberation.
This concludes the knowledge of the desire for liberation.
Now begins the discourse on the knowledge of contemplation by way of reflection.

757. Thus, desiring to be liberated from all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) that comprise the various states of existence, modes of birth, destinies, stations, and abodes along with their subdivisions,

he further grasps those very same conditioned phenomena by applying the three characteristics through the knowledge of contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa), in order to be liberated from the entire range of the conditioned.
Thus, he sees all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as impermanent through such reasons as: their non-finality, their being temporary,

their being delimited by arising and passing away, their disintegration, their instability, their fragility, their lack of endurance, their nature of change, their worthlessness, their dissolution, their being conditioned, and their nature of death.

Because of constant oppression, because it is suffering, because it is the basis of suffering, because it is a disease, because it is a boil, because it is an arrow, because it is a calamity, because it is an affliction,
because it is a plague, because it is a misfortune, because it is fear, because it is a disaster, because it is no refuge, because it is no shelter,

because it is no protection, because it is a danger, because it is the root of calamity, because it is a murderer, because it is subject to taints, because it is the bait of Māra, and because it is subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to illness.
One sees [the body] as suffering through such reasons as its being subject to sorrow, subject to lamentation, subject to despair, and subject to defilement.

One sees it as foul through such reasons as its being unlovely, malodorous, disgusting, repulsive, unworthy of adornment, deformed, and hideous—thus seeing it as foul because it is an adjunct to the characteristic of suffering.
One sees it as non-self through such reasons as its being other, empty, vain, void, ownerless, powerless, and lacking mastery—thus seeing it as non-self.

758. For one who sees in this way, having applied the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are said to be fully comprehended. But why does he comprehend them in this manner? It is for the purpose of providing the means for relinquishment. In this regard, there is this simile:
it is said that a certain man, thinking, "I shall catch fish," took a fish-trap and set it in the water.
Reaching his hand into the mouth of the trap, he seized a snake within the water by its neck, [thinking], "A fish..."
"I have caught it," he thought, and was delighted. Thinking, "I have indeed caught a great fish," he lifted it up;
but upon seeing it, he recognized it by the sight of the three *sovatthika* marks as being a snake. Terrified, perceiving the danger, and becoming weary of having seized it, he desired to release it.
Seeking a means to do so, he withdrew his hand starting from the tip of the snout.
Raising his arm and brandishing it over the serpent's head two or three times, he weakened the snake and released him,
saying, "Go, you wicked snake! Then, quickly climbing onto the embankment of the pond,
he stood looking back along the path he had come, thinking, "Oh, how I have been delivered from the mouth of that great serpent!"
In this context, the time when that man was satisfied after seizing the snake by the neck, thinking it was a fish,
is like the time when this practitioner is satisfied at the very outset after obtaining a personal existence.

His seeing the three auspicious marks after pulling the head out from the snake’s mouth is like this practitioner’s seeing the three characteristics in formations after performing the resolution of the compact.

The knowledge of the appearance of terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*) is like the time when that man became afraid. Then, the knowledge of contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa*) is like seeing the peril;

the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa*) is like becoming weary of grasping it. The knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*) is like the desire to let go of the snake;
and the application of the three characteristics to formations by means of the knowledge of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa*) is like employing the means for letting go.
Just as that man, having prodded the snake, weakened it, turned it back, and brought it to a state where it was incapable of biting,
releases it with a firm grip; even so, this practitioner of yoga, by applying the three characteristics, prods at formations, weakens them,
and brings them to a state where they are incapable of appearing again in the form of permanence, pleasure, beauty, or self, [and thus] releases them with a firm grip.
He releases it. Therefore it was said: “In order to accomplish the means for releasing, he comprehends in this way.
At this point, the knowledge of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa*) has arisen for him. With reference to this, it was said:
“When one attends to [the body] as impermanent, what knowledge of reflection arises? [The answer is: suffering. When one attends to it as non-self...”
"What is the knowledge of reflective contemplation that arises? When one attends to things as impermanent, the knowledge of reflective contemplation regarding the sign arises.

When one attends to them as suffering, the knowledge of reflective contemplation regarding occurrence arises. When one attends to them as non-self, the knowledge of reflective contemplation regarding both the sign and occurrence arises."
And here, "one reflects upon the sign" means that one knows the sign of formations by way of the characteristic of impermanence, [realizing it is] "unstable and temporary.
Granted, knowledge does not arise later after having first known [the object]; however, for the sake of conventional expression, it is stated thus, as in such passages as:
"Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises," and so forth. This is according to the method of identity (*ekattanaya*).
Or rather, it should be understood that this was stated by taking the preceding and the following [terms] as one.
In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the other two pairs of terms as well.
The knowledge of contemplation through reflection is concluded.

The Discussion of the Knowledge of Equanimity Towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇakathā). 760. Having thus comprehended with the knowledge of contemplation by reflection that "all formations are empty," he further comprehends the two-fold emptiness:
"This is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self. He, in this way...
Having seen neither himself nor anyone else standing as a possession of his own, he again grasps that fourfold emptiness taught here:
"I am nowhere, in relation to anything; nothing belongs to me anywhere, nor is there anything in me."
How so? For he does not see himself as "mine" anywhere;
nor does he see his self as something to be brought into the state of being a possession for anyone else.
Nor does he see it as something to be brought in by conceiving of it as a brother in the place of a brother, a companion in the place of a companion, or a requisite in the place of a requisite.
The meaning is "he does not see. Regarding the phrase "and nowhere mine," setting aside the word *mama* for a moment, "and nowhere" means that he does not see the self of another anywhere.
Now, bringing back the word *mama*, it means: "In anything whatsoever there is nothing belonging to me";
thus, he does not see that the self of another exists as something belonging to him in anything whatsoever.

The meaning is that he does not see himself in any place— whether in the position of a brother, or a companion, or a requisite— as something to be brought into the state of being a "something" (kiñcana) for another.
Thus, because he does not see himself anywhere, nor [see] that [self] as something to be brought into the state of being a "something" for another...
He sees [the self], but he does not see another’s self; he does not see another’s self as something to be brought into the state of being one's own property.
Therefore, by this, the fourfold emptiness (*suññatā*) has been discerned. 761.
Having thus discerned the fourfold emptiness, he further discerns emptiness in six ways.
How so? The eye is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, of permanence, of stability, of eternity, or of anything not subject to change...
[and so on] ...the mind is empty. Visible forms are empty... mental phenomena are empty.
Eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness. Eye-contact—and so on, the method should be applied up to aging and death.
762. Having thus discerned emptiness in six ways, he further discerns it in eight ways. Namely:
form is without core, devoid of core, and bereft of core—whether by way of the core of permanence, the core of stability, the core of happiness, or the core of self;
or by way of being permanent, stable, eternal, or not subject to change. Feeling... [and so on for the remaining aggregates].
