Perception... volitional formations... consciousness... the eye... [and so on] ...aging-and-death are without core, coreless, devoid of a core—whether by way of the core of permanence, the core of stability, the core of happiness, or the core of self;
or by way of being permanent, stable, eternal, or not subject to change. Just as a reed is without core, coreless, and devoid of a core; just as a castor-oil plant...
Just as the udumbara tree... just as the setavaccha tree... just as the pāḷibhaddaka tree... just as a mass of foam...
just as a water bubble... just as a mirage... just as the trunk of a plantain tree... just as a magical illusion is without core, devoid of core, and lacking any core—so too, form... and so on...
aging-and-death are without core, devoid of core, and lacking any core, whether by way of the core of permanence... or by way of that which is subject to changelessness.
763. Thus, having discerned emptiness (*suññatā*) in these eight ways, he further discerns it in ten ways:

he sees material form (*rūpa*) as void, as empty, as hollow, as empty, as non-self, as lacking mastery, as not acting according to one's will, as unobtainable, as being beyond one's control, and as secluded.
He sees feeling (*vedanā*)... [and so on] ...consciousness (*viññāṇa*) as void... [and so on].
"He sees it as secluded.
(764) Having thus discerned emptiness in ten ways, he further discerns it in twelve ways, as follows:
form is not a being, not a soul, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not a self, and not anything belonging to a self.
"It is not I, it is not mine, it is not another's, it belongs to no one at all. Feeling... [and so on] ...consciousness belongs to no one at all.
(765) Having thus grasped emptiness by way of twelve aspects, he again grasps emptiness by way of forty-two aspects through the comprehension of scrutiny:
"Form as impermanent... as suffering... as a disease... as a tumor... as a dart..."
As misery... as affliction... as alien... as disintegration... as an epidemic... as a calamity... as fear... as a misfortune...
as unstable... as fragile... as impermanent... as non-refuge... as non-shelter... as non-protection... as having become a non-protection...
as empty... as vain... as void... as non-self... as unsatisfactory... as fraught with peril... as subject to change... as worthless... as the root of misery.
He sees [form] as a murderer... as disintegration... as subject to taints... as conditioned... as the bait of Māra... as subject to birth... as subject to aging...
as subject to illness... as subject to death... as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair...
as arising... as passing away... as unsatisfactory... as a danger... and as an escape. He sees feeling... and so on... consciousness as impermanent... and so forth.

He sees it as an escape. And this has been said: “Seeing form as impermanent... [and so on] ...as an escape, he looks upon the world as empty. Seeing feeling... [and so on] ...consciousness as impermanent... [and so on] ...as an escape, he looks upon the world as empty.
“Always mindful, O Mogharāja, look upon the world as empty.”
“Having uprooted the view of self, one may thus transcend death;
the King of Death does not see one who contemplates the world in this way.
(766) Having thus seen [all things] as empty and applied the three characteristics, one who comprehends conditioned phenomena [abandons] both fear and delight.
Having utterly abandoned conditioned phenomena, he became indifferent and neutral; he no longer grasps at "I" or "mine," like a man who has cast off his wife.

Suppose a man had a wife who was beloved, dear, and pleasing to him, such that he could not endure being apart from her for even a moment and cherished her exceedingly; yet he saw that woman with another man...
Seeing her standing, sitting, speaking, or laughing, he would become angry and displeased, experiencing excessive dejection.

At a later time, having seen a fault in that woman and desiring to be released from her, he would dismiss her and no longer grasp at her as "mine. From that point on, [he would see her] with anyone...
Even upon seeing someone doing anything whatsoever, one should neither become angry nor fall into dejection; rather, one should simply remain indifferent and neutral.

In the same way, this person—desiring to be liberated from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*)—while comprehending those formations through the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*), does not perceive anything to be grasped as "I" or "mine," and having abandoned both fear and delight, [proceeds].
He remains indifferent and neutral toward all conditioned phenomena.

For one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind withdraws, recoils, turns back, and does not extend further toward the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings.
Either equanimity or repulsion becomes established.
Just as, for example, when a lotus leaf is slightly tilted, drops of water roll off it, shrink back from it, turn away from it, and do not spread out;
even so... [and] just as, for example, a chicken’s feather or a piece of sinew.
Just as something thrown into a fire shrinks back, recoils, turns away, and does not spread out, even so his mind regarding the three realms of existence...
[as before] ...either equanimity or revulsion becomes established. Thus, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations has arisen for him.
767. Now, if he views Nibbāna, the state of peace, as peaceful, then all the occurrence of formations...

Having relinquished [them], it leaps into Nibbāna itself. If one does not see Nibbāna as peace, then—like the "direction-crow" of seafarers—it continues to proceed with formations alone as its object.
It is said that when merchants going by sea set out on their ships, they take along a so-called "direction-crow.
When their ship is driven by the wind toward a foreign land and the shore is no longer visible, [the crow serves as their guide].
Then they release a directional crow. Standing on the rim of the well, it leaps into the air and traverses all the cardinal and intermediate directions;
if it sees the bank, it goes straight toward it. If it does not see it, it returns again and again and clings to the very rim of the well.
In the same way, if the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations [sees] the state of peace, Nibbāna...
If he sees [the goal] continuously, having relinquished the entire process of conditioned formations (*saṅkhārappavatta*), he enters exclusively into *nibbāna*.
If he does not see it, it proceeds again and again, taking only conditioned formations as its object.
This is like flour being rolled into a ball on a well-polished surface, or like cotton that has been spun being beaten. In various ways...
Having comprehended formations and abandoned both fear and delight, he stands with equanimity toward the investigation of formations by way of the threefold contemplation.
Standing thus, having attained the state of being an entrance to the threefold liberation,
he becomes a condition for the classification of the seven noble persons.
768. Herein, because it proceeds by way of three kinds of contemplation, it attains the state of being the three gateways to liberation through the predominance of the three faculties.
For the three contemplations are called the three gateways to liberation. As it is said:
"These three gateways to liberation lead to the escape from the world: [the contemplation of] all formations as limited and circumscribed..."
These three are: through the contemplation [of all formations] as impermanent and the leaping of the mind into the signless element;
through the inciting of the mind toward all formations and the leaping of the mind into the desireless element;
and through the contemplation of all phenomena as other and the leaping of the mind into the empty element.
“The doors to liberation lead to the world’s transcendence.
In this context, “delimited and circumscribed” means both by way of delimitation and by way of circumscription through [observing] arising and passing away.
For in the contemplation of impermanence, one first delimits [formations] by thinking, “Before their arising, formations did not exist,” and then [observes] their course...
Investigating them, he perceives them as being enclosed, seeing that "they do not go beyond their own age; they simply vanish right here.

"By way of mental agitation" means by way of causing a sense of urgency in the mind. For it is through the contemplation of suffering that one causes the mind to feel urgency regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"By way of perceiving them as other" means by way of perceiving them as non-self (*anattā*), thus: "I am not this; this is not mine."
Thus, it should be understood that these three terms are stated by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth.
For this very reason, it is said in the subsequent answer to the question: "To one who attends to [formations] as impermanent, they appear as destruction;
to one who attends to them as suffering, they appear as terror; to one who attends to them as non-self, they appear as void."
769. But which are those liberations of which these contemplations are the gateways? They are these three: the signless, the desireless, and the void.
For it has been said: "One who attends to [the object] as impermanent and is abundant in resolution attains the signless liberation.
One who attends to it as suffering and is abundant in tranquility attains the desireless liberation."
“He attains it. One who attends to [the aggregates] as non-self, being rich in wisdom, attains the void liberation.
And here, the signless liberation is the noble path that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object through the signless aspect.
For it is “signless” because it has arisen in the signless element, and it is “liberation” because it is liberated from the defilements. By this very same [principle...]

It should be understood that it is "wishless" when it proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object through the mode of the wishless (*appaṇihita-ākāra*), and it is "emptiness" when it proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object through the mode of emptiness (*suññata-ākāra*).
Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the Abhidhamma: "At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the dismantling [of the aggregates]..."

"For the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual desires, one enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is wishless and empty"—thus only these two liberations are mentioned; this is said with reference to the approach to insight in its direct sense.
For although insight-knowledge is described in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*—
“Knowledge of contemplation of impermanence releases adherence to permanence; knowledge of contemplation of suffering releases adherence to pleasure;
knowledge of contemplation of non-self releases adherence to self—thus it is the void liberation by way of releasing adherence.
In this way, it is called the void liberation by way of releasing adherence.
“Knowledge of contemplation of impermanence releases the sign of permanence;
knowledge of contemplation of suffering releases the sign of pleasure; knowledge of contemplation of non-self releases the sign of self.
Thus, it is called ‘the signless liberation’ by way of releasing the sign. In this way, it is the signless liberation through the relinquishing of signs.
“Knowledge of contemplation of impermanence releases longing for permanence; knowledge of contemplation of suffering releases longing for pleasure;
knowledge of contemplation of non-self releases longing for self—thus it is the ‘wishless liberation’ by way of releasing longing.
Thus it is called the wishless liberation by way of releasing longing.
It has been stated. Nevertheless, because it does not abandon the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), it is not "signless" (*animitta*) in the absolute sense.

In the absolute sense, however, it is both "emptiness" (*suññatā*) and "wishless" (*appaṇihita*). And it is by way of its arrival that liberation is specified at the moment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Therefore, it should be understood that only these two liberations—namely, the wishless and the empty—are what have been spoken of. This...
This concludes the discussion on liberation here.
As for what was stated, "it serves as a condition for the classification of the seven noble persons," therein are:

the follower by faith (saddhānusārī), the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutto), the body-witness (kāyasakkhi), the one liberated both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutto), the follower of the Dhamma (dhammānusārī), the one attained to view (diṭṭhippatto), and the one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutto).
These, then, are the seven noble persons (*ariyapuggala*); for their classification, this knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*) serves as the condition. 772.

For one who attends to [formations] as impermanent, being abundant in resolution, acquires the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*); such a person is a "follower by faith" (*saddhānusārī*) at the moment of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*). In the remaining seven instances, he is "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*). 773.
But one who attends to them as suffering, being abundant in tranquility, acquires the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*); such a person...
In all cases, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhi). However, having attained formless jhāna and reached the highest fruit, he is called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta).

But he who, attending to [the aggregates] as non-self, possesses abundant feeling and acquires the faculty of wisdom, becomes a "follower by Dhamma" (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the stream-entry path. Having attained vision in the six stages, he is "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta) at the highest fruit.
For this has been said:

“When one attends to [the aggregates] as impermanent, the faculty of faith becomes preeminent. Because the faculty of faith is preeminent, one attains the path of stream-entry; therefore, one is called a ‘faith-follower’ (saddhānusārī). Likewise:

“When one attends to [the aggregates] as impermanent, the faculty of faith becomes preeminent. Because the faculty of faith is preeminent, the fruit of stream-entry is realized; therefore, one is called a ‘liberated by faith’ (saddhāvimutto),” and so forth. Furthermore, it is said:
“One who is liberated by believing is a faith-liberated one (*saddhāvimutta*). One who has touched and realized [the goal] is a body-witness (*kāyasakkhi*).
One who has reached the view is one attained-to-view (*diṭṭhippatto*). One who is liberated while believing is a faith-liberated one.
One who first touches the contact of jhāna and subsequently realizes cessation, Nibbāna, is a body-witness. ‘Formations are suffering; Nibbāna is bliss.’”
"Cessation" is known, seen, understood, realized, touched, and reached by means of wisdom; thus one is "attained to vision.
Regarding the other four: one who follows through faith, or who follows and proceeds by means of faith, is a "follower by faith" (*saddhānusārī*).
Likewise, one who follows the Dhamma consisting of wisdom, or who follows by means of the Dhamma, is a "follower of the Dhamma" (*dhammānusārī*). By means of formless jhāna...
And because he is liberated both by means of the noble path and [by means of concentration], he is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).
"Liberated while understanding" means "liberated through wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*); such is how the meaning of the terms should be understood.
This concludes the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*).
778. However, this [knowledge] is identical in meaning to the two preceding kinds of knowledge. Thus the ancients said: “This knowledge of equanimity towards formations receives three names:
in the beginning it is called ‘knowledge of the desire for deliverance’; in the middle it is called ‘knowledge of contemplation of reflection’;
and at the end, having reached its culmination, it is called ‘knowledge of equanimity towards formations’.”
779. It is also stated in the Pāḷi:

“How is it that the wisdom of desire for deliverance, of reflection, and of composure regarding formations is knowledge of equanimity towards formations? The wisdom of desire for deliverance, of reflection, and of composure regarding arising is knowledge of equanimity towards formations. [The wisdom of desire for deliverance, of reflection, and of composure regarding] occurrence... [and so on].”
“Wisdom as the desire for deliverance, as reflexion, and as composure regarding the signs... and so on... and regarding despair, is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
‘Arising is suffering’... and so on... ‘it is a terror’... and so on... ‘it is worldly’... and so on... ‘arising is formations’... and so on... ‘despair is formations’:
wisdom as the desire for deliverance, as reflexion, and as composure regarding these is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.”
780. Therein, "desire for deliverance, reflection, and composure" refers to desire for deliverance, reflection, and composure.
Thus, in the preliminary stage, for one who is weary through the knowledge of disenchantment, the desire to abandon arising and so forth is "desire for deliverance.

The "reflection" in the middle stage is the act of reflecting for the purpose of employing the means to deliverance. The "composure" at the conclusion is the state of equanimity after having delivered oneself.
Stilling. It is with reference to this that it was said: “Arising is formations; one looks on with equanimity at those formations, thus it is equanimity about formations,” and so forth.
Thus, this is indeed one single knowledge.
Furthermore, by this scriptural passage as well, it should be understood that this is one alone. For it is said: “And that which is the desire for deliverance...”
"Both reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*) and equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) are states that have the same meaning; only the phrasing is different.
(782) Now, for this clansman who has thus attained equanimity towards formations, his insight has reached its culmination and becomes "leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*).
Whether it is called "insight that has reached its culmination" or "leading to emergence," it refers precisely to the triad of knowledges beginning with equanimity towards formations.
This is its name. For she has reached the "crest" (sikhā), that is, the state of excellence; thus she is "one who has reached the crest" (sikhāppattā). She goes toward emergence (vuṭṭhāna);
thus she is "one who goes toward emergence" (vuṭṭhānagāminī). "Emergence" refers to the Path, because it emerges from the object clung to as an external sign and from what proceeds internally;
she goes toward that, thus she is "one who goes toward emergence," meaning she is joined with the Path.
783. Herein, this is the matrix for the purpose of clarifying the emergence from the objects of misapprehension:
having misapprehended internally, one emerges from the internal; having misapprehended internally, one emerges from the external; having misapprehended externally, one emerges from the external;
having misapprehended externally, one emerges from the internal; having misapprehended form, one [emerges] from forms...
One emerges; having focused on the form realm, one emerges from the formless realm; having focused on the formless realm, one emerges from the formless realm;
having focused on the formless realm, one emerges from the form realm; one emerges from the five aggregates all at once;
having focused on impermanence, one emerges from impermanence; having focused on impermanence, one emerges from suffering and from non-self.

Having adhered to [the formations] as suffering, one emerges from them as suffering, as impermanent, and as non-self; having adhered to them as non-self, one emerges from them as non-self, as impermanent, and as suffering. How so?
Here, a certain person first adheres to internal formations; having adhered to them...

He sees. However, since the emergence of the path does not occur through the mere vision of the internal alone, but must also be seen externally, he sees even the aggregates of another and even non-clung-to formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
At times he contemplates internally, and at times externally. As he thus contemplates, within himself—
At the time of contemplating internally, insight joins with the path; this is called "having entered within, emerging from within.
But if, at the time of contemplating externally, insight joins with the path, this is called "having entered within, emerging externally.
This same method applies to entering externally and emerging externally.
And internally, even in the emergence [from concentration].
785. Another person, from the very beginning, adheres to form; having adhered, he sees both primary form (*bhūtarūpa*) and derived form (*upādārūpa*) as a mass.
However, since emergence does not occur through the mere seeing of form alone, [he must also see] the formless (*arūpa*).

It must indeed be seen. Therefore, having taken that form as an object, one sees the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that have arisen in dependence upon it as "this is the formless," and thus one sees the formless. At times he comprehends form, and at times the formless.
As he thus comprehends, at the time of comprehending form, insight joins with the path; this is called "emerging from form after having been intent upon form."

But if, at the time of contemplating the formless, his insight joins with the path, this is called "emerging from the formless after having been intent upon the formless. This same method applies to emerging from both the formless and the formed after having been intent upon the formless.

However, when one emerges in exactly the same way after being intent upon the thought, "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation," one is said to emerge simultaneously by means of the five aggregates.

787. One person, from the very beginning, comprehends formations as impermanent. However, since emergence does not occur through the mere comprehension of them as impermanent alone, but must also be comprehended as suffering and as non-self, he therefore comprehends them as suffering and as non-self.
For one who has practiced in this way, emergence occurs at the time of comprehending them as impermanent; this is [the path] regarding impermanence.
Having applied himself [to the object], he is said to emerge by way of impermanence.
However, if his emergence occurs at the time of comprehending it as suffering or as non-self, this is called "having applied himself to it as impermanent, he emerges as suffering or as non-self.
This same method applies to the remaining modes of emergence when one has applied oneself to it as suffering or as non-self.
788. And herein, whether one is intent upon impermanence, or suffering, or non-self, at the time of emergence, there is emergence by way of impermanence.
All three types of persons abound in resolve; they acquire the faculty of faith;
they are liberated by the signless liberation; and at the moment of the first path, they are followers by faith (*saddhānusārī*) in seven respects.

They are liberated through faith. However, if there is emergence from suffering, all three persons abound in tranquility, acquire the faculty of concentration, are liberated by means of the signless liberation, and are body-witnesses in every respect.
Furthermore, he for whom formless jhāna serves as the basis becomes one liberated in both ways regarding the highest fruit.

Then, as they emerge from [the perception of] non-self, all three persons become abundant in feeling, acquire the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), and are liberated by the void liberation (suññatavimokkha).

At the moment of the first path, they are followers by Dhamma (dhammānusārino); having attained vision in six respects, they are those liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) at the fruit of the highest attainment.

789. Now, twelve similes should be understood for the purpose of clarifying this insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāmini-vipassanā*), together with the preceding and succeeding knowledges. This is their summary verse (*uddāna*):
“The bat, the black snake, the house, the cow, the *yakkhinī*, and the boy;
hunger, thirst, cold, heat, darkness, and by poison.”
These similes could be brought forward from any point in the knowledge beginning with the appearance as terror;
however, when they are brought forward at this particular stage, everything from the appearance as terror up to the knowledge of the fruit becomes clear.
Therefore, it is said that they should be brought forward right here.

790. Regarding the *vaggulī*: it is said that a certain flying-fox (*vaggulī*) thought, "I shall find flowers or fruit here," and having settled upon a five-branched *madhuka* tree, she touched one branch but did not see there any flower or fruit fit to be taken.
Just as with the first, so too with the second, the third, and the fourth. She even touched the fifth branch...
Having searched, she saw nothing. Thinking, "Alas, this tree is fruitless;

there is nothing here worth taking," she relinquished her attachment to that tree, climbed straight up a branch, poked her head out through a gap in the foliage, looked upward, sprang into the air, and alighted upon another fruit-bearing tree.
In this context, the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) is to be seen as like the bat; the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are like the five-branched honey-tree;
the practitioner’s adherence (*abhinivesa*) to the pentad of aggregates is like the bat’s settling upon it;

and the practitioner’s examination of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is like the bat’s grasping one branch after another and, finding nothing there worth taking, moving on to grasp the remaining branches.
Having surveyed that [tree] and not seeing anything there worth grasping, he surveys the remaining aggregates;

this is like the tree-climber’s relinquishing his attachment to the tree. For the yogi who has become disenchanted by seeing the characteristics of impermanence and so forth in all five aggregates, there arises the triad of knowledge beginning with the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*); this is like climbing further up the straight branch.
For the meditator, the knowledge of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is like lifting the head and looking upward;
the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa) is like leaping into the air; and the knowledge of the fruit (phala-ñāṇa) is like perching on another fruit tree.

The simile of the black snake has already been explained in the section on the knowledge of reflection (paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa). However, in this context, regarding the coordination of the similes, the "releasing of the snake" refers to the knowledge of reflection.

The knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is like [the state] of one who has departed; the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa) is like the position of one looking back at the road already traveled after having released [the burden];
and the knowledge of the fruit (phala-ñāṇa) is like the position of one who has gone and stands in a place of fearlessness—this is the distinction.
792. Regarding "house": it is said that when the master of the house has eaten his evening meal, ascended to his bed, and fallen asleep, the house [is empty].
It was ablaze; having awakened and seen the fire, he thought, “It would be well indeed if I could escape without being burned.
Looking about, he saw a path, and having emerged, he went quickly to a place of safety and stood there.
In this regard, just as the master of the house, after eating and ascending to his bed, fell asleep, so too does the foolish worldling [perceive] within the five aggregates: “I...”

The grasping [of the aggregates] as "mine. Just as the time of being terrified upon waking and seeing the fire, so is the knowledge of the appearance of fear (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*) after having entered the right practice.
Just as looking toward the path of escape, so is the knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*).
Just as the sight of the path, so is conformity (*anuloma*). Just as the act of escaping, so is the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*). Just as traveling with speed...
Knowledge of the path is like reaching a place of safety; knowledge of the fruit is like standing in that place of safety.
793. Regarding the "cow": it is said that one farmer fell asleep during the night, and his oxen broke through the fence and fled.
At dawn, he went there and, looking about, realized they had escaped; following their tracks...
Having gone there, he saw the king’s oxen. Thinking, “These are my oxen,” he began to lead them away. At dawn, however, realizing, “These are not my oxen;
they are the king’s oxen,” he became terrified, thinking, “I must flee right now before the king’s men seize me as a thief and bring about my ruin. Abandoning the oxen, he fled with great speed.
He stood in a place free from fear. Therein, the grasping of the aggregates by the foolish worldling as "I" and "mine" is like the king's oxen being seized [by someone] thinking, "These are my oxen.

The yogi’s perception of the aggregates as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self" by way of the three characteristics is like the recognition at dawn that they are the king's oxen. The knowledge of the appearance of terror is like the time when one is afraid.
The desire to be released is like the desire to depart after having cast off [the burden]; the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) is like the casting off; the path (*magga*) is like the flight;
and the fruit (*phala*) is like standing in a place of safety after having fled.
794. Regarding the term "Yakkhī": it is said that a certain man lived in cohabitation with a female spirit (*yakkhinī*). During the night...
Thinking, "She is asleep," he went to the charnel ground and ate human flesh.
Following her, wondering, "Where is she going?", he saw her eating human flesh; realizing she was a non-human being, he thought, "I will flee before she eats me.
Terrified, he fled with great speed and stood in a safe place. There—
The grasping at the aggregates as "I" and "mine" is like cohabiting with a female spirit (yakkhinī);

the recognition of the aggregates' three characteristics after seeing them as impermanent and so forth is like knowing, upon seeing a woman eating human flesh in a charnel ground, "This is a female spirit";

the manifestation of fear is like the time of being terrified; the desire for liberation is like the desire to flee; and the abandoning of the charnel ground is like [the departure from the aggregates].
The change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) is like [the initial] movement; the path (magga) is like fleeing with speed; the fruit (phala) is like standing in a place of safety. 795. Regarding "the child":
it is said there was a certain woman who was greedy for her son.
While sitting on the upper terrace of the palace, she heard the sound of a child in the street and thought, "Is my son being harmed by someone? She went in haste, thinking, "It is my own son," and...
She took another man’s son, perceiving him through her perception (*saññā*). Having recognized him as "this is another man’s son," she felt ashamed;
looking here and there, thinking, "Lest someone should say of me, 'This woman is a child-thief,'" she set the boy down right there and quickly climbed back up to the palace and sat down.
In this case, the taking of another man’s son occurred through the perception that it was her own son.

The grasping at the five aggregates as “I” and “mine” is like [the mother’s] perception; the perception that “this is another’s child” by way of the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) is like the perception that “it is not I, nor mine”;
the manifestation of fear (bhayatupaṭṭhāna) is like being struck with alarm; the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa) is like looking here and there;
the conformity (anuloma) is like setting the child down right there; and having set him down, [walking] along the street...
The lineage (gotrabhu) is like the time of standing still; the path (magga) is like the act of climbing the palace; the fruit (phala) is like sitting down after having climbed.

(796) Furthermore, these six similes—of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, darkness, and poison—are stated for the purpose of showing that for one established in insight leading to emergence, there is a state of inclining, leaning, and tending toward supramundane states.
Just as a man overcome by hunger and suffering from great famishment longs for food of delicious flavor,

even so this practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara), touched by the famishment of the round of existence (saṃsāra), longs for the food of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) which has the taste of the Deathless (amata).

And just as a thirsty man, with his throat and mouth parched, longs for a drink composed of many ingredients, even so this practitioner of yoga, touched by the thirst of the round of existence, longs for the noble Eightfold Path (ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga) as his drink.

Just as a person touched by cold longs for heat, even so this practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara), touched by the cold of the oil of craving within the cycle of existence (saṃsāravaṭṭa), longs for the fire of the Path that burns away the defilements (kilesa).

And just as a person touched by heat longs for cold, even so this practitioner of yoga, scorched by the eleven fires of suffering within the cycle of existence, longs for Nibbāna, the allaying of those eleven fires.

Just as a man enveloped in darkness longs for light, even so this practitioner of yoga, shrouded and completely covered by the darkness of ignorance, longs for the light of knowledge, which is the cultivation of the path.

And just as a man struck by poison longs for an antidote that destroys the poison, even so this practitioner of yoga, struck by the poison of the defilements, longs for Nibbāna, the deathless medicine that crushes the poison of the defilements. Therefore it was said: "To him who, in this way..."
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind recoils, shrinks back, turns away, and does not extend toward the three realms of existence...
[and so on] ...toward the nine abodes of beings. Either equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
This is just as when a lotus leaf is slightly tilted; all this should be understood according to the method already explained above.
And to this extent he is called one who "lives withdrawn," with reference to whom it was said:
"For the bhikkhu who lives withdrawn,
resorting to a secluded seat..."
“They say that is his harmony,
who does not show himself in becoming.
Thus, this knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa), having established the state of the practitioner’s reclusiveness, [leads] further to the Noble Path as well.

It determines the specific distinction of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*), path factors (*maggaṅga*), jhāna factors (*jhānaṅga*), the way of practice (*paṭipadā*), and the liberations (*vimokkha*). For some elders say that the basis-jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) determines the distinction between the enlightenment factors, path factors, and jhāna factors.
Some say that the aggregates (*khandha*) which serve as the object of insight (*vipassanā*) determine it.
Some say that the individual's inclination (*puggalajjhāsaya*) determines it. Regarding their various assertions, this...
It should be understood that it is specifically the insight leading to emergence in the prior stage (*pubbabhāga*) that determines [the plane of rebirth].
798. Herein, this is the sequential explanation: for by the determination of insight, the path arises even for a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*);
and for one who attains meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the path arises even without making jhāna the basis (*pādaka*); and for one who makes the first jhāna the basis...
Even for one who has generated the path after having comprehended miscellaneous formations, the [paths] belong only to the first jhāna.
In all these cases, there are seven factors of enlightenment, eight factors of the path, and five jhāna factors.
For their preliminary insight, whether accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity, at the time of emergence, reaches the state of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

It is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*). In the system of the fivefold jhāna, when the second, third, and fourth jhānas are made the basis (*pādaka*) for the paths that have been produced, the jhāna in those respective orders consists of four factors, three factors, and two factors. However, in all cases, there are seven path-factors (*maggaṅga*).
In the fourth [path], there are six enlightenment-factors (*bojjhaṅga*). This distinction arises both from the restriction of the basis-jhāna and...
And it occurs by way of the fixed sequence of insight (vipassanā-niyama). For even their preliminary insight may be accompanied by joy (somanassa) or accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā);

however, the insight leading to emergence is invariably accompanied by joy. But in the path produced by taking the fifth jhāna as its basis, there are two jhāna factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—and six or seven enlightenment factors and path factors respectively.
This distinction also occurs by way of the double restriction. For according to this method, preliminary insight is either accompanied by joy or accompanied by equanimity;
however, the path leading to emergence is invariably accompanied by equanimity.
The same principle applies even to the paths produced by taking the formless jhānas as the basis. Thus, having emerged from the basic jhāna and having comprehended any formations whatsoever—
The attainment that has emerged in the vicinity of the path already produced makes itself conform to the nature of that path, just as the color of the ground conforms to the color of a lizard.

According to the second Elder’s teaching, however, whichever attainment one emerges from and whichever factors of that attainment one comprehends before the path is produced, the path becomes similar to that specific attainment.
In this case too, the rule regarding insight (vipassanā) should be understood according to the method already stated.

800. According to the third Elder’s teaching, whichever jhāna one takes as the basis (pādaka) in accordance with one's own inclination, and whichever jhāna-factors one contemplates (sammasita), the path that is produced will be similar to that specific jhāna.
However, that [path] is not accomplished by mere inclination alone without either the basis-jhāna or the contemplated-jhāna. This matter is established by the Nandakovāda Sutta.
It should be illustrated. Here too, the fixed order of insight (vipassanā) is to be understood according to the method already stated.

Thus, first of all, it should be understood that equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) determines the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the path factors (maggaṅga), and the jhāna factors (jhānaṅga).
801. However, if this [equanimity] from the beginning suppresses the defilements with difficulty, with effort, and with volitional activity (sasaṅkhāra)...
When one is unable to suppress the defilements, it is called the "painful progress. Conversely, it is the "pleasant progress.
However, when the defilements have been suppressed and insight proceeds slowly toward its maturation and the manifestation of the path, it is called "slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiññā*).
Conversely, it is "quick direct knowledge" (*khippābhiññā*). Thus, this equanimity regarding formations stands in the position of that which is to be arrived at.
Each [path] receives the name of its own respective path; thus, the path acquires four names.
However, this practice (paṭipadā) is different for some bhikkhus, while for others it is the same across all four paths.
For the Buddhas, however, all four paths were characterized by pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā). The same was true for the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati).
For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, however, the first path was easy to practice and swift in direct knowledge;
the three subsequent paths were difficult to practice and sluggish in direct knowledge.

Just as with the modes of practice (*paṭipadā*), so too the dominant factors (*adhipati*) differ for some bhikkhu across the four paths, while for others they remain the same throughout all four. Thus, equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) [is distinguished] by the specific mode of practice.
It determines. As to how it determines a specific liberation, that has already been explained above.

Furthermore, the term "path" (magga) receives its name for five reasons: either by its own essence (sarasena), or by its opposite (paccanīkena), or by its qualities (saguṇena), or by its object (ārammaṇena), or by its arrival (āgamanena).
For if equanimity regarding formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), having comprehended formations as impermanent...

He emerges; he is liberated by means of the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*). If he emerges after having comprehended [formations] as suffering, he is liberated by means of the desireless liberation (*appaṇihitavimokkha*).

If he emerges after having comprehended them as non-self, he is liberated by means of the void liberation (*suññatavimokkha*). This is what is called "emergence by way of its own essence" (*sarasato nāma*).

For, by means of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), he effects the resolution of the compactness of formations and [abandons] the signs of permanence, the signs of stability, and the signs of eternity.

Because he has come having abandoned [craving], it is "signless" (*animitta*). Because he has come having abandoned the perception of pleasure and having dried up longing and aspiration through the contemplation of suffering, it is "desireless" (*appaṇihita*).

Because he has come having abandoned the perception of self, being, and person through the contemplation of non-self, and because he has seen conditioned phenomena as empty, it is "empty" (*suññata*); this is its name derived from its opposite.

Furthermore, it is called "void" (*suññata*) because it is void of lust and the rest; "signless" (*animitta*) because of the absence of the signs of form and so forth, or specifically the signs of lust and so forth; and "wishless" (*appaṇihita*) because of the absence of the longing for lust and so forth—this is its name according to its qualities.
Moreover, it is called "void," "signless," and "wishless" because it takes as its object Nibbāna, which is void, signless, and wishless—this is its name according to its object.
Now, arrival is twofold: arrival by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and arrival by way of the path (*magga*). Among these, arrival by way of insight occurs in the path.
One attains the arrival at the path within the fruit. For the contemplation of non-self is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*); the path of emptiness-insight is "empty.
The contemplation of impermanence is called "signless" (*animittā*); the path of signless-insight is "signless.
However, these names are not obtained according to the Abhidhamma method; they are obtained according to the Sutta method. Therein:

For they say that the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), having made the signless Nibbāna its object and thus itself becoming "signless," stands in the place where it is to arrive and bestows the name upon the Path. Therefore, the Path is called "signless.
Furthermore, it is indeed logical that through the arrival of the Path, the Fruit is also signless. Contemplation of suffering dries up the aspiration for conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Because it has come from that [equanimity], it is called "wishless"; the path of wishless insight is wishless, and the fruit of the wishless path is wishless.
Thus, insight gives its own name to the path, and the path [gives its name] to the fruit;
this is the name according to the source of arrival (*āgamanato*). In this way, this equanimity regarding formations determines the specific liberation.
The knowledge of equanimity towards formations is completed.
804. Discourse on Conformity Knowledge:
For one who practices, develops, and cultivates that knowledge of equanimity towards formations, resolute confidence (*adhimokkha-saddhā*) [arises].
A more powerful state arises; energy is well-sustained, mindfulness is well-established, the mind is well-concentrated, and a sharper equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) emerges.

Then, thinking "Now the Path will arise," he comprehends those formations as impermanent, suffering, or non-self through equanimity toward formations, and sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Immediately after the life-continuum...

In the same manner as was done with equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) arises taking formations as its object— either as impermanent, or as suffering, or as non-self. Then,
having turned back from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), immediately after that functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*) which has arisen,
it occurs in an uninterrupted succession of mental states, likewise [taking] formations [as its object].
Taking that as its object, the first impulsion-consciousness arises; this is called "preliminary work" (*parikamma*).
Immediately after that, taking those same formations as its object, the second impulsion-consciousness arises; this is called "access" (*upacāra*).
Immediately after that as well, taking those same formations as its object, the third impulsion-consciousness arises; this...
"Conformity" (anuloma) is what is said. This is its specific name.
However, generally speaking, all three of these—repetition (āsevana), preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), and conformity (anuloma)—may appropriately be called by those names.
To what is it conforming? It conforms to both the preceding and the succeeding parts; for it conforms to the eight preceding [moments].
It conforms to the insight-knowledges (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) because it performs their proper function, and it conforms to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) that follow.
For, since it proceeds by taking conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as its object through the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, it is said:

"Indeed, the knowledge of arising and passing away has seen the arising and passing away only of those phenomena that possess arising and passing away," and "Indeed, [it has seen] only those that possess dissolution..."
"Indeed, contemplation of dissolution has seen dissolution"; "Indeed, that which is fearful has appeared as fearful to the appearance-of-fear";
"Indeed, contemplation of danger has seen danger in that which is dangerous"; "Indeed, the knowledge of disenchantment has become disenchanted with that which is to be disenchanted with";
"Indeed, the knowledge of desire-for-deliverance desires deliverance from that which is to be delivered from."

It conforms to the true function of these eight knowledges as they speak, in effect: "It has arisen," "It has indeed been reflected upon by the knowledge of reflection," and "It has indeed been looked upon with equanimity by equanimity toward formations";
and it is through that [equanimity] that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment follow above.
Because it is to be attained through practice.
For just as a righteous king, seated in the place of judgment, having heard the decision of the judges,
abandons any course of error and, remaining impartial, expresses his approval by saying, "So be it," regarding that decision— so too [is this practice].
It conforms to the ancient royal law; this is how it should be understood.
For conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) is like the king, the eight knowledges are like the eight chief judges, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are like the ancient royal law.
In this regard, just as the king, saying "Let it be so," [approves] the decision of the judges...

It conforms to the duty of a king; likewise, this knowledge arising with reference to formations by way of impermanence and so forth conforms to the eight knowledges through their performing their respective functions, and further, to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
For that very reason, it is called "knowledge conforming to the truths."
Knowledge of conformity is finished.
805. Furthermore, this knowledge of conformity is the conclusion of the insight leading to emergence, which has formations as its object.
It exists. However, the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) is the culmination of the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*).
Now, for the sake of non-confusion regarding that very insight leading to emergence, this correlation with the Suttas should be understood.
It is as follows:
For this insight leading to emergence is described as "non-identification" in the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta:
"Monks, depending on non-identification, resorting to non-identification, abandon that equanimity which is unified and based on unity; transcend it.
Thus it is called non-identification.
In the *Alagaddasutta*, it is stated as "disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated," thus it is called disenchantment (*nibbidā*).

In the *Susimasutta*, it is stated as "First, Susīma, is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*); afterwards is the knowledge of Nibbāna," thus it is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
In the *Poṭṭhapādasutta*, it is stated as "Perception, Poṭṭhapāda, arises first; afterwards comes knowledge," thus it is called the summit of perception (*saññagga*).
In the Dasuttara Sutta, it is stated as “the factor of striving for complete purity, which is the purification of knowledge and vision of the way.

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is stated by three names thus: “The desire for deliverance, the contemplation of reflection, and equanimity regarding formations—these states have the same meaning, differing only in expression.
In the Paṭṭhāna, it is stated by three names thus: “adaptation to change-of-lineage; adaptation to cleansing.”

In the *Rathavinīta Sutta*, it is stated: "But, friend, for the sake of purification by knowledge and vision of the way is the holy life lived under the Blessed One? Thus, purification by knowledge and vision of the way is described.
In these various names, that pure insight which leads to emergence has been extolled by the Great Seer.
"One who desires to emerge from the great terror of the mire of suffering in *saṃsāra* should constantly apply effort therein, being of a wise nature.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Visuddhimagga*, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way," in the Section on the Development of Wisdom.
22. The Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision:
The First Discussion on Path-Knowledge 806.

From this point on, there is change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*). Because it stands in the place of adverting to the path, it is neither purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*)...
It does not partake in the purification by knowledge and vision; rather, it remains intermediate and indeterminate.

However, because it falls within the stream of insight (*vipassanā*), it is designated as "insight. As for the four paths—the path of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the path of non-returning, and the path of arahantship—knowledge regarding these is called "purification by knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).
In this regard, for one who wishes to accomplish the knowledge of the first path, there is nothing else whatsoever that needs to be done.
For whatever he ought to do has already been performed by him while generating insight up to the conclusion of conformity.

However, for him whose knowledge of conformity has thus arisen, those three types of conformity-knowledge [serve to remove] the coarse obscurations of the truths according to their respective strengths.
When that [state] has vanished, the mind does not leap forward toward any conditioned phenomena;
it does not settle, does not resolve upon them, does not cling, does not adhere, and is not bound by them.
Like water on a lotus leaf, it shrinks back, recoils, and turns away. All objects of signs and all objects of occurrence are seen as obstacles.
It appears. Then, when all objects consisting of signs and their occurrences have appeared as obstacles, at the conclusion of the repetition of conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa),
it takes as its object the signless, non-occurrence, unconditioned cessation that is Nibbāna— thereby transcending the lineage of worldlings,
the designation of worldling, and the plane of worldlings, and entering the lineage of the Noble Ones, the designation of Noble One.

As one enters the noble plane, the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) arises—having reached its peak, being the summit of insight, and non-returning—which, directed toward Nibbāna as its object, establishes itself as a condition for the Path in six ways: by way of proximity, contiguity, repetition, decisive support, presence, and absence;
and which constitutes the first turning toward, the first application of attention, and the first act of coordination.
It was with reference to this that it was said:
“How is it that wisdom regarding emergence and turning away from the external is knowledge of change-of-lineage? It overcomes arising, thus it is ‘change-of-lineage’ (gotrabhu).
It overcomes occurrence... [and so on] ...it overcomes despair, thus it is ‘change-of-lineage’. It overcomes the sign of formations externally, thus...”

"The change-of-lineage (gotrabhu): it 'launches out' into non-arising, thus it is change-of-lineage. It launches out into non-occurrence... [and so on] ...into cessation, Nibbāna, which is without despair;
thus it is change-of-lineage. Having overcome arising, it launches out into non-arising; thus it is change-of-lineage. All of this should be expanded in detail.

807. Herein, this is a simile illustrating how the *anuloma* (adaptation) and *gotrabhū* (change-of-lineage) states, though occurring in a single cognitive series through a single adverting consciousness, nevertheless operate upon different objects:
Just as a man wishing to leap across a great trench and establish himself on the opposite bank might run with speed and seize a rope hanging down from a tree branch on this side of the trench;
Just as one who, having taken hold of a pole or a staff and leaped across, with his body leaning, tending, and inclining toward the opposite shore,
reaches the upper part of that shore, lets go of it, and falling onto the opposite shore with a thud, lands slowly and gains a firm footing— just so this practitioner of yoga,

desiring to be established in Nibbāna, which is the opposite shore of the realms of existence, the matrices of being, the destinations, the stations, and the abodes, by means of the contemplation of rise and fall and so forth...
Having run with speed and tied himself to a branch of the tree of his own person, he seizes— by means of adaptation-adverting— the rope of form or one of the staves such as feeling and so forth,
taking it to be "impermanent," "suffering," or "non-self"; and without letting go of that,
having leaped over by means of the first conformity-consciousness, with the second [conformity-consciousness] his body becomes inclined, sloping, and leaning toward the further shore.

With a mind inclined, sloping, and leaning toward Nibbāna as if it were the further shore, and having now become close to the Nibbāna that is to be attained— just as one who has reached the upper part of the further shore with the third [impulsion]— it releases that formation as its object through the cessation of that consciousness and,
by means of the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū-citta), falls into Nibbāna, which is the further shore consisting of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata). However, when there is a single object...
Like that man who is trembling because he has not yet attained the habituation [to the path], he is not yet well-established; thereafter, he becomes established by means of path-knowledge.
In this context, the conformity [knowledge] is able to dispel the darkness of the defilements that conceal the truths, but it is not able to take Nibbāna as its object.
The change-of-lineage [knowledge] is able to take Nibbāna itself as its object, but not the darkness that conceals the truths.

To divert [the mind]. In this regard, there is this simile: It is said that a certain man with keen vision, thinking, "I shall know the conjunction of the stars," went out during the night and looked upward to see the moon;
however, because it was obscured by clouds, the moon was not visible. Then a wind arose and dispersed the thick clouds. Another...
...the medium, and another the subtle. Then, that man, seeing the moon in a cloudless sky, recognized its conjunction with the constellations.
In this analogy, the three kinds of clouds represent the thick, medium, and subtle darkness of the defilements that obscure the truth;
the three winds represent the three types of conformable consciousness; the man with keen vision represents the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa); and the moon represents [the path].

Nibbāna is like the destruction of each individual cloud by each successive wind; it is the removal of the darkness that conceals the Truths by each successive conformable consciousness (*anuloma-citta*).

Just as that man sees the pure moon in a cloudless sky, so too, when the darkness concealing the Truths has vanished, the knowledge of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) beholds the pure Nibbāna.
For just as those three winds are able only to disperse the clouds that obscure the moon, but are not able to see the moon itself,
so too the conformable [knowledges] are able only to dispel the darkness that obscures the Truths, but are not able to see Nibbāna.
Just as that man is able only to see the moon, but not to disperse the clouds, so too...
The knowledge of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is able to see only Nibbāna, but it cannot dispel the darkness of the defilements.

For this very reason, it is called the "adverting" of the Path. Although it is not itself an act of adverting, it stands in the place of adverting and ceases as if having given a signal to the Path, saying, "Be produced in this way.
And the Path, without relinquishing the signal given by that [knowledge], proceeds.

By means of a continuous succession [of moments] in the Avīci hell, that knowledge arises as it pierces and shatters the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion—things never before pierced and never before shattered—as it follows them without interruption. 809.
Here is a simile for this: it is said that a certain archer, having had a hundred wooden shields set up at a distance of eight usabhas, [shot at them].
Having wrapped his face with a cloth and fastened his quiver, he stood at the edge of the wheel.
Another man, having turned the wheel, would give a signal with a staff when the arrow-head was facing the target board.
Without letting go of the signal from the staff, the archer would shoot the arrow and pierce the hundred boards. In that regard:
The knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) is like the perception of the target-stick,

and the knowledge of the path (magga-ñā� Just as an archer, without letting go of his perception of the target-stick, pierces a hundred shields, so too the knowledge of the path, without letting go of the perception given by the knowledge of change-of-lineage,
takes Nibbāna as its object and breaks through and shatters the previously unbrokeable and unshattered aggregates of greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is the shatterer of despair.

(810) Not only does this path bring about the disillusionment with the mass of greed and so forth, but it also dries up the ocean of suffering—the cycle of existence whose beginning is unknown—and closes all doors to the states of misery;
furthermore, it brings about the manifestation of the seven treasures of the noble ones.
It abandons the eightfold wrong path, pacifies all enmities and fears,
brings one to the status of a legitimate son of the Fully Enlightened One, and conduces to the acquisition of many hundreds of other benefits.
Thus, the knowledge associated with the path of stream-entry— which bestows such manifold benefits— is "knowledge of the path of stream-entry."
The knowledge of the first path is concluded.
Discourse on the person who has entered the stream (sotāpanna):
Immediately following this knowledge, there arise two or three resultant consciousnesses that constitute its fruition.
They arise. For it is precisely because supramundane wholesome states have immediate fruition that it is said:
"They call concentration 'the immediate' (ānantarika)," and "He attains the immediate [fruit] slowly for the destruction of the taints," and so forth.
Some, however, say there are one, two, three, or four fruition-consciousnesses; that should not be accepted.
For at the conclusion of the repetition of the conformity [cognitions], change-of-lineage knowledge arises. Therefore, at the very least, there must be two moments of conformity consciousness.
Indeed, a single moment does not receive the condition of repetition, and a single adverting process consists of a maximum of seven moments of consciousness.
Consequently, for one who has two moments of conformity, the third is change-of-lineage and the fourth is the path-consciousness.
There are three fruition-consciousnesses (*phalacitta*). For one who has three conformities (*anuloma*), there are four:

the fourth is the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), the fifth is path-consciousness (*maggacitta*), and there are two fruition-consciousnesses. Therefore it is said: "Two or three fruition-consciousnesses arise.
However, some [hold that] for one who has four conformities, there are five: the fifth is change-of-lineage and the sixth is path-consciousness, and there is one [fruition-consciousness].

They call this the "fruit-consciousness" (*phalacitta*); however, because it enters [the attainment] at the fourth or fifth moment and not beyond that—since it is close to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)—that [definition] is rejected.
Therefore, it should not be accepted as the essential meaning.
At this point, he becomes the second noble person, known as a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). Even if he were extremely negligent...
Having offered [the sacrifice] seven times, and having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans, one becomes capable of making an end to suffering.
At the conclusion of the fruit, however, his consciousness descends into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Then, interrupting the life-continuum, mind-door adverting consciousness arises for the purpose of reviewing the path. When that has ceased—

In succession, there are seven impulsion moments of reviewing the Path. Then, having descended into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), adverting and the subsequent moments arise in that same manner for the purpose of reviewing the Fruit and so forth.
Through the arising of these, one reviews the Path, reviews the Fruit, reviews the defilements abandoned, and [reviews] the remaining defilements.
He reviews [them]; he reviews Nibbāna.
For he reviews the path, thinking, "Indeed, by this path have I come";
then he reviews the fruit, thinking, "This benefit has been obtained by me"; then he reviews the defilements abandoned, thinking, "These very defilements have been abandoned by me."
Then, [the practitioner] reviews the defilements to be abandoned by the three higher paths, thinking: "These indeed are the defilements remaining for me.
And at the conclusion, he reviews the deathless Nibbāna, thinking: "This Dhamma has been penetrated by me as an object.
Thus, there are five kinds of reviewing for a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer. And just as it is for the stream-enterer, [so it is for the others].
The same applies to the once-returner and the non-returner. However, for the Arahant, there is no such thing as reviewing the defilements that remain.
Thus, all these together constitute the nineteen kinds of reviewing.
This is merely the maximum limit; for even those in training (sekkhā) perform reviewing of the defilements already abandoned and those remaining.
Or rather, it was not. For it was precisely due to the absence of such reflection that Mahānāma asked the Blessed One:
"What dhamma, indeed, has not been abandoned within me, because of which at times even states of greed persist, having seized my mind?
All of this should be understood in detail.
The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Second Path: 813.

Having thus reflected, that noble disciple who has attained stream-entry either remains seated on that very seat or, at another time, applies himself to the practice for the sake of reaching the second stage, through the attenuation of sensual lust and ill-will.

He practices. Having brought together the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, he rubs with his knowledge that very mass of formations—divided into form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; he turns it over and enters the path of insight.

As he practices in this way, at the conclusion of equanimity towards formations, by means of a single advertence, there arise the knowledge of conformity and the knowledge of change-of-lineage according to the method already described.

When [the change-of-lineage knowledge] has arisen, immediately following the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), the path of once-returning arises. The knowledge associated with that is "knowledge of the path of once-returning.
The second knowledge is finished.
Discussion of the third path-knowledge.
814. Immediately after this knowledge, the resultant consciousnesses are to be understood in the same manner as previously described.
Up to this point, he is called the fourth noble person, the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī), who is capable of making an end of suffering after having come back to this world only once more.
Following that, the reviewing is exactly as described before.

Having reflected thus, that noble disciple who is a once-returner either remains seated on that very seat or at another time applies himself to the practice for the sake of attaining the third stage— the complete abandonment of sensual lust and ill will.
Having brought together the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, he regards that same conditioned process as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

He rubs it with knowledge, turns it over, and enters the path of insight. As he practices in this way, at the conclusion of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), in the manner already described, when the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma*) and the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) arise through a single adverting moment, the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) arises immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage.
The knowledge associated with that is "knowledge of the path of non-returning."
The Third Knowledge is finished.
815. The discussion of the knowledge of the fourth path:
immediately after this knowledge as well, the resultant consciousnesses are to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Up to this point—

This one is called the non-returner (anāgāmī), the sixth noble person (ariyapuggala). He is of spontaneous birth (opapātika), attains final nibbāna there (tattha-parinibbāyī), and is subject to the nature of not returning;
by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), he does not come back again to this world. After that, the method of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa) is exactly as previously stated.
Having reviewed in this manner, that noble disciple who is a non-returner, either while sitting on that very seat or at another time, [reviews his attainment].

Or, at another time, he applies himself to the attainment of the fourth stage for the sake of abandoning without remainder lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

Having brought together the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, he rubs that very same conditioned state with the knowledge that it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self; he turns it over and enters the path of insight.

For one who has practiced in this way, at the conclusion of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), in the manner already described, when the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma*) and the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) have arisen through a single adverting moment, the path of arahantship arises immediately after the change-of-lineage. The knowledge associated with that is "knowledge of the path of arahantship.
The fourth knowledge is completed.
The Discussion of the Person Who is an Arahant (Arahantapuggalakathā). 816.
Following this knowledge, the resultant consciousnesses are to be understood in the same manner as previously described.
Up to this point, he is called the eighth noble person, the Arahant, who has destroyed the great taints, who bears his final body, and who has laid down the burden.
"One who has attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, liberated through right knowledge—he is the supreme recipient of offerings in the world with its devas.

Thus, regarding what was said: "Knowledge of these four paths—the path of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the path of non-returning, and the path of arahantship—is called purification by knowledge and vision"—that [knowledge] proceeds according to this sequence.
This was said with reference to the four knowledges that are to be attained.

Now, in order to understand the power of this very purification by knowledge and vision consisting of the four knowledges, [the following] is stated: 817. Discourse on the Requisites of Enlightenment. Now, for the purpose of understanding the power of this very purification by knowledge and vision consisting of the four knowledges—
The fulfillment of the factors conducive to enlightenment, the application of the power of emergence,
and the abandoning of those phenomena which are to be abandoned by whichever means;
and the tasks such as full understanding and so forth, which were described at the time of clear realization.
And all of these should be understood according to their true nature. 818.
In this context, "the state of the factors of enlightenment being complete" means the completeness of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*). These are:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), and the five powers (*bala*).

The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path— these thirty-seven states are called "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*) because they belong to the side of the noble path,
which has received the name "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) in the sense of awakening. "Belonging to the side" means being situated in a state of assistance.

819. It is called *paṭṭhāna* because it stands forth (*patiṭṭhāna*) by leaping forward and springing upon various objects. Mindfulness itself is the foundation, thus it is "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

Furthermore, its fourfold division arises from its occurrence by way of grasping the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self in the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, and by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.
Therefore, they are called the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
820. That by which one exerts oneself is "exertion" (*padhāna*). A beautiful exertion is "right exertion" (*sammappadhāna*). Or, that by which one rightly exerts oneself is right exertion.
Or, it is "exertion" because it is beautiful due to being free from the deformity of the defilements, and it is [called] exertion because it brings about welfare and happiness.
It is called *sammappadhāna* because it brings about excellence (*seṭṭhabhāva*) and because it is the cause of the state of striving (*padhānabhāva*). This is a designation for energy (*vīriya*).

Since this energy accomplishes the task of abandoning unwholesome states that have arisen and preventing those not yet arisen from arising, as well as the task of causing wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise and maintaining those already arisen, it is fourfold;
therefore, they are called the "four right strivings" (*cattāro sammappadhānā*).
821. *Iddhi* (success) is so called in the sense of accomplishment as previously stated.

Because it is the precursor to that [accomplishment] which is associated with it, and because it is the causal basis for that [accomplishment] which has become its fruit, it is called a *iddhipāda* (basis of success). This is fourfold by way of desire (*chanda*) and the rest;
therefore, they are called the "four bases of success. As it is said: "The four bases of success: the basis of success consisting of desire..."

“The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to desire, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to energy, and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to investigation. These are exclusively supramundane.

However, mundane states are also included, as they are acquired through the predominance of desire and so forth, according to such statements as: “If a bhikkhu, making desire his dominant influence, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind—this is called concentration due to desire. Thus, there are also mundane factors obtained by way of the predominance of desire and the rest.
822. It is called a faculty (*indriya*) in the sense of predominance (*adhipati*), which is defined as overcoming, because it overcomes lack of faith, laziness, negligence, distraction, and delusion.
And it is called a power (*bala*) in the sense of unshakability, because it cannot be overcome by lack of faith and the other hindrances.
Both of these are fivefold according to faith and the rest; therefore, they are called the five faculties and the five powers.
823. Furthermore, for a being who is awakening, mindfulness and the others are the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) by way of being constituent parts.

And through the sense of leading to liberation, right view and the others are the eight factors of the path (*maggaṅga*). Therefore it is said: "The seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path. 824.
Thus, these thirty-seven states conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), while occurring during mundane insight (*vipassanā*) in the preliminary stage...
The foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body arises for one who comprehends the body in fourteen ways;

the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of feelings arises for one who comprehends feelings in nine ways; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the mind arises for one who comprehends the mind in sixteen ways;
and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of phenomena arises for one who comprehends phenomena in five ways.

The first right effort (*sammappadhāna*) occurs at the time of striving for the non-arising of unwholesome states by seeing unwholesome states that have arisen in another person—which had never previously arisen in one’s own self—and thinking:
“This has arisen in him because he practiced in such a way; I shall not practice in that manner, so that this will not arise in me.
It is the seeing of unwholesome states that have reached manifestation in oneself.
The second [right effort] is at the time of striving for abandonment. The third is for one striving to arouse either jhāna or insight that has never before arisen in this present existence.
The fourth right effort is for one repeatedly arousing what has already arisen so that it does not decline.
The basis of psychic power consisting of desire is at the time of producing the wholesome by making desire the primary factor.
At the time of abstaining from wrong speech, it is "right speech"; thus they are found in various moments of consciousness.

However, at the time of the arising of these four knowledges, they are found in a single moment of consciousness. Excluding the four right endeavors, thirty-three factors are found at the moment of the fruition (phalakkhaṇa).

825. Thus, when these states are found within a single moment of consciousness, mindfulness alone—having Nibbāna as its object—is called the "four foundations of mindfulness" by virtue of its accomplishment of the tasks of abandoning the perception of beauty and so forth regarding the body and the other aggregates.
Likewise, a single energy is called the "four right endeavours" by virtue of its accomplishment of the tasks of not allowing unarisen states to arise and so forth.
However, in the remaining [factors], there is no lessening or increasing.
Furthermore, among them:
nine are of one kind, one is twofold, then fourfold and fivefold;
eightfold and ninefold as well—thus they become sixfold.

"Nine are of one kind": desire (*chanda*), consciousness (*citta*), rapture (*pīti*), tranquility (*passaddhi*), equanimity (*upekkhā*), intention (*saṅkappa*), speech (*vācā*), action (*kammanta*), and livelihood (*ājīva*)—these nine are of only one kind by way of being the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) starting with desire; they do not belong to any other category.
"One is twofold": faith (*saddhā*) stands in two ways, by way of being both a faculty (*indriya*) and a power (*bala*). Then "four are fivefold": another... [text ends]

The meaning is that one is fourfold and another is fivefold. In this context, concentration (*samādhi*) is one [factor] that exists in four ways by way of being a faculty (*indriya*), a power (*bala*), a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and a path-factor (*maggaṅga*).
Wisdom (*paññā*) is fivefold by way of those same four and by way of the category of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
"And eightfold and ninefold" means that another one is eightfold and another one is ninefold.
Mindfulness is established in eight ways by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path factors.
Energy is ninefold by way of the four right endeavors, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path factors.
Thus—these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment remain unmixed, numbering fourteen.
