From the perspective of their constituent parts, they are sevenfold; from the perspective of their thirty-seven classifications, they are so.

Because they fulfill their respective functions, because they are described according to their own specific natures, and because they all come into being whenever the Noble Path arises—thus do they all occur.
Thus, first of all, the state of having the factors of enlightenment complete should be understood here.
827. The Discourse on the Conjunction of Emergence and Power:
"Conjunction of emergence and power" means both emergence and the conjunction of power. For mundane insight, because it has the sign as its object...
Because it does not cut off both the sign—the cause of occurrence—and its arising, the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) neither emerges from the sign nor from occurrence.
However, because it takes Nibbāna as its object, it emerges from the sign; thus, there is an emergence from one side. Therefore he said: "Wisdom in the turning away from emergence externally..."

“the knowledge of change-of-lineage. Likewise, it should be understood that all [the following] are to be explained: “It is change-of-lineage because, having turned away from arising, it enters into non-arising; having turned away from occurrence,” and so forth.

Moreover, these four knowledges emerge from the sign because their object is signless, and they emerge from occurrence because they completely sever its arising; thus, they are "emergences from both sides."
Therefore it was said:
"How is it that wisdom regarding emergence and turning away from both is knowledge of the path?
At the moment of the stream-entry path, right view—in the sense of seeing—emerges from wrong view and from the defilements that follow upon it."

It emerges from the internal aggregates and it emerges from all external signs. Therefore, it is said that wisdom in the turning away through emergence from both sides is knowledge of the path. Right livelihood; right effort in the sense of exertion; right mindfulness in the sense of establishment;
and right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from wrong concentration, emerges from the defilements and the aggregates that follow upon it, and emerges from all external signs.
Therefore, it is said: “Wisdom concerning emergence and turning away from both sides is knowledge of the path.”

“At the moment of the path of the once-returner, right view in the sense of seeing … right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from the gross fetter of sensual lust and the fetter of ill will, and from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to ill will … [and so on] … At the moment of the path of the non-returner,

right view in the sense of seeing … right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from the residual fetter of sensual lust and the fetter of ill will, and from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to ill will … [and so on] …”

“At the moment of the path of arahantship, right view in the sense of seeing … [and so on] … right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance;
it emerges from the defilements that accompany them and from the aggregates; and it emerges from all external signs.”
Therefore it is said: “Wisdom regarding emergence and turning away from both sides is knowledge of the path.

At the time of developing the eight mundane attainments, the power of serenity (samatha) is predominant; at the time of developing the contemplations such as impermanence, the power of insight (vipassanā) is predominant.
However, at the moment of the Noble Path, these two states proceed in union.
In the sense of not overstepping one another. Therefore, in these four kinds of knowledge, there is a conjunction of both powers. As it was said:
"The unification and non-distraction of the mind when emerging from defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates is concentration, having cessation as its domain;
[the unification and non-distraction] when emerging from defilements accompanied by ignorance and from the aggregates is insight in the sense of contemplation."
"Insight has cessation as its domain. Thus, in the sense of emergence, serenity and insight have a single flavor, they are yoked together, and they do not overstep one another.
Therefore it is said: 'He develops serenity and insight yoked together in the sense of emergence.
In this way, the conjunction with the power of emergence should be understood here.

The Discussion on the Abandoning of States to be Abandoned (Pahātabbadhammapahānakathā) 829. Regarding these four knowledges, it must be understood which states are to be abandoned by which knowledge, as well as their abandonment. For these [knowledges] function accordingly.

They are the abandoners of those states known as the fetters (*saṃyojana*), defilements (*kilesa*), wrongness (*micchatta*), worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), stinginess (*macchariya*), perversions (*vipallāsa*), bonds (*gantha*), bad ways (*agati*), taints (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), misapprehensions (*parāmāsa*), clingings (*upādāna*), underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), stains (*mala*), unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*), and types of consciousness-arisings (*cittuppāda*). In this context,
they are called "fetters" because they bind sentient beings to the aggregates (*khandha*) by means of the aggregates, to karma by means of its fruit, and to suffering.
Ten factors, beginning with lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*), are so called. For as long as those [factors] persist, these [fetters] do not cease.

Among them, lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—these five are called the "higher fetters" (*uddhaṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*) because they bind one to the aggregates and so forth produced in the higher realms.
Personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), and lust for sensual pleasures (*kāmarāga*)...

"Repulsion" refers to these five lower fetters (*adhobhāgiya-saṃyojana*), so called because they bind one to rebirth in the lower realms through the aggregates and other factors that lead to such rebirth.

"Defilements" (*kilesa*) refers to these ten states: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; for they are defiled in themselves and cause the associated mental states to become defiled.
"Falsehoods" (*micchatta*) refers to wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, and wrong action, so called because they function in a mistaken way.

Wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—these are eight factors. Together with wrong liberation and wrong knowledge, there are ten. "Worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) refers to these eight:
gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain, blame and praise, because they possess the nature of never ceasing while the world persists.
Here, however, by way of metaphorical designation for the cause, it refers to the attachment based on gain and the other [worldly conditions].
It should be understood that this inclusion of aversion (paṭigha) based on such grounds as loss and so forth is accomplished by the mention of the "worldly conditions" (lokadhamma).

"Miserlinesses" (macchariyāni) refers to the five types of miserliness— namely, miserliness regarding one's dwelling, miserliness regarding families, miserliness regarding gain, miserliness regarding the Dhamma, and miserliness regarding praise—
which function by way of intolerance toward others sharing in these matters, such as dwellings and the rest.

Perversions (*vipallāsa*) are these three: the perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), the perversion of mind (*citta-vipallāsa*), and the perversion of view (*diṭṭhi-vipallāsa*), which occur with respect to objects that are actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul, yet are regarded as "permanent," "pleasurable," "self," and "beautiful" respectively.
Fetters (*gantha*) are four, beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*), because they fetter both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the material body (*rūpakāya*). For indeed, they are:

the bodily fetter of covetousness, the bodily fetter of ill-will (*byāpāda*), the bodily fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa*), and the bodily fetter of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth" (*idamsaccābhinivesa*).
These are called the bodily fetters.

"Wrong course" (*agati*) is a designation for doing what should not be done and failing to do what should be done out of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; for it is called a wrong course because it is a path that should not be traveled by the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Taints" (*āsava*) means they flow from the object down to the stage of the *gotrabhū* and up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), or else they flow through the doors that have not been restrained.

Because they flow out like water from the holes of a jar, or because they cause the suffering of *saṃsāra* to flow forth in the sense of constant oozing, this is a designation for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view, and ignorance.

Furthermore, because they drag one down into the ocean of existence and because they are difficult to cross over, they are called "floods" (*oghā*). And because they do not allow for separation from objects of attachment nor for separation from suffering, they are also called "yokes" (*yogā*); these are likewise designations for those very same states.
"Obstructions" (*nīvaraṇāni*) refers to the five beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), in the sense of being a hindrance, an obstruction, and a concealment of the mind.

"Misapprehension" (*parāmāsa*) is a designation for wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), because it functions by overstepping the true nature of this or that phenomenon and grasping at a false nature beyond it.
"Clingings" (*upādānāni*) refers to the four beginning with clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), as described in every aspect in the exposition of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

The *anusayas* (underlying tendencies) are the seven beginning with sensual lust, as they are described as the underlying tendency of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, the underlying tendency of lust for existence, and the underlying tendency of ignorance, in the sense of being firmly rooted.
For these, because they are firmly rooted, they indeed lie latent (*anusenti*) by way of being the cause for the repeated arising of sensual lust and the rest; thus they are called *anusayas*.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are three [unwholesome roots] because they are themselves impure like the mixture of oil, lac, and mud, and because they cause others to become impure.
They are called "unwholesome courses of action" (akusala-kammapatha) both by virtue of being unwholesome actions and by virtue of being paths to the miserable destinies.
These are: killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and covetousness.
Ill will and wrong view—these are the ten.
Unwholesome arisings of consciousness: eight rooted in greed, two rooted in hatred, and two rooted in delusion—these are the twelve.
Thus, among these phenomena such as the fetters and so forth, these [preceding factors] are, as appropriate, the causes of their abandonment. How so? Among the fetters:

To that extent, these five factors—the view of a self-existent body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa), and sensual lust and aversion leading to states of deprivation (apāyagamaniyā kāmarāga-paṭighā)—are to be abandoned by the first knowledge.
The remaining gross forms of sensual lust and aversion are to be abandoned by the second knowledge;

the subtle forms are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; and all five types of lust for the fine-material realm (rūparāga) and so forth are indeed to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. Furthermore, beyond this:

Wherever we do not establish a restriction by means of the word "only" (*eva*), it should be understood that in each such case, whatever we shall describe as "to be abandoned by higher knowledge" (*upariñāṇavajjha*) becomes abandonable by higher knowledge precisely because its state of leading to rebirth in the states of misery and so forth has already been destroyed by the preceding knowledges.

Among the defilements (*kilesa*), wrong view and doubt are abandonable by the first knowledge; hatred is abandonable by the third knowledge; and greed, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread are abandonable by the fourth knowledge.
Among the wrong states, wrong view, false speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood—these are to be abandoned by the first knowledge.
Wrong intention, malicious speech, and harsh speech—these are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; here, it should be understood that "speech" refers specifically to volition.
Idle chatter, wrong effort, lack of mindfulness, wrong concentration, and lack of knowledge regarding liberation are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Aversion toward worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) is to be abandoned by the third knowledge; attachment (*anunaya*) is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge—some say that attachment to fame and praise is also to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. The forms of stinginess (*macchariya*) are indeed to be abandoned by the first knowledge. Among the perversions (*vipallāsa*):
the perversions of perception, mind, and view regarding the impermanent as permanent and the non-self as self;

and the perversions of view regarding suffering as pleasure and the foul as beautiful—these are to be abandoned by the first knowledge. The perversions of perception and mind regarding the foul as beautiful are [also] to be abandoned by the first knowledge.
The perception and mental distortion that there is pleasure in what is suffering are to be abandoned by the third knowledge.

Among the fetters (*gantha*), the fetters of attachment to rules and observances, and the fetter of dogmatic adherence to "this is the truth," are to be abandoned by the first knowledge; the fetter of ill will is to be abandoned by the third knowledge, and the other is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.
Wrong courses of conduct (*agati*) are to be abandoned by the first knowledge alone.

Among the taints (*āsava*), the taint of views is to be abandoned by the first knowledge; the taint of sensual desire is to be abandoned by the third knowledge; the other two are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. The same method applies to the floods (*ogha*) and the yokes (*yoga*).

Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of doubt is to be abandoned by the first knowledge; the three—sensual desire, ill will, and worry—are to be abandoned by the third knowledge; sloth-and-torpor and restlessness are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. Misapprehension is to be abandoned by the first knowledge alone.

Regarding the *upādānas* (clinging), because all mundane phenomena (*lokīyadhamma*) are included under "sensual desire" (*kāma*) by way of the objects of desire (*vatthukāma*), even lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms falls under clinging to sensual desire (*kāmupādāna*). Therefore, that [lust] is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge (*ñāṇa*), while the remaining [types of clinging] are to be abandoned by the first knowledge.

Regarding the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the underlying tendencies of views and doubt are abandoned by the first knowledge; the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion are abandoned by the third knowledge; and the underlying tendencies of conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance are abandoned by the fourth knowledge.
Regarding the stains (*mala*), the stain of hatred (*dosamala*) is abandoned by the third knowledge, while the others are abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Among the unwholesome courses of action (*akusalakammapatha*), killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and wrong view—these five are to be abandoned by the first knowledge (*paṭhamañāṇavajjha*).

The three consisting of malicious speech, harsh speech, and ill will are to be abandoned by the third knowledge (*tatiyañāṇavajjha*). Frivolous talk and covetousness are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge (*catutthañāṇavajjha*).

Among the unwholesome types of consciousness (*akusalacittuppāda*), the five associated with the four types of views and that associated with doubt are to be abandoned by the first knowledge alone. The two associated with aversion (*paṭigha*) are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. The remaining ones are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

And that which is to be abandoned by something is said to be "abandoned by that. Therefore it was said: "Thus, these [states] are, as appropriate, the causes for the abandoning of these states, such as the fetters.
831. But do these [paths] abandon these states when they are past or future, or rather when they are present? What follows from this?
If, first of all, they abandon them when they are past or future, then effort would be fruitless. Why? Because of the non-existence of those things to be abandoned. Or if—
Even so, it would be fruitless because those defilements that must be abandoned through effort still exist;

furthermore, it would follow that the cultivation of the Path is itself defiled, or else that the defilements are dissociated [from the mind]. Yet, there is no such thing as a present defilement that is dissociated from the mind.
This is not a unique objection, for in the very Canon it says: "This [Path] abandons defilements in the past..."
Having said, "One abandons past defilements, one abandons future defilements, and one abandons present defilements," he then said again:

"If one abandons past defilements, then one is exhausting what is already exhausted, ceasing what has already ceased, making vanish what has already vanished, and bringing to its end what has already ended. One abandons that which, being past, no longer exists."
“It does not abandon past defilements”—this has been rejected.

Likewise: “If it abandons future defilements, then indeed it abandons what is unborn, abandons what is unarisen, abandons what is unproduced, abandons what is unmanifested. It abandons that which is non-existent in the future. And so forth.
Having said this, it was rejected [by the opponent] that "one does not abandon future defilements.
Likewise: "If one abandons present defilements, then surely one who is lustful abandons lust; one who is hateful abandons hatred; one who is deluded abandons delusion;
one who is bound up abandons conceit; one who is misapprehending abandons views; one who has fallen into distraction abandons restlessness; and one who has fallen into error..."
Having stated, "One abandons doubt and the latent tendency that has become firmly rooted; dark and bright phenomena proceed as if yoked together;

there is a path-cultivation that is subject to defilement," and having rejected everything by saying, "One does not abandon defilements in the past, nor in the future, nor does one abandon defilements in the present," [he concluded]: "In that case, there is no cultivation of the path."

At the conclusion of the question—"There is no realization of the fruit, there is no abandoning of the defilements, there is no breakthrough to the Dhamma"—he first asserted, "Indeed, there is cultivation of the path...
[and so on]... there is breakthrough to the Dhamma," and when it was asked, "In what way? this was said:
“Just as if there were a young tree that had not yet borne fruit, and a man were to cut it down at its root:
those fruits of that tree which had not yet been born would remain unborn;
they would not come to be, they would not arise, and they would not become manifest, even though unmanifested. In the same way, arising is the cause, arising is the condition.”
Having seen the danger in the arising of defilements, the mind leaps forward toward their non-arising;
because the mind leaps forward toward their non-arising, those defilements which would have arisen through the condition of accumulation do not arise while unarisen...
[and so on] ...they do not become manifest while unmanifested. Thus, with the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of suffering. Activity is the cause... [and so on].

The sign is the cause... [and so on] ...accumulation is the cause... Because the mind leaps forward into non-accumulation, those defilements that would have arisen through the condition of accumulation do not arise; they remain unborn...
indeed, they do not become manifest while remaining unmanifest. Thus, through the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of suffering.
In this way, there is the development of the path, there is the realization of the fruit, and there is the abandoning of the defilements.

“There is the realization of the Dhamma. What is illustrated by this? The abandoning of defilements that have already been acquired by the stages (bhūmi) is what is illustrated. But are those defilements acquired by the stages past, future, or present? They are indeed called “arisen” (*uppanna*) by way of having been acquired by the stages.
For “arisen” has many divisions according to whether it is occurring, has become past, has been displaced, has made room [for another], or has been acquired by the stages. Among these:
All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) characterized by the possession of arising, aging, and dissolution are called "presently arisen" (vattamānuppanna).
Wholesome and unwholesome states that have ceased after experiencing the flavor of their object are called "arisen having passed away after being experienced" (anubhūtāpagata);

and all other conditioned things that have ceased after reaching the three stages of arising and so forth are called "arisen having passed away after having come to be" (bhūtāpagata). As for those [karmic results] previously performed...

Kamma described by such methods as "kammāni" (deeds), even when it is past, is called "arisen by way of making room" because, having prevented other results, it stands having made room for its own result;
and because that result, though yet unarisen, will necessarily arise in the room thus made, it is so termed. [This applies] to that which has not been eradicated in those respective planes.
Unwholesome [states] are called "arisen by way of having reached their plane" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*).
Herein, the distinction between the "plane" (*bhūmi*) and that which has "reached its plane" (*bhūmiladdha*) should be understood.

For the "plane" refers to the five aggregates belonging to the three realms, which serve as the object of insight (*vipassanā*). That which is "reached by the plane" refers to those states capable of arising within those aggregates.
It is born of defilement. For that reason, when that plane has been attained, it is said to be "attained as a plane" (*bhūmiladdha*);

however, this is not by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*). For even all past and future aggregates, though fully understood (*pariññāta*), can give rise to defilements in those whose taints are destroyed;
for example, Soreyya the merchant [gave rise to lust] taking the aggregates of Mahākaccāna and Uppalavaṇṇā as his object.

It is like [the case of] the young brahmin Nanda and others. Furthermore, if that were called "acquired by the plane" (*bhūmiladdha*), then because it could not be abandoned, no one would ever abandon the root of existence (*bhavamūla*).
Rather, it should be understood as "acquired by the plane" in the sense of its objective basis (*vatthu*);
for wherever aggregates arise that have not been fully understood through insight (*vipassanā*), from the moment of their arising onwards, within them—
The root of the round, which is the class of defilements, underlies [the aggregates]. It should be understood as "having acquired its soil" in the sense of being unabandoned. 835.

And herein, for whichever person the defilements have underlain within whichever aggregates in the sense of being unabandoned, those very aggregates are the basis for those defilements, and not the aggregates belonging to others.
This applies also to past aggregates in the case of those whose underlying tendencies have not been abandoned.
For defilements, only the past aggregates are the basis, not the others. This same principle applies to the future and so forth.

Likewise, among the aggregates of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), only the sense-sphere aggregates are the basis for those defilements whose underlying tendencies (anusaya) have not been abandoned, not the others. This same principle applies to those of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

Furthermore, regarding the aggregates of any noble person (ariyapuggala) such as a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and so on, whichever specific class of defilements rooted in the round of existence [remains] in their aggregates...

Whatever aggregates have been abandoned by whichever respective path do not receive the designation "plane" (bhūmi) because they serve as the basis for those various root-defilements of the round that have already been abandoned.

Since an ordinary person has not abandoned any of the root-defilements of the round whatsoever, whatever action he performs—whether wholesome or unwholesome—occurs. Thus, for him, there is [the cycle] conditioned by karma and defilements.
The round (of existence) revolves. Of this round, the root is in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) alone, and not in the aggregates of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth.

Or rather, it should not be said that it is in the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) alone and not in the aggregates of form and so forth. Why? Because it lies latent (*anusayita*) without distinction in all five aggregates.
How so? Like the sap of the earth in a tree. For just as a great tree, being established upon the surface of the earth...
Depending upon the essence of earth and the essence of water, and conditioned by them, the tree grows with roots, trunk, branches, twigs, shoots, leaves, flowers, and fruits;

filling the sky and persisting through a succession of seeds as a lineage of trees until the end of the eon, that essence of earth and so forth resides only in the roots, not in the trunk and so on...
[and so on] ...or only in the fruit, not in the roots and so on.
It should not be said [that it is so]. Why? Because it follows all roots and so forth without distinction.

However, just as when a certain person, disgusted with the flowers, fruits, and so on of that very tree, strikes the poison-thorn called *maṇḍūkakaṇṭaka* in the four directions, then that tree, touched by the contact of that poison, [loses] its earth-essence and water-essence...
Just as that seed, having been consumed and having reached a state where it no longer possesses the quality of germination, would be unable to produce a new continuity,

even so the clansman who is weary of the process of the aggregates initiates the cultivation of the four paths within his own continuity— just as that man [planted] trees at the four quarters of the earth extending for a league. Then, his continuity of aggregates...

Because all defilements rooted in the cycle of existence have been completely consumed by that contact with the four paths, all categories of kamma—such as bodily action and the rest—become mere functional states.
Consequently, due to the quality of not producing further renewed existence in the future, they are unable to generate a continuity of existence in another life.
Merely through the cessation of the final consciousness, one attains parinibbāna without fuel, like a fire without a substrate, being without any further clinging.
In this way, the distinction between the plane (*bhūmi*) and that which has attained the plane should be understood.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of what has arisen, by way of: manifestation, being grasped as an object, being suppressed, and not being eradicated.
Among these, only that which is currently occurring is "arisen by manifestation. However, when [an object] has come into the range of the eye and so forth...

Although a class of defilement does not arise in the preliminary stage with respect to an object, it is nevertheless called "arisen through the apprehension of the object" because it arises invariably at a later time due to the very fact that the object was previously apprehended;

this is like the class of defilements that arose for the Elder Mahātissa while he was walking for alms in the village of Kalyāṇī upon seeing an unwholesome form. [This applies] to serenity and insight.
A class of defilements that has not been suppressed by means of any [of the mundane paths] is called "arisen but not suppressed" because, although it has not entered the mental continuum,
there is no cause to prevent its arising. However, even when suppressed by means of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā),
it is called "arisen but not eradicated" because it has not been uprooted by the Noble Path and has not transcended the nature of arising.
It is like the arising of defilements in an elder who had attained the eight meditative attainments while traveling through the air,
upon hearing the song of a woman with a sweet voice as he was gathering flowers in a grove of blossoming trees;
and this threefold [arising] occurs only when the object has been seized, suppressed, or not yet eradicated by one who has attained that particular level.
It should be understood that it "falls under inclusion.

838. Thus, when these aforementioned varieties have arisen, that which is called the fourfold "arisen"—namely, the present, the past, the departed, and the occasioned—is not something to be abandoned by any knowledge, because it is not an object of the path. As for that which...

Now, this "arisen" refers to that which is characterized as obtained by the plane, grasped as an object, un-suppressed, and not yet eradicated. Since each respective mundane or supramundane knowledge arises by destroying that state of being arisen, therefore all of it must be abandoned.
Thus, in this context, one should understand those phenomena which are to be abandoned by what means, as well as their abandonment.
The Discussion of the Functions Beginning with Full Understanding: The functions beginning with full understanding,
which were stated at the time of clear realization— all of those should be understood according to their true nature.

For at the time of the realization of truth (saccābhisamaya), within each one of these four knowledges, these four functions—full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), realizing (sacchikiriyā), and developing (bhāvanā)—are stated; they should be understood according to their true nature.
For it has been said by the ancients:
"Just as a lamp performs four functions simultaneously— without priority or sequence— it consumes the wick,
dispels darkness, reveals light, and exhausts the oil; even so,
the knowledge of the path realizes the four truths simultaneously— without priority or sequence— through the realization of full comprehension regarding suffering."
He realizes: he realizes the origin through the realization of abandoning; he realizes the path through the realization of development;
he realizes cessation through the realization of actualization. What is meant by this?
Taking cessation as his object, he reaches, sees, and penetrates all four truths.”

And this has also been said: "Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—all of this should be understood.

Furthermore, it has been said: "The knowledge of one possessing the path is knowledge regarding suffering, knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this context, just as a lamp burns up the wick, so does path-knowledge fully understand suffering.

Just as it dispels darkness, so does it abandon the origin. Just as it makes light manifest, so does it develop the path—consisting of states such as right intention—by way of being a co-nascent and other types of conditions. Just as it consumes moisture, so does it bring about the exhaustion of the defilements.
"He realizes cessation"—thus should the application of the simile be understood.

Another method: just as the rising sun, appearing simultaneously and without priority or sequence, performs four functions—it illuminates all forms, dispels darkness, displays light, and allays the cold—so too [does the practitioner].
In the same way, path-knowledge... [as before] ...realizes cessation through the clear comprehension of realization.
Here too, just as the sun illuminates all forms, so does path-knowledge fully understand suffering (*dukkha*).
Just as it dispels darkness, so does it abandon the origin (*samudaya*). Just as it displays light, so does it [reveal the path] by way of its status as a co-nascent and other types of conditions.
He develops the path. Just as it allays the cold, so too he realizes the cessation that is the subsiding of the defilements;
in this way the application of the simile is to be understood. 841.
Another method: just as a boat performs four functions simultaneously—neither before nor after—[namely] reaching the near shore...
It abandons, it cuts the stream, it carries the cargo, and it reaches the further shore; even so, path-knowledge...
[as before] ...realizes cessation through the clear realization of actualization.
Here too, just as the boat abandons the near shore, so does path-knowledge fully understand suffering. Just as it cuts the stream, so does it abandon the origin.
Just as one carries a load, so too does he develop the path through the conditionality of co-nascence and the rest;
just as one reaches the further shore, so too does he realize cessation, which is the further shore. In this way, the correlation with the simile should be understood.

842. Thus, at the moment of the penetration of the truths, for this knowledge—which functions in a single moment by way of four functions—there are four functions that are penetrated simultaneously in sixteen aspects, in the sense of their being suchness. As it has been said:

“In what sense are the four functions identical in their penetration through the sense of suchness? Through sixteen aspects, the four functions are identical in their penetration through the sense of suchness.
For suffering, there is the sense of oppression, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of changeability, and the sense of suchness.
For the origin, there is the sense of accumulation, the sense of source, the sense of bondage, the sense of obstruction, and [the sense of suchness].”

The meaning of suchness (*tathaṭṭha*). For cessation (*nirodha*), there are the meaning of escape (*nissaraṇaṭṭha*), the meaning of seclusion (*vivekaṭṭha*), the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhataṭṭha*), the meaning of the deathless (*amataṭṭha*), and the meaning of suchness (*tathaṭṭha*).

For the path (*magga*), there are the meaning of outlet (*niyyānaṭṭha*), the meaning of cause (*hetuṭṭha*), the meaning of seeing (*dassanaṭṭha*), the meaning of dominance (*adhipateyyaṭṭha*), and the meaning of suchness (*tathaṭṭha*).
By these sixteen aspects, the four truths are comprised within the single category of the meaning of suchness. That which is comprised as one is oneness (*ekatta*).
“That which is unity is penetrated by a single knowledge; thus, the four truths are penetrated as one. 843. Herein, it might be asked:
since there are other meanings for suffering and the rest, such as disease, abscesses, and so forth, why are only four stated?
To this we reply: because they are manifested through the vision of the specific truths. “In that regard, what is [the knowledge] regarding suffering?”
“Knowledge”: by such methods as “the wisdom and understanding that arise with reference to suffering,” knowledge of the truths is described according to each truth as its respective object.

Furthermore, it is described by way of the accomplishment of the function regarding the remaining truths while taking one truth as the object, according to the method beginning: “Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees its origin.”
In this context, when one takes each truth as an object, first, through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*),
even though suffering has the characteristic of oppression by its own nature, because it is accumulated, conditioned, and heaped up by the origin which has the characteristic of accumulating,
its aspect of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*) becomes manifest. Furthermore, because the Path (*magga*) removes the torment of the defilements...

It is very cool; therefore, by the seeing of that path, the meaning of "peace" becomes manifest, just as the ugliness of Sundarī became manifest to the Venerable Nanda upon seeing the celestial nymph.
However, there is no need to say more here than this: by the seeing of cessation, which is not subject to change, the meaning of "changelessness" becomes manifest.

Likewise, through the vision of suffering, the meaning of origin as accumulation—by way of its intrinsic nature—is made manifest, just as the fact that food is the cause of disease is revealed by seeing a disease arising from unsuitable food.
Through the vision of cessation as disjunction, the meaning of bondage is revealed. And through the vision of the path as the outlet, the meaning of obstruction is revealed.
Likewise, by seeing cessation—which has the characteristic of escape—and by seeing origination, which is non-secluded, the state of seclusion becomes manifest.
By the vision of the path, the state of the unconditioned is revealed;

for in this beginningless saṃsāra, the path has never been seen before, and since it too is conditioned due to having causes and conditions, the unconditioned nature of the causeless dhamma is exceedingly clear.
Furthermore, by seeing suffering, its meaning as the deathless (*amata*) becomes manifest; for suffering is poison, while Nibbāna is the deathless.

Likewise, regarding the Path which has the characteristic of leading out, by seeing the origin [of suffering], its meaning as the cause becomes manifest through the thought: "This is not the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna;
this is the cause. By seeing cessation, its meaning as vision [becomes manifest], as do the most subtle forms.
It is like the clarity of the eye when one sees, "My eyes are indeed clear.
Through the vision of suffering, there is the sense of supremacy, just as the majesty of a lord is seen through observing the wretchedness of people afflicted by many diseases;
thus, here each [truth] is defined by its own specific characteristic, while the other three are defined by the vision of the remaining truths.
Four meanings have been stated for each [of the truths] by way of their manifestation.
However, at the moment of the Path, all these meanings reach penetration through a single knowledge that performs the four functions regarding suffering and the other truths.
As for those who maintain that there is a separate realization (nānābhisamaya) for each, the refutation of their view has already been stated in the *Kathāvatthu* of the Abhidhamma.

844. Discussion of the Analysis of Full Understanding and the Other [Three] Functions: Now, regarding those four functions beginning with full understanding that have been mentioned—full understanding is threefold, and likewise are abandoning and realization.
Two kinds of development are intended; therein, the analysis must be understood.
There are three kinds of full understanding: full understanding as the known, full understanding as investigation, and full understanding as abandoning; thus, full understanding is threefold.
Having thus stated, "The wisdom of direct knowledge is knowledge in the sense of having known," [it continues]: "Whichever phenomena..."
“Those things are directly known; those various states are known”—thus it is stated in brief. In detail, it is stated by way of the method beginning: “Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known.
And what, bhikkhus, is everything that is to be directly known? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be directly known,” and so forth.
This is called the full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*). Its exclusive domain (*āveṇika-bhūmi*) is the direct knowing of name-and-form together with their conditions.
846. Having thus stated, "The wisdom of full understanding is knowledge in the sense of scrutinizing," [the Sutta] then explains it briefly as:
"Whatever states have been fully understood, those very states have been scrutinized. And by way of such passages as: "Bhikkhus, everything is to be fully understood.
And what, bhikkhus, is everything that is to be fully understood? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be fully understood," and so forth.
What has been explained in detail is called "full understanding by scrutinization" (*tīraṇapariññā*).

Its exclusive domain extends from the stage of the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*)—proceeding by way of scrutinization as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—up until the stage of conformity (*anuloma*).
847. Having thus stated, "Wisdom of abandoning is knowledge in the sense of relinquishing," [it continues]: "Whichever phenomena have been abandoned..."
The full understanding by abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*) is that which proceeds according to the method stated in detail as:
"Those respective phenomena have been relinquished," and "By the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), one abandons the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*)," and so forth.
Its scope extends from the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) up to the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*); this is what is intended here.

Or alternatively, since both the full understanding as knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*) and the full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*) have that same purpose, and because those phenomena which one abandons are necessarily both known and investigated, it should be understood that, by this method, the triad of full understandings is also the function of path-knowledge.

Likewise with abandoning: for abandoning consists of suppression-abandoning (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*), partial eradication-abandoning (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), and complete eradication-abandoning (*samuccheda-pahāna*).

Full understanding is likewise threefold. In this context, the suppression of adverse states such as the hindrances by means of various mundane concentrations—just as moss is suppressed by a jar placed in water containing moss—is called "abandoning by suppression.
In the Pāli, however, it says: "And the abandoning of the hindrances by suppression is the first..."
When it is said, “for one developing jhāna,” the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) alone is mentioned; this should be understood as being stated because it is the most evident.
For the hindrances do not suddenly overwhelm the mind either before or after the jhāna, whereas applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors do so at the very moment of absorption.
Therefore, the suppression of the hindrances is what is manifest.

849. Furthermore, just as darkness is dispelled by a lamp kindled during the night, the abandonment of each respective state to be abandoned occurs through the very counteractive mode of the various factors of knowledge that constitute insight;

this is called "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*). For example, first, the abandoning of the personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) occurs through the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpapariccheda*).

By the discernment of conditions, there is the removal of the views of no-cause and irregular cause, as well as the stain of doubt. By the comprehension of the aggregates, there is the removal of the grasping at a collective [self] as "I" and "mine.
By the definition of what is the path and what is not the path, there is the removal of the perception of a path where there is no path.

By the vision of arising, there is the removal of the annihilationist view. By the vision of passing away, there is the removal of the eternalist view. By the appearance of terror, there is the removal of the perception of safety where there is danger.
Through the vision of danger, there is the abandoning of the perception of gratification; through the contemplation of disenchantment, the perception of delight;
through the desire for deliverance, the state of not desiring deliverance; through reflective contemplation, the lack of reflective contemplation; through equanimity, the lack of equanimity;
and through conformity, the grasping that is contrary to the truths.
Or again, among the eighteen great insights: by the contemplation of impermanence, [one abandons] the perception of permanence;
by the contemplation of suffering, the perception of pleasure; by the contemplation of non-self, the perception of self; by the contemplation of disenchantment, delight;
by the contemplation of dispassion, lust; by the contemplation of cessation, origination; by the contemplation of relinquishment, grasping; by the contemplation of destruction...

By means of the perception of density, [one abandons] accumulation; by means of the contemplation of vanishing, [one abandons] accumulation; by means of the contemplation of change, the perception of permanence;

by means of the contemplation of the signless, the sign; by means of the contemplation of the desireless, longing; by means of the contemplation of emptiness, misapprehension; by means of insight into phenomena with higher wisdom, the misapprehension of grasping at a core;
by means of knowledge and vision according to reality, the misapprehension of delusion; and by means of the contemplation of danger...

The abandoning of adherence to a basis occurs through the contemplation of reflection; the abandoning of non-reflection occurs through the contemplation of reflection; and the abandoning of adherence to bondage occurs through the contemplation of turning away.
This too is simply abandoning by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

850. In this regard, just as the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth occurs through the seven [contemplations] beginning with the contemplation of impermanence, that has already been explained under the contemplation of dissolution.

Contemplation of destruction (*khayānupassanā*), however, is the knowledge of one who sees destruction in the sense of impermanence by means of effecting the resolution of the compact mass. Through that, the perception of a compact mass is abandoned.
Contemplation of fall (*vayānupassanā*) is stated as follows:
"By way of the sequence of the object, both are determined as one."
"Adherence to cessation" is insight into the characteristic of vanishing.
Thus, having seen the dissolution of formations both through direct perception and through inference, there is adherence to that very cessation known as dissolution;
by means of that, the exertion [of grasping] is abandoned. For whatever purpose one might exert oneself, those...
For one who thus contemplates with insight, "Thus is the nature of aging," the mind does not incline toward grasping.

Contemplation of change (*vipariṇāmānupassanā*) is the observation of the occurrence of things otherwise by transcending their respective limits, such as the sevenfold set of materiality (*rūpasattaka*), etc.;
or it is the observation of change in two ways regarding what has arisen, namely through aging and death. By means of that, the perception of permanence (*dhuvasaññā*) is abandoned.
Contemplation of the signless is precisely contemplation of impermanence; by means of it, there is the abandoning of the sign of permanence.
Contemplation of the desireless is precisely contemplation of suffering; by means of it, there is the abandoning of longing for pleasure and aspiration for pleasure.
Contemplation of emptiness is precisely contemplation of non-self; by means of it, there is the abandoning of the dogmatic adherence that "there is a self."
Insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) is as follows:
“Reflecting upon the object and contemplating its dissolution,
and the manifestation [of that object] as empty— this is insight through higher wisdom.”

Having been told this, one understands the object such as visible form, and having seen the dissolution of that object and of the consciousness that had that object, one practices insight by taking emptiness through the mode of dissolution, thinking:
"Only formations dissolve; the death of formations is all there is; there is nothing else.
This, being both higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*) and insight into phenomena (*dhammesu vipassanā*), is so called.

What is called "insight into phenomena through higher wisdom" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) brings about the abandonment of the adherence to grasping at a core, because by means of it one has clearly seen the absence of a permanent core and the absence of a self-core.

"Knowledge and vision in accordance with reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is the discernment of mentality-materiality together with its conditions; by means of that, [the views] such as "Did I exist in the past? and so forth...
Furthermore, there is the abandoning of the adherence to delusion that occurs in such ways as “the world arises from a Creator.

Contemplation of danger is the knowledge that sees danger in all states of existence, etc., which has arisen by way of the appearance of terror; through this, there is the abandoning of the adherence to a basis, [realizing] that “nothing at all is seen to be worth clinging to.
Contemplation of reflection is the knowledge of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa*) which provides the means for relinquishing; through this, there is the abandoning of non-reflection.
Contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*) consists of both equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and conformity (*anuloma*).
For at that time, his mind shrinks back from, recoils from, and turns away from the entire range of formations, like a drop of water on a slightly sloping lotus leaf; thus it is said.
Therefore, by means of that [contemplation], there is the abandoning of adherence to fetters, such as the defilement-adherence to the fetter of sensual desire and so forth.
The meaning is that there is the abandoning of the active defilements. Thus, abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgappahāna) should be understood in detail.

In the Pāḷi, however, it is stated only in brief: "And abandonment by substitution of opposites occurs for one who develops concentration partaking of penetration regarding the various types of views."

851. Furthermore, that abandonment of the phenomena such as the fetters, by means of the knowledge of the Noble Path—such that they do not arise again, just as a tree struck by a thunderbolt does not grow again—is called "abandonment by eradication" (*samucchedappahāna*).
With reference to this, it was said: "And abandonment by eradication belongs to one who develops the supramundane path leading to the destruction [of the taints]. Thus.
Among these three types of abandonment, it is only abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*) that is intended here.

However, since for that practitioner the prior stages of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and abandonment as a factor (*tadaṅga*) also serve that same purpose, it should be understood that, in this manner, all three types of abandonment constitute the function of path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*). This is like one who, having slain a rival king, has attained the kingdom.
For even that which was done prior to that is all said to be "done by the king" as "this and that.

852. Regarding "realization" (*sacchikiriyā*): although it is divided into two types—mundane realization and supramundane realization—it becomes threefold through the further division of the supramundane into seeing and cultivation. In that regard, [of] the first jhāna...

The "contacting" (*phassanā*) of the first jhāna and so forth—occurring in such passages as, "I am a gainer, I am a master; the first jhāna has been realized by me"—is called mundane realization (*lokisañcikiriyā*).
"Contacting" means the touching through the contact of knowledge (*ñāṇaphassa*) by way of direct experience, having attained [it] and thinking, "This has been attained by me.
It is with reference to this very meaning that it is said: "Realization is wisdom in the sense of contacting."
Having stated "knowledge," the description of its realization is given as: "Whatever states have been realized, those very states have been touched.
Furthermore, there are those states which, even without being produced within one's own continuum, are known solely by a knowledge that does not depend on another.
These have been realized. For this very reason it was said: "Bhikkhus, everything is to be realized.
And what, bhikkhus, is everything to be realized? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be realized," and so forth. Furthermore, it was said:
"One who sees form realizes it; one who sees feeling... [and so on] ...one who sees consciousness realizes it."
"One who sees the eye... [and so on] ...old age and death... [and so on] ...sees and realizes Nibbāna, which has the Deathless as its goal.
Whatever states have been realized, those very states have been contacted.
At the moment of the first path, however, the seeing of Nibbāna is "realization by seeing"; at the moments of the remaining paths, it is "realization by development."
Both of these two types are intended here. Therefore, it should be understood that the function of this knowledge is the realization of Nibbāna by way of both seeing and development.
(853) Regarding the phrase "the two developments are intended," there are only two developments: mundane development and supramundane development.
It is intended. Therein, mundane cultivation (*lokīyabhāvanā*) is the arising of mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and the perfuming of the continuum (*santāna*) by means of them.
Supramundane cultivation (*lokuttarabhāvanā*) is the arising of supramundane virtue and so forth, and the perfuming of the continuum by means of them.
Among these, it is the supramundane that is intended here. For supramundane virtue and the rest produce this fourfold knowledge.
Because it acts as their conascent condition and so forth, and because it perfumes the mental continuum by means of them, this is the function of the supramundane development.
Thus:
"The functions such as full understanding and the rest, which were stated at the time of clear realization..."
And all of these should be understood according to their true nature.
To this extent, it is said:
“A wise man, established in virtue, should develop the mind and wisdom.”

Thus, what was stated for the purpose of showing the method for developing wisdom as it has been brought forth in its own form—that "it should be developed by one who, having accomplished the two purifications that constitute the root, accomplishes the five purifications that constitute the body"—is thereby explained in detail.
And the question, "How should it be developed? has also been answered.
Thus ends the Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision, in the Section on the Development of Understanding, composed in the *Visuddhimagga* for the delight of virtuous people.
The Twenty-Third Chapter:
The Exposition of the Benefits of the Development of Wisdom;
An Exposition of the Benefits.
854. As for what was asked—"What is the benefit of the development of wisdom?"—we shall speak to that. This so-called development of wisdom possesses hundreds of benefits.
It would not be easy to explain its benefits in detail even over a long period of time.

Briefly stated, however, its benefits are the destruction of various defilements, the experiencing of the flavor of the noble fruits, and the capacity to attain the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
The benefit to be understood here is the accomplishment of the state of being worthy of offerings and so forth.
855. Regarding the discourse on the destruction of various defilements:
therein, from the point of delimiting name-and-form onwards, there is the destruction of various defilements by way of the personality-belief view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and others.

This has been stated; this is the benefit of the development of mundane wisdom. That which was stated regarding the destruction of various defilements, such as the fetters, at the moment of the Noble Path—this should be understood as the benefit of the development of supramundane wisdom.
Like a thunderbolt falling with terrifying force upon a mountain of rock...
Like a fire fanned by the force of the wind in a forest,
like the sun dispelling the darkness with its radiant, blazing orb,
he [dispelled] that which had pursued him for a long time and was the source of every misfortune.
For wisdom, when developed, shatters the web of defilements;
therefore, one should know this visible benefit here and now.
The Discussion on the Attainment of Fruition.
856. “Experiencing the flavor of the noble fruits”: this is not only the destruction of the defilements;
experiencing the flavor of the noble fruits is also a benefit of the development of wisdom. For “noble fruit” refers to the fruits of recluseship, such as the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.
The experience of its flavor occurs in two ways: during the course of the path and during the occurrence of the attainment of fruition.
In this context, its occurrence within the course of the path has already been shown.
Furthermore, for the sake of those who say, "The fruit is merely the abandoning of the fetters;
there is no other distinct state," this sutta should also be cited: "How is it that wisdom is the subsiding of the effort?"... [and so on].
What is knowledge of the fruit? At the moment of the stream-entry path, right view—in the sense of seeing—emerges from wrong view;
it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon it, and it emerges from all external signs.
Right view arises because of the subsiding of its associated [defilements]; this is the fruit of the path. Thus it should be expanded in detail.
“The four paths that are not included [in the mundane sphere], and the four fruits of recluseship—these states have an immeasurable object.
Furthermore, such statements as “A sublime state is a condition for an immeasurable state by way of proximity-condition” serve here as proofs.
To show the occurrence of the attainment of fruition, however, this line of inquiry is undertaken: What is the attainment of fruition?
Who enters it? Who does not enter it? Why do they enter it? How does the entering come about?
How is there maintenance? How is there emergence? What is immediate to the fruit? And what is the fruit immediate to? 859.
In this context, what is the attainment of fruition? It is the absorption (appanā) in cessation that belongs to the noble fruit.
860. Who enters these attainments, and who does not? All worldlings (*puthujjana*) do not enter them. Why? Because they have not attained them.

All noble ones (*ariya*), however, do enter them. Why? Because they have attained them. But those in higher stages do not enter the lower stages, because [the attainment] has become tranquilized through their transition to the state of another person (*puggalantara*). As for those in the lower stages...
And [the two lower fruits] are not [included] because they have not yet been attained. However, the conclusion here is that each person enters into the fruition of their own respective fruit.
Some, however, say: "Even stream-enterers and once-returners do not enter [these attainments]; only the two higher ones enter them. And this is their reason:
"For these two are those who bring concentration to perfection. But that [reason] applies even to an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*).
It is for no reason at all that one enters upon the mundane concentration attained by oneself. What is the use here of such deliberation on what is a cause and what is not?
Is it not stated in the Pāḷi itself: “Which ten change-of-lineage states arise by way of insight?
For the sake of attaining the stream-entry path, there is arising, occurrence... [and so on] ...distress, and the sign of external formations.”
"It overcomes, thus it is 'change-of-lineage' (gotrabhū). For the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, it overcomes the path of once-returning...

for the sake of attaining the fruit of arahantship... for the sake of attaining the dwelling in emptiness... for the sake of attaining the dwelling in the signless, it arises and overcomes the sign of external formations;
thus it is 'change-of-lineage'. Therefore, all noble ones [attain] their respective fruits.
One must conclude that they "attain" [the jhānas] for this reason.
Why do they attain them? For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
Just as a king experiences the happiness of sovereignty and deities experience celestial happiness, so too do the Noble Ones [think], "We shall experience the noble supramundane happiness."
Having determined a limit for their journey, they enter the attainment of fruition at whatever moment they desire.
How does its entry come about, how its maintenance, and how its emergence? First of all, its entry comes about in two ways:
through non-attention to any object other than Nibbāna, and through attention to Nibbāna.
and non-attention. As it is said: “There are, friends, two conditions for the attainment of the signless deliverance of mind:
non-attention to all signs and attention to the signless element.
This, moreover, is the sequence for entering [this attainment]. For a noble disciple who desires the attainment of the fruit, having gone into seclusion—
One who is in seclusion should contemplate formations by way of their arising and passing away, and so forth.

For such a person practicing gradual insight into the process of occurrence, immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) which has formations as its object, the mind enters into cessation by way of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
And here, because of the inclination toward the attainment of fruition, even for one still in training (sekkha), only the fruition arises, not the path.

But as for those who say, "A stream-enterer, having established insight with the thought, 'I shall attain the attainment of fruition,' becomes a once-returner; and a once-returner becomes a non-returner," they should be told:
"If that were so, a non-returner would become an arahant, an arahant a paccekabuddha, and a paccekabuddha a Buddha. Therefore, this is nothing [of consequence], and according to the Pāḷi itself—"
Nor should it be understood as "rejected. Rather, this alone should be accepted:

even for one in training (sekkha), only the fruit (phala) arises, not the path (magga). And as for that fruit, if he has attained a path belonging to the first jhāna, only a fruit belonging to the first jhāna arises;
if it belongs to any other [jhāna] such as the second and so on, only a fruit belonging to that particular jhāna, such as the second and so on, arises.
Thus, first of all, there is its attainment. For it is said:
"Friend, there are three conditions for the persistence of the signless deliverance of mind:
non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element, and prior mental formation."
There are three ways in which there is stability for it. Herein, "prior volitional formation" refers to the delimitation of time prior to the attainment.
Because it has been delimited by the thought, "I shall emerge at such-and-such a time," there is stability for it as long as that time has not yet arrived. Thus there is stability for it.
865. “There are, friends, two conditions for emerging from the signless liberation of mind:
attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element. Because of this statement, its emergence occurs in two ways.
Therein, “all signs” refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. And although—
One does not attend to all of these together by way of a comprehensive inclusion; rather, this is stated as a general summary.

Therefore, its emergence should be understood as follows: for one who attends to whatever has been the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), there is emergence from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
866. What is immediately after the fruit, and what has the fruit as its immediate successor? First, regarding the fruit:

either another fruit or the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs immediately after it. As for the fruit itself, there is that which follows the path, there is that which follows the fruit, there is that which follows change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and there is that which follows the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Among these, in the cognitive process of the path...

Immediately after the path, each preceding [path] is related to each succeeding [fruit]; immediately after the fruits, each preceding [fruit] is related to each succeeding [fruit]. Among the attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), each preceding [fruition] is related to the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*).
And here, "change-of-lineage" should be understood as conformity (*anuloma*). For this is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*:
"For an Arahant, conformity is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*). For those in training (*sekkhā*)..."
“Anuloma is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of the proximity condition.

That fruition by which emergence from cessation occurs is immediately subsequent to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*). Therein, with the exception of the fruition that arises within the cognitive sequence of the path (*maggavīthi*), all remaining fruition is said to proceed by way of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). Thus it is in the cognitive sequence of the path.
Or, by way of its arising in the attainment of fruition:
The supreme fruit of recluseship is peaceful, with the deathless as its object and beautiful; it is lovely, with its feverish distress allayed, and it has vomited out the bait of worldly things.
Pervaded by pure, vital, and blissful happiness—
happiness that is exceedingly sweet, like nectar and honey—
that is the unsurpassed, essential flavor of that noble one’s bliss.
Because the wise person, having developed wisdom regarding the fruit,
attains it, therefore this experience of the flavor of the noble fruit here is called the benefit of the development of insight.
867. Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation:
It should be understood that the capacity to attain the attainment of cessation is not merely the experience of the flavor of the noble fruits;
rather, this capacity to attain the attainment of cessation is also to be known as a benefit of this development of wisdom.
Herein, this is the method of inquiry for the purpose of clarifying the attainment of cessation:
What is the attainment of cessation? Who attains it? Who does not attain it? Where do they attain it? Why do they attain it?
How is there the attainment of it? How is its maintenance? How is the emergence from it? For one who has emerged, to what is the mind inclined?

What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has attained cessation? Is the attainment of cessation conditioned (*saṅkhata*) or unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), mundane (*lokiya*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*), accomplished (*nipphanna*) or unaccomplished (*anipphanna*)?
868. In this context, what is the attainment of cessation? It is that which, by way of successive cessation, [brings about] the cessation of mind and mental factors.

Non-arising (*appavatti*). Who enters this attainment and who does not? All ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), dry-insight non-returners (*sukkha-vipassaka-anāgāmin*), and arahants do not enter it.

However, non-returners who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti-lābhin*) and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) do enter it. "Because of being endowed with two powers and three..."

For it is said: “Wisdom consisting in mastery through the subsiding of formations, by means of the sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge and the nine modes of conduct of concentration, is the knowledge of the attainment of cessation.

And this accomplishment does not belong to anyone other than non-returners whose taints are destroyed and who have attained the eight attainments; therefore, only they enter that attainment, and no others.
869. But which are the two powers here... [etc. ...and what is mastery? There is nothing for us to say here; all this has already been stated in the exposition (*niddesa*) of that summary (*uddesa*).
As it was said: "By 'two powers' means the two powers: the power of serenity (*samatha-bala*) and the power of insight (*vipassanā-bala*). What is the power of serenity?
One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction by way of renunciation is the power of serenity. By way of non-ill-will... by way of perception of light... by way of non-distraction... [etc.]"

One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction through in-breathing while contemplating relinquishment... and through out-breathing while contemplating relinquishment is the power of serenity (*samathabala*).
In what sense is it the power of serenity? It is the power of serenity because by means of the first jhāna one is unshaken by the hindrances;
by means of the second jhāna, by thought and examination... [and so on]... up to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The power of serenity is that by which one is unshaken by the perception of the base of nothingness.
The power of serenity is that by which one is unshaken, unmoved, and undisturbed by restlessness, by the defilements associated with restlessness, and by the aggregates.
This is the power of serenity. “What is the power of insight? The contemplation of impermanence is the power of insight. The contemplation of suffering... the contemplation of non-self...”
Contemplation of disenchantment… contemplation of dispassion… contemplation of cessation… contemplation of relinquishment is the power of insight.
Contemplation of impermanence in form… [and so on] …contemplation of relinquishment in form is the power of insight.

Contemplation of impermanence in feeling… in perception… in volitional formations… in consciousness… in the eye… [and so on] …contemplation of impermanence in aging-and-death. Contemplation of relinquishment in aging-and-death.

The power of insight (*vipassanābala*). In what sense is it the power of insight? It is called the power of insight because it does not waver from the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence;
it does not waver from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering; it does not waver from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self;
it does not waver from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment; it does not waver from lust through the contemplation of dispassion...

"It trembles" means... through the contemplation of cessation, it does not tremble regarding origination; through the contemplation of relinquishment, it does not tremble regarding grasping—this is the power of insight (*vipassanā-bala*).

It does not tremble, does not waver, and does not shake with regard to ignorance, the defilements accompanied by ignorance, and the aggregates—this is the power of insight. This is the power of insight.
“And with the subsiding of three formations: of which three formations?
For one who has attained the second jhāna, the verbal formations—applied thought and sustained thought—have subsided.
For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the bodily formations—inhalation and exhalation—have subsided. [And] for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling...”
For one who has attained [jhāna], perception, feeling, and mental formations are stilled. Through the stilling of these three formations:
"By means of the sixteen modes of knowledge"—by which sixteen modes of knowledge? The mode of knowledge consisting in the contemplation of impermanence.
Contemplation of suffering… of non-self… of disenchantment… of dispassion… of cessation… of relinquishment… and contemplation of turning away are the modes of knowledge.
The path of stream-entry is a mode of knowledge. The attainment of the fruit of stream-entry is a mode of knowledge.
The path of once-returning… [and so on] … the attainment of the fruit of arahantship is a mode of knowledge. By means of these sixteen modes of knowledge.
“By the nine modes of conduct of concentration (samādhicariyā). By which nine modes of conduct of concentration?
The first jhāna is a mode of conduct of concentration; the second jhāna... [and so on] ...the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a mode of conduct of concentration.

The applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind for the sake of attaining the first jhāna... [and so on] ...[for the sake of attaining] the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
Initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind for the sake of attainment. By means of these nine modes of practice regarding concentration.
"Mastery" refers to the five kinds of mastery: mastery over adverting, mastery over attaining, mastery over resolving, mastery over emerging, and mastery over reviewing.
One adverts to the first jhāna wherever, whenever, and for as long as one wishes.
Mastery of adverting is the absence of sluggishness in adverting. Mastery of attainment is the absence of sluggishness in attaining the first jhāna wherever, whenever, and for as long as one wishes.

…pe… Mastery of resolution is the absence of sluggishness in resolving. …pe… Mastery of emergence is the absence of sluggishness in emerging. …pe… Mastery of reviewing is the absence of sluggishness in reviewing.

"There is no [delay]" refers to mastery in reviewing. Regarding the second [attainment]... pe ... one adverts to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception whenever, however, and for as long as one wishes... pe ... one reviews it.
"There is no sluggishness in reviewing" refers to mastery in reviewing. These are the five masteries."
870. And here, the description as "by sixteen modes of knowledge" is the highest possible case. However, for a non-returner (anāgāmin), it occurs by means of fourteen modes of knowledge.
If this is so, why does it not occur for a once-returner (sakadāgāmin) by twelve and for a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) by ten?
It does not occur because they have not yet abandoned the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure, which is an obstacle to concentration. This is the case for them.
For that [hindrance] has not been abandoned. Therefore, the power of serenity (*samatha-bala*) is not fulfilled;

when it is unfulfilled, they are unable to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which is to be entered by means of two powers, because of the deficiency of those powers. But for the non-returner (*anāgāmī*), that [hindrance] has been abandoned;
therefore, he possesses fulfilled power. Because his power is fulfilled, he is able [to attain it]. Thus the Blessed One said:
—“For one emerging from cessation, wholesome *nevasaññānāsaññāyatana* is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
Indeed, this was stated in the *Mahāpakaraṇa* of the *Paṭṭhāna* with reference specifically to the emergence from cessation of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
871. Where do they attain it? In the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*). Why? Because of the presence of successive attainments (*anupubbasamāpatti*) therein.
In the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*), however, there is no arising of the first jhāna and so forth. Therefore, it is not possible to attain [the attainment of cessation] there.
Some, moreover, say it is because of the absence of a physical basis (*vatthu*).

Why do they attain it? Having become weary of the diversity in the occurrence of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), they attain it with the thought: "Becoming mindless even in this very life, we shall dwell in happiness having reached cessation, which is Nibbāna."

873. How does his attainment come about? For one who has performed the preliminary duties by exerting himself through both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), and who brings the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) to cessation—in this way his attainment comes about.
For he who exerts himself solely through serenity remains after reaching the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; whereas he who [exerts himself] solely through insight...
He exerts himself and, having attained the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he remains therein.

However, one who, having exerted himself by means of both [the preliminary and the actual practice] and having performed the prior duties, brings about cessation (*nirodha*) in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), enters that attainment; this is the summary here.
This, however, is the detailed account: Here, a bhikkhu desiring to enter cessation, having finished his meal and having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, [proceeds].
In a secluded place, he sits down on a well-prepared seat, having crossed his legs in the full lotus posture,
set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Having entered the first jhāna and emerged from it,
he contemplates the formations therein as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
This insight (vipassanā), moreover, is threefold: insight that grasps formations, insight for the attainment of fruition, and insight for the attainment of cessation.

In this context, whether the insight that grasps formations is dull or sharp, it certainly serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the Path. As for the insight for the attainment of fruition, only the sharp kind is required.
[These] are similar to the development of the path. However, for the insight leading to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is appropriate that it be neither too dull nor too sharp.
Therefore, with insight that is neither too dull nor too sharp, he contemplates those formations (*saṅkhāra*).
