Then, having entered the second jhāna and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations therein. Thereafter...
The third jhāna … [as before] … Then, having entered the base of infinite consciousness and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations therein.
Likewise, having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it, he performs the fourfold preliminary duty:
not disturbing what is bound by various ties, honoring the Saṅgha, inviting the Teacher, and delimiting the duration of the journey.
875. Therein, "not disturbing what is tied separately" means that whatever bowl or robe, bed or bench, dwelling house, or any other kind of requisite belonging is not tied together with this bhikkhu,
but remains separate, he should ensure it is not disturbed by fire, water, wind, thieves, rats, or the like.
It shall not perish; thus it should be resolved.

This is the method for making the resolution: "May this and that [article] within these seven days not be consumed by fire, not be carried away by water, not be destroyed by wind, not be stolen by thieves, and not be gnawed by rats and the like."
When he had thus resolved, for those seven days no danger whatsoever befell him.
However, had he not so resolved, he would have been destroyed by fire and other such perils, as was the case with the Elder Mahānāga.

It is said that the Elder entered a village belonging to his mother, a female lay follower, for alms. After the lay follower had given him rice-gruel, she had him sit in the assembly hall. There, the Elder [entered] cessation...
Having entered [that attainment], he sat down. While he was sitting there, the assembly hall was consumed by fire;
the remaining monks each took their own seats and fled. The village dwellers gathered together, and seeing the Elder, they said, "This is a lazy monk!
The fire, having burnt the grass, bamboo, and wood, stood surrounding the Elder. The people [took] water-jars...
Having brought water, extinguished [the fire], removed the ashes, leveled the ground, and scattered flowers, they stood there paying homage.
The Elder, emerging at the predetermined time, saw them and thought, "I have become known.
He rose into the air and went to Piyaṅgudīpa. This is called "not disturbing what is bound in various ways."

In the case of a lower garment (*nivāsana*) or an upper robe (*pāvuraṇa*) that are joined together as one, or of a seat upon which one is sitting, there is no need for a separate act of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
One protects them by means of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) alone, as in the case of the Venerable Sañjīva. For it has been said:
"The psychic power of the Venerable Sañjīva was through the expansion of concentration; the psychic power of the Venerable Sāriputta was through the expansion of concentration."

876. *Saṅghapaṭimānanaṃ* means the waiting for or looking toward the Saṅgha. The meaning is that as long as this bhikkhu has not arrived, the formal act (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha shall not be performed. Furthermore, in this context, the actual waiting is not the preliminary duty;
rather, the mental advertence (*āvajjana*) to wait is the preliminary duty. Therefore, one should advert thus: "If, during these seven days..."
"If the Saṅgha wishes to perform any formal act, such as a *jattikamma*, while I am sitting having entered cessation,
I shall emerge at that very moment, provided no monk comes to call for me.
Having made this resolve and entered [cessation], he emerges at that very time.
But if one does not do so, and the Saṅgha, having assembled and not seeing him, asks, "Where is such-and-such a bhikkhu?
and upon being told, "He has entered the attainment of cessation," the Saṅgha dispatches a certain bhikkhu, saying, "Go and summon him in the name of the Saṅgha.
Then that bhikkhu stands within hearing distance and says to him, "The Saṅgha, friend, is waiting for you."

Emergence occurs as soon as it has been spoken. Such indeed is the weighty command of the Saṅgha. Therefore, having adverted to it, one should attain [the attainment] in such a way that emergence occurs by itself.
877. Regarding "the Teacher’s summons": here too, the only task is the adverting to the Teacher’s summons. Therefore, that too—

One should attend to it thus: "If, while I am sitting having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days, the Teacher should lay down a training rule regarding some matter he has encountered, or should teach the Dhamma on account of some particular occasion, I shall emerge immediately as soon as anyone comes to call me.
Having made this resolve and sitting thus, one emerges at that very moment.
But as for one who does not do so, when the Teacher has assembled the Saṅgha and, not seeing him, asks,
"Where is such-and-such a bhikkhu?", and it is said, "He has entered the attainment of cessation," he sends a certain bhikkhu, saying, "Go and summon him in my name. Then,
that bhikkhu stands within earshot of him and says, "The Teacher summons the Venerable One."
Emergence occurs as soon as it has been spoken. For the Teacher’s summons is indeed weighty; therefore, having adverted to it, one should attain [jhāna] in such a way that one emerges by oneself.
878. "The delimitation of the duration" means the delimitation of the life-span. By this monk, in the delimitation of the duration...

One must become highly skilled. Having adverted to one's own life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*)—thinking, "Will my life-formations continue for seven days or will they not?"—one should then enter the attainment.

For if one enters the attainment without having adverted to the life-formations that are to cease within seven days, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is unable to ward off death. Death occurs before the cessation [of the formations].
Because there is no intermediate state between [the base of nothingness and] the attainment, he emerges from the attainment. Therefore, this must be adverted to before entering the attainment.
As for the remainder, it is permissible not even to advert to it; however, this [base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception] must indeed be adverted to—thus it is said.
Having thus entered the base of nothingness and emerged, and having performed this preliminary duty, he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He enters [the attainment]. Then, after passing over one or two mental moments (*cittakkhaṇa*), he becomes mindless and touches cessation (*nirodha*).
But why do mental states not proceed for him beyond those two moments? Because it is the preliminary application (*payoga*) for cessation.
For this bhikkhu, having yoked together the two factors of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), this is the ascent to the eight attainments.
The application belongs to successive cessation, not to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
because it is the application for cessation, [the mind-moments] do not proceed beyond two moments of consciousness.
However, that bhikkhu who, having emerged from the base of nothingness, does not perform this preliminary duty and instead enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
He enters [the attainment], but he is unable to remain without consciousness thereafter; turning back, he settles once more in the base of nothingness itself.
Here, the simile of a man who has never traveled a certain path should be told:
it is said that a certain man, having never before traveled a particular road, comes upon a water-filled ravine or deep, muddy water in the middle of it.
Having crossed over and reached a stone heated by the fierce sun that had been set aside, he descends into the ravine without even adjusting his lower garment or cloak;
then, out of fear of damaging his requisites, he returns once more to the bank.

Even after stepping on the stone, his feet become so scorched that he steps back down onto the near side. In this regard, just as that man—because of his failure to adjust his lower garment and cloak—
Just as one who has merely descended into a cave, or merely stepped upon a hot rock, turns back and remains right where he was before,

so too the practitioner of yoga, because his preliminary duties have not been performed, turns back as soon as he has entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and remains in the base of nothingness.
Just as a man who has previously traveled that path, upon reaching that place, puts on one garment firmly,
takes another in his hand, crosses the ravine, and having merely stepped upon the hot rock, proceeds further;
even so does the bhikkhu who has performed the preliminary duties enter the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having entered [the attainment], she remains having touched cessation while being without consciousness thereafter.

880. How is there a "standing"? For one who has thus attained, there is a standing by way of the delimitation of time and by way of the absence of interruption through the exhaustion of the intermediate life-span, the formal act of the Saṅgha, or the Teacher’s summons.

881. How is there an "emergence"? There is emergence in two ways: for a non-returner, through the arising of the fruit of non-returning; and for an arahant, through the arising of the fruit of arahantship.
882. "When he has emerged, to what does his mind incline? It inclines toward Nibbāna. For this was said:

"Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, his mind inclines toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, and tends toward seclusion. 883.
"What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has attained [the attainment of cessation]? This matter, too, is stated in the Sutta. As it is said:
—“Friend, in the case of one who has died and passed away, his bodily formations have ceased and subsided; his verbal formations...
his mental formations have ceased and subsided; his life-span is exhausted, his heat has been quenched, and his faculties have perished.
And in the case of this bhikkhu who has entered the cessation of perception and feeling, his bodily formations also...”
“Volitional formations of speech have ceased and subsided; volitional formations of mind have ceased and subsided;
yet life has not been exhausted, heat has not subsided, and the faculties are unimpaired.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the attainment of cessation is conditioned (*saṅkhata*) or unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), mundane (*lokiya*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*), and so forth: it is conditioned, it is unconditioned, and it is mundane.
Nor should it be called "supramundane. Why? Because it does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
However, since it is said to be "attained" by virtue of one who enters it, it is appropriate to say that it is "accomplished," not unaccomplished.
Thus, this attainment, which is peaceful and practiced by the Noble Ones—
Having developed noble wisdom, the wise enter that which is reckoned as Nibbāna in this very life;
therefore, they possess the capacity for this attainment as well.
"By means of wisdom regarding the Noble Paths, it is called 'the benefit.
(885) Regarding the discourse on the accomplishment of being worthy of offerings and so forth:
"The accomplishment of being worthy of offerings and so forth" does not refer merely to the capacity for entering the attainment of cessation.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the attainment of the state of being worthy of offerings and so forth is also a benefit of this development of supramundane wisdom.
For, by developing this fourfold wisdom without distinction, a person of developed wisdom becomes one worthy of offerings,
worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and an unsurpassed field of merit for the world, including its devas.
886. Specifically, however, having first developed the wisdom of the first path, one who arrives with weak insight and dull faculties is called "one who has seven births at most";
after wandering through seven existences in the happy realms, he makes an end of suffering.
One who arrives with middling insight and middling faculties is called "one who goes from family to family" (*kolaṃkolo*); [he wanders] two or three times...
Having wandered and transmigrated through various families, he makes an end of suffering.
One who has arrived at sharp insight and possesses sharp faculties is called a "one-seeder" (ekabījī); having produced only one human existence, he makes an end of suffering.
Having developed the wisdom of the second path, he becomes a "once-returner" (sakadāgāmī); having come to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.
888. Having developed the wisdom of the third path, one becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). Due to differences in the faculties (*indriya*), he is fivefold:

one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (*antarā-parinibbāyī*), one who attains Nibbāna upon arrival (*upahacca-parinibbāyī*), one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*), one who attains Nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*), and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (*uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī*).
Here, he has reached his final destination. Among these, "one who attains Nibbāna in the interval" refers to one who, in whatever state among the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*)...
Having been reborn, one attains final nibbāna without even reaching the midpoint of the lifespan.

An "one who attains nibbāna upon arrival" (upahacca-parinibbāyī) is one who attains final nibbāna after having passed beyond the midpoint of the lifespan. An "one who attains nibbāna without exertion" (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī) is one who generates the higher path without exertion or effort.
An "one who attains nibbāna with exertion" (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī) is one who generates the higher path with exertion and effort.
"One who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm" means that having been reborn there, he ascends from that point upward as far as the Akaniṭṭha existence and attains final nibbāna there.
Having developed the wisdom of the fourth path, some become liberated through faith, while others become liberated through wisdom.

Some are liberated both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta), some are possessors of the three knowledges (tevijja), some are possessors of the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiñña), and some have attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and are great ones whose taints are exhausted (mahākhīṇāsava).
With reference to this, it was said: "At the moment of the path, he is called one who unbraids that tangle;
at the moment of the fruit, having unbraided the tangle, he becomes the most worthy of offerings in the world with its devas."
Thus there are manifold benefits in the cultivation of noble wisdom;
therefore, the discerning person should take delight therein.
(890) And at this point—
"Established in virtue, a wise man, developing his mind and wisdom,
the ardent and prudent bhikkhu shall disentangle this tangle."—
In this verse, the development of wisdom along with its benefits is elucidated within the *Visuddhimagga*, which is taught by way of the headings of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Thus ends the exposition on the benefits of the development of wisdom, titled "The Exposition of the Benefits of the Development of Wisdom," in the Section on the Development of Wisdom within the Path of Purification composed for the delight of virtuous people.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Concluding Remarks. 891.
And at this point—
“Having established himself in virtue, a wise man, developing the mind and wisdom,
the ardent and discerning bhikkhu can unravel this tangle”—
having set down this verse, we said:
“Now, regarding this verse spoken by the Great Seer,
I shall explain its meaning— divided into virtue and the rest— exactly as it is.
Having obtained the going-forth in the Conqueror’s teaching, which is so very difficult to find...”
"The secure and straight path to purification, which comprises virtue and the rest—
those here who desire purity but do not know it as it truly is,
do not attain purification, even though they strive with diligence, O yogis."
“This Path of Purification, which brings joy to them,
contains well-purified determinations and is based on the method of teaching of the Mahāvihāravāsins—
I shall speak it; listen to me as I speak it with care.”
"All you who desire purity, O virtuous ones, listen attentively.
Thus it was spoken. And therein—
The exposition of the meanings of those categories beginning with virtue,
as set forth according to the method of the commentaries of all five Nikāyas—
having collected almost all of that together with its definitive analysis— [is here presented].
Since this has been expounded free from all faults of confusion,
therefore those practitioners who desire purification and possess pure wisdom should indeed apply themselves with reverence to this Path of Purification.
Of the illustrious Theras, the foremost exponents of the Vibhajjavāda,
dwellers of the Mahāvihāra, who were well-versed in their own lineage;
of the venerable Saṅghapāla, whose conduct was pure and austere.
Having accepted this request from one who is devoted to the conduct of the Vinaya, intent upon the practice,
and whose mind is adorned with virtues such as patience, gentleness, and loving-kindness,
I have composed this work.
By the power of the accumulation of merit attained by one who desires the endurance of the true Dhamma,
may all living beings prosper in happiness.
And may this Path of Purification remain here without any obstacles.
The recitation section consisting of fifty-eight units is completed.
May all the world’s aspirations, which are based upon what is wholesome,
be fulfilled without obstacle, very swiftly, indeed very swiftly.
895. Adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a multitude of virtues such as morality, conduct, uprightness, and gentleness;
capable of plunging into the depths of his own system and those of other systems; possessed of analytical discernment (*paññā-veyyattiya*);

a great grammarian whose unimpeded radiance of knowledge shone upon the Teacher’s Dispensation—including the Three Pitakas and their commentaries—and who was graced by the beauty of sweet and noble speech flowing forth from the happiness produced by perfection of expression.

By the one who speaks what is fitting and supreme, the best of debaters, the great poet, whose intellect is unimpeded regarding the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with qualities such as the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and who is an ornament to the lineage of the Elders dwelling at the Mahāvihāra—
by him whose name was taken by his teachers as Buddhaghosa, possessing vast and purified intelligence, [this work was composed].
The Elder, who was to be addressed as Mudantakhedaka, composed the work called the *Visuddhimagga*.
May it remain in the world for as long as there are seekers of deliverance from the world,
showing to noble sons the method for the purification of virtue and the rest.
"Even the name 'Buddha'— the Great Seer, the Elder of the World, whose mind is pure and who is such-like— prevails in the world.
Thus ends the discourse on the Path of Purification, composed for the delight of virtuous people.
According to the calculation of the Pāḷi text, however, it consists of fifty-eight recitation sections (bhāṇavāra).
Thus ends the treatise on the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga).
